### 🌅 Opening Activity: Cutting the Seven Pieces

**🧰 You need:** 1 cereal-box card cut to an 8-inch square · a ruler or any straight edge · 1 pencil · scissors (adult only).

1. Rule a line corner to corner and cut along it. Two big triangles. She holds the card flat while you cut.
2. Cut one of those in half again, then work the other down into a medium triangle, two small ones, a square and a slanted four-sided piece.
3. Seven pieces on the table and no picture yet. Let her push them round, then leave them until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Tangram Animals

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The seven cut pieces
- 4 sheets of paper for tracing outlines
- 1 pencil and 1 permanent marker
- 1 envelope or freezer bag to keep the set in
- A clear table or a tray to work on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Hand her all seven and ask her to make the square they came from. Leave her with it a while. She does not have to get it.
2. Build a cat together on a sheet of paper: big triangle for the body, the square for the head, two small triangles for ears. She sets the ears.
3. Draw round the finished cat in pencil, lift the pieces off and go over the outline in marker.
4. Do a boat and a house the same way, tracing each one before you break it up.
5. Let her invent the fourth. Trace it and write her name for it along the bottom, spelling and all.
6. Everything goes in the envelope with **TANGRAM** on the front. She is back at it by 4:15.

> 💡 **Tip:** When she pushes a piece in upside down, leave it. Turning a
> shape over until it drops into the gap is the skill, and your hand on the
> piece ends it.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Arrow Trail

Walk out with a job: at every corner she lays an arrow of sticks, stones or
scuffed gravel pointing the way you came. Four or five is plenty. On the way
back she reads her own arrows and gets you home. The ground is frozen hard, so
they sit where she put them. Check tomorrow.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and reaching across his own
> body now. Sit him near the table with a cardboard tube, then set a second
> past his right shoulder so he has to swing an arm over for it. He ends up
> with one in each hand, passing them back and forth. On the walk, carrier
> facing out, and the crows are the loudest thing he hears all morning.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Puzzle Swap

A second set of seven comes off the other cereal box: two builders, two trays,
a timer.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The seven tangram pieces from this morning
- A second set cut from another cereal box
- 2 trays or baking sheets
- 2 sheets of paper
- 1 marker
- 1 dish towel
- An egg timer or the phone timer

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cut the second set with her calling out which piece comes next. She watched at 8:00 and remembers more of the order than you expect.
2. One set on each tray, sitting opposite each other with the timer between you.
3. Two minutes on the clock. Build a picture on your tray without showing her while she builds one on hers.
4. Slide your tray alongside hers with your picture still standing on it. She clears her own tray and copies yours piece by piece. Set the timer again.
5. She will get stuck. Let her pick her tray up and turn it round rather than point at the piece she needs.
6. One round from memory, three pieces only. Build a small shape, give her a slow count of five, drop the dish towel over it and let her go. Three she can hold in her head at this age. Asking for seven ends the afternoon.
7. Let her set the timer for the last round, then tip both sets into one pile and build one enormous animal.

> 💡 **Tip:** Rebuilding someone else's picture is harder than making your own,
> and she will say so. Tell her you find it harder too.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One set only, taking turns to build on the same tray.
- Solve the four outline cards and stop there.
- Cut a third set and mail one piece to a grandparent.
- Draw round every piece on one sheet and color them in.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Meet a friend at the park**, and take the outline cards
- The park on your own if nobody is free
- A café, with the tangram envelope in your bag
- The short loop past this morning's arrows
- The big supermarket, and let her find seven of something

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him a baking sheet of his own on the floor
> and one wooden spoon. At 7 months he babbles in long runs of *bababa* and
> *dadada* with the shape of sentences in them, so answer him. Wait for the
> pause, say something back, wait again. He takes the turn.

### 🌍 Around the World: China and the Tangram 🧩

The seven pieces on your table are Chinese and they are old. The puzzle is
called *qi qiao ban*, seven boards of skill, and Chinese printers were selling
books of tangram figures by the early 1800s. Sets traveled, and by 1818 Europe
and America were in the middle of a tangram craze, thousands of shapes, every
one using all seven pieces and nothing else.

> **✨ Try it:** Cut her lunchtime sandwich into the same seven shapes and
> let her rebuild the square on the plate before she eats it.

> *Did you know?* Two mathematicians proved in 1942 that only thirteen tangram
> shapes have no dents in the edges.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sharing and turn-taking are different skills, and one is much easier.**
> Azlyn will hand you a tangram piece when you say *your turn* and refuse to
> hand over the same piece when you say *share it*. Turn-taking has a shape
> she can hold in her head. It comes back, and something outside her decides
> when: a timer, the end of a round, a count. Sharing asks her to give a thing
> up now with no visible return, and most three-year-olds manage the first a
> year or more before the second. You already put a timer or a count on it, so
> the return is something she can hear coming, and the piece leaves her hand.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Seven small card pieces and a 7-month-old who mouths
> everything do not go together. Build on the table, sweep before you put
> Kreston down, and count the pieces back into the envelope every time. The
> scissors are adult only and go back up out of reach between cuts, not onto
> the table where she is working.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Drawing It Onto the Card

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of cereal-box card · crayons · 1 printed photo of her, in case the drawing does not happen · 1 glue stick.

1. Give her the card blank side up and ask for a drawing that goes to the edges. Big shapes, heavy color, no white left. A photo does the same job if she is not in the mood.
2. Sit and draw your own beside her without commenting on hers.
3. Tell her what happens at 9:15: you cut it into pieces. Let her add anything she wants first.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Jigsaw with Words on the Back

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 sheets of cereal-box card
- Her drawing, or a printed photo
- 1 glue stick
- Scissors (**adult only**)
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 freezer bag or envelope for storage
- 1 tray to build on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Glue the drawing onto the second sheet and press it under a heavy book for ten minutes.
2. While it presses, write ten things you love about her on the back of an envelope. Specific ones. *You hold the door open for Kreston* beats *you are kind*.
3. Turn the card face down and draw ten chunky pieces on it in marker. Fat lobes, nothing thinner than her finger. Write one of your ten inside each.
4. Cut along the lines with her holding the card steady. The scissors go back on the shelf as the last piece comes free.
5. Jumble the pieces picture side up on the tray and let her build it. Hand her the edges and wait to be asked about the middle.
6. Turn the puzzle over one piece at a time and read what is on the back. All ten, including the ones she talks over.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut the pieces bigger than looks right. A puzzle she can finish gets built forty times. One that beats her goes in the drawer by Tuesday.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Winter Bird Match

Sketch three birds on a scrap of paper before you go, whichever three turn up
in January: a crow, a robin, a fat pigeon. Give her a crayon to tick each one
off. The hedges are empty, so they show up from a long way off. Home when all
three are ticked, or when her hands get cold.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and passing things hand to
> hand. Give him two cardboard tubes while Azlyn cuts: he takes the second
> with the empty hand, then moves the first across to free it up. That
> handover is new this month. Keep card offcuts and the open glue stick away
> from him.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: One Piece Each

Five big pieces go out to five people, and the picture arrives when the last
comes back.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 sheet of card, cut into 5 large pieces
- Crayons
- 1 marker
- 5 envelopes or paper bags
- Masking tape

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cut one sheet of card into five big pieces with curvy edges. Write a name on the back of each: you, Joseph, Azlyn, Kreston, and a grandparent or the teddy.
2. Let her hand them out. She reads the names off the backs by shape.
3. Each person takes their piece away and decorates it. Nobody looks at anybody else's. Kreston's is ten seconds of your hand round his on a fat crayon.
4. Post each piece into its envelope and seal it.
5. Collect what you can before you leave for the aquarium at 2:30. She does the asking, and somebody needs chasing twice.
6. The rest come back at dinner. Build it on the table with everybody there, tape the joins and hang it where she eats breakfast.
7. Let her point out whose is whose, and say one thing you like about each.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not tidy anyone's piece, including Kreston's. Five different
> hands is the picture.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Three pieces instead of five, done in ten minutes at the table.
- Cut the morning jigsaw down into twenty pieces and try again.
- Draw on one sheet together, taking turns with the crayon.
- Mail a piece of card to a grandparent and ask for it back decorated.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The aquarium**, the week's big outing, and the dark rooms suit Kreston
- Indoor playground if the aquarium line is a Saturday one
- The pet store, for fish at a tenth of the price
- A walk to water, a river or a pond, and count what moves in it
- Home, blankets, and the jigsaw on the floor

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The aquarium is built for a 7-month-old. Dark
> walls, lit tanks, slow-moving things at his eye height in the carrier. His
> long-distance vision is close to yours now, so he follows one fish across a
> tank. Twenty-five minutes, then out before the noise stacks up.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Being told what someone loves about you is different from being praised.**
> *Good girl* and *well done* are verdicts. They land on a performance, and
> the next performance has to earn them again. The ten things on the back of
> those pieces describe her instead, and she has to do nothing to keep them
> true. She holds the door for Kreston. She sings to herself in the bath.
> Nothing on that list can be failed. Children who hear a running verdict on
> their effort get more careful about trying things they might lose at, and
> children who hear themselves described build a steadier picture of who they
> are. The puzzle puts it in her hands.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Ten jigsaw pieces and a 7-month-old on the floor means the
> tray stays at table height and the count goes back in the bag every time.
> Glue sticks come apart in a mouth, so the lid goes on and the stick goes up
> whenever you leave the table. Crayons snap into mouth-sized pieces, so keep
> your hand round Kreston's for his ten seconds and put the crayon straight
> back in the box. The scissors are adult only.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Closing the Boxes

**🧰 You need:** the six containers · six small treasures · 1 tray.

1. Lay the six out with a treasure beside each. Let her look inside and handle the lids.
2. She drops a treasure in and you shut them together. Name each closing out loud: screw, clip, zip, tape, knot, band.
3. Push the tray into the middle of the table and leave it shut until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Six Ways to Open a Thing

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 plastic screw-lid jar
- 1 clip-lid tub
- 1 ziplock bag
- 1 shoebox taped shut with masking tape
- 1 bag tied with string
- 1 tub held shut with an elastic band
- 6 small treasures inside: stickers, raisins, a small toy
- 1 tray

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Put the tray in front of her and sit on your hands. She picks the order and keeps what she gets out.
2. Count to twenty before you offer anything, then offer a word and not a hand: *turning*, or *find the corner*.
3. The screw lid is hardest, because two hands go opposite ways at once. If she is stuck, she holds the lid still and turns the jar.
4. The knotted string will beat her. Loosen it to one loop and hand it back so the last pull is hers.
5. When all six are open, count the treasures. Shut them again, and she picks which fastening goes on which.
6. Now she loads them and hands you the tray. Struggle out loud with the elastic band.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say what her hands are doing. *You are pushing and turning at the
> same time.* She gets words for a thing she worked out.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Gate Latch Walk

Walk the street and try every fastening you are allowed to touch. The park
gate with the drop bolt, the churchyard latch, your back gate, the catch on
the recycling bin, the brake on the stroller. Cold metal takes a firmer hand than
a plastic lid.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months. Seal something rattly inside
> a clip-lid tub and hand it over. He cannot open it, so he shakes it, bangs
> it and passes it hand to hand. Hide a toy under a dish towel while he
> watches, and the first time he pulls it off he will look up at you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Wall She Fits Through

A flattened box stands between two chairs with a hole in it, and the only way
across is through.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large flattened cardboard box
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (**adult only**)
- 2 dining chairs
- Packing tape
- 1 blanket for the floor

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread the blanket, lay the box flat and draw round her while she lies on it, arms out. Leave that outline uncut, because it is the last hole of the afternoon.
2. Cut a dinner-plate circle high in the panel while she stands back, and put the knife away before the box goes upright.
3. Tape the box between the chair backs so it stands like a wall, blanket underneath.
4. She goes through the circle first. Starting easy is why she is still going at the fourth.
5. Take the box down, cut a new hole, stand it back up. A tall slot, a mail slot low down she crosses on her belly, one cut too small on purpose. Knife away before it goes up.
6. Let her name each shape and work out her own way through. She tries head-first twice before discovering feet.
7. Her own outline comes last, and cutting it takes the middle out of the wall. She walks through the shape of herself and the wall goes with her.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut the next hole while she is still enjoying the last. The
> activity dies the moment she stands and watches you measure.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One hole, one box, and she goes through it forty times.
- Crawl tunnel out of two chairs and a blanket instead.
- Post small toys through a slot in a shoebox lid and shake them out.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A playground you have never been to**, and let her lead once you are there
- Your usual park, if the new one is a parking lot with a swing
- The woods loop, for gates, stiles and cold mud
- A drive to somewhere with a view, staying in the warm car

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Lie him on the blanket on the far side of the
> wall so Azlyn comes through and lands next to him. A face appearing where a
> wall was is peekaboo, and at 7 months nothing is funnier. At the playground,
> a bucket swing with your hand on him, two or three pushes and out.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Puzzles build a skill that has nothing to do with puzzles.**
> Six lids is a morning of Azlyn trying a thing, failing, and trying a
> different thing. That loop is the skill and it travels. Researchers who
> follow children into school find that staying with a hard task predicts
> school outcomes as strongly as anything they can measure at four. A closed
> container is a good place to practice, because the problem is honest: the
> lid is off or it is not, no adult decides whether she did well, and the
> treasure pays out the second she solves it. She sets her own difficulty,
> picking which one to attack next. You keep your hands still and she banks
> another minute.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Elastic bands, raisins and a ziplock bag are hazards for a
> 7-month-old. Work at the table, count the six treasures in and out, and pick
> the band up the moment it comes off. The craft knife is adult only and goes
> out of reach between every cut, not onto the arm of the sofa. Sit a bag of
> shopping on each chair seat to hold them down, stay beside her while she goes
> through, and tape the box so it pulls loose rather than dragging a chair over
> on her. Never leave Kreston beside the standing box wall on his own.

## 🌟 Day 25: The Memory Tray 🌟
**📅 Monday, January 25, 2027**
**Theme:** Puzzles & Problem Solving

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Cut sixteen palm-sized cards from the week's offcuts, leave them in a shoebox lid with the crayons, and put a clean tray and a dish towel on the table.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Filling the Tray
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: What's Missing from the Tray (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: She Leads the Way Home (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Pairs She Draws Herself (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Pairing the Socks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Pairs Cards
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Two Books on the Sofa
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Filling the Tray

**🧰 You need:** 1 tray · the run of the house · 1 dish towel.

1. Hand her the tray and send her round the house for eight things bigger than her fist. You veto nothing that fits the rule.
2. Lay them out in two rows of four and name each one out loud. Let her shuffle them until it looks right to her.
3. Cover the tray with the dish towel and leave it on the table. Say nothing about what happens next.

### 🎨 The Main Event: What's Missing from the Tray

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 tray
- 8–10 household objects bigger than her fist: mug, wooden spoon, hairbrush, sock, apple, board book, sponge, shoe
- 1 dish towel to cover the tray
- Paper and a pencil for keeping score

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Uncover the tray and name all eight, pointing at each. Give her a slow count of ten.
2. Cover it. She turns round or shuts her eyes. Take one object off and sit on it.
3. Uncover and let her name what has gone. If she stalls, name the ones still there and let her hear the gap.
4. Drop to six objects if eight is too many, go up to ten when eight stops being work.
5. Swap over. She takes one while you look away, and you work it out loud: *sock, apple, book, and the spoon was next to the book*.
6. Keep score in tally marks, hers and yours, and leave the tray out so she can run it on whoever walks in.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her win most of them. A three-year-old who is getting them
> right stays at the table. One stretched every round leaves after four rounds.

### 🌳 Get Outside: She Leads the Way Home

Walk ten minutes out from the door, taking three or four turns, then hand the
job over: she gets you home. Name what you pass on the way out, the red door,
the mailbox, the dog behind the fence. January sun sits low enough to change
how the street looks coming back, so expect one wrong turn and let her walk
into it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and working on Azlyn's
> question: does a thing still exist when nobody can see it. Play peekaboo
> with the dish towel over your face, then over a toy. Give him the wooden
> spoon off the tray and let him drop it from the high chair. He is checking
> that it lands every time, and it does.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Pairs She Draws Herself

Sixteen blank cards, eight drawings done twice, and a memory game she made
herself.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Card offcuts cut into 16 palm-sized cards
- Crayons
- 1 marker
- 1 shoebox lid to keep them in

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the sixteen cards out blank side up and tell her the job: eight things, each drawn twice, so every card has a twin.
2. Start her off. Draw a red circle on one card, hand her the second, and let her copy it. Wobbly copies are fine.
3. She picks the other seven. A fish, a sun, a spot, whatever comes. Draw one of each pair yourself if her hand gets tired.
4. Go over the faint crayon lines in marker so they read from across the table.
5. Play with four pairs first. Eight cards face down in two rows, turn two over, and put them back the same way up in the same place if they do not match.
6. Add pairs as she holds it. Twelve cards, then all sixteen. Stop adding the round before she starts guessing at random.
7. Everything goes in the shoebox lid and stays out for 4:15. She plays it again on her own with the cards face up.

> 💡 **Tip:** Put the cards back in the exact spot they came from. Half of this game is her remembering *where*.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Six cards, three pairs, played on the sofa.
- Match the pairs face up as a sorting game and skip the memory part.
- Draw the eight things on paper instead and cut them out together.
- Play snap with the finished cards instead of pairs.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Green space and a ball**, the Monday slot, and a ball is warmer than a bench
- The neighborhood park if the grass is under water
- A walk with one job: find five things you saw this morning
- The big field, for running in a straight line until she stops
- Round the block on the scooter while the light holds

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him two of anything identical, two wooden
> spoons or two cups, one for each hand. At 7 months he holds both and studies
> them, and the banging-together stage is weeks off. On the grass, sit him on
> a folded blanket where he can watch the ball go past. He turns his whole
> body after it.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Working memory is the thing she is building.**
> The tray game runs on the same system Azlyn uses to follow you round the
> house: working memory, the part that holds a few things in mind while doing
> something with them. At three she can hold two or three items, which is why
> *go upstairs, get your socks and bring down the blue cup* arrives as one
> item, and it is seldom the right one. The tray gives the same system a
> workout she volunteered for. Eight objects sit above her ceiling, so she
> leans on the layout and the gap in the rows, which is memory strategy
> showing up early.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Count the sixteen cards into the shoebox lid and out of it
> every time, and keep the tray of objects up at table height while Kreston is
> on the floor. Sweep under the table before he goes down. Crayons snap into
> mouth-sized pieces, so the broken halves go in the trash as they happen, and
> the wooden spoon he drops off the high chair is the only thing off that tray
> he gets.

## 🌟 Day 26: Two Ways to Sort 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, January 26, 2027**
**Theme:** Puzzles & Problem Solving

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill a laundry basket with twenty or thirty mixed things, take the knives out of the silverware drawer, and put a cookie or stickers aside for tomorrow.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Basket of Everything
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Sorting It Twice (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Two Bags, One Rule (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Every Lid Has a Box (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Sorting Bowls
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: After Swimming, Straight to Pajamas
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Basket of Everything

**🧰 You need:** the full basket · 4 bowls or paper bags · masking tape and a marker.

1. Tip the basket out on the floor and sit in it with her. Half of it she has not seen for weeks and she will greet all of it.
2. Ask her to put two things together that go together. Take whatever reason she gives, including *they are both Kreston's*. Three or four times.
3. Line the four bowls up beside the pile and say nothing about what goes in them. The sorting starts at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Sorting It Twice

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 basket of 20–30 mixed household objects and toys
- 4 bowls or paper bags
- Paper and a marker for labels
- Masking tape

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Four bowls, four colors. Tape a colored scrap to each or write the color word on it. She sorts the whole pile, and the two-color ones are hers to call.
2. Walk her along the four bowls and count each one out loud. Announce the winner.
3. Tip the lot back into one pile.
4. Same objects, new rule: things that need two hands, things that fit in one. Two bowls. She will complain about starting again, then beat her own time.
5. Third round is hers. She sorts by a rule she keeps secret and you work it out from what lands in each bowl. Guess wrong twice before you get there.
6. Her rule will be *things I like* and *things I do not*. Both count. Write it on the paper, read it back and tape it to the bowl.

> 💡 **Tip:** The moment worth waiting for is the second sort, when a red spoon
> that was a red thing an hour ago becomes a two-hands thing. Say so out loud.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Two Bags, One Rule

Two paper bags and one rule set at the front gate: things that came off a tree
in the left bag, things that never did in the right. Late January hands over
brown leaves, bare twigs, a seed head, a bottle cap, gravel. The arguments are
the good part. Ten minutes of collecting is plenty in this cold.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months. Give him his own bowl with
> two objects too big to swallow and watch what he does. He takes them out and
> does not put them back, because putting things into a container comes around
> nine months. Today he empties, you refill, and he thinks that is the game.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Every Lid Has a Box

The kitchen floor gets the version with a real result, and by six she has
fixed two things you meant to fix in November.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- All the tupperware boxes and lids
- The silverware drawer, **knives removed first**
- 1 dish towel
- 1 dishpan
- Masking tape and a marker for labeling shelves

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Take every knife and skewer out of the drawer and onto the top of the fridge before she comes into the kitchen.
2. Tip all the tupperware onto the floor. Lids in one heap, boxes in another, three feet apart.
3. She matches. Hand her the three most obvious, then stand back. A lid that almost fits is the best part of the job.
4. Any box with no lid goes in the dishpan, out of the house or into the craft pile. She makes the call.
5. Stack the matched boxes biggest at the bottom and put them back on the shelf. Tape a label on the shelf edge and let her say what to write.
6. Now the drawer. Tip it onto the dish towel and let her sort each piece back into its slot: forks, spoons, teaspoons, a bowl for the odd stuff.
7. Leave the drawer open. She checks her own work at 4:00 when she does the forks.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not re-sort behind her tonight. She walks past that drawer
> forty times this week, and every time she opens it she sees something she
> got right.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- The lids only, and stop when the tupperware is done.
- Sort the toy basket into two boxes, one of them for the thrift store.
- Pair the shoes by the front door, all facing the same way.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the Tuesday anchor, and the fourth of the year
- The indoor play center if the pool is shut
- A warm café and a window seat, if nobody has it in them
- Home, a warm bath instead, and an extra book at five

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes too if he is up for it. At 7 months he
> sits supported in the water and splashes with intent. The pool hall throws
> his own voice back at him, so he shouts at the ceiling and waits to hear it
> again. Hold him chest to chest at first, twenty minutes and out before he
> cools.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Classification is quiet, invisible math.**
> Before Azlyn can count six forks she has to decide what a fork is and that
> these six are all one kind of thing. Sorting is where that gets settled.
> Every bowl she fills is a set, every argument about the two-color ones is
> her testing where the edge of a category sits, and number is built on top of
> that. The second sort does something further. Running a new rule over the
> same objects, color one hour and size the next, is the flexible half of the
> job, and it is harder than the first sort. You have her pairing socks and
> sorting silverware already. Same task, real result.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Knives, skewers and anything with a point come out of the
> drawer before she is in the room and stay out until it goes back. Small
> sorted objects stay off the floor while Kreston is down there, and the
> basket goes up on the table between rounds. Never leave the drawer open at
> her height with the sharp things still in it.

## 🌟 Day 27: Describe It First 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, January 27, 2027**
**Theme:** Puzzles & Problem Solving

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Leave an empty pillowcase and a clean tray on the table, hide the cookie or the stickers, and check you have two rolls of masking tape for tomorrow.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Choosing the Secret Objects
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Bag You Can't See Into (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Eyes Shut, Five Sounds (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Picture Clues (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Mystery Bag on Her Own
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Flashlight and One Long Book
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Choosing the Secret Objects

**🧰 You need:** 1 pillowcase or tote bag · a wander round the house · 1 tray.

1. Send her round for things that feel different, one out of every room. Rough, cold, furry, prickly, smooth.
2. Feel each one before it goes in, hands only and eyes on the ceiling. Give her three words for it and ask for three back.
3. Mail them all into the pillowcase and stand it where she can see it and not reach in. She will try anyway.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Bag You Can't See Into

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 pillowcase or tote bag
- 8–10 objects with different textures, all bigger than a fist: orange, hairbrush, scrubbing brush, wooden spoon, washcloth, shoe, mug, bath sponge
- 1 tray to lay the guessed ones on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sit opposite each other with the bag between you. One rule: hand goes in, eyes stay out.
2. Whoever's turn it is finds one object and says three things about it before anybody guesses. *Hard, cold, round.*
3. Go first so she hears what three things sounds like. Take your time and be wrong at the end.
4. Her turn. She will blurt the answer out, at least twice. Ask for one more thing and let her hold it while she thinks.
5. Objects come out onto the tray as they are named. When the bag is empty, cover it and see how many she can list.
6. Last round the other way: you describe one from memory, hands on the table, and she finds it in the bag by feel.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her the words she is missing while her hand is on the object. *Bumpy* and *ridged* and *cold at one end* land now and vanish later.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Eyes Shut, Five Sounds

Stop on the path, both shut your eyes, and count five sounds off on her
fingers. There are no leaves this week so sound carries: a crow, a car, a dog,
a plane, your own boots on the grit. Do it again by a road and behind a hedge,
and ask which was louder. She points at the road with her eyes still shut.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and his mouth is still his
> best instrument for finding out what a thing is. Give him a washcloth, a
> wooden spoon and a silicone spatula, one at a time. Put words on each while
> he works it over. Keep the bath sponge in the bag and out of his reach,
> because it comes apart in bits.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Picture Clues

Six drawings, taped round the house, each sending her to where the next one
waits.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper cut into 6 cards
- Crayons
- Masking tape
- 1 small prize: a cookie or a sticker
- 1 teddy to hide

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Hide teddy first with the prize under him, somewhere she walks past twenty times a day.
2. Draw six clues, one per card: the bath, the fridge, her boots, the sofa, the kitchen trash can, and last of all teddy's spot. Rough drawings are fine.
3. Tape clue one where she will start. Every card sends her to the place drawn on it, where the next waits.
4. Walk it with her and carry nothing. She holds the card, she decides where the drawing means, she gets to be wrong about the fridge.
5. She finds teddy, gets the prize and eats it standing up in the hall.
6. Now she hides teddy and draws your six clues. No help with the drawings, however long they take.
7. Follow her clues as drawn, including the one that makes no sense. Ask what it is and take the answer she gives.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will want to tell you where teddy is about four clues in. Ask her to whisper it to the wall and go on hunting. Holding a secret for ten minutes is work.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Three clues instead of six, run in the kitchen alone.
- Hot and cold, called out loud, with no cards at all.
- Hide the same object ten times and get faster each round.
- Draw a map of the downstairs and mark an X on it.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The indoor play center**, the Wednesday slot, and it is too cold for the park
- Indoor playground with the quiet session, if the big one is full of the school-pickup crowd
- The library, a week early, and take out something with flaps in it
- The store, and let her carry one thing and pay for it
- A friend's house with the mystery bag in your coat pocket

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The baby area at the play center is his. Sit him
> in the ball pit shallows with a hand on his back, because at 7 months he
> sits well but tips at speed. Mirrors at his level beat any of the toys.
> Twenty minutes, then out to somewhere quieter.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Describing before guessing is the whole skill.**
> Guessing is fast and closes the thinking down. Describing keeps it open and
> costs her more, because she has to find words for weight, temperature,
> texture and shape while her hand is the only thing telling her anything.
> Every one of those words is a category she can carry to the next object.
> Teachers call this attribute language, and children with plenty of it find
> it easier later to explain how they got to an answer, which is most of what
> school asks them for. The rule you set at the top, three things before
> anybody guesses, is what does the work.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The bath sponge comes apart in bits, so it goes back in the
> bag between turns and the bag stays off the floor. Hide the cookie somewhere
> Kreston cannot get to, and let Azlyn eat it before you put him down. Press
> the tape ends flat on every clue you stick up at his height, and pull them
> all off the walls once the hunt is over.

## 🌟 Day 28: Dead Ends 🌟
**📅 Thursday, January 28, 2027**
**Theme:** Puzzles & Problem Solving

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Flatten the last cereal boxes and stand them in the baking tray with the masking tape and the ping-pong ball. Scissors up out of reach.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Cutting the Maze Walls
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Maze in a Tray (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: She Picks Every Turning (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Maze You Walk (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Teddy Does the Maze
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Week's Puzzles, Laid Out
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Cutting the Maze Walls

**🧰 You need:** cereal-box card · scissors (adult only) · 1 baking tray · masking tape.

1. Cut the card into strips two fingers wide. She counts them into a pile as they come off, and you want about fifteen.
2. Fold each strip along its length so it stands on its own edge. Let her fold all fifteen and leave the crooked ones crooked.
3. Stand a few loose in the baking tray and let her shove them round with one finger. Nothing gets taped down until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Maze in a Tray

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 baking tray or shallow box lid
- Cereal-box card cut into strips
- 1 roll masking tape
- Scissors (**adult only**)
- 1 ping-pong ball, or a tight ball of foil
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Draw the route on paper first. Start at one corner, finish at the other, four turns between. Mark three dead ends and let her put an X on each.
2. Tape the first walls into the tray along the route you drew, gaps wide enough for the ball.
3. Build in the three dead ends. Say nothing about them at all.
4. Give her the ball and let her tilt. She will hit the first dead end inside ten seconds and look up at you. Look back and keep quiet.
5. Once she has all three worked out, hand her the tape and tell her the maze is hers to change. She will open the dead ends up.
6. Last run on the floor, tray held in two hands, standing over it. Time her, then let her time you and be slower.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep the walls low enough to see over. She has to watch the ball
> go the wrong way to know it went wrong, and a tall wall turns it into luck.

### 🌳 Get Outside: She Picks Every Turning

Out the front door and every junction is hers. She calls left or right, you
walk it, no steering and no hints. Turn back at twenty minutes and let her get
you home. Some of her turns are dead ends, somebody's driveway or a fence, and
those are the good ones. The cold sits in her hands this week, so mittens on.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months. The ping-pong ball and the
> foil stay up on the table, so give him something too big to swallow: a
> soccer ball, or a rolled-up towel. Roll it across him at walking pace so he
> follows it over his own midline and reaches across. He may push himself
> backwards trying and end up under the sofa, which is how a lot of babies
> move first.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Maze You Walk

Tape on the floor, cushions for corners, teddy at the finish, and this time the
thing going through the maze is her.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 rolls masking tape
- 4 sofa cushions
- 2 dining chairs
- 1 teddy for the end
- Paper and a marker to draw the plan first

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Draw the plan together on paper. She can copy the tray maze or invent a new one, but three dead ends go on it first.
2. Clear one room end to end. Lay the tape two lines at a time so she watches a corridor appear rather than a finished puzzle.
3. Cushions and chair legs go on the corners where tape on the floor stops reading as a wall.
4. Teddy waits at the finish. She starts on the taped X by the door.
5. First run she walks it. Second run on all fours, third on tiptoe, fourth carrying teddy back the other way without touching a wall.
6. Hand her the tape and let her turn one dead end into a door.
7. Leave it down for the evening and make everybody walk it to get to dinner, including whoever comes in at six.

> 💡 **Tip:** Run it once yourself, out loud, saying what you think at each
> turn. *That is a wall, so I am going back to the last corner.* She takes the
> words for her next run.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One straight tape corridor with two turns and nothing else.
- Drive toy cars round the tray maze instead of rolling the ball.
- Draw a maze on paper and let her find the way out with a finger.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The post office**, with a letter she mails herself
- The hardware store, for the aisles that go on forever
- The grocery store, and she navigates to the bananas
- The playground on the way home, twenty minutes

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Put him at the finish next to teddy, so Azlyn's
> arrival is the reward for the pair of them. He is 7 months and picking at
> edges with his fingers, so press the tape ends flat and pull up anything
> that has lifted. In the post office line, hand him something to hold before
> he decides for himself.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Dead ends are the point of a maze.**
> A maze with no wrong turns in it is a corridor. The three dead ends make
> Azlyn stop, look at where she has got to, decide the route was wrong and go
> back. That is a different job from pushing harder at the same thing.
> Psychologists call dropping a plan that is not working cognitive
> flexibility, and three is about when it arrives. Her first move at a dead
> end will be to shove the ball into the wall again. Wait. The second thing
> she tries is the one worth having, and you gave her a wrong turn she can
> survive, with nothing riding on it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The ping-pong ball and any foil balls or dried beans in the
> tray are a choking hazard for Kreston. Build at table height, count the ball
> back in at the end of every run, and sweep before he goes down on the floor.
> The scissors are adult only and go back up out of reach between cuts.

## Week 5: Forest Friends 🌲
**📅 January 29 – February 4, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

Azlyn prints four animal coats on Friday morning and builds the animals after
lunch, then spends the rest of the week finding places for them to live. A
tree up the living room wall on Saturday, a forest floor in a baking tray on
Sunday, tracks across the hall on Monday, feeders outside the window on
Tuesday, a cave in a cardboard box on Wednesday. Every day inherits the day
before it. By Thursday she has a forest in the house and enough of it in her
head to tell the whole week back to you through a lit sheet.

February arrives on Monday, and Groundhog Day lands on Tuesday the 2nd as a
bonus note inside the afternoon: people in America gather round a hole to
watch a woodchuck come up and check the weather. It sits an inch from
Wednesday's hibernation cave, so the two can talk to each other. The cold does
the rest of the work this week. Frost on the grass until the sun comes round
the houses, bare branches with every old nest showing, and shadows that run
long at eleven in the morning.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Patterns she can carry on.** Spot, spot, stripe down a paper strip, then finishing the row without you.
- **Where forest animals live.** Roots, trunk, branches, top, and which animal belongs at which height.
- **Reading evidence.** A print, a chewed leaf and a tuft of wool add up to an animal she never saw.
- **Waiting, and holding still on purpose.** She fills four feeders on Tuesday and the birds come on Thursday; she hibernates on Wednesday while you count to twenty.
- **Telling the week back.** Two tours, a puppet show, and a shadow fox that swells up the sheet as she walks him toward the flashlight.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Patterns are the beginning of algebra
- Explaining to someone else is how understanding gets locked in
- Loose parts beat finished toys
- Evidence and inference, a big idea learnable at three
- Delayed payoff is a muscle, and this is a gentle way to work it
- Pretending to sleep is real self-regulation practice
- Shadows are confusing at three, and the confusion is worth exploring

---

## 🌟 Day 29: The Animal Coats 🌟
**📅 Friday, January 29, 2027**
**Theme:** Forest Friends

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Cut six long strips from a paper bag or the back of the wrapping paper, and stand the paints, four saucers and a stack of newspaper at one end of the table.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Stamp Hunt
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Printing the Animal Coats (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Bark Rubbing Walk (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Building the Forest Family (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Animal Line-Up
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and a Forest Story
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Stamp Hunt

**🧰 You need:** 1 grocery bag · the recycling · the odds drawer.

1. Hand her the bag and one job: find things that make a mark. A cork, a fork, a spool of thread, a tube end, a bottle cap.
2. Press each find into your palm and ask what shape it would leave. Take her guesses without fixing them.
3. Line the winners along the table edge in the order she wants to use them. That is the plan for 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Printing the Animal Coats

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Long paper strips cut from a paper bag or the back of wrapping paper, 6
- Washable non-toxic poster paint in brown, black, white and orange
- 1 saucer or old plate for each color
- Cardboard tube ends, 1 cork, 1 fork, 1 crumpled piece of paper towel
- 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
- Newspaper for the table

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread the newspaper, lay one strip in front of her the long way, and pour a thin puddle of each color into its own saucer.
2. Start the fawn. Two spots with the cork, a stripe dragged with the back of the fork, two spots again. Say it as you print: *spot, spot, stripe.* Hand her the cork on the third repeat.
3. Raccoon next. Wide dark and pale bands from a tube squashed flat, alternating down the strip like a ringed tail. She takes over after two.
4. Owl on the third strip: rings from the open end of a tube, rows of them, brown on brown.
5. Fox on the fourth: orange the whole length with the crumpled paper towel, then a white tip.
6. Hand her the last two strips with no pattern to follow. Those two are hers, printed however she likes. Lay all six flat to dry, wash hands, then walk the row and ask what comes next on the four you started.

> 💡 **Tip:** Print the first repeat and stop. She finishes the strip. A pattern she completed is one she can read back at you an hour later.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Bark Rubbing Walk

Take paper and a fat crayon with the wrapper peeled off. Rub the crayon on its
side over paper held flat against four different trunks. Oak comes out deep
and ridged, birch close to smooth, and she feels the difference through the
paper before she sees it. January bark holds the wet, so work the sheltered
side of each trunk.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and passes things from hand to
> hand now. Give him a wooden spoon and a folded washcloth, the second set out
> to his side so he has to reach across his body for it. He keeps up a running
> commentary at both of them while Azlyn prints. On the walk, hold his open
> palm flat against a trunk for a second.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Building the Forest Family

The strips are dry by one o'clock. Wrapped round a cardboard tube and taped,
each one stands up on the table by itself.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The printed strips
- Cardboard tubes, 4–6
- 1 roll masking tape
- Scissors (**adult**)
- Card scraps for ears, tails and beaks
- 1 permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the dry strips out and ask which animal each one is. Take her answer even when the raccoon has turned into a zebra.
2. Wrap the fawn strip round a tube with the pattern facing out and tape the seam on the inside. She holds, you tape.
3. Cut ears, a tail and a beak from the card scraps. She draws the shape, you cut on her line.
4. Tape the pieces where she points, including the ears you would have put somewhere else.
5. Stand each animal on the table as you go so the row grows in front of her.
6. Write every name on the base in marker. Fox is a name and so is Bibby.
7. Give them an address: a shelf, a windowsill, the corner of the table. They stay there all week.

> 💡 **Tip:** Tape the seam inside the tube where her fingers cannot find it. A seam she can pick at comes apart by Sunday, and these four have a week of work ahead.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One strip, one tube, one animal, and stop there.
- Draw faces onto plain tubes and skip the printing.
- Sort the dried strips by color, then by pattern.
- Line the animals up by height and photograph them.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Grandparents, or whoever in the family is nearest**, and she takes one animal to show them
- A friend's house, if the Forest Family needs an audience under five
- The park, back to the trees she rubbed this morning
- A café with a window seat and paper for one more rubbing
- A drive out to somewhere with more trees in it than houses

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Keep him off the tape and the tube ends and give
> him a big offcut of card instead, wider than his own mouth. At 7 months he
> pulls at paper with both hands and turns it over hunting for the other side.
> He runs a long string of sound at you while he works, so answer as though he
> asked you something.

### 🌍 Around the World: Japan, *Shinrin-yoku* 🌲

In Japan, *shinrin-yoku* means forest bathing, a walk with nothing to achieve.
No route, no distance, no finish. You go in among the trees and use your
senses: what you can hear, what you can smell, how bark feels under a hand.
Japanese doctors send patients out to do it, and the walk counts as treatment.

> **✨ Try it:** Green tea and a rice ball, eaten under a tree with your coats
> on. Ten minutes of sitting and listening counts as the whole practice.

> *Did you know?* Japan's forestry ministry invented the word *shinrin-yoku* in
> 1982, and the name came before any of the science did.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Patterns are the beginning of algebra.**
> Azlyn printed spot, spot, stripe, spot, spot, stripe down a paper strip this
> morning, and the work underneath it is what a nine-year-old does with x. A
> pattern is a rule that holds while the pieces change. Once she can say what
> comes next on the raccoon strip, she can find the rule in a row of cups, a
> clapped rhythm or a line of numbers, because one skill sits under all three.
> Researchers who track early math find pattern work predicts where a child
> lands later, alongside counting, and it adds something counting does not.
> You never have to name it. Print the first repeat, hand her the cork, and
> let her carry the rule to the end.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Kreston is 7 months and everything he reaches goes in his
> mouth. Corks, tube ends and card scraps go up out of reach the moment you
> stop watching, on a shelf and not the table edge. Washable non-toxic paint
> only. The scissors stay with you.

**📅 Saturday, January 30, 2027**
**Theme:** Forest Friends

### 🌙 Prep Tonight

- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Tearing the Trunk

**🧰 You need:** brown paper bags or a flattened box · masking tape · the cleared wall.

1. Tear the paper into long ragged strips instead of cutting it. A torn edge looks like bark, and her hands can do it all.
2. Lay the strips end to end along the floor and stand her beside the line.
3. Ask where the branches should start. Tape a tab on the wall at that height and leave the pile until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Tree That Fills the Wall

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Brown paper bags, a flattened cardboard box, or the plain side of wrapping paper
- 1 roll masking tape
- Scissors (**adult**)
- Green paper, newspaper or magazine pages for leaves
- 1 permanent marker
- The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape the torn strips to the wall as a trunk, floor to shoulder height, wider at the bottom. Overlap them until no wall shows.
2. Add branches from the shorter strips. She decides how many and where, and crooked ones stay crooked.
3. Tear leaves from the green paper or magazine pages and tape them along the branches in handfuls.
4. Draw a line along the baseboard and run roots below it. That line is the ground.
5. Sort the animals. Ask where each one lives: roots, trunk, branches, top. Tape a card shelf at that height and stand it there.
6. Write the four layers up the wall in marker: **roots, trunk, branches, top.** Read them out with her, bottom up.

> 💡 **Tip:** Build it at her height. A tree she can reach the top of is one she keeps adding to all week, and the ceiling end is yours.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Choosing Her Tree

Walk the route and let her pick one tree to be hers for the year. She has to
give a reason, and any reason counts. Put both arms round the trunk to see
whether they meet, then count the big branches. Photograph her against it
today, the last Saturday in January, and again in April, July and October.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and tracks Azlyn across a room
> now. Lay him on his back under the wall tree to look up at the leaves. Tape
> one green paper leaf at the height of his hand, off to one side so he has to
> reach across his body for it. He crumples it and passes it over.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Forest Tour

She knows where every animal on that wall lives. This afternoon she says it
out loud to an audience that cannot get up and leave.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The wall tree
- 1 flashlight
- 1 cardboard tube, for a megaphone
- Paper scraps and 1 crayon, for tickets
- Your phone, to record one tour for Joseph
- A chair each for the teddies, and a cushion on the floor for Kreston

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set the chairs in a row facing the tree with a teddy in every one. Kreston sits at the end, propped against the cushion.
2. Make tickets. She scribbles on the paper scraps and hands one to every seat, Kreston included.
3. Give her the tube and the flashlight. The tube is her voice and the flashlight is her pointer.
4. Take a seat and be the audience. Who lives at the top. Why does nobody live in the roots. What happens up there when it rains.
5. Let her be wrong. Owls in the roots is a claim, and a claim beats a correct answer copied off you.
6. Record one tour start to finish with no retakes. Joseph gets it tonight.
7. Swap over. You give the tour, and she corrects you before you finish the first sentence.

> 💡 **Tip:** Ask for the tour twice with an hour in between. The second runs longer and adds something she worked out in the gap.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- A tour of one animal, thirty seconds, done.
- Draw the tree on paper and label the layers together.
- Hide the animals round the room and have her put each one back at its height.
- Give the whole tour to Joseph on a video call.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The botanical garden**, greenhouse first if the wind is up
- A garden center with an indoor plant section, the same trees in miniature
- The park with the biggest trees you know, for the shapes of them bare
- A churchyard or an arboretum, both good for old trunks in winter
- A café near the garden and a hot chocolate on the way home

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At 7 months the wet warm air of the greenhouse,
> the smell and the change in sound as the door shuts all land at once, and he
> goes still and stares. Carry him facing out and stop at three plants, his hand
> under yours on one big rubbery leaf. Back home he props against a cushion at
> the end of the row.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Explaining to someone else is how understanding gets locked in.**
> Azlyn giving the tour is doing harder work than Azlyn being told. To explain
> the tree she has to put the parts in an order, find words for the joins, and
> run into the bits she does not have. Researchers call it self-explanation,
> and children who talk their way through a problem hold on to it longer than
> children who watched a demonstration. Her audience does not need to follow a
> word. Kreston and three teddies do the job as well as an adult, because the
> value sits in the telling. Ask one real question at the end and let the
> silence run while she hunts for the answer.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Kreston sits on the floor against a cushion for the tour and
> never on a dining chair. At 7 months he goes over sideways with no warning.
> The leaf taped at his height and every loose end of masking tape come away
> the moment you stop watching, because both go straight to his mouth. The
> scissors stay with you, up on a shelf between cuts.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Odds and Ends Hunt

**🧰 You need:** the bowl of odds and ends · 1 baking tray · 1 jar lid.

1. Tip the bowl into the middle of the table and let her go through it.
2. Give her three words: **log**, **rock**, **leaf**. Ask which things in the pile could be each. A cork can be a log, a bottle cap a rock.
3. Set the jar lid in the middle of the empty tray and tell her it is the pond. Nothing else goes in until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Forest Floor Tray

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 baking tray or a large shallow box lid
- Soil, sand or torn brown paper for the ground
- Corks, clothespins, bottle caps, cotton balls, fabric scraps
- 1 jar lid for the pond
- Small stones and twigs from the yard
- 1 pitcher of water

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread the ground first: soil, sand, or brown paper torn small. Her hands do it. Sweep at the end.
2. Press the jar lid in and let her pour water from the pitcher. Refill it rather than telling her to go careful.
3. Lay the corks as fallen logs and the clothespins as branches. Stand the twigs up as trees, pushed in or taped to the tray edge.
4. Build one hollow under a cork to sleep in, and one heap of cotton balls for a nest.
5. Ring the pond with the small stones. Ask what is missing and put in whatever she names.
6. Leave one corner bare. You collect for it at 10:30 and fill it after lunch, so tell her that now.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her the whole bowl, not a chosen handful. Deciding which cork is a log is the part she came for.

### 🌳 Get Outside: What's Under the Leaves

Take a paper bag and turn over the leaf litter at the bottom of a hedge. The
underneath of January is wet, dark and busy: leaves gone to skeleton, a pill
bug, an empty snail shell, twigs going soft. Lift one stone, look, and put it
back as you found it. Fill the bag with moss, bark and four good twigs.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and everything goes to his
> mouth. Keep him clear of the tray and give him a bowl of his own with a
> wooden spoon and a folded washcloth in it. On the walk, hold one big dry leaf
> out for him to grab. He gets it to his mouth in under a second, so keep hold
> of your half.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Moving the Animals In

The collecting bag has sat by the front door since eleven. Empty it into the
bare corner of the tray, and the Forest Family moves in on top.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The forest floor tray
- The collecting bag from this morning
- The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 spray bottle, or a spoon and a cup of water, for rain
- 1 permanent marker for name labels

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip the bag onto newspaper beside the tray and go through it piece by piece. She decides what goes in.
2. Press the moss down as ground cover and lean the bark against a cork for a roof.
3. Bring the animals over one at a time. Each one needs somewhere to sleep and she picks the spot.
4. Write each name on masking tape and stick it on the tray edge below that animal.
5. Make it rain, one squeeze of the spray bottle or a spoonful tipped from a height. Watch where it runs and who chose a bad spot.
6. Move whoever got wet. Ask why the new place is drier and take her reasoning as it comes.
7. Lift the tray onto the table when she has finished. It comes down again tomorrow.

> 💡 **Tip:** Rain is the best thing here and she will ask for it eleven times. Set the number before you start, three rains, and hold the line, or the tray is soup by two.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- A shoebox lid and four things, and stop there.
- Draw the forest floor on paper instead of building it.
- Sort the collecting bag into two piles, alive and not alive.
- Float the bark in the dishpan and see what else floats.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A nature hunt walk** with a list of five: something red, rough, round, soft, and older than her
- The same hedge again with a flashlight as the light goes
- A woodland path, for trees she has not met yet
- The duck pond, to see what the water does in January
- A warm bath with the moss and twigs on a tray beside it, if the weather has turned

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes on the hunt in the carrier facing out
> with a hat over his ears. Stop three times and hold him up to touch a wall, a
> wet leaf, a cold gate. Name each one as his hand lands. At 7 months he answers
> every name with a run of sound, so leave him the gap to put it in.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Loose parts beat finished toys.**
> A bowl of corks, clothespins and bottle caps puts a decision in front of
> Azlyn on every piece she picks up. The cork has to become a log, and she
> makes it one. Architects and playworkers call these loose parts: the more a
> material can turn into, the longer a child stays with it and the more she
> says. A toy fox stays a fox for as long as you own it. Her cork is a log,
> then a seat, then a bear, and each change is a thought she had. Keep a bowl
> of them where she can reach and top it up from the recycling.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Small stones, corks and bottle caps sit at mouth height for a
> 7-month-old. The tray lives on the table between sessions and never on the
> floor while Kreston is loose in the room. Soil and leaf litter mean hands
> washed before the snack. Tip the pond out when she has finished.

## 🌟 Day 32: Who Came Past in the Night 🌟
**📅 Monday, February 1, 2027**
**Theme:** Forest Friends

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Lay the flour trail tonight in the room you can shut the door on, hide the animal at the end, and leave the paw stamps and the sieve on the table.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Four Feet
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Track Trail (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Footprints in the Frost (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Laying a Trail for Joseph (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Print Book
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Books on the Floor Cushions
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Four Feet

**🧰 You need:** paper · 1 crayon · the 2 paw stamps · one shut door.

1. Draw four feet on one sheet: a bird's, a duck's, a grown-up's, and a paw with four toes. Draw them rough; she will still read them.
2. Ask whose is whose and take the wrong answers without fixing them. Then ask what each foot is good at. Gripping, swimming, walking, digging.
3. Press one paw stamp onto the paper dry so she meets the shape before the trail. Something came through the house in the night, and that door stays shut until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Track Trail

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- All-purpose flour, 2 cups, in a sieve or a small bowl
- 2 paw shapes cut from a sponge or thick card
- Dark paper or a dark towel for the prints to show up on
- 3 clues: a chewed leaf, a tuft of wool, a few crumbs
- 1 hidden animal from the Forest Family, or any toy animal
- 1 dustpan and brush

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Open the door and stand back. Let her look before anybody says a word.
2. Follow it from the start on hands and knees. Count the prints out loud and let her take over.
3. Stop at every clue and ask the same question: what does this tell us. A chewed leaf says it eats plants, a tuft of wool says it is furry, crumbs say it went past the trash can.
4. Find the animal at the end. She lifts whatever it is hiding under and says the name.
5. Now walk it backwards, animal to door, and ask which way it was going. This is the hard part.
6. Sweep up together. Keep half a cup of flour back for after lunch.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not tell her who it was at the start. Guessing wrong for ten minutes and finding out at the end is the whole activity.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Footprints in the Frost

Early February holds frost on grass and car roofs until the sun comes round,
and a mild morning gives you soft mud instead, which takes a print better.
Walk the shaded side of the street and read what crossed it in the night: a
cat's prints along a wall, bird feet in a puddle, her own boots on white
grass. Send her across the lawn, then turn her round to see what she left.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and sits solid with both hands
> free. Put him at the far end of the trail on a blanket with a wooden spoon
> and let Azlyn crawl toward him. He tracks her the whole way and laughs before
> she arrives. Keep him off the floured floor, and out in the frost hold his
> bare palm on a cold car roof for one second.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Laying a Trail for Joseph

Joseph walks in at six tonight with no idea there is anything on the floor.
Azlyn spends the afternoon making sure there is.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The paw stamps and the flour
- Paper and crayons for arrow cards
- 1 roll masking tape
- One thing to hide at the end, chosen by her
- 1 flashlight
- 1 dustpan and brush

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Walk the route with her first, no flour, and let her fix where it starts and ends. Follow her decision even when it goes through the kitchen twice.
2. She chooses what waits at the end and hides it herself, out of your sight.
3. Print the prints. She presses the stamp, you sieve a little flour onto the sponge between presses.
4. Make three arrow cards. She draws them, you tape them at Joseph's eye height rather than hers.
5. Add two clues of her own. Ask what each is meant to tell him and write her answer on the back.
6. Walk it once as a test, her leading and you playing Joseph. She will fix two things.
7. Turn the lights down at six and hand him the flashlight at the door.

> 💡 **Tip:** Write her clues down word for word. She will not remember the reasoning by Friday.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One arrow, one hidden thing, thirty seconds of trail.
- Lay the trail outside in chalk instead of flour.
- Draw round everybody's shoes and match them back to feet.
- Press a toy animal's feet into playdough.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The big slide playground**, and check under the swings for tracks
- The neighborhood park, for the muddy path along the far end
- A field walk, for the biggest frozen puddles you can find
- The woods loop, looking for holes in banks and under roots
- Another trail upstairs, if the wind has made outside a bad idea

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He goes in the stroller with a blanket over his
> legs and a hat over his ears. February wind at the top of a slide is a
> different thing at his height, so keep him low and moving. Five minutes on
> the baby swing and no more. He is passing things hand to hand now, so give
> him two rings for the walk home.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Evidence and inference, a big idea learnable at three.**
> A chewed leaf on the floor and a fox at the end of the hallway are different
> kinds of thing, and Azlyn spent the morning getting from one to the other.
> Scientists call the move inference: the leaf is what you can see, the fox is
> what you worked out. Three-year-olds do this better than the age suggests,
> as long as the evidence sits in front of them. Ask *what does this tell us*
> instead of *who was it*, and she has to say the middle step out loud. That
> middle step is the whole of science, and she will use it on you
> within a week.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Flour on a hard floor is slippery in a way that puts adults
> down as fast as children. Sweep between rounds, keep it off tile and
> laminate near the stairs, and never lay a trail on a staircase. Sieve it
> rather than throwing it, so nobody breathes a cloud.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 33: Feeding the Birds 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, February 2, 2027**
**Theme:** Forest Friends

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Bring the four feeders in off their branches and stand them by the sink with the string, the four foods and the swimming bag.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Bird Menu
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: What the Birds Take First (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Hanging the Feeders (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Binoculars and the Bird Chart (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Topping Up the Seed Tub
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Window Seat
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: After Swimming, Two Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Bird Menu

**🧰 You need:** paper · crayons · a saucer of seed, oats and raisins.

1. Put the saucer in front of her and let her sort it. Seeds here, oats there, raisins in their own heap.
2. Ask which a bird would go for first. Write her answer as a menu, one line per item, with her drawing of the bird beside it.
3. Pin the menu on the window the feeders hang outside. She checks it against real birds all week.

### 🎨 The Main Event: What the Birds Take First

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The four feeders from January 17, brought in off their branches (or 4 clean yogurt pots and string, if the wind took them)
- Warm soapy water, 1 dish brush and a cloth
- 4 foods, a cup of each: sunflower seeds, mixed birdseed, oats and breadcrumbs, raisins
- Masking tape and 1 marker
- String, 1 ball
- 1 tray

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Line the four feeders up on the table and tip what is left of each into its own saucer. She puts them in order, emptiest to fullest.
2. She scrubs the pots in the warm soapy water and stands them on the tray. Sixteen days of birds leave a lot behind.
3. Fill each pot with one food and one food only. She will want to mix them, and a mixed pot answers nothing.
4. She draws a label for each one and you tape it on: a sunflower, a scatter of seed, a spoonful of oats, a raisin.
5. Re-tie the strings and pull every knot tight. A pot that swings loose in a February wind empties itself in a day.
6. Walk her past the menu she pinned on the window at 8:00 and ask which pot empties first. Write her answer on the menu.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will want raisins in every pot, because raisins are the good one. Let her put them in the pot she thinks the birds like least, and the test still works.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Hanging the Feeders

Hang all four in new places this time, well apart, where she can see them from
a window and a cat cannot reach. A clothesline, a bare branch, a hook under
the eaves, a fence post. She picks every spot and you lift her to the high
ones. February is the hard month out there, and four foods in four spots ask a
better question than four in one.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months and passes things from hand to
> hand all day. Give him a clean yogurt pot and a wooden spoon beside the
> table and let him swap them over. He bangs the two together inside ten
> minutes. The seed, the string and the raisins stay well out of reach.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Binoculars and the Bird Chart

Nothing will come to those feeders today. Birds take a day or two to find a
feeder that has moved, so build her somewhere to sit and wait.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Cardboard tubes, 4
- 1 roll masking tape
- Paper and crayons for the chart
- Cushions and a blanket for the window seat
- 1 pencil
- The Groundhog Day note: February 2, when a woodchuck is said to come up and check on winter

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape two tubes side by side for her pair, and two more for yours. Nothing goes round her neck: she holds hers to her eyes with both hands.
2. Let her color both pairs.
3. Build the window seat: cushions under the window, blanket over her knees, chart and pencil beside her.
4. Draw the chart with her. Five rows, one bird per row, a tick box at the end.
5. Sit and watch. Ten minutes is a long time at three, so set the deal now: watch, something else, watch again.
6. Tick nothing, and treat that as an answer. Ask why and write her reason at the bottom.
7. Tell her what today is. February 2, Groundhog Day. Ask what she thinks the woodchuck saw.

> 💡 **Tip:** Leave the chart on the windowsill with the pencil. She ticks it on Thursday when a chickadee turns up.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One tube, one eye, and stop there.
- Draw birds out of a book instead.
- Count everything that moves outside for five minutes.
- Put crumbs on the windowsill and watch the sill instead.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one
- The quiet hour, if the after-school crowd is in
- Indoor playground if the pool is shut
- A warm café and the new binoculars, aimed at the pigeons
- Straight home, if the morning ran long

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He swims too if he is coming. At 7 months he sits
> supported in the water and slaps at it, and twenty minutes is enough before
> he goes cold. Hold him chest to chest for the first few minutes, so the echo
> and the shouting arrive with your face in front of him. Get him dry and
> dressed before you deal with yourself.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Delayed payoff is a muscle, and this is a gentle way to work it.**
> She filled four feeders this morning and no bird came this afternoon. That
> gap is the thing worth having. Waiting well builds through small waits with
> something visible at the end, and a feeder outside the window is the
> friendliest version. Nobody is asking her to sit still in front of a
> marshmallow. She hung it, she can see it, and the birds arrive on Thursday.
> Say out loud that they need a day or two to find it, so the wait carries a
> reason instead of an unexplained no. A three-year-old who waited and turned
> out right takes that with her.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Old feeders carry droppings, so both pairs of hands get
> washed with soap after the scrubbing and again after the hanging, before
> anybody eats. Loose seed on the floor is choke-sized for a 7-month-old, so
> sweep before Kreston goes down. The string gets tied outside and the ball
> comes straight back indoors, because a loop of string at toddler height is a
> strangulation risk. The binoculars stay stringless for the same reason: no
> cord long enough to go over her head, on those or on anything else in the
> house.
