## 🌟 Day 34: The Long Sleep 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, February 3, 2027**
**Theme:** Forest Friends

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Empty the biggest box in the house, check inside for staples, and stand it on its side in the corner with a folded blanket beside it.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Winter Sleepers
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Bear Cave (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Empty Nests in Bare Trees (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Waking the Bears (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **The Library** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks and the Napkins
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Nesting the Animals
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Library Book in the Cave
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Winter Sleepers

**🧰 You need:** the Forest Family animals or any toys · 1 blanket · the sofa.

1. Line the animals along the arm of the sofa. Ask which of them she thinks sleeps the whole winter.
2. Hand her the four that do in this house's version: bear, groundhog, chipmunk, bat. Tuck them under a corner of the blanket together.
3. Ask what a sleeping animal needs. Take her list as it comes, and tell her the cave gets built at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Bear Cave

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large cardboard box, big enough for her to sit up in
- Newspaper or scrap paper to tear for leaves
- 1 blanket and 1 cushion
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 flashlight
- The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the box on its side with the opening facing away from the window. Run a hand round the inside for staples and tape over the ones you find.
2. Tear the paper into leaves together. Fill a grocery bag and let the tearing run as long as she wants.
3. Line the floor of the cave with the leaves, the blanket over them, and the cushion at the back wall.
4. Tape a flap of card across part of the opening so the inside goes dark. She decides how much light gets in.
5. Send her in with the flashlight and stay outside. Give her five clear minutes on her own before you ask a single question.
6. Move the animals in one at a time, each to a spot she picks. Then get in with her, turn the flashlight off, and let the cave go dark.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her tear far more paper than the cave needs. Two hands pulling in opposite directions is work she can keep up for twenty minutes.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Empty Nests in Bare Trees

Nests show up in February and vanish again in April, so this is the month to
look. Walk the road and the park with your eyes up and count the dark clumps
in the bare branches. Some are nests, some are a knot of twigs. Find the
highest and the lowest. Nobody is home in any of them, so say so.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months. Sit him at the cave mouth
> propped on a cushion with you beside him, and let Azlyn crawl in and out past
> him. The light drops as she goes in and comes back as she comes out, and he
> turns his head after it. Give him a big sheet of paper to crush in both hands.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Waking the Bears

The cave is dark and lined by lunchtime. Azlyn runs the afternoon on a wooden
spoon and a pan lid, and winter ends whenever she says it does.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The cave
- 1 wooden spoon and 1 pan lid
- 1 blanket each
- 1 cup of warm milk and a snack, for eating inside
- Books about bears or winter, 2–3
- 1 flashlight

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Everybody hibernates. Into the cave or under a blanket, eyes shut, and hold it while you count to twenty out loud.
2. Bang the pan lid once with the spoon. That is spring. Everybody wakes, stretches and comes out slow.
3. Go round again with her holding the spoon. She decides how long winter lasts, three seconds the first time and two minutes the fourth.
4. Change one rule each round. Sleep standing up. Sleep in a pile. Sleep with the flashlight on. Sleep and snore.
5. Creep past a sleeping bear without waking it, then swap and let her creep past you. Getting caught is the fun of it, so get caught.
6. Take the milk and the snack into the cave and eat in there with the flashlight on.
7. Read the books in the cave and finish with everybody asleep and nobody banging anything.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her hold the pan lid for most of the rounds. Deciding when winter ends is a lot of power for a three-year-old.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- A blanket over two sofa cushions instead of a box.
- Sleeping lions, the quiet version, five minutes and done.
- Draw what a bear dreams about all winter.
- Sort the animals into sleepers and stay-awakes.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Library**
- **The library**, and ask at the desk for one book about bears and one about winter
- Indoor playground if the library is shut or packed
- The park on the way back, for twenty minutes of running
- A café, with both new books read cover to cover
- The bookshop window, if the library run is not happening today

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Sit him in the board-book corner at the library
> while Azlyn chooses. At 7 months he mouths every book he gets hold of, and he
> holds one in each hand and swaps them. Let Azlyn pick his and carry it to the
> desk. At home the pan lid stays well away from his ears.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Pretending to sleep is real self-regulation practice.**
> Azlyn lying still with her eyes shut while you count to twenty is doing
> something hard on purpose. She wants to move, she knows the rule, and she
> holds herself to it anyway. Researchers call that inhibitory control, and
> games with a stop-and-go rule build it better than being told to sit still,
> because the rule belongs to the game. The round where she holds the pan lid
> works harder: running the stop and the go for somebody else takes more
> control than following it. Freeze games, musical statues and sleeping lions
> sit in the same family. Reach for one on the afternoons she is
> climbing the walls.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Kreston is 7 months and cannot get himself out of anywhere.
> He goes in the cave only with you in it, and never on his own for a second.
> Torn paper and loose blankets stay clear of his face. Check the box for
> staples before either of them climbs in, and tape over every one you find.

## 🌟 Day 35: The Shadow Forest 🌟
**📅 Thursday, February 4, 2027**
**Theme:** Forest Friends

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Flatten two cereal boxes onto the table with the scissors and a marker, put fresh batteries in the flashlight, and clear the wall.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Guess the Shadow
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Shadow Animals (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Longest Shadow (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Puppet Show Behind the Sheet (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Flashlight and the Wall
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Last Story of the Week
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Guess the Shadow

**🧰 You need:** 1 flashlight · a pale wall · 3 toy animals · your hands.

1. Turn the big light off, sit her facing the wall, and hold the flashlight behind your shoulder.
2. Put one animal in the beam. Ask which one it is before she turns round.
3. Move it closer to the flashlight and let the shadow swell. Hand her the flashlight until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Shadow Animals

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Cereal boxes or thick card, 4–5
- Scissors (**adult**)
- Craft sticks, straws or pencils
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 flashlight
- A pale wall or a white door

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Draw the four animals on the cereal box: fox, owl, deer, raccoon. Big simple outlines, no detail inside. You draw, she directs.
2. Cut them out. Card this thick is adult work: she holds the box flat while you cut.
3. Tape a craft stick low on the back of each, so her hand stays out of the beam.
4. Test the first one against the wall. If the ears are too small or the legs have joined into a block, cut wider and test again.
5. Do the same to all four. Deer antlers have to be fat, and an owl needs a notch between its ear tufts.
6. Line them up and test from across the room. Any animal she cannot name goes back for cutting.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut everything fatter than looks right. Thin legs and fine antlers vanish on the wall.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Longest Shadow

Stop at the feeders on the way out. The sunflower seeds have gone down, and a
chickadee comes back for more if you hold still. Let her tick the chart when
you get in. The sun stays low all day in early February, so shadows run long.
Stand her on the sidewalk at eleven, draw round her shadow in chalk, and pace
it out in her steps. Come back past the chalk mark on the way home.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 7 months. Lay him on his back and hold
> the flashlight above him off to one side, your hand between the beam and his
> face. Move your fingers through it. He follows the shape across the ceiling,
> loses it, finds it again. Outside, park him with the low sun behind him and
> wave from a few feet back.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Puppet Show Behind the Sheet

A sheet clipped across a doorway turns the week into something she can
perform. She has four animals, one flashlight, and an audience.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 white or pale sheet
- Clothespins or binder clips, 6
- A doorway, or 2 dining chairs back to back
- 1 flashlight
- The shadow puppets
- Paper and crayons for tickets and a poster

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Clip the sheet across the doorway, pulled tight, floor to above her head. Two chairs back to back work if clips will not hold.
2. Stand the flashlight behind the sheet on the floor or a low stool, aimed at the middle.
3. Test the distance. Close to the sheet the fox is small and sharp; back near the flashlight he is huge and soft.
4. Make the poster and the tickets. She draws, you write the words she dictates.
5. Sit the audience down: Kreston propped on cushions, teddies either side, whoever else is home.
6. She tells the week back through the puppets: coats on Friday, the tree on Saturday, somebody past in the night on Monday. Give her the day and she supplies the rest.
7. Swap sides at the end. You run the fox, and the last five minutes go with the flashlight off.

> 💡 **Tip:** Move the flashlight back further than feels right. A flashlight against the sheet gives one bright spot and four tiny animals.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Flashlight and bare hands on the wall, no sheet and no puppets.
- Shadow shapes on the ceiling from under a blanket.
- Draw round the puppets' shadows on paper and color them in.
- Retire the puppets into the forest floor tray and stop there.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The garden center**, for the indoor trees and a warm greenhouse in February
- The hardware store, for flashlights and a spare set of batteries
- The park on the way back, for the low sun and the long shadows
- The grocery store, and she chooses one thing for Friday breakfast
- Home and the sofa, if the show ran long and nobody wants a coat on

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The garden center is warm and bright, so sit him
> on your lap for ten minutes. Hold a big leaf out to one side, where he has
> to reach across himself. At 7 months that cross-body reach is new work. At
> the show he sits in the front row, and moving shapes on a lit sheet hold him
> longer than a book.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Shadows are confusing at three, and the confusion is worth exploring.**
> Ask Azlyn what a shadow is made of and you get real thought in the answer
> and no truth in it. Three-year-olds treat a shadow as a thing that belongs
> to an object and travels with it, rather than as blocked light. The real
> version takes a couple of years of flashlight time. Every test today feeds
> that version: close to the sheet, back near the flashlight, one hand in the
> beam. Hold off on the tidy explanation. Give her the flashlight, let her run
> the tests, and answer the questions she asks rather than the ones she has
> not reached.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Loose craft sticks and straws stay off the floor while Kreston
> is down. They splinter, and they fit down his throat, so count them onto the
> table and back off it. Card this thick is yours to cut and the scissors stay
> with you. Clip the sheet where it can come down without bringing anything with
> it, a door frame rather than a curtain pole or a shelf. Stand the flashlight on
> the floor instead of a stack of books, and with the room lights off keep
> Kreston inside arm's reach the whole time.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>
<a id="backup-jan"></a>

# 🌧️ January — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

These five pages sit outside the 365. Reach for them when the day you had
planned will not run: ice on the sidewalk and a stroller that will not go
over it, a fever that arrived at 3:00 in the morning, or an hour where the
plan in front of you needs more hands than you have. The two weather days
are full days built for a January where nobody is leaving the house, so
everything on them comes out of your own kitchen. The two sick days run on
no clock at all.

---

<a id="jan-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — Cold Enough to Keep

Freezing rain since before it got light, the ground hard under it, and dark
again by five. The door stays shut today. The cold is still the subject, and
it comes in through the kitchen instead of the front step.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put the fruit bowl, the salt and a ball of string on the counter, stand the vinegar and a clean jar with a lid beside them, and clear the sill above the warmest radiator.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: What Lives in the Cold
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Drying the Apple Rings (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Twenty Seconds of Weather (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Tray of Things That Keep (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎬 Movie Hour: The One She Picks (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Checking the Apple String
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Tray She Ranked
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and Three Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: What Lives in the Cold

**🧰 You need:** the fridge · the cupboard · 2 dish towels laid on the floor.

1. Let her take ten things out of the fridge and ten out of the cupboard, one at a time, and stand each one on its own towel.
2. Swap two over while she watches. Ketchup on the cupboard towel, dried pasta on the fridge towel. Wait for her to object.
3. Ask what would happen to the milk if it lived in the cupboard. Take her answer as it comes, tell her you will show her at 9:15, and put it all back.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Drying the Apple Rings

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3 apples, or any firm fruit in the bowl; with no fruit in the house, 1 potato or 2 thick slices of bread
- 1 sharp knife (**adult only**)
- String, about a yard, and 2 clothespins
- 1 saucer and 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Slice the fruit across into rings about as thick as her fingernail. You cut, she counts them into a bowl and tells you when to stop.
2. Set two rings aside on a saucer. That saucer gets nothing done to it, and it does more work today than anything else on the table.
3. Thread the rest of the rings onto the string with a gap between each one, hang it across the sill above the warm radiator, high up and well past her reach, and pin each end with a clothespin so it cannot slide.
4. Write the date on the saucer, and look at it together every time either of you walks past it.
5. Check the apple string at 4:00 as her job. Almost nothing will have changed, and the almost-nothing is the honest answer to how long this takes.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not skip the saucer that gets no treatment. The ring on the string means nothing to her without a brown one sitting beside it to compare against.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Twenty Seconds of Weather

Coats, hats and boots on as though the walk were happening, because the
getting ready was half of what the walk did for her. Open the back door,
stand on the mat together, and count to twenty out loud while the cold works
on your faces. Shut it. Then run five laps of the downstairs to get warm
again and count those too. Three rounds of that. She gets the weather on her
skin, the door stays shut the rest of the day, and the running gives her back
what the walk would have.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 6 to 7 months, sitting with his hands
> free and rocking on hands and knees. Fill a small plastic bottle with cold
> water, tape the cap down hard, and let him hold it for a minute at a time
> while you slice. Cold in the hands is new information for him. Bring him to
> the open door with a hat on for five of the twenty seconds, facing out, and
> then get him back in the warm. The apple string and the knife stay above
> head height the whole morning.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Tray of Things That Keep

The morning hung fruit up to see what warm air takes out of it. This
afternoon she eats her way across a cupboard full of food other people
already made last, then packs a jar of her own and waits a day for it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large plate or tray
- Six of these, or any six the cupboard holds: raisins, dried apricots, olives, pickles, jam, honey, canned peaches, dried beef
- 1 teaspoon each
- 1 clean jar with a lid
- 1 carrot, half a cucumber or any firm vegetable in the drawer
- White vinegar, 1/2 cup · water, 1/2 cup · sugar, 1 tablespoon · salt, 1 teaspoon
- 1 marker and a strip of paper for the label

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set the six foods around the tray with a spoon each. She tastes them in whatever order she picks, and she is allowed to spit one out.
2. Ask her to lay them in a line from the one she would eat again to the one she would not. Write the order down and read it back to her.
3. Give her the one fact under all six: every one of them was made to last past the week it was picked in. Then let her have her favorite twice.
4. Peel the vegetable into sticks together. She snaps them to the length she wants and packs them into the jar herself.
5. Measure the vinegar, water, sugar and salt into a cup. Hand her the lid and let her shake it until the sugar has gone.
6. Pour it over the sticks, screw the lid down tight, and let her write the date on the label however her writing comes out.
7. Put the jar in the fridge and tell her it is tomorrow's snack. The waiting is the part she will remember.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will hate at least one of the six and say so at volume. Write that one down with the same care as the ones she liked. The ranking belongs to her, and it is the reason she keeps tasting.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Skip the tasting. Pack the jar and stop there.
- Dry whatever else is in the fruit bowl on the sill and hang it in the window.
- Line up everything in the fridge door from what lasts longest to what spoils first.
- Read the dates on six packets and find the one that runs out soonest.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Sit him at the table end in his chair where he
> can watch the jar being shaken. At 6 to 7 months the sound of something
> rattling in a container holds him longer than the container does. Give him a
> clean metal spoon and a small unbreakable cup of his own to bang and mouth.
> Nothing off the tray reaches him: honey waits until he is one, raisins and
> olives are choking hazards at his size, and the vinegar gets a hard no.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Preservation is a surprisingly big idea.**
> Food goes bad because something alive is eating it before you get to it.
> Cold slows those things down, salt pulls the water out from under them,
> vinegar sours the ground they grow in, and drying takes away the water they
> need. Azlyn will not hold all four of those today, and she does not have to.
> She holds one comparison: the ring on the saucer went brown and soft, the
> ring on the string went hard and pale, and both of them came off the same
> fruit an hour apart. Running two versions of a thing and looking at the
> difference is the method behind most of what she will learn later, and she
> can do it at three.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The knife is adult-only and goes back out of reach between
> cuts, on a high shelf and not the counter edge. Hang the apple string above
> her head and take it down the moment the rings are dry. A loop of string at
> toddler height is a strangulation risk. Radiators get hot enough to burn, so
> the rings sit on the sill above and never on the metal. No honey for Kreston
> before his first birthday, and no raisins, olives or carrot sticks.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jan-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — What Everything Is Made Of

Snow came down in the night and froze under a skin of ice, so every sidewalk
is a slide and the light goes again by five. A whole day indoors makes the
house feel smaller by about eleven in the morning. Today she goes through it
room by room and finds out that the house she knows is made of four or five
things.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand an empty laundry basket by the sofa with a roll of masking tape and a marker in it. Dig out the coin jar, the dullest copper you own, and the ketchup.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Back of Her Hand
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Coldest Thing in the House (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Sixty-Second Snowstorm (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Coins That Come Back (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🛁 The Afternoon Bath (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks Back in the Drawer
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Basket by the Sofa
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Two Books Under the Lamp
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Back of Her Hand

**🧰 You need:** 1 metal spoon · 1 wooden spoon · 1 dish towel · a clear counter.

1. Lay all three side by side and leave them for five minutes so they come to the same temperature as the room.
2. Show her the test: back of the hand, held flat, counting to three. Cheek for the ones that pass.
3. Ask her which is coldest. She picks the metal one, and the three have been sitting together the whole time. Tell her you are going hunting for the coldest thing in the house at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Coldest Thing in the House

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 laundry basket
- 4 dish towels laid out on the rug as the four groups
- Masking tape, cut into labels, and 1 marker
- Paper and a pencil for the list
- 1 metal spoon, carried as the thing everything gets compared against

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Walk the house room by room with the basket. She tests with the back of her hand and takes anything that feels cold. Her wrong ones come too.
2. Tip the basket out on the rug and line the finds up, coldest at one end. She sets the order and she can retest as often as she wants.
3. Read the line back to her from cold to warm, and write it down in that order.
4. Now the second sort. Write **metal**, **wood**, **plastic** and **cloth** on four strips of masking tape, stick one to each towel, and read them to her. Every object lands on a towel.
5. She will put things in the wrong group, and the painted ones will be the ones that beat her. Let her tap them, weigh them in her hand and scratch a corner with a fingernail before she commits.
6. Stand back and look at the two arrangements together. Most of what she called cold is sitting on the metal towel. Say that out loud once and let it sit.

> 💡 **Tip:** The whole house is one temperature this morning, and that is what makes this worth an hour. Metal pulls the heat out of her hand faster than wood does, so it feels colder while measuring the same. She does not need those words today. She needs to notice that the spoon and the cutting board disagree.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Sixty-Second Snowstorm

Tip the paper recycling onto the floor and crumple the lot into snowballs
with her. Fifty is a good target and she will lose interest at thirty, so
crumple the rest yourself. Run a line of masking tape across the middle of
the room, put her on one side and you on the other, and set a timer for sixty
seconds. One rule: get the snow off your own side. Count what is left when
the timer goes, sweep it back to the middle and run it again. Three rounds
takes more out of her than the walk would have, and the cleanup is one bag.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 6 to 7 months and mouths everything he
> can reach. Sit him propped against the sofa with this morning's wooden spoon
> and metal spoon and watch which one he keeps. Cold metal on his gums is a
> sensation he has not had before. Keep him out of the room while the paper is
> flying. Wet paper tears into pieces the size of his mouth, so sweep the floor
> at his eye level before he goes back down, and give him one clean sheet to
> crumple at the edge of the room with you sitting beside him.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Coins That Come Back

The morning was full of cold things she was told to leave as they were. This
afternoon she takes the dullest metal in the house and makes it shine, and
the change happens under her own hands inside a minute.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 20 or so dull coins, copper ones for preference
- Ketchup, 2 tablespoons, or 1 tablespoon of salt stirred into 3 tablespoons of vinegar
- 1 small bowl and 1 old teaspoon
- 2 rags or a cut-up t-shirt
- 1 bowl of clean water and a dish towel
- The forks and spoons out of the drawer

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Line the coins up on a rag and let her pick the three ugliest ones.
2. Stand one of those three aside where she can see it. Nothing happens to that coin all afternoon, and it is the one that proves the rest.
3. Drop the others into the bowl of ketchup and let her push them under with the spoon. Count to sixty out loud together.
4. Fish one out and rub it with the rag. It comes up bright. Hand her the rag and let her do every remaining coin herself.
5. Rinse them all in the clean water and dry them, because ketchup left sitting on metal marks it.
6. Line the bright coins up next to the one you left alone and ask her to tell you what happened. Write her explanation down word for word.
7. Finish on the silverware. A dry rag and ten minutes of buffing the forks, and she leaves them ready on the counter for 4:00.

> 💡 **Tip:** Sixty seconds is a long minute for a three-year-old. Count it out loud with her, or she fishes them out at twenty and the trick fails on her.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Coins in ketchup and nothing else. Ten minutes, same result.
- Polish one object each and stand them in a row on the windowsill.
- Sort the coin jar by size, then by how bright each one is.
- Wash the plastic toys in a bowl of warm soapy water on a towel on the floor.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Coins stay on the table and off the floor the
> whole afternoon. Count them into the bowl and count them back into the jar
> before he comes down. Give him the wooden spoon and an unbreakable cup on
> the rug where you can see him. He is rocking on hands and knees and getting
> further with it every week, so what sat out of his reach on Monday is inside
> it by Friday. Get down at his eye level and check the floor before you put
> him on it.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sorting by material is harder than sorting by color.**
> Color sits on the surface and she can call it from across the room. Material
> hides. A wooden spoon and a plastic spoon come in the same shape and often
> the same color, and telling them apart means picking both up, feeling the
> weight, tapping them and holding them against her cheek. She has to gather
> evidence and hold a rule in her head while she gathers it, which is a bigger
> job than matching what she sees. Expect wrong groups, and expect painted
> wood and coated metal to break her rule. The arguing over the hard ones is
> the part that teaches, so let those arguments run long.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The temperature test is for cold things. Say the rule out
> loud before she starts and again after lunch: she tests nothing on the
> stove, nothing on a radiator, nothing plugged in, and she asks you first
> every single time. Coins are one of the most swallowed objects there is, so
> count them out and count them back before Kreston is on the floor. Keep the
> vinegar and the bowl at the back of the counter, and wash her hands before
> the snack.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jan-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Day She Stays on the Sofa

This is the flat day. She is hot, she wants you inside arm's reach, and
anything with a beginning and an end is past her. Everything on this page can
be picked up and dropped without a word, and none of it needs cutting,
setting up or clearing away.

### 🕗 The Shape of the Day

- **Whenever she wakes** · 🛋️ Making the Spot, and no decisions asked of her
- **Once she is in it** · the first drink, small and often
- **When lying still stops working** · 🫱 Lap Things: one at a time, dropped the moment it stops holding
- **After the first long sleep** · more Lap Things, or the movie, with no guilt attached to either
- **The middle of the day** · 😴 The Rest Block
- **When she asks for food** · small, bland, and only when she asks
- **Before the afternoon dip** · a warm bath if she has it in her, a warm washcloth if she does not
- **The end of the day** · bed an hour early and the same book twice

### 🛋️ Making the Spot

Build her one place and let her stay in it. Sofa, her pillow from her own
bed, the blanket she picks, a towel underneath in case of the bowl, and a
lidded cup of water within her reach and not yours. Put a bucket or a mixing
bowl on the floor beside her and show her where it is, so she does not have
to call for it. Move a lamp so the overhead light can stay off.

Set the day up so she never has to move for anything. Fetching is your job
today, and the fetching is most of what she wants from you.

### 😴 The Rest Block

Sleep is the medicine here, and the rest block is the plan rather than the
gap between plans. Half shut the curtains, drop the sound in the house, and
lie on the floor beside the sofa where she can see you. Skip the screen for
the first stretch, because she will fight sleep to keep watching. An hour is
a good aim and forty minutes is a win. If Kreston goes down at the same time,
put your own head on the arm of the sofa and take the twenty minutes. You are
on the third night of broken sleep too, and nobody else in the house is going
to schedule that for you.

### 🫱 Lap Things

- **The Window List** · she names everything that goes past and you write it on the back of an envelope
- **The Story With Her Name In It** · you make it up as you go, and she chooses what happens next when she has it in her
- **The Warm Washcloth** · a bowl of warm water on the floor and a cloth she wipes her own face and hands with
- **Five Minutes on One Page** · one page of a picture book held open that long, hunting for small things in the corners
- **The Popsicle That Counts as a Drink** · for a raw throat, and it goes on the fluids tally
- **Every Photo Named Out Loud** · your phone on airplane mode and the camera roll gone through one picture at a time

### 🍵 When She Asks for Food

Fluids matter today and food does not. Water, diluted juice, milk if it stays
down, popsicles, ice chips, soup broth from a mug. Offer small amounts often
rather than a meal she has to face down. Toast, banana, plain rice, dry
cereal by the handful. She eats again when she is better, and pushing a plate
at her today costs you both more than the missed meal does.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

He is 6 to 7 months, sitting on his own and rocking on hands and knees, and
every week that rocking gets him a hand's width further, so anything of hers
left within reach of his blanket is his. Set his blanket and a basket of his
own things on the far side of the room where he can see her and not reach her,
and take the playpen or travel crib out if you have one, since today is the
day it earns its space. Wash your hands between them and keep her cup, her
spoon and her washcloth off his patch. The odds are he catches it anyway, and
the handwashing still buys you a couple of days. Feed him and change him on a
schedule you set out loud, because she cannot wait for anything today and he
will get skipped otherwise.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A day off has to be visibly protected or it doesn't happen.**
> A sick day is a day off nobody chose, and it disappears the same way a
> chosen one does. The delivery still comes, the message still gets answered
> on your knees by the sofa, and the thing you meant to do at four gets tried
> at four. Clear it out loud instead. Cancel the visit in front of her, take
> the appointment off the calendar where she can see the line through it, and
> tell her the day has nothing in it now. She hears that you moved the world
> for her, which is most of what she wants while she feels this bad, and you
> stop spending the day in two places at once.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Keep the fluids going and count wet diapers or trips to the
> bathroom, because dehydration moves faster in a three-year-old than in you.
> Call the doctor for fast or labored breathing, a fever over 102°F that will
> not come down or lasts past three days, a child too drowsy to rouse, no wet
> diaper in eight hours, or any rash that does not fade when you press a glass
> against it. Never give aspirin to a child. Check the label and the weight
> before every dose, and write down the time you gave it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jan-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Better But Not Well

The fever went in the night and she woke up asking for things. She has about
an hour of energy in her with nothing behind it, so the trap today is a plan
built for a well child. Give her a small version of a normal day and let her
come back to full size on her own schedule.

### 🕗 The Shape of the Day

- **Whenever she wakes** · 🛋️ Moving the Spot, which is the whole event
- **The first good hour** · 🫱 Things She Can Do From Sitting, one at a time
- **When she gets sharp with you** · the energy has run out. Back to the blanket
- **After the first long sleep** · food, and more of it than yesterday
- **The middle of the day** · 😴 The Rest Block, and she will fight it
- **When she asks for food** · say yes to almost all of it
- **Before the afternoon dip** · one job with a visible end
- **The end of the day** · an early bath and no plans made out loud for tomorrow

### 🛋️ Moving the Spot

Rebuild her camp in a different room. Kitchen table with a blanket over her
knees, the floor by the window, your bed with the good pillows, anywhere that
is not yesterday's sofa. A change of room does more for a bored recovering
child than any activity you could put in front of her, and it costs you four
minutes and an armful of bedding.

Take the whole kit with her: cup, blanket, bowl within reach, the same lamp.
Then move it again after lunch if the second room stops working.

### 😴 The Rest Block

She will refuse it today, and she still needs it. Take sleep off the table
and ask for lying down instead. Curtains half shut, a story playing, and
nothing she has to answer. Forty minutes flat on her back does most of what a
nap would have, and about half the time she goes under anyway. Sit with her
for the first five minutes, then get up and go do the thing you have not
managed for two days.

### 🫱 Things She Can Do From Sitting

- **The Drawing She Doesn't Have to Explain** · a hardback book under the paper for a desk, crayons loose on the blanket, and no questions about what it is
- **The Button Tin on a Tray** · sort them however she likes, tip them out, do it again
- **The Order Pad** · she writes an order from the blanket however her writing comes out and you fetch it, one item at a time
- **Rolling It Back** · she rolls a ball across the floor to you from where she sits and you roll it back, for as long as it holds her
- **Reading to Kreston** · board books held up from the sofa while he sits below her on his blanket
- **Joseph on Speaker** · him or a grandparent, and she does the talking with the phone flat on her chest
- **One Sticker Sheet, One Page** · no rules, no theme, and the sheet is hers alone

### 🍽️ When She Asks for Food

Her appetite comes back before her energy does, and it comes back crooked.
Say yes to toast at four in the afternoon and soup for breakfast. Keep
offering fluids at the same rate as yesterday even though she looks better,
because she stops asking before she has caught up. Put a small plate in front
of her rather than a full one, and let her ask for seconds. Asking for
seconds is a better sign than a plate she clears without noticing.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

Today she wants him near, and near is now the problem. He is 6 to 7 months,
he mouths everything he reaches, and half of what she is playing with fits in
his mouth. Put him on his blanket below her rather than beside her, run the
button tin on a tray at sofa height, and count the buttons back in before he
gets floor time. Give her one job that involves him and ends: holding the
book up for three pages, passing him one toy at a time, singing him the song
he likes. She gets to be the older one again for ten minutes, which is worth
more to her right now than anything you could hand her on a tray.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **"What is it?" is the question to stop asking.**
> She finishes something on the blanket and hands it over. The reflex is to
> ask what it is, and she will invent an answer to satisfy you, which turns
> her drawing into a test with one right answer she has to guess. Say what you
> see instead. You used the blue three times. That line runs right off the
> edge. This bit here is pressed so hard it went through the paper. She will
> tell you what it is inside a minute, or she will tell you it is nothing at
> all, and both of those are fine. At three the movement and the mark are the
> point, and the naming arrives later on its own.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Buttons, coins and small sorting objects stay on a tray at
> sofa height and get counted back into the tin before Kreston is on the
> floor. A button is the right size to block a 7-month-old's airway. She can
> be around other children once she has gone 24 hours with no fever and no
> medicine holding it down, and not before. Keep giving fluids at yesterday's
> rate, and call the doctor if a fever comes back after a clear day.

## 🎲 January — Extra Ideas

Ten minutes, no plan, and a dark afternoon to fill. Nothing here needs a
shopping trip or more than one instruction.

### 🎲 Alternative Activities

- **The Dark by Five Countdown** · she checks the window every fifteen minutes and shouts when the streetlights come on
- **The Hallway Tow** · she kneels on a bath towel holding the front edge and you pull her from the bedroom door to the kitchen and back
- **Every Shoe in the House** · lined up biggest to smallest along the hall with yours at the end
- **The Two-Minute Race** · a timer, one room, and everything that lives somewhere else goes in a basket
- **The Upside-Down Meal** · dinner food at breakfast time, eaten on a blanket on the floor
- **The Teddy Toboggan** · send soft toys down the stairs on a cushion and mark whose goes furthest
- **Three Mugs, Three Temperatures** · cool, warm and warmer, and she picks the one that is right
- **The Fogged Mirror** · run the hot water, let the mirror steam up and draw in it with a finger
- **Ten Things You Can Hear From the Sofa** · sit still, eyes shut, and count them off on her fingers
- **The Reverse Tidy** · you put things in the wrong rooms and she finds all six
- **The Boot Check** · every pair of boots by the door tried on by the wrong person

### 🎨 Alternative Arts & Crafts

- **The Frost Picture** · white crayon on white paper, then a wash of watery blue over the top
- **The Salt Bloom** · sprinkle table salt into a wet blue wash and watch the blotches open while it dries
- **The Cotton Swab Snow** · white paint dots on the darkest paper in the house
- **The Cold Tea Map** · dab cold tea on paper with a cloth, dry it on the radiator, and it comes out old
- **Fork Prints** · dip the tines in paint and print grass, fences and hair
- **Bubble Wrap Stamping** · paint on a scrap of packing wrap, press it down, peel it up
- **The Paper Chain Down the Banister** · cut strips, loop them, and stop when the chain reaches the bottom step
- **The Cereal Box Sign** · cut the front off, draw on the plain side, and tape it to her bedroom door
- **The Torn Paper Hill** · no scissors at all, and the ragged edge is the point
- **The Handprint Bird** · her hand printed sideways, then a beak and a leg added in marker
- **The Envelope Book** · three envelopes stapled down one side and something small posted into each page

### 👶 Kreston's Turn

*He is 6 to 7 months this month: sitting on his own, mouthing everything he
can reach, and rocking on hands and knees.*

- **The Muffin Tin of One Thing Each** · a spoon, a lid and a washcloth in separate cups for him to pull out
- **The Basket He Can Empty** · a low basket of safe objects taken out one at a time, refilled by you, emptied again
- **The Mirror at Floor Level** · an unbreakable mirror propped against the sofa for him to rock toward
- **The Cushion Step** · one sofa cushion laid flat with a favorite toy on top, close enough to reach across from sitting

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Small parts**: buttons at the bakery counter on Day 39, dyed pasta on Day 46, stamps and coins on Day 48, lentils and beans on Day 52, pasta and cut straws on Day 54, crayon stubs and keys on Day 55. Sweep before Kreston is down, count them out and count them back in, and treat Day 40's balloons as the worst of the list.
- **String and cord**: the floss that cuts the buns on Day 42, the heart garland on Day 45, the pasta necklaces on Days 46 and 54, the gallery line on Day 56, the string telephone on Day 62. The hung ones come down the moment the activity ends, and no cord or beaded necklace goes on a baby.
- **Adult-only steps**: the oven runs on five days and hits 475°F for the pizzas on Day 38, and Day 63 simmers a pan of orange peel for an hour. Hot trays come out at Kreston's head height, so block his route before one goes in, and the craft knife on Days 43 and 51 goes back up between cuts.
- **Salt dough and playdough are not food.** The month mixes them three times, on Days 39, 52 and 61, and both carry far more salt than anything on her plate. Kreston's piece goes in a small rigid pot with the lid taped on hard, never in a food bag.
- **Standing water**: the dishpans on the floor on Days 46 and 58, and swimming on all four Tuesdays, Days 40, 47, 54 and 61. Kreston can drown in a dishpan's depth, so tip it out the moment she finishes and stay within arm's reach of both children at the pool.
- **February cold**: three walks go hunting frost and ice, Days 37, 38 and 46, and Day 58 puts her bare palms on cold metal. Take the salted side of the path, keep one hand free for her, and gloves go back on the moment she says cold.

## Week 6: Little Bakery 🥐
**📅 February 5 – February 11, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

Four things make bread, and she counts them on her fingers on Friday morning
before anything goes in the bowl: flour, water, salt, yeast. The rest of the
week takes them apart one at a time. The yeast gets its own jar and then its
own balloon, the dough gets punched flat and stretched until it tears, and the
same lump comes back as rolls, a pizza base and a tray of cinnamon buns. She
follows one loop all week, from dry powder foaming in warm water to a hollow
knock on the bottom of a crust.

No holiday lands in this week, so the shape comes from the theme. Four days
run on a hot oven, three of them on real dough. Monday and Wednesday run on
playdough, paper and a pretend shop counter, and they sit there to give your
kitchen a day off.
Thursday takes the whole thing out of the house: she boxes what she baked,
walks a round she scouted that morning, and hands it over at four front doors.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Yeast is alive and it eats.** A jar of foam at eight thirty, a balloon standing up by eleven thirty, and an hour of waiting she can see the point of.
- **Hands that knead, roll, cut and press.** Ten minutes of heavy work at the table on Friday, a rolling pin on Monday, and floss pulled through a log of dough on Thursday.
- **Her own words hold still on paper.** She dictates a recipe, you read it back the same way twice, and by Thursday she picks *butter* out of the page on her own.
- **Words for what her mouth finds.** Soft, chewy, seedy, holey. Five breads on five numbered plates and one word each.
- **Numbers doing a job.** Twelve pastries counted onto a tray, a price written on every one, buttons counted into the register and back out at closing.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Auditory attention is trainable, and it underpins reading
- Dictated stories are the bridge to real literacy
- Cabin fever is a real physiological thing, not a bad attitude
- Pretend play is where self-control gets built
- Regression during illness is expected, not a setback
- Boredom on the mend is a good sign, and a useful one
- On the days you use this page instead of the plan

---

## 🌟 Day 36: The Dough That Wakes Up 🌟
**📅 Friday, February 5, 2027**
**Theme:** Little Bakery

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Set the flour, salt, sugar, a packet of active dry yeast and a clean jam jar on the table, and stand 100 g of butter out for tomorrow.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Fizzing Jar
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Four Things Make Bread (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Walk Past the Bakery (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Rolls and the Hollow Knock (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Bread Basket
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Her Own Piece of Dough
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Warm Kitchen
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Fizzing Jar

**🧰 You need:** 1 clean jam jar · active dry yeast, 1 packet · sugar, 1 tsp · warm water, 100 ml · 1 teaspoon.

1. Fill the jar a third full, cold water in first and hot run in after, until it feels like bath water on your wrist. Let her test it with one finger.
2. Tip in the yeast and the sugar and let her stir. Then walk away for ten minutes.
3. Come back and look. The top has gone beige and foamy and smells of beer. Tell her the yeast is alive and has been eating the sugar.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Four Things Make Bread

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Bread flour, 500 g
- Active dry yeast, 1 packet (7 g)
- Salt, 1 tsp
- Sugar, 1 tsp
- Warm water, 300 ml
- Vegetable oil, 1 tbsp
- 1 large mixing bowl
- 1 clean dish towel
- The jam jar of woken yeast from 8:00

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Count the four things on her fingers before anything goes in the bowl: flour, water, salt, yeast.
2. Flour into the bowl, salt to one side, and let her punch a well in the middle. The yeast goes in the well, then the oil and the warm water.
3. She mixes with one hand until it comes together as a shaggy lump. It sticks to her. Leave it sticking.
4. Turn it onto the table and knead: push with the heel of your hand, fold, turn a quarter, push again. Say the four words out loud and hand it over.
5. Ten minutes of that between you. She will manage two and wander off, so take it on and hand it back when she returns. The lump goes from ragged to smooth.
6. Oil the bowl, drop the dough in, cover it and stand it somewhere warm. Mark its height on the outside with a strip of tape.

> 💡 **Tip:** Kneading is heavy work and it settles a wound-up morning better than any instruction to calm down. Give her all ten minutes.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Walk Past the Bakery

Walk to whichever store near you bakes on the premises. The supermarket counter
counts. Cold February air holds the smell tight to the doorway, so the last
four steps are the good ones. Count the shapes through the glass: rounds, long
ones, braids, rolls with seeds. Buy one thing and let her carry it home in her
own hand.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** **Kreston turns 8 months today** and he is
> crawling, which changes what a kitchen is. Set him up at the far end of the
> room with two metal spoons and a plastic bowl. Banging two objects together
> is new this month and needs both hands working to one plan. Say happy eight
> months out loud.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Rolls and the Hollow Knock

The dough has doubled by one o'clock and it holds the dent when she pushes a
finger in.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The risen dough
- 1 baking tray and baking paper
- Extra flour for the table
- 2 tbsp milk and a pastry brush or a spoon
- 1 wire rack or a cold plate
- Oven gloves
- Butter for the first one, eaten warm

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip the dough onto a floured table and let her press all the air out of it. It sighs down and she will want to do it twice.
2. Cut it into eight or ten pieces. She cuts, you even them up afterwards without saying so.
3. Show her the roll: hand cupped over the piece, palm circling, dough turning underneath. Hers come out as lumps and lumps bake fine.
4. Space them on the lined tray a hand's width apart, cover, and leave them thirty minutes. Oven on to 425°F.
5. Brush the tops with milk and bake fifteen to eighteen minutes. She watches through the glass and the door stays shut.
6. Out onto the rack. Once one has cooled enough to hold, turn it over and knock the bottom with a knuckle. Hollow means baked through, so let her knock every one.
7. Butter the first and eat it standing up in the kitchen before anyone suggests plates.

> 💡 **Tip:** Knock on a raw one before the tray goes in. She needs the dull thud at one thirty to hear the hollow one an hour later.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- A store-bought pack of dough, and skip to the knocking.
- Shape the whole batch as one loaf and cut a cross in the top.
- Roll long snakes and braid three of them together.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A friend's house**, and she carries a bag of the rolls to the door herself
- The park, for the swings before the light goes
- The corner store for butter and jam, both chosen by her
- A café, where somebody else has done the baking
- Back past the bakery window to see what has sold out

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston gets a soft roll with the crust off, torn
> small, sitting upright with you in front of him. Stranger wariness is
> arriving this month, so at the friend's house keep him on your hip for the
> first ten minutes. He comes off you when he leans off you and not before.

### 🌍 Around the World: Bread Everywhere 🥖

Almost everywhere on earth makes a bread from the same short list. India tears
**naan** off the wall of a clay oven. Mexico presses **tortillas** flat between
two hands. Ethiopia ferments **injera** until it turns sour, and it works as
the plate as well as the bread. France buys a **baguette** twice a day because
it goes stale by evening.

> **✨ Try it:** Buy one bread you have never eaten, tear it at the table and
> eat it with your hands. Azlyn decides whether it beats her rolls.

> *Did you know?* Injera is cooked on one side only, which is why the top is
> covered in tiny holes.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Auditory attention is trainable, and it underpins reading.**
> Azlyn knocking the bottom of a roll and deciding whether it sounds hollow is
> doing fine listening work: two sounds held side by side, one picked out from
> the other. That skill sits underneath reading. Before she can match a letter
> to a sound she has to hear that *bat* and *pat* start with different mouths,
> and children who catch small differences in sound learn to read with less
> effort later on. Kitchens are good ground for it. The kettle, the fizzing
> jar, the knock on a crust, the oven timer. Name a sound out loud and she
> starts collecting them.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Kreston is crawling and the oven runs at 425°F today, with hot
> trays coming out at his head height. Block his route to the oven door with a
> chair or the stroller before the dough goes in, and check it is still there
> before you open the door. Never leave the oven door open to cool with him
> loose in the room.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Choosing Off the Shelf

**🧰 You need:** the baking cupboard · a stool to stand on · paper and a pen.

1. Open the cupboard and get her up to eye level with the shelf. Read out what is in each tub and let her hold the ones with lids.
2. She picks the additions for her recipe. If that is sprinkles and mashed banana together, it is sprinkles and mashed banana together.
3. Write her choices at the top of a fresh page under her name. Nothing gets vetoed.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Recipe She Tells You

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Soft butter, 100 g
- Sugar, 100 g
- All-purpose flour, 200 g
- 1 egg
- Her chosen additions: raisins, chocolate chips, cocoa, sprinkles or a mashed banana
- 1 bowl and a wooden spoon
- 1 baking tray and baking paper
- Paper and a pen for her words

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sit down with her and ask how it is made, starting with the first thing into the bowl.
2. Write every word as it comes. *And then you shake it a lot.* *Two hundred sugars.* Do not tidy the order or fix the grammar.
3. Read it back from the top. She will change things. Cross out and write the new version underneath so both stay.
4. Now make it off her page. Quantities come from the list above, order comes from her.
5. Roll the mixture into walnut-sized balls, flatten them onto the lined tray with gaps between, and she adds her extras where her page says.
6. Bake at 350°F for twelve to fifteen minutes until the edges brown. Read her recipe out loud once more while they bake.

> 💡 **Tip:** Where her order makes a mess of it, follow it and say out loud what happened. A batch that comes out odd beats one you fixed behind her back.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Frost Patch Hunt

Go out before the sun reaches the shady side of the street. Frost survives
where it has not: north-facing walls, the ground under parked cars, grass in
the shadow of a hedge. Give her five patches to find and a fingernail to
scratch each one. A mild night leaves you nothing white, so hunt the cold
instead: the slab that stays dark, the dew standing on a car roof, the metal
gate that stings her palm. Put her bare hand flat for one second, then back in
the mitten.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and stranger wariness has
> landed, so the far end of the table will not do. Sit him where he can see
> your face while you write, with a wooden spoon and a plastic tub to bang
> together. Outside, hold his bare palm on the frost for a second and watch his
> face.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Her Page in the Cookbook

This afternoon her recipe becomes a page in a book with her name on the front.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper, 5–6 sheets
- The written recipe from this morning
- Crayons or markers
- Tape or glue
- 1 cereal box cut flat for the cover
- String and a hole punch, or a stapler
- A permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Trim the sheets to a size her hands can turn and lay them in order.
2. Tape the morning's recipe onto the middle page, butter stain and crossings-out and all.
3. She draws one ingredient per sheet on the pages before it: butter, sugar, egg, flour, her own addition. Write the word underneath in your own hand, big.
4. Cut the cereal box flat for the cover and let her color it. Ask her the name of the book and write it across the front word for word.
5. Punch two holes down the left edge of every sheet and thread the string. Three staples down the spine work as well.
6. Read it back cover to cover, turning the pages at her pace.
7. Stand it on the kitchen shelf with the real cookbooks, at her height.

> 💡 **Tip:** She matches the shape of the word to the picture she made, and by Thursday she will find *butter* on the page unprompted.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One page only, her drawing on one side and her words on the other.
- Photograph each step of the morning and stick the photos in instead.
- Add a page for a recipe she invents that nobody has to make.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum**
- **The museum**, first Saturday of February and the second of the year
- The indoor play center, if the parking lot beats you
- The park, and a bag of yesterday's rolls if any survived
- A café, and she orders her own thing out loud
- The Saturday market, for a stall with something baked on it

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston goes in the carrier facing in today. At 8
> months a museum is a room full of unfamiliar faces at his eye level, and your
> chest is where he turns back to between looks. Find one low thing with lights
> or a mirror and sit on the floor while he works it. Twenty-five minutes is a
> full visit.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Dictated stories are the bridge to real literacy.**
> Azlyn cannot write and she can compose. Those two come apart at three, and
> taking her recipe down word for word lets the second run ahead of the first.
> She watches her own speech turn into marks you read back the same way twice,
> which is the idea underneath all of reading: the marks hold the words.
> Teachers call it language experience, and children who dictate to an adult
> arrive at writing with more to say and less fear of a blank page. Keep her
> wrong grammar in. Her sentence made the trip onto paper whole and comes back
> the same.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Raw egg and raw flour both carry a real infection risk and she
> will eat some of the mixture. Hold it to one small spoonful, or set a
> spoonful aside before the egg goes in. Kreston gets none of it raw, and
> cookies are sugar all the way through, so he skips the baked ones too. The
> bowl goes in the sink and not on the floor.

- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: One Pizza Each (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Plates
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Flour Tray
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Long Bath After the Flour
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Punching It Down

**🧰 You need:** the overnight dough, cold from the fridge · flour · a dish towel.

1. Take the bowl out and let her look first. The dough has climbed the sides overnight and smells sour.
2. Give her one instruction: fist in, all the way. The whole thing sighs to a third of its height and she will laugh.
3. Leave it under the dish towel to come to room temperature. Cold dough will not stretch, so the wait is an hour.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Dough That Fights Back

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The overnight dough (500 g bread flour, 7 g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 300 ml water, 1 tbsp oil)
- Or a 500 g pack of ready-made pizza dough, if last night got away from you
- Flour for the table, a good handful
- 2 baking trays
- 1 tbsp oil for the trays
- 1 dish towel

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Flour the table well. Cut the dough in half and give her one half.
2. Show her both flat hands pushing out from the middle, then work yours.
3. She will tear hers. Pinch it shut, carry on, and say out loud that dough mends and paper does not.
4. Once it is about tray-sized, lift an edge and let it hang from her hands. It stretches under its own weight and springs back when she lays it down. Let her try yours as well.
5. Lay both bases on the oiled trays and push them to the corners with her fingertips. Bumpy is right.
6. Cover them with the dish towel until one o'clock.

> 💡 **Tip:** Flour her hands and keep it off the dough. Flour worked in makes it tough, and hers has four hours of poking ahead of it.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Stamping the Ice

Take the route with puddles. February ice is thin and goes white where air got
trapped underneath. It cracks under a boot with a sound she will chase down
the path. Stamp one, then lift a plate of ice out of another and hold it
against the sky. A mild week leaves the puddles open, so pick the deepest one
instead and stand a stick in it to mark the water line. Wet gloves come home in
a pocket.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and shuffling, so the floured
> floor is his now. Sweep before you put him down, then give him a scrap of
> dough shut in a small rigid pot with the lid taped on hard. Raw dough is
> dangerous eaten and a food bag is a suffocation risk at his age, so he gets
> the pot and never the bag, and it comes back the moment you stop watching. He
> shakes it, drops it and goes after it. On the walk, hold a plate of ice above
> the stroller for him.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: One Pizza Each

Everything comes to the table in small bowls at one o'clock and nobody builds
anybody else's.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The stretched bases
- Tomato sauce, or a can of chopped tomatoes
- Grated cheese, 200 g
- Whatever is in the fridge in small bowls: ham, corn, peppers, olives, mushrooms
- 1 spoon per person
- Dried herbs
- Oven gloves and a board

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set the bowls in a line down the table, a spoon standing in each.
2. Sauce first. Show her the spoon spiralling out from the middle, then let her do her own. The edges she misses stay missed.
3. Cheese by the handful. Everyone works down the line taking what they want, and nobody comments.
4. She will build yours as well. Eat whatever she puts on it.
5. Oven as hot as it goes, 475°F if you can get it. One tray at a time, top shelf, ten to twelve minutes, until the edges blister.
6. Out onto the board, herbs over the top, and cut hers into strips.
7. Eat at the table. This is Sunday lunch and the big meal of the day.

> 💡 **Tip:** Put one bowl out with something in it she has refused for a month. Sitting near a food, touching it and putting it back down is most of the road before she eats it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Store-bought bases or split pittas, same line of bowls.
- One big pizza cut into pieces instead of one each.
- Faces on the pizzas, built out of the toppings.
- Sauce and cheese only, and no argument about the rest.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The sunset walk**, out at three for the long shadows, then back at the window by five when the sun goes
- The park while the bases proof, if one o'clock ran late
- A drive up to anywhere with a view west, and stay in the warm car
- The duck pond, and back before the cold gets into her hands
- Round the block counting the west-facing windows with the low sun in them

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston eats before the pizzas go in, then takes
> a strip of cooled plain base at the table. At 8 months he brings both hands
> and his gums to it and most of it ends up on the tray. Wrap him warm for the
> walk and use a hat with a chin strap, since a loose one is off his head
> inside a minute.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Cabin fever is a real physiological thing, not a bad attitude.**
> Six weeks into winter, Azlyn is short of two things her body runs on:
> daylight and room to move. Morning light sets the clock that governs her
> sleep and her mood, and a February day indoors gives her a fraction of what
> an August one hands over. Add a body built to cover a few miles a day and a
> house that allows eight steps in a line, and the four o'clock meltdown reads
> as a shortage of both. Twenty minutes outside under flat gray cloud beats an
> hour under a lamp. Yours counts too, and you run the same shortage she does.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The oven goes to 475°F today and Kreston is shuffling, so
> block his route to it with a chair or the stroller before the first tray goes in,
> and check the block is still there before you open the door. Melted cheese
> holds its heat long after the crust has cooled. Cut hers into strips and
> leave them three minutes on the board before the plate reaches her. If there
> is ice underfoot on the walk, take the salted side of the path and keep one
> hand free for her.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 39: The Bakery Opens 🌟
**📅 Monday, February 8, 2027**
**Theme:** Little Bakery

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Rinse two 500 ml plastic bottles from the recycling, stand them upside down to dry, and find two balloons that have not perished.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Coloring the Dough
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Twelve Pretend Pastries (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Mud Bakery (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Counter Opens (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Wiping the Counter
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Minding the Shop
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Closing the Shop
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Coloring the Dough

**🧰 You need:** all-purpose flour, 2 cups · salt, 1 cup · warm water, 1 cup · oil, 2 tbsp · food coloring · 1 big bowl.

1. Flour and salt in the bowl, her hands in to mix them dry. Then oil and warm water, stirred until it leaves the sides.
2. Knead it on the table for two minutes while it is warm, then split it into three.
3. Press a hollow into each piece, three drops of a different color into each, and let her fold it in. Her hands come out patchy and wash clean by lunch.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Twelve Pretend Pastries

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- No-cook playdough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup warm water, 2 tbsp oil
- Food coloring, 2–3 colors
- 1 table knife
- 1 rolling pin or a straight-sided glass
- 1 fork for pressing marks
- Paper cupcake liners, or squares of baking paper
- 1 baking tray as the display tray

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Line the tray with the cupcake liners first, so it looks like a store window.
2. Croissants: roll a ball, flatten it, cut a triangle, roll from the wide end and curve the ends in. Do one, hand her the knife, let hers come out fat.
3. Braids: three snakes rolled under her flat palms, pinched at the top and crossed over one another.
4. Buns and rings: balls pressed with the back of the fork, and snakes joined end to end for doughnuts.
5. Keep going until the tray is full. Count them on out loud, one to twelve, then backwards when the dough runs out.
6. Stand the tray on the counter you are about to build. None of it gets baked and she will ask twice.

> 💡 **Tip:** Make one wrong on purpose. She corrects you, and correcting an adult's croissant buys her more practice than praise ever will.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Mud Bakery

Take an old baking tray, a wooden spoon and a plastic tub to the muddiest
patch you can reach. February mud is soft to the top of a boot and cold enough
to hold a shape. She makes mud pastries to match the ones on the kitchen
counter and counts them the same way. Leave them there for the frost.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and everything reachable goes
> to his mouth on its way to being understood, so the pastry tray lives above
> his line all day. Give him a whole sheet of baking paper instead, too big to
> get into his mouth. He crushes it, drops it, hears it land and leans over to
> look.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Counter Opens

A dining chair turned side-on is the counter. She takes the inside, you take
the sidewalk side and the customer's part for the afternoon.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 small table or a chair as the counter
- Paper bags or envelopes, 6–8
- Paper and a marker for price signs
- A coin purse of buttons or bottle tops as coins
- 1 dish towel as an apron
- 1 shoebox as the register
- The tray of pastries

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set the counter where she says. Tray on top, shoebox register beside it, dish towel in her waistband as the apron.
2. Write the price signs with her, a number and a drawing on each, and she decides every number.
3. Be the first customer. Say good morning, ask for two things by name and wait for her to name a price.
4. Pay in buttons, one at a time, counted out loud into her hand. She puts them in the register and shuts the lid.
5. Bag the order and let it take as long as it takes. Folding the top over twice is the part she will want again.
6. Swap over. She comes in with the coin purse and you get one item of her order wrong on purpose.
7. Closing time at two thirty. Count the buttons out of the register, cover the tray and turn the sign round.

> 💡 **Tip:** Stay in role when she goes off script. If a croissant costs a hundred buttons, count out a hundred. Stepping out to explain money ends the game.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Carry the tray round the house and sell door to door.
- Line the pastries up by size and photograph the window.
- One customer, one order, then she runs it on her own.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The field walk**, boots on, with the far hedge as the turning point
- The neighborhood park, if the field is under water
- One lap of the block with a paper bag, delivering to nobody
- The green space with a ball, after an hour behind a counter
- The yard with a bucket of water, poured over the mud pastries

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is a customer. Sit him on your lap at the
> counter and let Azlyn hand him an empty paper bag, which he
> chews and then waves at her. At 8 months he checks your face to work out what
> a new thing is for, so take it back with a big thank you.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Pretend play is where self-control gets built.**
> Azlyn behind that counter holds a rule in her head, and she holds it longer
> than she holds one of yours. That might be ten minutes or twenty,
> depending on the morning. Shopkeepers wait. They hand the bag over. They
> leave the stock alone. Nobody is enforcing any of it and she does it anyway,
> because the role says so. Children in role play stand still longer, wait
> longer and stay with a dull job longer than the same children asked to do the
> same thing without the pretend.
> Every minute she spends being a baker is practice at what you will want at
> five, in a classroom.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Playdough carries far more salt than food and Kreston will
> have it in his mouth the second he is near the tray. Keep the tray above his
> reach and wipe the table before he goes on the floor. Buttons and bottle tops
> are choking-sized for an 8-month-old. Count them into the coin purse at the
> start and back into the register at closing.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>
