- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Reading What She Chose
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Rolling the Paper Cones

**🧰 You need:** 4 sheets of paper or thin card · masking tape · 2 rubber bands.

1. Roll one sheet into a cone with a wide mouth and a hole at the point big enough for her ear. Hold it closed while she winds the rubber band on.
2. She rolls the next two herself, one fat and one thin. Crooked is fine, and turns out to be useful.
3. Hold each one to her ear and say nothing about which sounds best. She finds that out at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Ear Trumpet Test

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4 sheets of paper or thin card
- 1 roll masking tape
- 2 rubber bands
- A ticking clock, or your phone playing something quiet in the next room
- 1 saucepan and a wooden spoon, for the far-away noise
- Crayons for decorating the winner

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Send the noise away first. A ticking clock in the next room, or the saucepan and spoon at the far end of the hall.
2. Bare ears first. Let her tell you how much she gets from where she stands.
3. Cone one against one ear, other ear covered with her hand. Same sound, same distance. Ask her better or the same.
4. Cone two, then cone three, in that order, at that distance, with nothing else changed between goes.
5. She calls the winner, even where you would have picked another. Tape that cone so it holds its shape.
6. She decorates the winner with crayons and it is hers for the day. The other two go on the shelf until 4:15, and she says what happens to them.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep the sound the same and change one cone at a time. She is running a fair test without the words for it, and swapping the noise halfway wrecks the hour.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Listening Stop

Walk to a bench or a low wall and stop dead for two minutes. Nobody talks. Hold
up a finger for each sound she catches: a car, a crow, a door, a plane, wind in
a bare hedge, her own breathing. Early March carries sound further than summer
does, with no leaves out yet to soak it up. Take the trumpet and let her aim it
at the furthest one.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and turns his whole head to a
> sound now instead of moving his eyes and giving up. Sit behind him and shake a
> set of keys to one side, then the other, and watch the head come round. Once
> Azlyn has finished testing, hand him the saucepan and the wooden spoon. A pan
> is the loudest thing in the house and he knows it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The String Telephone

Two cups and five meters of string between two rooms. She works out the rule
before you get to say it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 paper cups or clean yogurt cups
- 3–5 meters of string
- 1 pencil or skewer to pierce the cups (**adult only**)
- 2 paperclips or matchsticks to anchor the knots
- Scissors (**adult only**)

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Pierce one small hole in the bottom of each cup yourself, dead center, with her hands well back.
2. Thread the string in from the outside and knot it round a paperclip inside the cup so it cannot pull back through. She holds the cup while you tie.
3. Test it across one room, both of you standing, string pulled tight. You talk, she listens, then swap over.
4. Let the string go slack and try again. She gets nothing, and she will tell you before you ask. Run it round a door frame into the next room and it dies at the corner too. Leave her to find the straight line that brings it back.
5. Whisper down it. That is the run that convinces her, because she can see your mouth moving and hears nothing without the cup at her ear.
6. Take it down, wind the string up and put it away before you do anything else.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her the listening end first. A three-year-old handed the talking end shouts into the cup, and a shout crosses the room through the air anyway.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One cup and one length of string, held to the ear like a stethoscope.
- Tap a message down the radiator pipe and listen at the other end.
- Hide a ticking clock and let her find it by ear alone.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Library**
- **The library**, and let her ask for the book out loud instead of pointing
- The indoor play center if the library is packed with a school group
- The park, for the swings on the way back
- The thrift store, for a book she gets to keep

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Take him to the library and put him down in the
> board-book corner. At 8 months he chews books, which is what board books are
> for, and he bangs two together before he opens either. New faces at storytime
> may be too much this month, so sit at the edge with him facing you.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Testing before committing is a habit worth encouraging.**
> Azlyn made three cones and found out which one worked before any of them got
> decorated. That order matters more than the cones do. A three-year-old who
> tries the rough version first is learning that a plan is a thing you check, and
> the check costs her nothing here, because the materials are paper and tape.
> Engineers call it prototyping and Azlyn calls it trying it out. You back it up
> every time you let a poor idea run to its end instead of heading it off,
> because the cone that heard nothing taught her as much as the one she kept.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Take the string telephone down and put the string away the
> second you finish. A loop of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk,
> and Kreston crawls now, so it never stays up while you make a cup of tea.
> Scissors and the skewer stay with you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="day-63"></a>

## 🌟 Day 63: Following Her Nose 🌟
**📅 Thursday, March 4, 2027**
**Theme:** My Body & Senses

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill the six pots after she is in bed, foil and a band over each one with a few holes pierced through, and pare one curl of peel off an orange for the sixth pot.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Six Pots with Holes in the Lid
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Smell Words (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Wet Earth and Woodsmoke (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The House That Smells of Oranges (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Smell Pots Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Her Words from All Week
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Six Pots with Holes in the Lid

**🧰 You need:** the six filled pots · masking tape · 1 marker.

1. Set the six in a row on the table and let her look at them without opening a thing.
2. Show her how to waft: cupped hand over the top, a pull of air toward her face. Nose down on the foil gets her a lungful of cinnamon.
3. She lines them up, the one she likes best at one end and the one she likes least at the other. Nothing gets written down yet.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Smell Words

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 small jars or yogurt cups with foil lids
- Rubber bands or masking tape
- Cotton balls
- Ground coffee, ground cinnamon, orange peel, a dried herb, a sliver of soap, a drop of vanilla
- Masking tape for labels and a marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sit opposite her with the six pots on your side of the table and hand them across one at a time.
2. Ask for a word and stop there. A word for it, not the name of it. Sit through the silence while she looks.
3. Write her word on a strip of masking tape and stick it on that pot. Her spelling if she has any, your handwriting if she does not.
4. If she names the thing, take that as her word too. Coffee is a word.
5. Go round a second time in a different order. Two or three words will change, and both versions go on the tape. Read the six labels back at the end and let her move any pot she wants to.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not tell her what is in the pots. Naming them ends the sniffing, because she has the answer and no reason to go back.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Wet Earth and Woodsmoke

Early March smells of wet ground. Lift a handful of soil from a flower bed, a wet
stone, or a dead leaf from under a hedge and hold it up to her. Rain on cold
earth releases a smell with a name of its own, petrichor, and she knows it long
before she has the word. Then go hunting: a chimney with smoke, trash day, a
laundry vent. One word each.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and knows your smell better than
> your face on a bad day, which is why your sweater settles him faster than a toy.
> Hold him in the kitchen doorway once the oranges start and watch his face open
> up. Hold the third orange yourself, cut side toward him, and let him get his
> nose into it. Peel breaks off in hard pieces under a gum, so it stays in your
> hand and never in his.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The House That Smells of Oranges

Peel and cinnamon go on the stovetop at the lowest setting, and the house changes
around her while she draws.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 small saucepan and water
- The peel of 2 oranges
- 1 cinnamon stick or a spoon of ground cinnamon
- 1 wooden spoon
- Paper, crayons and washable paint
- This week's written-down words, to read back at the end

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Peel two oranges with her. She pulls the pieces off in whatever sizes come away.
2. Drop the peel into the pan with the cinnamon and enough water to cover it. Back burner, lowest heat, handle turned in.
3. Set her up at the table beside the kitchen with paper, crayons and paint, and no subject.
4. Say nothing about the smell. It arrives on its own over about fifteen minutes, and she will be the one who mentions it.
5. Top the water up as it drops. She can hand you the pitcher.
6. Halfway through, read her the week's written-down words: the touch words, the taste words, this morning's smell words.
7. Ask which one she wants to keep. Write that word big across the top of whatever she has drawn, and put it on the fridge.

> 💡 **Tip:** Hold off asking her what she has drawn. If she wants you to know, she tells you, and the question turns her paper into a test she can get wrong.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Orange peel and cloves pushed into a pomander, no stovetop involved.
- Warm cinnamon toast and eat it while it fills the kitchen.
- Bury the six pots in a basket of rice and let her dig them out.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The grocery store**, and let her pick the fruit by smell before it goes in
- The bakery, for the doorway more than the bun
- The market, if it runs today
- A loop past the pizza place, the florist and the laundromat, naming each one

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At 8 months he sits up in the cart seat and takes
> in a store that is loud, bright and full of strangers, so twenty minutes is
> plenty. Keep him facing you rather than out, and give him something cold from
> the chiller to hold, too big to fit in his mouth.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **She tells you what it is once nobody has asked.**
> You already describe more of it than you think. *You used a lot of red down
> this side* and *that line goes all the way to the corner* are sentences she
> can answer, and she answers them. The one that stalls her is *what is it?*,
> because she hears a test with one right answer, and half the time she did not
> set out to make a thing at all. Stay with what her hands did. You pressed hard
> here and soft here. She picks up the words for it, carries no pressure to have
> meant anything, and nine times in ten she tells you what it is herself, on her
> own timing.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A pan simmering on the stovetop for an hour with a crawling
> 8-month-old in the house. Back burner only, handle turned in, and it goes off the
> heat if you leave the kitchen. Ground cinnamon and coffee sting in the eyes, so
> the pots stay lidded and go up high when she is done with them.

<a id="backup-feb"></a>

# 🌧️ February — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

February is the month the plan breaks. Ice sets in for three days. One of the
children comes down with something, and the day on the page wants an oven and a
walk you have no intention of taking. These five pages cover that. Two of them
are full days for weather that keeps you in, two are for a child who is ill,
and the last one is a list you can open with ten minutes of warning and no plan
at all. Everything on these pages runs on what is already in the house, because
the weather that cancels the walk cancels the store run with it. Use them in
place of any day this month and put the printed one back in the week whenever
you feel like it.

---

<a id="feb-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — The Course Through the House

> *For the morning everything outside is glazed. Ice down the front steps, ice
> across the sidewalk, and no stroller is crossing that. She has energy for a
> two-mile walk and nowhere to spend it, so the hall becomes the walk.*

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stack the sofa cushions at one end of the hall, and put the masking tape, a wooden spoon and a saucepan lid on top of them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Clearing the Runway
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Six Stations Down the Hall (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Ten Laps (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Judge's Chair (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🛋️ Down Time: Cushions, a Blanket and Something on the Screen (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Rebuilding Station Three
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Long Warm Bath
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Clearing the Runway

**🧰 You need:** the hall, or the longest run of floor in the house · masking tape · 1 envelope and a pen.

1. Walk the length of it together and take out everything that would hurt to land on. The plant, the basket of coats. She carries what she can into another room and you take the rest.
2. Tape a line across the floor at each end. She decides which one is the start and stands on it to make it official.
3. Ask her what should happen in the middle. Write every answer on the back of the envelope, the ones you can build and the ones you cannot. The stations at 9:15 come off that list.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Six Stations Down the Hall

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The cleared hall, taped at both ends
- Sofa cushions, 3–4
- 2 dining chairs
- 1 blanket or a bath towel
- 4 books, to weight the blanket corners
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 cardboard box with the flaps cut off, or the laundry basket
- 1 saucepan lid and 1 wooden spoon
- The envelope of her ideas

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Station one is a straight line of tape down the middle of the floor, three steps long. Heel to toe, arms out, and the floor either side counts as water.
2. Station two is the cushions, spaced a small stride apart. She works out the gap that suits her legs, so lay the first two and hand her the rest.
3. Station three is the two chairs a body's length apart with the blanket over the top, weighted with a book at each corner. She crawls through it.
4. Station four is the box on the floor. In with both feet, out with both feet, and the box has to still be where it started.
5. Station five is hers. Take one thing off the envelope and build it however she describes it, down to the parts you would fix.
6. Station six is the finish. Hang the pan lid on a door handle at her shoulder height and give her the spoon. One tap and the lap is over. Run the whole course yourself first, badly, while she watches.

> 💡 **Tip:** Build it too easy. A course she clears on the first go gets run
> twenty times, and she raises the difficulty herself by lunchtime.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Ten Laps

The sidewalk is a sheet of ice and the walk is off, so the forty-five minutes
go into laps. Tape a strip of paper to the door frame at the finish and let her
mark it after each one. Change one thing every couple of laps and say what it
is: backwards through station two, teddy under one arm, a cup of water carried
the whole way, feet only on the tape. Ten is the number to aim at, and she will
pass it. Sit down at the finish and be the person who is there every time she
comes around.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and crawling with a
> destination in mind, which is his version of the same work. Put him at one
> end of the cleared floor with something he wants at the other, well clear of
> the run while anybody is on it. He travels the length of the hall on his
> hands and knees and arrives pleased with himself. Let Azlyn be the thing at
> the far end and he goes twice as fast.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Judge's Chair

The course is built and she has run it thirty times. This afternoon she sits
down and everybody else runs it, under rules she makes up as she goes.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The course, still up from this morning
- 1 dining chair set at the finish line
- Paper and a marker for the scorecard
- 1 dish towel as the flag
- Everybody in the house
- The pan lid and the spoon

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set her chair where she can see all six stations at once. That chair is the job and nobody else sits in it.
2. Make the scorecard together. One row per person, names written big while she watches, and she draws a face beside each one so she can find them again.
3. She says the rules out loud before anybody runs. Take all of them, including the rule that you have to hop at station four.
4. You go first. She drops the dish towel to start you and marks your row when you tap the lid. Get station three wrong on purpose and let her rule on whether it counts.
5. Everybody in the house takes a turn. Carry Kreston through on your hip, station by station, and let her mark his row too.
6. Swap over. She runs, you take the chair, and you read your marks back the way she read hers.
7. At the end she says who won. Leave the result standing, whoever it favors.

> 💡 **Tip:** Play it straight when she changes the rules mid-race. A judge who
> gets argued with stops judging, and the whole ninety minutes runs on her
> holding a job nobody is taking off her.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One station only, the cushions, jumped until she is done with it.
- Move the whole course into her bedroom and leave the hall alone.
- Everybody runs it in slow motion, and last one to the lid wins.
- Take the course down together, station by station, and stop there.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He does his lap on your hip with a hand on each
> station as you pass it, and Azlyn marks his row. After that, lay one cushion
> flat on the floor with something he wants on the far side. At 8 months a
> climb with a reason on the other side of it holds him for a long stretch, and
> he is working on getting a knee up onto things. Stay beside him for the
> tipping-over part.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Specific recognition beats general praise, every time.**
> Azlyn hears *good girl* several times an hour and it stops landing by
> Wednesday. Say the thing you saw instead. *You got both feet on that cushion
> and held your arms out to stay up* hands her a fact about her own body that
> she can use on the next lap. Children who get described stay with a hard task
> longer and take bigger risks inside it, because the words carry information
> and no verdict to live up to. Description is also cheaper on a morning when
> your patience has gone, since you are reporting what happened. She starts
> reporting back within a week, and her reports are worth hearing.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Check what is under and beside every jumping station before
> she starts. Radiators, door frames and the corner of a bookshelf are what
> hurt, so move the cushions rather than trusting her aim. The two chairs need
> a hand test for wobble before she crawls under them, and the blanket goes
> over the backs and not across her head. Keep Kreston out of the run while
> anybody is on it. A crawling 8-month-old cannot get out of the way of a
> three-year-old at full speed, and she cannot stop.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="feb-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Lamps On at Eleven

> *For the wild one. Wind against the glass, snow going sideways and banking up
> on the sill, the lamps on all morning and dark again by five. Nobody is going
> out, and the weather is the thing she keeps looking at.*

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put both flashlights on the kitchen counter and check they work. One flashlight and a charged phone covers the whole day if the other is dead, so nobody needs batteries. Leave a pen and an old envelope on the windowsill.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Counting the Gusts
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Bangs and What Makes Them (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Parade That Beats the Wind (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Pretend Power Cut (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🔦 Free Play: Still No Lights (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Collecting the Flashlights Into One Place
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Blanket Over Two Chairs
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Every Lamp in the House, Switched On by Her
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Counting the Gusts

**🧰 You need:** the window the weather hits hardest · 1 old envelope · 1 pen.

1. Two chairs at that window and the lamp off behind you, so the glass shows the street instead of the room.
2. Every time the wind moves something out there, she makes a mark on the envelope. A branch, a trash can lid, the snow going flat across the road. Count the marks at the end of ten minutes.
3. Ask her which one was the biggest and what it hit. Tell her the noises in the house get their names at 9:15, and leave that sitting.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Bangs and What Makes Them

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The whole house, one room at a time
- Paper and a marker for the list
- 1 old towel, rolled
- Thick card or a folded cereal box, for wedging
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 heavy book

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Start in the room with the most noise in it. Stand still, both of you, and wait for a bang without talking over it.
2. Track it down together. Put her hand flat on the thing while it is moving, so she meets the vent flap or the loose pane herself.
3. Name it and write it on the list in her words. *The clacky one. The one that goes whoosh.* Draw a small picture beside each so she can read the list back.
4. Fix what can be fixed from indoors. Card folded and wedged under the door that slams, the rolled towel along the bottom of the drafty one, a strip of tape across the rattling vent, a book against the blind that keeps knocking.
5. Walk the house again and listen. She reports which noises stopped and which ones beat you, and the ones that beat you get a circle.
6. Read the list back at the end, both columns. Six noises with names and causes hold better than one house full of banging.

> 💡 **Tip:** Answer the question she asks and stop there. *That is the fence
> gate, it swings when the wind pushes it* is the whole answer, and adding
> reassurance she did not ask for tells her there was something to be reassured
> about.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Parade That Beats the Wind

Nobody is walking anywhere in this, so put the noise indoors. Saucepan, wooden
spoon, an upturned plastic tub, a set of keys, feet. Parade the loop of the
house, kitchen to hall to living room and around again, loud on the straight
bits and silent through one doorway you nominate. Three laps loud, one lap on
tiptoe, then back to the window to see how much deeper the snow on the sill has
got and to work out who is winning, the parade or the weather. Kreston rides on
your hip through all of it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 8 months and checks your face before he
> decides what a bang means. A gust that rattles a window will send his eyes
> straight to you, so let him see the same face you would wear on a still day
> and carry on with what you were saying. Sit him on your knee for the parade
> and let him hit the upturned tub with a flat hand while you hold it steady.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Pretend Power Cut

The lamps have been on since breakfast and the snow has not let up. At one
o'clock every switch in the house goes off on purpose, and the afternoon
happens in one room with two flashlights.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 flashlights, or one and a phone
- Blankets, 2, and every cushion in the room
- 1 pitcher of water and 2 cups
- The afternoon snack, whatever is in the cupboard that needs no stove

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Announce it at one and let her be the one who walks the house turning switches off. Lamps, kettle, the hall light. The heating stays on and she does not need to know that.
2. Work out together what a real one would need and go and collect it: flashlights, blankets, water, food that needs nothing done to it. She carries what she can and names each thing as it goes in the pile.
3. Pick one room, shut the door and build the camp on the floor. Cushions, blankets, both flashlights standing on end so the light bounces off the ceiling.
4. Hands in the beam. Show her one shape, a bird or a dog, then hand the flashlight over and let her invent the rest against the wall.
5. Eat the snack down there. Food on the floor in a half-dark room is most of the appeal, and it buys you twenty minutes.
6. Turn one flashlight off, then the other, and sit in the dark for as long as she wants. Four seconds counts. Talk the whole time so she can hear where you are.
7. At five, when the real dark arrives outside, walk the house together and let her put every lamp back on. Say the room name as each one comes up.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her a flashlight of her own for the whole ninety minutes and
> do not ask for it back. Holding the light is what makes the dark hers instead
> of something happening to her.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One flashlight, one blanket over two chairs, and read in there.
- Shadow shapes on the ceiling from flat on your backs.
- Keep the lights on and eat the snack under the kitchen table instead.
- Call somebody and let her tell them how deep the snow is getting.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes into the camp in the carrier on your
> front for the dark stretch, where your voice arrives through your chest
> before it arrives through the air. At 8 months a room he knows with the light
> gone is a new room, and your heartbeat is the thing that makes it an old one
> again. Once the flashlights are on, sit him in the cushions facing Azlyn and
> let him watch the shapes move. He gets no flashlight of his own today.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Children take the reading off your face before they take it off the weather.**
> A gust hits the window and Azlyn looks at you before she decides how to feel
> about it. Psychologists call that social referencing, and it runs hard from
> the end of the first year: children read a trusted adult's face and voice and
> take the reading as information about the world. Kreston is doing the same
> thing at 8 months in its purest form. Your eyebrows carry more weight than
> your explanation does. Naming the noise and giving it a cause in a flat voice
> does more than any amount of *there is nothing to be scared of*, which
> arrives as a tone she can hear straight through. Handle the snow in front of
> her the way you would handle it alone.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Flashlights today, never candles, with a crawling 8-month-old
> and a three-year-old holding the light. Check the flashlight cases are shut
> tight and the battery compartments screwed down before either child touches
> one. Loose batteries are a medical emergency if swallowed, and a button cell
> burns through a throat in hours, so count them in and out and keep the spares
> in your pocket. Stay back from the windows while the wind is throwing
> anything around outside, and leave the trash cans, the porch chairs and the
> steps until it drops. Nobody goes out to clear snow with both children
> indoors on their own, and the front steps stay off limits to her until you
> have salted them.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="feb-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Day That Asks Nothing

> *For the worst of it. Fever, no appetite, and a three-year-old who wants to
> be held and does not want to be moved. Nothing on this page needs setting up,
> cutting or cleaning, and every part of it can be abandoned halfway.*

### 🛏️ Before Anything Else

Make one nest and keep her in it. A pillow and her own blanket on the sofa,
the curtains half open for gray daylight, a cup with a lid, a bowl within
reach, a towel folded under her head that you can swap without moving her. The
day has one job, and the nest is where it happens. Cancel whatever was on for
today out loud in front of her, because she will hear you do it and stop
worrying about it.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day

There are no clock times today. Work off her instead.

- **Whenever she wakes.** Get fluids in before food. A cup with a lid and a straw, or a teaspoon if the cup is too much. Take her temperature once and write the number and the time on the back of an envelope you keep on the counter.
- **The first long stretch.** She lies down and you sit with her. This is the rest block and it is the day's main event.
- **When she asks for food.** Whatever she asks for, in a small amount, on a small plate. Toast, yogurt, a banana, plain crackers. Appetite goes first and comes back last.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** One low-demand thing off the list below, on a lap or lying down, for as long as it holds and no longer.
- **The dip itself, somewhere around mid-afternoon.** Fever climbs in the late afternoon most days. Expect the worst hour to land here and plan nothing across it.
- **The end of the day.** Warm bath if she wants one, skipped without argument if she does not. Early bed, in your bed or hers, whichever gets everybody the most sleep.

### 😴 The Rest Block

Give the middle of the day to lying still, and give it hours rather than
minutes. Take the tablet and the television out of the decision by leaving
them off from the start; a screen keeps a sick three-year-old awake and wanting
more of it. Lie down with her if she will not settle alone. She may sleep, and
sleep is what her body is asking you for. Read the same thing over her head in
a low voice while she drifts, and stop when she stops answering.

### 🛋️ Things She Can Do Without Sitting Up

**One Book, Four Times.** She picks it, you read it, she picks it again. The
repetition is the comfort, and a familiar book asks nothing of a tired brain.
Read it flat, at half your usual speed, and let her turn the pages when she
has a hand free.

**Her Whole Year on the Phone.** Open the photos and scroll backwards from
today with her on your chest. Name who is in each one and where it was.
Christmas, the museum, the box house in January. She narrates more than you
expect and it costs her nothing.

**Counting the Sips.** Fluids are the whole medical plan on a day like this
and she will refuse a cup. Count instead: ten sips, one at a time, out loud,
with a rest between each. Ice chips, watered juice, a popsicle from the
freezer, a spoon of yogurt. Little and often beats a full cup at any point.

**The Ceiling Story.** Both of you flat on your backs looking up. Start a
story about somebody her age and let it wander nowhere in particular. She joins
in when she has it in her and lets it run over her when she does not.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

Kreston is 8 months, crawling, and he will head for her the moment he is on the
floor, which is the one place he cannot be today. Ask somebody whose face he
already knows to have him for two hours if there is anybody to ask, and a
morning out is worth more to you today than any amount of tidying. A face he
has not met costs more than the two hours buy back at 8 months, so a familiar
one or nobody. Otherwise he goes where he can see you and not reach her: a
travel crib in the same room, the high chair pulled up beside you, or the
kitchen floor behind a gate with his own things. Keep his cup, his spoon and
her cup on different counters. He will catch it anyway, and washing your hands
between the two of them still shortens the odds. His naps hold their usual
times, and those two stretches are the only two-handed hours you get, so do
the things that need two hands then.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **The third day of a cold is the worst one for both of you.**
> Most of the ordinary winter viruses run to a shape: a day of it coming on,
> a hard middle, then a turn. Day three is where the fever tends to sit
> highest, where her sleep has been broken enough to show, and where your own
> reserves have gone, since you have been up for two nights and had no daytime
> to recover in. Knowing the shape is worth something. She is where she is
> meant to be at this stage, the clinging and the crying are the illness rather
> than a slide backwards, and the turn tends to arrive by the fourth or fifth
> day. Plan nothing across it and let the day cost what it costs.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Call the doctor rather than waiting it out for any of these:
> a fever over 104°F, a fever in a child who is hard to rouse or floppy, a
> rash that does not fade when you press a glass on it, trouble breathing or
> fast breathing at rest, a stiff neck, dry pants and no trip to the toilet in
> eight hours, or a fever running past three days. Trust yourself over the
> list if she looks wrong to you. Never give aspirin to a child, check the
> dose on the bottle against her weight rather than her age, and write down
> the time of every dose on the envelope, because you will not remember it at
> three in the morning. Kreston is 8 months and takes nothing at all without
> the doctor saying so, including anything left over from Azlyn.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="feb-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Bored, Not Better

> *For the mend. The fever has broken, she is complaining that there is nothing
> to do, and she is still one bad hour away from the sofa. The bar stays low
> and everything on this page can be done from a lying start.*

### 🛏️ Before Anything Else

Move the nest. Yesterday's pillow and blanket go from the bedroom to the sofa,
or from the sofa to a floor pile in whichever room you are working in. The
change of scene is most of the medicine today. Put a tray on the coffee table
within her reach with her cup, a plate of small food and whatever she is
carrying around this week, so she can start something without calling you in
from the kitchen.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day

Still no clock times. She will tell you where the edges are.

- **Whenever she wakes.** Bring the drink to her and watch how she takes it. Her hands and her voice tell you both more about how she is doing than any question you could ask.
- **The good stretch, which comes early.** The best hours today land in the morning, so spend them. One job with an end to it, then a book, then stop while she still has some left.
- **When she asks for food.** Appetite comes back sideways. Offer what she asked for yesterday and was refused, and let her leave most of it.
- **The rest block after lunch.** Shorter today and it still happens, whatever she says about it.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** The bath, warm and long, and back into pajamas afterwards even though it is the middle of the day.
- **The end of the day.** Same bedtime as a well day, and hold it. A child who slept all afternoon yesterday needs the shape back.

### 😴 The Rest Block

She will fight this one, because she feels better than she is. Take the
argument out by lying down with her yourself and putting a timer on for twenty
minutes, out loud, where she can see it. She can look at books, and her body is
horizontal for the whole twenty either way. Most children on the mend fall
asleep inside the first five minutes of an argument they were winning.

### 🛋️ Things She Can Do From the Sofa

**The Jobs She Can Do Lying Down.** Bring the work to her. A laundry basket of
socks matched into pairs on her stomach. The crayon box tipped out on a
cushion and put back in some order she invents. The silverware basket and a
tray, sorted into forks, spoons and the blunt knives, while Kreston is asleep
or behind the gate. One job at a time, and take the tray away when it is
finished so the finish is visible.

**The Spoon on the Mug.** Give her a teaspoon and a mug on the tray and one
rule: two taps means she needs you, and you will come every time. She uses it
eleven times in the first hour and about twice after that. A child stuck on a
sofa with no way to reach the adult in the next room shouts, and this stops the
shouting.

**The Tally on the Envelope.** Prop her where she can see out and give her a
pen and an envelope. One mark per car, or per bird, or per person with an
umbrella. Come back later and count them together, then start a second row and
see which row wins.

**The Sofa Menu.** She dictates what the house eats tonight and you write it
down as a menu, her words as they come. Read it back, let her change it twice,
and then cook whatever version she landed on. Being in charge of one real
decision does more for a bored convalescent than any activity.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

Kreston is 8 months and today he goes back on the floor near her, which is what
they both want. Set him up at the end of the sofa with something he can work at
on his own: a wipes box stuffed with a burp cloth to haul out, or a shallow box
of things too big to swallow. Azlyn can hand him things from where she is
lying, and passing something down to him is a job she will take on for twenty
minutes. Sweep the floor before he goes down, twice if the crayons came out.
Watch his own nose and temperature today, because he is four or five days
behind her on whatever she had, and stranger wariness makes him harder to hand
to anybody else the week he comes down with it himself.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Coming back to normal needs a smaller version of normal first.**
> Azlyn is bored, which is the clean signal her body has finished the work. The
> pull is to hand her the whole day back at once, and a full day today puts her
> flat again by four. Give her the shape without the load: the same meals at
> the same points, one job, one bath, the same bedtime, and nothing that runs
> longer than twenty minutes. Routine is what tells a small child which
> category today belongs in, and a recognizable day is how she works out that
> the ill part is over. Children on the mend hold their gains better when the
> markers come back before the demands do. Add the demands tomorrow.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Illness that turns back around is worth a phone call. A fever
> that clears and then returns, a cough that gets worse after several days of
> getting better, or ear pain arriving late all point at something on top of
> the first virus, and none of them is a wait-and-see. Playgroup, the pool and
> anybody else's kitchen wait until she has gone a full day without a fever and
> has eaten a proper meal. The silverware basket comes to her while Kreston is
> asleep or behind the gate, and the socks or the crayons take its place the
> moment he is back on the floor beside the sofa. Keep her cup and her spoon
> separate from Kreston's for the rest of the week and wash your hands between
> the two of them.

## 🎲 February — Extra Ideas

> *Ten minutes of warning and no plan. Everything here runs on what is already
> in the house, and none of it needs the weather to cooperate.*

### 🎲 Alternative Activities

- **The Cupboard Nobody Sorts.** Everything out of one low cupboard, sorted her way, and back in before lunch.
- **The Weight Line.** Five cans from the pantry, lifted one at a time and lined up lightest to heaviest.
- **Statues Until the Song Stops.** Music on, everybody dancing, and she runs the pause button.
- **Hide the Spoon.** One wooden spoon hidden in one room, and warmer or colder called out from the doorway.
- **The Cushion Island Game.** Every cushion on the floor, and the floor between them counts as water.
- **The Big Pile of Shoes.** Every shoe in the house tipped out and matched into pairs, biggest to smallest.
- **Washing the Windows From the Inside.** A spray bottle of water, a cloth each, and her half of the glass is hers.
- **The Cold Doorstep Minute.** Coats on, sixty seconds on a salted step in the falling snow, back in for something warm.
- **The Phone Call to Somebody Far Away.** She dials, she talks, and you stay out of the conversation.
- **The Grocery List She Dictates.** She says what the house needs and you write every item down, including the four cakes.
- **Everything That Fits in a Shoebox.** A hunt through the house, and a long argument about the things that almost fit.

### 🎨 Alternative Arts & Crafts

- **Foil Animals on a Plate.** Kitchen foil squeezed into creatures that have to stand up on their own.
- **The Junk Mail Chain.** Strips looped and taped end to end until the chain crosses the room.
- **Two Crayons, Two Hands.** One in each fist on a big sheet, both arms moving at once.
- **The Sticky Wall.** Plastic wrap taped across a doorway sticky side out, and torn tissue pressed onto it.
- **The Drawing That Comes Through the Paint.** Heavy crayon first, then a watery wash over the top of it.
- **Tape Under the Paint.** Masking tape shapes stuck down, painted over, peeled off when dry.
- **Printing With What Is in the Fridge.** A halved potato, the end of a celery bunch and a fork, pressed into paint.
- **Soap Drawings on the Mirror.** A dry bar of soap on the bathroom mirror, wiped off with a warm cloth after.
- **Drawing With Her Feet.** Paper taped to the floor and a fat crayon held between her toes.
- **The Torn Cloud Sky.** White paper torn into lumps and glued across a page of gray.
- **The Family Drawn From Behind.** Everybody in the house drawn from the back of the head, and guessed at afterwards.

### 👶 Kreston's Turn

*He is 8 months this month: crawling or shuffling, banging two things together,
and wary of any face he does not know.*

- **The Muffin Tin and Four Cloths.** A washcloth pushed into each cup for him to haul back out.
- **Two Lids and a Loud Floor.** A pan lid in each hand on the kitchen floor, banged together for as long as you can stand it.
- **The Face That Comes Back.** A dish towel over your head, then off, ten times, and he pulls it the last few.
- **The Cold Spoon From the Fridge.** A metal teaspoon chilled for ten minutes, his to hold and chew while his gums work.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Seed-sized everything**: cress seed, soaked beans, loose rice, rubber bands, the trap's chocolate coins. Count them out, count them back, and sweep before he goes down.
- **Balloons**: Day 77 is catching day, and burst pieces are the worst choking hazard in the house for both children. Use the scarf instead any time Kreston is on the floor.
- **Anything he can pull up on**: the tent chairs all circus week, the paper bin, the laundry basket nest, the oven door. Weight it, push it to a wall, or lift the activity onto the table.
- **String and cord**: the tent flag line, the nest, the leprechaun trap and the sorting circles all use it. Take it down the moment the activity ends.
- **Adult-only steps**: scissors most days, the craft knife on mud kitchen day, the oven through forty minutes of soda bread. Scissors go back out of reach between cuts, not down on the table.
- **Water, and there is more of it this month**: the mud kitchen sink, the pond edge on the frog egg walk, the gutters running after March rain, swimming every Tuesday. That sink holds enough to drown Kreston, so tip it out every time you step away, and stay within arm's reach of both children at the pool.
- **Spring specific**: daffodil bulbs and yew are poisonous, and both grow along the route she collects on, so nothing she picks goes near a mouth. Wash hands after soil and after raw egg, and Easter Sunday's dyed eggs are for looking at.

## Week 10: Circus Adventures 🎪
**📅 March 5 – March 11, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

A bedsheet goes over four dining chairs on Friday morning and the big top
stays up until Thursday. Every day after that adds one act underneath it. She
tumbles on a comforter and names her own six tricks, builds a sound desk out of
the low cupboards, lifts a hundred-kilo barbell made of newspaper, draws four
clown faces off her own reflection, walks a rope taped down the hall with a
rice sock on her head, and catches scarves that fall slow enough to give her
time. The morning builds the act and the afternoon plays it.

Thursday is the show. She draws the poster with herself as the star, delivers
three of them to the doorsteps she picks, sells tickets from a box by the tent
door and announces every act through a paper cone in the order she set at
breakfast. Film that one end to end. The tent comes down on Thursday evening
and the barbell goes out with the recycling, so the poster and four minutes of
wobbly video are what is left of the week.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Balance she can feel changing.** Heel to toe along a rope, arms out sideways, a rice sock on her head that falls the moment she looks down.
- **Telling two close sounds apart.** Seven noise-makers on one desk, eyes shut, picking the keys out from the pasta jar.
- **Four feelings with a face and a word each.** Happy, sad, cross and surprised, pulled in a mirror and drawn on paper plates she keeps.
- **What heavy does to her body.** Sorting the counter into two piles, hauling the barbell overhead, loading a basket until it stops moving.
- **Running an order she set herself.** Her names on the trick cards, her numbers on the tickets, her five acts on the fridge list nobody is allowed to change.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Interoception, the sense nobody lists
- Adjectives are the scaffolding for thinking
- Auditory discrimination is the reading skill nobody mentions
- Body awareness is a sense too
- Naming a feeling reduces its intensity, and the drop is measurable
- Teaching a child to notice her own body settling is a lifelong tool
- What a self-portrait tells you about her thinking

---

## 🌟 Day 64: The Big Top Goes Up 🌟
**📅 Friday, March 5, 2027**
**Theme:** Circus Adventures

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Cut six sheets of red paper into long strips, and stand the big sheet, the clothespins, the masking tape and four heavy books beside the dining chairs.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Marking Out the Ring
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Big Top (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Flags in the March Wind (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Ringmaster (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Inside the Big Top
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and Two Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Marking Out the Ring

**🧰 You need:** 1 roll masking tape · 2 meters of string · a clear patch of floor.

1. Push the sofa and the coffee table back to the walls with her. She picks which end of the room the ring goes in.
2. Hold one end of the string down in the middle and let her walk the other end round you, laying tape as she goes. The circle comes out lopsided. Leave it lopsided.
3. Tell her a tent goes over that circle at 9:15, then leave her to walk the line while you clear breakfast.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Big Top

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large bedsheet, or 2 single sheets
- 4 dining chairs, or a drying rack and 2 chairs
- 8 clothespins or bulldog clips
- 1 roll masking tape
- Red paper, 6 sheets, cut into long strips
- String, 2 meters
- 4 heavy books to weight the edges

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Stand the four chairs on the tape circle, backs facing out, as far apart as the sheet will reach.
2. Drape the sheet over the top and clip it to the chair backs. Clips hold where a tucked edge slides off the moment she leans on it.
3. Ask her where the door goes. Clip that edge so she can lift it and drop it, and put it on the side you can see from the kitchen.
4. Tape the red strips down the outside, roof to floor, all the way round. You hold each strip, she sticks the tape.
5. Weight all four outside edges with the books. Nothing goes on the roof.
6. Tape a paper flag to the string, run it from the top of the tent to the back of one chair, and get in with her.

> 💡 **Tip:** It stays up until Thursday, so build it to survive her crawling in and out forty times. More clips and heavier chairs beat a neat sheet.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Flags in the March Wind

Tape three paper flags to three sticks and take them out. The wind arrives in
gusts this month, so walk to the open end of the park and hold the flags up
where nothing blocks them, then round the side of a building where the air
goes still. She will find the windiest spot on the street before you do.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** **Kreston turns 9 months today.** He pulls himself
> up on anything that stays put. Sit him at the sofa edge, outside the ring,
> with a fat wad of red strips taped together at one end. He works the loose
> end with finger and thumb, a skill about two weeks old, and it holds him a
> while. Stay beside him, because a strip that comes free goes to his mouth. He
> waves at the flags outside. Wave back and he does it again.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Ringmaster

The tent has a door and nobody has been announced through it yet. The hat
takes the longest, so it comes first.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 cereal box or 2 sheets thick card
- 1 pair of scissors (adult only)
- Black paper, or a black crayon (paint works)
- Packing tape and masking tape
- 1 sheet of paper rolled into a cone
- 1 wooden spoon or cardboard tube for the baton
- 1 ribbon, scarf or old belt
- Every teddy in the house, for the audience

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cut a strip of card long enough to go round her head, tape the ends into a ring, and check it sits above her ears.
2. Cut a card circle wider than the ring for the brim, snip tabs round the inner hole, and tape the tabs up inside the ring. She holds, you cut.
3. Cover the outside with black paper, or hand her the crayon and let her do it. The patches she misses stay missed.
4. Roll the sheet of paper into a cone, tape the seam, and let her test her voice through the narrow end.
5. Tie the ribbon over one shoulder and under the other arm. She chooses the shoulder.
6. Line every teddy along the hallway. She walks the parade with the baton, announcing each one by name, and the parade ends inside the big top.
7. Let her announce you, and then be whatever she introduced you as.

> 💡 **Tip:** Some children never get past the cone. If the parade never happens, the afternoon still worked.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Hat only. Skip the sash and the parade.
- A megaphone each and a conversation from opposite ends of the hall.
- Empty the dress-up box and make nothing at all.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Grandparents or family**, and she arrives in the hat
- The park, and the flags go back out
- A friend's house with the megaphone in the bag
- The café with the window seat, if the wind has won

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He is the front row. At 9 months he waves, and a
> parade of teddies coming down the hall toward him beats any of it. Sit him
> propped in the tent doorway so he can watch her coming. Take the flag string
> down off the tent before he is on the floor near it.

### 🌍 Around the World: China: Acrobatics 🎪

Chinese acrobatics runs back more than two thousand years, to village harvest
festivals where people showed off with whatever was to hand: plates, jars,
tables and chairs. Those props are in the acts today, and a troupe will spin
a stack of dinner plates on thin sticks or balance a heavy jar on a bare head.

> **✨ Try it:** Eat lunch in the tent the way a troupe eats between shows,
> bowls of noodles on the floor. Let her spin the empty bowl on the back of a
> wooden spoon afterwards.

> *Did you know?* Han dynasty acrobats performed with jars, tables and plates
> from their own kitchens.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Interoception, the sense nobody lists.**
> Sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell get all the attention. Azlyn is also
> building interoception, the sense that reads her own insides: hunger,
> thirst, a full bladder, a heart going fast after she has run round a tent.
> That wiring is half built at three, so she can be starving and tell you she
> is fine, then come apart over a sock. You are already doing the thing that
> helps. Name the signal out loud when you spot it (*your tummy is rumbling,
> that means hungry*), and name the state she is in when she comes off the
> parade. Each label hands her a word for something she can feel and cannot
> yet place.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Kreston will haul himself up on the chair legs holding the
> tent and bring the whole frame down on top of himself, so stay in the room
> while he is near it. Loose paper strips go to his mouth, so sweep them up
> before he is down and keep his wad taped. The books weight the outside edges
> and never the roof. The scissors stay with you. String at his height is a
> strangulation risk, so take the flag line down before he is on the floor.

## 🌟 Day 65: Acrobats 🌟
**📅 Saturday, March 6, 2027**
**Theme:** Circus Adventures

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fold the comforter in half on the living room floor, cut six cards out of a cereal box, and stand the rice and three clean socks on the counter for this afternoon.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Building the Soft Floor
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Building the Soft Floor

**🧰 You need:** 1 comforter or 3 folded blankets · 4 sofa cushions · masking tape.

1. Drag the comforter into the ring and let her lay it out. Fold it double where she says she is going to land.
2. Wall the far edge with the cushions. Check what is behind her head rather than in front of her, and move the coffee table now.
3. Run a strip of tape along the near edge as the start line. She will test the mat by throwing herself on it, which is the test you wanted.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Six Tricks and a Bow

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 comforter, or 3 folded blankets
- 4 sofa cushions
- 6 index cards, or 6 pieces cut from a cereal box
- 1 marker
- 1 roll masking tape for the start line
- A phone, for filming one trick

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Show her a move, let her try it, then ask what it is called. Write her name for it on a card in marker, big enough to read from the other side of the room.
2. Six moves: a forward roll, a log roll down the length of the comforter, a bridge on hands and knees, a candle on her back with her hips on the mat and both legs straight up, a jump with a half turn, and a stork balance on one foot.
3. Every move ends on the tape line with a bow. The bow is how she knows a trick has finished.
4. Lay the six cards face up. She picks the running order and performs the set from start to end.
5. Film the one she is proudest of and watch it back with her once.
6. Leave the cards on the mat. She runs the set again at 4:15 with nobody watching.

> 💡 **Tip:** Spot her with your hands ready and off her. A forward roll goes wrong at the moment an adult lifts her halfway through it.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Every Low Wall on the Street

Walk the usual route and stop at every low wall, curb and painted line on it.
She goes along the top with a hand in yours, then without. March leaves the
bottoms of walls wet and green, so pick the dry ones and expect one soaking
anyway. Count the walls on the way out and see whether her number holds
coming back.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months. Put him on the far corner of
> the comforter, clear of the tumbling, with one cushion to pull up on. A soft
> floor is harder work than a hard one, and you will see him sink, plant a
> hand wider and try again. He tires faster on the comforter than on the kitchen
> floor, and he wants it more.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Beanbag on Her Head

Three rice socks take ten minutes to make and get used every day for the rest
of the week.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3 clean socks
- 2 cups rice or dried lentils (flour in a double freezer bag if you have neither)
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 tray
- 1 paperback book
- A phone timer

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Fill each sock a third full, knot it twice, and turn the cuff back over the knot. She pours, you knot.
2. Run a line of masking tape from one end of the hall to the other with a bend in the middle of it.
3. She walks the line with one sock on her head. It falls. She starts again from the beginning, and she will insist on that rule herself.
4. Stack the second sock on top of the first and let her find out how much less her head can move.
5. Add the tray held flat in both hands, with the paperback on it and one sock on her head.
6. Time a run with the phone and say the number out loud. Then ask for a slower one and time that.
7. Put a sock on your own head and let her walk you down the line.

> 💡 **Tip:** Arms out sideways do more for her balance than anything you can say about it. Put your own arms out and she copies without being asked.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Three tricks instead of six, then stop.
- Rice socks only, thrown and caught on the mat.
- Balance a sock on your head and let her knock it off.
- Cushions on the floor and a jumping game with no cards.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum**
- **The museum**, first Saturday of the month
- Whichever gallery has a floor she can sit on, if the rest is packed
- The indoor play center, if it is raining sideways
- The park with the low wall she liked this morning

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Take him in the sling for the first half of the
> museum. At 9 months he pulls up on anything at knee height, so find the room
> with a carpeted corner or a low bench and put him down there for twenty
> minutes. Let Azlyn choose which room he sees.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Adjectives are the scaffolding for thinking.**
> Azlyn named six moves this morning and you wrote her words down. Describing
> words are the tools she sorts the world with. Nouns hand her the objects,
> and adjectives let her hold a quality on its own, so *heavy* stops belonging
> to one can and becomes something a box, a basket and a brother can each be.
> *Slower*, *higher* and *softer* are the first measuring she does without a
> ruler. Feed her the ones she is missing while her body is still doing the
> thing: *that roll was tighter than the last one.* An adjective attached to
> something she can feel sticks better than one off a page.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Move the mat away from the coffee table, the fireplace and
> the radiator before she rolls, and check what is behind her head, not in
> front of her. Double-knot every rice sock and check them for leaks between
> goes. Loose rice on the floor is a choking hazard for a 9-month-old with a
> pincer grip, so sweep before Kreston goes down.

## 🌟 Day 66: The Circus Band 🌟
**📅 Sunday, March 7, 2027**
**Theme:** Circus Adventures

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill a screw-top jar with dried pasta, find the comb, the saucepan lid and four thick rubber bands, and stand three empty shoeboxes by the door.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: One Noise Each

**🧰 You need:** the kitchen cupboards · a tray or upturned box · her.

1. Open the low cupboards and give her one job: find five things that make five different noises. The tray takes whatever she brings out.
2. Take each one in turn and make its noise once. She copies it with her mouth.
3. Ask her which two sound closest. Leave her answer alone and put the tray out for 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Sound Effects Desk

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 upturned box or tray as the desk
- 1 saucepan lid and 1 wooden spoon
- 1 comb and a sheet of baking paper
- 1 empty plastic bottle with its lid
- 1 shoebox and 4 thick rubber bands
- Dried pasta in a screw-top jar
- 2 sheets of paper to rip
- A bunch of keys or a bell
- Masking tape and a marker for labels

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set the desk on a table at her height and lay the noise-makers out in a row she decides on.
2. Build the two that need building: fold the baking paper over the comb to hum through, and stretch the four rubber bands across the open end of the shoebox.
3. Play each noise and let her say which circus act it belongs to. Write her answer on masking tape and stick it on: the drum roll, the trapeze, the clown falling over, the lion.
4. Sit with your back to her and call an act. She shuts her eyes and finds the right one.
5. Swap over. She calls the acts, you play them, and you get one wrong on purpose.
6. Run the whole set in order, loud to quiet, as a show for Kreston.

> 💡 **Tip:** Put the keys next to the pasta jar and let her work at telling them apart.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Birds Are Back

Stand still at the end of the street and listen before you walk anywhere. Early
March is when the singing starts up again, and there is more of it before nine
than at any other hour. Hold up a finger for every different bird she hears.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and turns his head to a sound
> before he turns his body. Bang the wooden spoon on the saucepan lid at the
> far end of the room and watch him find you, then do it from behind him. Give
> him the plastic bottle, lid taped on hard and checked before he gets it. He
> bangs it for a few minutes, then comes back to it two or three times across
> the hour.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Clown Shoes

A clown walks wrong on purpose, and she has to work out how first. The boxes
take an hour to build and the walking takes the rest.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 shoeboxes or cereal boxes
- String or wide elastic, 1 meter
- Packing tape
- Paint, or colored paper and glue
- 1 pair of scissors (adult only)
- A chair back to hold for the stand-up
- 1 sturdy hardcover book, for the step up
- One of your cardigans and a belt
- A full-length mirror

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cut two slits across the top of each box, a foot's width apart. You cut, she holds the box still.
2. Thread the elastic through and knot it underneath so it makes a strap over the top of her foot.
3. Line the inside with packing tape where her heel lands, because that corner goes first.
4. She paints or papers them, and the colors go on big, bright and uneven.
5. Put them on sitting down on the carpet, with her hand on a chair back for the stand-up.
6. She walks a length of carpet on her own first. Then she takes a hand in yours for one step up onto a book, a turn on the spot, and the walk back.
7. Put your cardigan on her with the belt round the middle and stand her in front of the mirror. Give her ten minutes in front of it with nothing to do.

> 💡 **Tip:** Boxes with the sides left tall stay on her feet. The moment you cut them down to look neat, they fall off at every step.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One box each and no straps. Slide them along the floor instead.
- Paint the boxes today and walk in them tomorrow.
- Giant shoes out of your rain boots and two pairs of socks.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A playground you have never been to**, one stop further than the usual one
- The usual playground, if the new one turns out to be built for big kids
- The woods, for sticks worth bringing home
- Somebody's yard, if anyone will have you

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The baby swing is the whole trip for him. At 9
> months he holds his head steady through a proper push and spends the rest of
> it watching Azlyn come down the slide. Wipe the seat before he goes in, and
> keep his hands off the metal chains, which pull the heat out of small
> fingers in March.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Auditory discrimination is the reading skill nobody mentions.**
> Azlyn shut her eyes this morning and picked one noise out of seven. Telling
> two close sounds apart is a skill of its own, and reading sits on top of it.
> A child who cannot hear the difference between the front of *bat* and the
> front of *pat* has nothing to hang a letter on, and the gap turns up in
> school as a reading problem when it started in the ear. Household objects
> beat an app for this, because the sounds are messy and she has to hold two
> of them side by side to choose. The two she keeps confusing are the ones her
> ear is still working on.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Thick rubber bands go straight into a 9-month-old's mouth
> and he can reach the shoebox from standing. Count them onto the desk and
> count them off, and keep the desk on a table, never the floor, while Kreston
> is loose. Bang the saucepan lid at the far end of the room from him. The
> scissors stay with you. The box shoes go on carpet, never on a hard floor,
> never on the stairs and never near the tent chairs. Stay within arm's reach
> for the first walk, and hold her hand for the step up onto the book.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Lifting Everything in the Kitchen

**🧰 You need:** six things off the counter · two clear patches of floor.

1. Line up a can, an empty mug, the bag of flour, a wooden spoon, a full bottle and a dish towel.
2. She lifts each one and puts it in one of two piles, heavy or light. Leave both piles as she sorts them.
3. Ask which is the heaviest thing in the row, then hand her the can and the flour at once and let her change her mind.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Hundred-Kilo Barbell

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 large cereal boxes, or 2 paper grocery bags
- Newspaper, a full stack
- 1 broom handle, or 3 paper-towel tubes taped end to end
- Packing tape
- 1 black marker
- 1 laundry basket
- 6–8 heavy books
- Masking tape for the lifting line

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She crumples the newspaper, you pack it, until a thumb pressed into the box meets no give.
2. Push one end of the broom handle into each box and tape the joint round and round. That joint is the whole barbell, so use more tape than looks sensible.
3. Write a giant **100** on each box. Let her say the number and copy it underneath.
4. Tape the lifting line at the far end of the room from Kreston. Lift from the line: to her knees, to her shoulders, over her head. Count each one out loud.
5. Carry it the length of the room and back with the number facing out, then set it down and bow.
6. Load the basket with books and let her drag it by one handle. She decides how many go in and takes one out when it stops moving.

> 💡 **Tip:** The barbell looks enormous and weighs nothing, and she is in on the joke. Ask for a strongman face and you will get a look you have never seen before.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Moving the Fallen Branches

March storms leave the park littered. Take a strong bag and shift fallen
branches into one pile at the edge of the field, biggest first. She will find
one too heavy and want it anyway, so take one end and give her the other.
Then ask her to sort the pile into what she can carry alone and what needs
two people.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and pulls to stand, so this
> week he is learning what holds his weight and what comes with him. Give him
> the empty laundry basket upended on the carpet. It takes his weight, and he
> will pull up on it, drop, and go again. The drop is practice too, and he is
> getting better at landing on his bottom.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Tightrope on the Floor

The rope goes down the hallway this afternoon and stays there until Thursday.
A line on the floor sets her the same problem a real tightrope does.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- A jump rope or length of clothesline, 3 meters (masking tape alone works)
- 1 umbrella, or a cardboard tube as the balance pole
- 2 sofa cushions
- One of Saturday's rice socks, or a folded dish towel
- Chalk, for the same line outside
- A chair back to hold at the start

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the rope flat down the hall and tape it to the floor every half meter so it cannot roll under her foot.
2. Walk it yourself first, heel to toe, arms out, and say nothing about how.
3. She holds the chair back for the first meter, then lets go and does the rest alone. Do not walk beside her with a hand out.
4. Hand her the umbrella across her body in both hands. The pole steadies her, and she will feel it work.
5. Put a cushion either side of the middle stretch, so stepping off the rope means stepping into something soft.
6. Rice sock on her head for one full length. Count her steps out loud so she has a number to beat.
7. Chalk the same line on the path outside, coats on, and walk it where the ground is uneven.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will go faster to stay upright. Ask for a slow walk and count her steps, because slow is what makes her use her feet.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Masking tape line only, no rope.
- Walk the line carrying a full cup of water.
- Set the cushions out in a row and jump the gaps instead.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The neighborhood park**, and the branch pile you started this morning
- The field with a ball and nothing else
- A walk with the chalk in your pocket for a line on every path
- The corner store on the way back, and she carries the bag the whole way home

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Sit him on the grass at the edge of the branch
> pile with one short thick stick, too fat to go far into his mouth. At 9
> months he bangs two things together on purpose, and a stick on a tree root
> will hold him longer than a toy would. Check the ground with your hand
> first.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Body awareness is a sense too.**
> Shut your eyes and touch your nose. The sense that got your hand there is
> proprioception, receptors in muscle and joint reporting where every part of
> you is without your eyes involved. Azlyn's version is still coarse, which is
> why she grips a paper cup like a hammer and misses the chair when she sits
> down. Weight is how the map gets calibrated. She braces for a hundred kilos,
> gets a broom handle and two boxes of newspaper, and adjusts. Every load she
> moves today sharpens that map, and a sharper map is what lets her pour her
> own drink next year.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Keep the barbell and the loaded basket off her feet, and load
> the basket where it will be dragged rather than carried up a step. Kreston
> pulls to stand and will grab the broom handle mid-lift, so the lifting line
> goes at the other end of the room from him, and nothing gets dragged across
> a floor he is sitting on.

**📅 Tuesday, March 9, 2027**
**Theme:** Circus Adventures

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put four paper plates, the hand mirror and four craft sticks on the table, and pack the swim bag before you go up.

- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch

- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Hat That Won't Stay On (90 min)

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Face in the Spoon

**🧰 You need:** 1 big metal spoon · her breakfast chair · you opposite her.

1. Hand her the spoon and let her find her own face in both sides of it. One side turns her upside down and she will go back to it.
2. Ask for a cross face, then a sad one, then a surprised one, and let her watch each one arrive in the spoon.
3. Say what her eyebrows are doing each time. Say nothing about the mouth yet, because that is the job at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Four Faces on Four Plates

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4 paper plates, or 4 circles cut from a cereal box (scissors, adult only)
- Crayons and washable poster paint
- 4 craft sticks or 4 cardboard tubes
- Masking tape
- 1 hand mirror
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Four plates on the table in a row, mirror propped up where she can see herself without holding it.
2. Happy first. She pulls the face in the mirror, looks at it, then draws it. Leave every wobbly eye where she put it.
3. Sad next. Ask what the corners of a sad mouth do and let her check in the mirror before she draws.
4. Cross, then surprised. By the fourth she will be telling you what the eyebrows do.
5. Write the feeling word on the back of each plate in marker while she paints the cheeks and the nose.
6. Tape a stick to the back of each one, low enough for her hand, and stand all four in a mug on the table.

> 💡 **Tip:** Four plates and four words is plenty. A fifth face turns a set she can hold in her head into a pile she cannot.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Puddle Mirror

Find a puddle with the sky in it and look down together. She makes the four
faces over the water and watches them arrive. Wind wrecks the picture, so hunt
out a sheltered one in the lee of a wall. Then let her jump in it, because a
puddle she has been careful of for ten minutes becomes unbearable. Rain boots on,
spare socks in the bag, swim things in the same bag.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and watches a face the way
> Azlyn watches the mirror. Hold him facing you and make the four faces, one
> at a time, with a pause after each. He will try one back, and the surprised
> one gets copied first because the mouth moves most. Let Azlyn do it as well.
> She gets a bigger response than you do.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Hat That Won't Stay On

One gag, repeated three times, is a whole clown routine. She has to know what
comes next before it can be funny to anybody but her.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 adult hat, or Friday's ringmaster hat
- 1 dining chair
- 1 broom
- The four plate faces
- Teddies and dolls for the front row
- A phone, filming

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Show her the gag once. Hat on your head, bend down for the broom, hat lands on the floor behind you, and you look everywhere for it except down.
2. Break it into three parts and name them with her: hat on, hat off, hunting for the hat. Three is as many as she can hold.
3. Run it through with her, counting the parts on your fingers as they happen. Do it four or five times until she is ahead of you.
4. Let her add one thing of her own. Whatever she adds stays in, including the bit where the broom falls over.
5. She picks up a plate face at the end to show the audience what the clown feels about it.
6. Line the teddies up and sit Kreston at the front, propped and facing the right way. Perform the whole thing and film it without stopping.
7. Watch it back once and ask her which part made him laugh.

> 💡 **Tip:** Rehearsal is the part she loves. Running the same three beats again and again is how she learns that a story can be planned, so let her call for a sixth go.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One gag, done four times, and nothing else.
- A puppet show with the plate faces over the back of the sofa.
- Photograph her pulling each of the four faces and stick them on the fridge.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one
- The indoor play center, if the pool is closed for a school session
- The library, a day early
- Ten minutes at the park on the way back, no longer

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He is in the water with you today. At 9 months he
> holds the rail and bobs, and he will spend the session watching the big
> children at the far end rather than his own hands. Both your hands stay on
> him. Get him out before the shivering starts, because he loses heat faster
> than Azlyn does and shows it later.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Naming a feeling reduces its intensity, and the drop is measurable.**
> Put a feeling into words and it loses height. Researchers call it affect
> labeling, and in scanner studies the people who name what they are feeling
> show a quieter amygdala and more work happening in the language areas.
> Azlyn has less of that machinery built than an adult, so she borrows yours.
> She drew four faces this morning and has four words to go with them. Hand
> her the word in the middle of the wobble (*you look cross, that is the cross
> plate*) and you are lending her the part of her brain that has not finished
> growing. She will point at a plate before she can say the word, and pointing
> counts.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Swimming this afternoon. Kreston stays within arm's reach in
> the water at all times, 20 minutes is plenty at 9 months, and no float or
> seat is a substitute for your hands. Paint goes on plates and paper, never
> on Kreston's skin, and washable non-toxic paint only while he is mouthing
> everything he can reach. The scissors stay with you.
