# 🌧️ March — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

March hands you three good afternoons and then takes them back. These pages are
for the mornings the plan does not survive the weather, and for the mornings
somebody wakes up hot and gets no further than the sofa. Two of the days here
need nobody to leave the house, and two of them need almost nothing from either
of you. The last page is for the ten minutes when you open the book with no
plan and a child already asking.

---

<a id="mar-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — The Visitor Who Got Rained In

Cold rain, the kind that comes sideways and turns the yard to soup. Nobody is
going out and nobody is coming over. Today the house gets a guest instead, and
Azlyn has to explain the whole place to him.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Sit a soft toy on the mat by the front door with a paper bag beside him, so she finds him there before you are up. Put a shoebox, a ball of string and a roll of masking tape on the counter for the afternoon.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Visitor at the Door
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Showing Him How It All Works (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Long Way to Every Room (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Bed He Has to Fit In (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Drying the Windowsills
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Box and Everyone Who Fits In It
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: A Book He Has Never Heard
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Visitor at the Door

**🧰 You need:** one soft toy she has not played with in weeks · a paper bag.

1. Let her find him. Tell her he came in out of the rain, his home is a long way off, and he cannot leave until it stops. Point at the window. The window is doing the arguing for you today.
2. Ask her three questions and take the first answer she gives: his name, where he came from, and one thing he has never seen before.
3. Write his name on the bag. Let her carry him around while you clear breakfast, and listen. She will start explaining the toaster to him without being asked, which is the 9:15 activity beginning an hour early.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Showing Him How It All Works

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The visitor
- 1 sturdy step stool
- 1 dish towel for spills
- 1 plastic cup
- Your worst pretend voice

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tell her the visitor needs to know how six things in this house work, and let her choose all six. Faucets, light switches, the toilet flush, the fridge door, the front door lock and the washing machine dial are the usual six, and hers may be stranger.
2. At each stop she does two jobs in order: tell him what it is, then make it work in front of him. Hold the toy at her height so he can see.
3. You are the visitor. Ask one stupid question per stop in his voice. *Does the water live in there? Where does it go after?* She has to answer him, and her answers are the point of the day.
4. At the sink, set the faucet to cold before she climbs the stool, and stand behind her. She fills the plastic cup for him, tips it back out, and dries the counter with the dish towel so the visitor sees the whole job.
5. At the end, ask her which one was hardest to explain. Go back to that one and let her try it again. She will do it better the second time.
6. Last lap, at speed: she names all six in the order she picked them. Count them off on her fingers with her.

> 💡 **Tip:** Leave her explanations alone. *The water comes down from the sky into the pipe* is close enough to true, and correcting it costs you the rest of the tour.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Long Way to Every Room

Rain on a window is worth ten minutes of watching and no more. She has a full
hour of legs in her and no yard to put it in, so give her the visitor to carry
and one rule: every room in the house, and no room twice. Every time you call
**switch**, she changes how she travels. Stomping, tiptoeing, crawling on all
fours with him balanced on her back, sideways along the wall, backwards with
one hand on the doorframe. Count the rooms out loud as she clears them and let
her decide whether the hallway counts as a room. Finish with the same lap done
as slow as she can manage, which is harder than the fast one and settles her
before snack.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and pulling himself upright on
> anything that holds still. Let him do his own tour along the sofa and the
> coffee table while she does hers. Move the sharp-cornered furniture out of
> the route first and put the fire guard or the stair gate across the stairs
> before either of them starts, because today they are both moving through the
> whole house. He waves now, so have her wave at him from each doorway and wait
> for the wave back. He will come to the doorframe to get it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Bed He Has to Fit In

The visitor is staying the night, since the rain has not let up. Morning was
talking and walking. This afternoon she measures, cuts and pads.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The visitor
- 1 length of string, about 3 feet
- 3 boxes of different sizes from the recycling, one a shoebox
- 1 roll masking tape
- Scissors (adult only)
- 1 washcloth, 1 clean sock, 1 dish towel
- Crayons

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay him flat on the floor and lay the string beside him. Pinch the string at his head and his feet, and cut it there. That piece of string is now the visitor.
2. Hand her the string and send her to the three boxes. She holds it across each one: too short, too long, right.
3. Cut the chosen box down to bed height yourself while she holds it steady. Tape the raw edge over so it stops scratching.
4. She makes it soft. Washcloth for a mattress, the rolled sock for a pillow, dish towel folded over for the blanket. Let her put him in and take him out until she is satisfied with the depth.
5. Crayons on the outside, and tell her he will be looking at the inside all night, so the inside earns some color too.
6. She picks where the bed goes and tells him one last time where the bathroom is.

> 💡 **Tip:** The string is doing the teaching. Measuring with an object instead of a number is where measurement starts for her, and she will use string on other things for weeks after this.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Make him a raincoat out of a plastic bag and a rubber band.
- Draw the route of the morning tour on one long strip of paper, stop by stop.
- Let her do the whole tour again for you on your phone camera, then watch it back over dinner.
- Set up the box bed as a hospital and let her decide what is wrong with him.
- Sort the recycling boxes into a row by size, biggest to smallest, and leave the row up.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him his own box, the biggest one, laid on its
> side on the floor. At 9 months he will pull up on the edge of it, drop things
> in, and lean over to find them again, which is the same investigation Azlyn is
> running with the string. Keep the string, the crayons and the masking tape
> rolls off the floor whenever you are not looking at him. His pincer grip is
> good enough now to pick up things you cannot see from standing height, and
> everything he picks up goes in his mouth.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Giving a tour is the best test of understanding there is.**
> Azlyn can tell you what a faucet is. Explaining one to somebody who has never
> seen it asks for something harder. She has to guess what the listener already
> knows, put the parts in an order, and notice the spot where her own
> explanation runs out. Researchers call it the protégé effect, and it shows up
> whenever children teach younger children: the tutor gains more than the
> student does. A soft toy works because he never gets bored and never argues.
> Listen for the moment she stops and says *wait*. That pause is her finding a
> hole in her own model, and she will fill it herself if you stay quiet for
> four seconds.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Cold faucet only when she is on the step stool, and stand
> behind her the whole time she is up there. Kreston is pulling to stand today,
> so the stair gate goes across before the tour starts and the stool goes away
> the second she steps off it. Never leave him alone in a room with the string,
> the tape rolls or the crayons.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="mar-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — Warm Water and a Gray Sky

Rain since before it got light, and the yard is a swamp. Everything that lives
by the back door is filthy. Today the house does not go out to the mud, so the
mud comes in and gets washed off at the sink.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put two dishpans, an old towel, a nail brush and an old toothbrush beside the sink, and set the bag of clothespins and a marker beside them for the afternoon. Stand the muddy boots on newspaper in the middle of the kitchen floor where she cannot miss them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Grubby Parade
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Dirty End, Clean End (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Ten Trips to the Drying Rack (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Clipped Up in Size Order (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Emptying the Rinse Bowl
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Cave Under the Kitchen Table
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Long Bath, No Hurry
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Grubby Parade

**🧰 You need:** 1 laundry basket · 1 old towel spread on the kitchen floor.

1. Hand her the basket and one instruction: find everything in this house with mud on it. Boots, the stroller wheels, the plastic animals that got left out, the trowel, the doormat, the ball.
2. Lay it all out on the towel in a line, dirtiest at one end. She will hit two things that look about the same, and sorting that out is the work. Let the argument run and do not settle it for her.
3. Count the line together. Tell her the number, and tell her every one of them is getting washed at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Dirty End, Clean End

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 dishpans or large mixing bowls
- Warm water, plus a squirt of dish soap in one bowl
- 1 nail brush and 1 old toothbrush
- 1 old towel spread on the floor
- 1 dish towel for drying
- 1 step stool
- An apron, or clothes you have given up on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Apron on her first, or the clothes you have given up on. Set the two bowls at one end of the towel, soapy first and rinse second. Keep the far end of the towel empty and tell her that end is the clean end.
2. Run one boot through the whole route while she watches: into the soap, scrub, into the rinse, out onto the clean end. Then hand her the nail brush and stop demonstrating.
3. Work down her line in the order she set this morning. Pass her one thing at a time so the floor stays walkable. The old toothbrush is for the boot treads and the stroller wheels, where the nail brush cannot reach.
4. When the soapy water goes brown, carry it to the sink together. She climbs the step stool and pours it out herself. Refill it and let her look at how much of the yard came off six objects.
5. At the end, ask which one turned out to be dirtiest and whether her line this morning had it right. Move it if she wants to.
6. Everything on the clean end gets patted with the dish towel by her and carried to the drying rack, which is the next hour.

> 💡 **Tip:** Warm water, not hot. Her hands are in it for forty minutes and a three-year-old will keep going long past the point where her skin has had enough.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Ten Trips to the Drying Rack

Wet things are heavy, and heavy is what her body wants on a day stuck indoors.
Stand the drying rack at the far end of the house from the kitchen and make her
walk every item down there one at a time. Count the trips out loud. Ten trips
is the target and she will want twenty. Load her up on the last few, one boot
in each hand, and let her feel the difference between carrying a wet washcloth
and carrying a wet boot. Push the pace with a countdown if she flags. Heavy
work through the arms and legs settles a wound-up child better than any sitting
activity you could offer instead, and today she has nowhere else to spend it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and hauling himself upright on
> whatever is nearest, which makes a drying rack the most dangerous object in
> the house today. Stand it against a wall, weight the base with a bag of flour,
> and keep him on the other side of a gate while it is loaded. Give him his own
> job on the floor near the towel: a shallow tray with an inch of warm water and
> two plastic lids. Stay within arm's reach of him the entire time that tray is
> out.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Clipped Up in Size Order

Morning was warm and wet and loud. This afternoon is a line, twenty clothespins
and a problem to solve.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 drying rack, or a length of string tied between two chair backs
- 20 clothespins, or binder clips and hair clips if the bag of pins runs short
- A basket of small clean laundry: washcloths, dish towels, socks, pillowcases
- The boots and plastic animals she washed this morning
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tie the line at her shoulder height so she can reach every inch of it without help. String between two chairs beats a rack for this.
2. Tip the basket on the floor and sort the pile into a size order first, smallest at one end, before anything goes up.
3. Clip them in that order, two clothespins each, one at each corner. Her hands will tire out around item six, so take the tight pins and leave her the loose ones.
4. Stand back with her and look down the finished line. Ask her to find the middle one, and let her put a marker dot on that clothespin so the middle stays findable.
5. Take three off while she covers her eyes, then hand them back and let her find the right gaps.
6. Give her the rest of the pile, the morning's boots and plastic animals included, and no instructions at all. She will invent an order of her own, and hers is worth more than yours.
7. Leave the line up overnight. Laundry in a March house takes until morning, and she gets to check it before breakfast.

> 💡 **Tip:** Clothespins are hard work for three-year-old fingers, and that is the reason to use them. Opening one takes the same pinch she will need for a pencil at five.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Fold the dry washcloths corner to corner and stack them into a tower.
- Wash the plastic animals a second time in a bowl of bubbles, for the bubbles.
- Give her a bowl of warm water and a paintbrush and let her paint the kitchen floor tiles until they dry off.
- Line the clean boots up by the door in size order, every pair in the house.
- Tape a sheet of paper to the window and trace the rain tracks down it with a crayon.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Clothespins pinch and they fit in a mouth, so he
> does not get any. Give him a laundry basket half full of dry washcloths
> instead, and sit him beside it. At 9 months he pulls things out one at a time
> with a thumb and finger and drops them over the edge, and he will run that
> loop for twenty minutes. Empty every bowl of water the moment you step away
> from it. A baby who has learned to pull up can get his face into standing
> water in an inch of it.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Water is the most reliable regulator you have, and it works in either direction.**
> A wound-up child and a flat one need opposite things, and warm and cold water
> hand you both. Warm water on her forearms slows her down. The temperature sits
> close to her skin, the resistance is steady, and there is nothing in it to
> win. Twenty minutes at a bowl on a stool buys more calm than any instruction
> you could give her. Cold runs the other way. A cool washcloth on the back of
> the neck, or her hands under the cold faucet for a count of ten, brings back a
> child who has gone floppy and whiny at four in the afternoon. Neither one
> costs anything, and both are available on a day the door stays shut.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Warm water only, tested on the inside of your own wrist first,
> and set the faucet to cold before she climbs the stool. Kreston can drown in
> the inch of water left in a dishpan, so every bowl gets emptied the moment you
> leave the room, with no exceptions for a quick errand. Weight or block the
> drying rack before he pulls up on it. Keep the clothespins in the basket and
> off the floor.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="mar-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Day It Peaks

She is hot, streaming, and has no interest in anything you can offer. There is
no schedule on this page and no clock times, because she will set both. Nobody
goes outside today. The rest block below is the day; everything else is
optional and can be dropped halfway through with no harm done.

### 🌙 Before She Wakes
> Make her spot on the sofa now: two pillows, the blanket she likes, a towel over the cushion under her head, a cup with a lid within her reach, and a bowl on the floor beside her in case. Put the tissues where she can get them herself. Fill a paper bag with ten small things from around the house and leave it behind the sofa, out of her sight until you want it.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day

- **Whenever she wakes.** Carry her to the sofa spot. No breakfast question yet. The cup, and nothing else.
- **After the first long sleep.** Fluids, one small thing from the bag, back down.
- **When she asks for food.** Take whatever she asks for and give it to her on the sofa.
- **The middle of the day.** The rest block. Curtains half shut, lights off, you on the sofa with her.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** A story with her eyes closed, or a movie, or nothing.
- **Early evening.** Bath if she wants it, bed an hour before you think.

### 🛋️ Where She Lands

Pick one spot in the house and keep her in it all day. Moving her from bed to
sofa to bed costs her more than it saves you, and a child who has one nest
knows where her cup is, where the bowl is and where you are. Keep it near where
you have to be. If the sofa is out of earshot of the kitchen, the day gets
harder for you by the hour.

Take the pressure off yourself early. A day of screens on a fever day has never
harmed a child and it buys you the hands to look after her. Put something long
and slow on, not something loud.

### 😴 The Rest Block

The middle of the day belongs to sleep, and it is the only thing on this page
that matters. She may nap for two hours, or she may lie still with her eyes
open for forty minutes, and both count. Draw the curtains halfway, kill the
overhead light, and lie down with her rather than leaving her to it. A hot
three-year-old settles faster with a hand on her back than with a door closed.

Guard it. Silence your phone, park Kreston somewhere safe first, and let the
laundry sit. Everything you skip today gets done tomorrow when she is a
notch better.

### 🤲 Three Things That Ask Nothing of Her

**The Bag You Bring to Her.** The bag you filled last night comes out from
behind the sofa: a spoon, a shell, a key ring, a hair clip, a photo, a pine
cone. Hand her one at a time and say nothing about it. She looks, keeps it on
the blanket or gives it back. No questions and no quiz. This runs for as long
as it runs and stops the second she turns her head away.

**Drawing on the Back of Her Hand.** Washable marker, her hand flat on the
blanket, and you draw. A cat, a boat, a sun, her name. She does nothing at all
except hold still and watch, and the light pressure on her skin does more for
her than the picture does. Ask before each one and stop when she has had
enough.

**The Story She Can Close Her Eyes For.** Tell her a story about her own day,
starting from waking up, and put everything ordinary in it. She woke up hot,
she came to the sofa, the blanket was blue. Slow down as you go and add nothing
exciting. She can keep her eyes shut for the whole of it, and half the time it
turns into the rest block on its own.

### 🥣 What She'll Take

Fluids beat food today and it is not close. Water, watered-down juice, milk if
she keeps it down, ice chips if she will not drink. Offer a small amount often
rather than a cup she has to face. A three-year-old who eats nothing for a day
and drinks well is fine. One who will not drink is the one to watch.

Food, if she asks: dry toast, plain crackers, banana, yogurt, cold fruit. Do
not make anything that needs cooking or that you will mind throwing away.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

He cannot be on that sofa today. At 9 months he pulls up on the cushions, goes
for her face and her cup, and gets everything she has within a day or two of
touching it. Set his floor up in the same room but out of reach, gated or
across the rug, so she can see him and he cannot get to her. His waving is new
and reliable now, so let them wave at each other across the gap. That counts as
contact for both of them.

Get him out of the house for a stretch if there is a second adult, or a
grandparent who will take a walk in the wind with the stroller. An hour with
one child is a different day from an hour with two. Wash your hands between
them, every time, and keep her cup and his separate.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Naming the darkest day is better than enduring it.**
> A cold runs to a shape. Symptoms climb for two or three days, top out, then
> fade across the week that follows, so the darkest day of it sits somewhere
> you can point at. You already treat today as that day. Saying it out loud is
> what changes the hours. Tell yourself this is the top, tell her tomorrow
> will be easier, and the day stops running open-ended for either of you. A
> bad stretch with an edge on it is easier to sit inside, for her as much as
> for you. Cancel what the week had in it, plan nothing, and guard your own
> sleep, because it is holding the rest of this up.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Call your doctor the same day for a fever in a child this age
> that passes 104°F, or any fever lasting more than three days. Go now, not
> tomorrow, for fast or labored breathing, a stiff neck, a rash that stays
> visible when you press a glass against it, a child too drowsy to wake
> properly, or no wet diaper or bathroom trip in eight hours. Never give
> aspirin to a child. Follow the dosing on the bottle by weight and write down
> the time of every dose, because you will not remember it by evening.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="mar-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Better, But Not Back

The fever broke overnight, she is bored by nine, and she is nowhere near ready
for a real day. Still no going out and still no clock times. Today has a rest
block in the middle of it, same as yesterday, and everything around it is a
shrunken version of a normal morning.

### 🌙 Before She Wakes
> Move her nest off the sofa and onto the floor, on a blanket with cushions, so she is at her own level and near her things. Fill the cup. Put a stack of catalogs and junk mail and a fat crayon beside it.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day

- **Whenever she wakes.** Dressed in clothes, not pajamas. It changes how she behaves all day.
- **After breakfast.** The smallest version of the morning, below. Ten minutes of each thing.
- **When she flags.** Stop before she asks you to. She will not ask.
- **The middle of the day.** The rest block, shorter than yesterday and still not skipped.
- **When she asks for food.** Lunch on the blanket, where she already is.
- **Late afternoon.** One quiet job with a visible end, then nothing.
- **Early evening.** Bed at the same time as yesterday, not the usual time.

### 🧺 The Smallest Version of the Morning

Give her the shape of a normal day at a tenth of the size. Ten minutes of
building, ten minutes of drawing, ten minutes of a song, and a sit-down in
between each one. The order matters more than the length, because the order is
what she has been missing since she went down. Announce each thing before you
start it and announce the end of it: *building now, then we stop.* Stopping on
time is the whole skill today. A recovering three-year-old will overshoot,
crash at two in the afternoon, and lose tomorrow to it.

Keep every one of them on the floor blanket. She stays where she is and the
activity comes to her.

### 😴 The Rest Block

Shorter today, and non-negotiable. Curtains half shut, a blanket, and you
beside her for the first ten minutes. She may not sleep, and lying down without
sleeping is still doing the work. Set an end to it that she can hear, a story
finishing or a timer, so she is not lying there wondering how long this lasts.

Bring her out of it slow. A drink first, then one small thing, then the
afternoon.

### 🛋️ Three Things She Can Do From a Blanket

**Circling What She'd Buy.** Hand her the catalogs and a fat crayon. Her job is
to circle everything in there she would have if she could. No cutting, no
sticking, no tidying up after. Come back every few minutes and ask her to show
you one thing she circled and why. She will talk more today than she has since
Monday, and talking is the sign she is on the mend.

**The Drawer She Empties and Refills.** Bring one drawer to her: the silverware
tray, the sock drawer, the drawer of chargers and rubber bands. She tips it out
on the blanket, sorts it however she likes, and puts it back. A job that
finishes where she can see it suits her right now, and it takes nothing out of
her. The silverware and the charger drawer come out only while Kreston is
gated or asleep. If he is on the floor with her, she gets the socks.

**Lunch Where She Is Sitting.** Sandwich cut in triangles, eaten on the blanket
with a dish towel under it for a plate. Sit down and eat yours beside her,
because a meal she has to travel to is a meal she will turn down today. Keep it
small; her appetite comes back a few days behind everything else, and a full
plate reads as a demand.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

He can come back in today, on the floor, at her level. Keep the cups apart and
keep him off her face for another day or two, and beyond that let them be near
each other. She has been away from him and he has noticed.

Give him a task in her sight line: a laundry basket he can pull up on, or a
plastic bowl with three lids in it for his thumb and finger to work at. At 9
months he will offer things to her and then take them straight back, and she
has enough left in her today to find that funny. Watch that he does not haul
himself up on her blanket and land on her, because he will try it within the
first ten minutes.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **The build-up is more than she can hold, and the crash afterwards is normal.**
> Her first good morning in days arrives with an appetite for all of it, and
> she has no way to meter that. Her temperature came back to normal ahead of
> her sleep, her appetite and her patience, so the reserve she spends this
> morning is thinner than it feels to her. The two o'clock crash is the normal
> end of a morning she enjoyed. You already stop each thing before she asks,
> and that keeps the crash small enough to sleep off. Take the tears at two as
> the receipt for a good morning, hold the rest block where it is, and put her
> down at yesterday's bedtime rather than the usual one.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The sorting drawer is the hazard on this page. Forks, knives,
> chargers, rubber bands and coins reach the floor the moment she tips the
> tray, and Kreston is back on that floor today with a pincer grip and a mouth.
> Hand her the silverware or the charger drawer only while he is gated or
> asleep, give her the sock drawer any time he is beside her, and sweep the
> blanket with your hand before you let him near it. Call your doctor if the
> fever comes back after a clear day, if a cough gets worse after several days
> of getting better, or if she starts pulling at an ear, because each of those
> sits on top of the first virus. Preschool, the pool and anybody else's
> kitchen wait until she has gone a full day with no fever and no vomiting and
> has eaten a real meal. Keep her cup and her spoon apart from Kreston's for
> the rest of the week and wash your hands between the two of them.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="mar-extras"></a>

## 🎲 March — Extra Ideas

Ten minutes, no plan, and a child already asking. Everything on this page uses
what is in the house or on the walk you were taking anyway.

### 🎲 **Alternative Activities**

- **The Deepest Puddle on the Street.** She stands a stick in each one and you rank them shallow, deeper, deepest.
- **Under the Umbrella, Listening.** She sits under an open umbrella in the rain with her eyes shut and names what she hears.
- **What the Wind Takes First.** Hold up a ribbon, a leaf and a paper towel off the back step and see which one goes.
- **Boot Prints Down the Hall.** A roll of paper down the hallway and one walk across it in wet boots.
- **The Warmest Spot in the House.** She hunts for it with the back of her hand and marks the winner with a sticky note.
- **Ten Things That Rattle.** She shakes her way around the kitchen cabinets and lines up the loudest five.
- **The First Warm Step.** On the first mild afternoon, shoes off on the back step for two minutes and nothing else.
- **Counting the Buds on One Branch.** Same branch every few days, and the number climbs all month.
- **The Race Between Two Raindrops.** Pick two on the window and call the winner at the sill.
- **Everything That Fits in One Boot.** She loads it, you both count what came out.
- **The Mud Footprint Guessing Game.** You press a print in the mud with a shoe and she works out whose it is.

### 🎨 **Alternative Arts & Crafts**

- **Rain-Spotted Paper.** Chalk dust or marker dots on paper, held out in the rain for five seconds and brought straight back in.
- **Three Jars of Mud Paint.** Dirt and water at three thicknesses, painted onto a flattened box with a stick.
- **The Wind Spinner Off a Cereal Box.** A spiral cut from card, hung on thread by the window that always leaks air.
- **Gray Day Paper Chain.** One strip for every gray day this month, in every gray she can find in the crayon box.
- **Tissue Paper on a Wet Window.** Colored tissue squares pressed to damp glass, backlit whenever the sun does show up.
- **The Egg Carton Bulb Tray.** Cups torn off, painted, upended and pushed into a tray as a row of crocuses.
- **The Puddle Painted From Memory.** Back from the walk, she paints the biggest one she saw, before she looks at a photo.
- **A Kite That Only Works Indoors.** Ribbons taped to a stick and run down the hall at full speed.
- **The Sock Puppet With a Cold.** One sock, a marker, a scrap of tissue, and a voice she has heard all week.
- **Stamping With the Bottom of a Boot.** Paint on the sole, one press per sheet, a whole line of them along the hall.
- **The Weather Wheel for the Fridge.** A paper circle in quarters, a card arrow, and one turn every morning.

### 👶 **Kreston's Turn**

- **The Cruising Rail.** Two chairs pushed until their edges overlap, so he can sidestep the whole length with a hand on each.
- **The Muffin Tin and Six Lids.** One plastic lid dropped into every cup, taken out again, and dropped back in with a thumb and finger.
- **Puffs on the Tray.** A handful of cereal puffs spread wide, worked at with thumb and finger, all through her main event.
- **Waving From the Window.** Whoever leaves the house waves from the path and waits there until he waves back.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Small parts, and his hand works on all of them now**: beans, stones, dry pasta, torn paper strips, snails, the bottle caps and buttons on the 27th. Count them out at table height and count them back into the tin, and use a flat fridge magnet for the test on the 25th, because a small strong one means surgery.
- **Standing water**: the pouring buckets on the 10th, the dam tray on the 19th, the float-test dishpan on the 25th, the pulp bowl on the 26th, swimming every Tuesday. Two inches drown him, so tip every container out as you step away and stay in arm's reach at the pool.
- **String and cord**: the coat hanger scale on the 10th, the blind cords by the window chair on the 16th, the wall strings on the 17th, the wild corner boundary line on the 22nd, the truck pull cord on the 24th. Take every length down as the activity ends, and tie the blind cords up out of reach before she climbs.
- **Everything sitting at his new height**: four mugs of dye water on the 7th, the celery jars on the 11th, the cardboard hide on the 21st, the perfume jars on the 30th, the soil-filled glass jar on May 6. Push the wet things past the middle of the table, and tape the hide to the chair legs.
- **Adult-only steps**: the stovetop on the 2nd and the 8th, the kitchen knife on the 8th, the craft knife on every cut bottle (rain gauge, rot jars, filter, worm tower) and on the cardboard hide, the adult scissors most days, the broken glass and cans on the 22nd. Tape every cut rim before either child touches it, and keep Kreston out of the kitchen while a pan is on the stove.
- **Spring specific**: raw egg through Week 14, soil, compost and worm bedding all month, daffodil sap, foxglove and lily in her hands on the 30th, wasps at the butterfly plate on May 1, ticks by May 5. Scrub both children before food and before anyone lifts Kreston, keep every flower out of both mouths, and check hairlines, necks and behind the knees when you come in.

## Week 14: Egg-cellent Science 🥚
**📅 April 2 – April 8, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

One object, seven days. She paints six eggs on Friday, stacks a pile of books
on four eggshells on Saturday, shuffles one along the hall on the tops of her
feet like a penguin on Sunday, and lifts two out of a vinegar jar with the
shells eaten off them on Monday. The egg is strong, fragile, cheap, edible and
the right size for her hand, and every day this week takes it apart another
way.

No holiday lands in these seven days. Easter was last Sunday, so the eggs on
the table are the plain kind. Monday the 5th carries the month's calendar
work: April's handprint goes up beside January's, Azlyn gets a fresh pencil
mark on the door frame, and Kreston turns 10 months and gets his first line
four below hers. Friday opens the week with a second new year, six painted
eggs standing on the dinner table and a new set of questions taped to the
shelf beside the January time capsule.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **A dome carries weight.** Four eggshells hold a stack of books, then cave under one thumb the other way up.
- **Real size at real scale.** Six eggs drawn true to size, hummingbird to ostrich, taped along the hall floor and walked.
- **Sorting by a rule the object doesn't show.** Feathers, fur, scales and six legs cut clean across color.
- **Wax and oil push water off.** On a shell, on paper, on her coat in the rain, and in a jar she shakes herself.
- **Cracking, whisking and cooking.** Twelve eggs on Saturday, then her own fork and her own pan on Thursday with your hand over hers.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Two new years in one book is a useful idea
- Sanctioned rule-breaking is good for a rule-following child
- Trying and failing at something an animal does easily builds real respect
- Children can't perceive their own growth, and showing it matters
- Sorting into families is a more advanced move than sorting by color
- Resist techniques teach a real idea: some things repel others
- Doing your own version beside her beats helping with hers

---

### 💛 A Note from Joseph

> My mark from New Year's Day is still up on that door frame near the top,
> and on Monday two new ones go under it, her April line and Kreston's first.
> Three months between her January mark and this one, about two fingers wide,
> and she will put her thumb in that gap and ask about it all week. Saturday
> is twelve of the cheapest eggs in the store and one rule, which is that the
> shells go in the bowl. I put that day in on purpose. She has had be careful
> out of me all winter, and one morning of the opposite squares it up a
> little. Photograph the four question sheets on Friday before they go in the
> envelope, because I want what she says about her brother now, in April's
> words, before she has better ones.

---

> 👶 **Kreston is 9 months this week**. He pulls to stand on anything at knee
> height, picks up single small things between finger and thumb, and waves at
> every face he passes. **He turns 10 months on Monday the 5th**, and starts
> cruising the furniture, pointing at what he wants, and stopping when you say
> no.

**📅 Friday, April 2, 2027**
**Theme:** Egg-cellent Science

### 🌙 Prep Tonight

### 🌅 Opening Activity: One Egg Each

**🧰 You need:** the 6 cooled hard-boiled eggs · 1 permanent marker · 1 tray.

1. Put the cold eggs on the table and count the people in the house with her. Four, and two spares for the ones that crack. If nothing got boiled last night, put six on now and count the names while they cook, then cool them under the cold tap.
2. She hands one egg to each name out loud. Write the first letter on each base with the marker while she decides whose is whose.
3. Line them up on the tray. Every one gets painted at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Spring New Year Table

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 hard-boiled eggs, cooled
- Washable non-toxic poster paint in 4 colors
- 1 narrow brush and 1 wide brush
- 1 empty egg carton, cut down, as a drying rack
- 1 tray
- 1 permanent marker
- Paper towels

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Paper towels over the table, the cut-down carton at one end as the drying rack, the four paints in a row.
2. She starts with her own egg. Wide brush, one whole color, then straight into a hole in the carton to dry while she does the next.
3. Once all six have a base color, hand her the narrow brush. Spots, stripes, a face, whatever belongs to the person the egg is for. She decides what Kreston's looks like.
4. Paint one yourself while she works, and take her instructions on it.
5. When they are dry to the touch, turn each over and write the name in marker beside the letter.
6. Stand all six on the tray in the middle of the dinner table. They stay there until she is done with them.

> 💡 **Tip:** Persian families have kept a table like this for three thousand years, one painted egg for every person in the house. Tell her that while she paints.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Watching for Nesting Birds

Birds are building all over the street in the first week of April, and this
morning she supplies them. Cut a dozen short lengths of wool, none longer than
her thumb, and let her drape them over a low shrub, a fence wire and the gate
latch. Add a pinch of moss and the hair off her brush. Count what she leaves
out, and come back before dinner to count what is gone.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and picks up single small
> things between finger and thumb. Give him the lid you cut off the egg carton
> and let him work the hinge with that new grip while Azlyn paints. On the
> walk he waves at everyone, so face him outward.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Spring Questions

The time capsule has sat sealed on the high shelf since New Year's Day. Three
months on, she answers a second set of questions and they go up beside it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper, 4 sheets
- 1 pencil
- Crayons
- 1 envelope
- Masking tape
- Your phone, to photograph the answers

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Show her the sealed box on the shelf first, and remind her when it goes back down.
2. One question per sheet, written across the top in pencil: favorite color, favorite food, best thing about Kreston, what she wants to do when it gets warm.
3. Write her answer underneath **word for word**. If she gives you a story instead of an answer, take the story.
4. Read all four back to her in her own words and let her correct you.
5. Turn the fourth sheet over. Crayons, and she draws everyone in the house, Kreston included.
6. Photograph all four sheets before they go anywhere near the envelope.
7. Fold them in, let her seal it and scribble on the front, then write **OPEN DECEMBER 31** across it and tape it to the shelf edge beside the box.

> 💡 **Tip:** Resist steering her toward a better answer. The version you want to read in December is the one where she says her favorite food is ice cubes.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Questions only. Skip the envelope and stick the sheets on the fridge.
- Draw the family on one big sheet and stop there.
- Look back at January's photos and name who is in each one.
- Let her interview you, and write your answers down the same way.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Meet a friend at the park**, and take two painted eggs to show
- The green with a ball, if the friend falls through
- A café with a window and something to watch
- The long way round, to see whether the wool has gone off the fence
- A drive out to see the blossom before the wind takes it

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He gets his handprint and his height on the wall
> on Monday, so today he sits in on the questions. Put him on the floor by the
> table with a sheet of paper of his own. At 9 months he tears, crumples and
> tastes it. Say his name in her answers out loud.

### 🌍 Around the World: Japan, *Tamagoyaki* 🍳

Japanese cooks make *tamagoyaki* in a small rectangular pan, pouring egg in
thin layers and rolling each new one onto the last until the omelette is a
block of ten or twelve layers. It goes into lunch boxes cold, cut into slices
that show every layer. Tokyo cooks sweeten theirs with sugar. Osaka cooks
leave it savory.

> **✨ Try it:** You cook it on Thursday, in two pans, one each. Until then,
> cut a slice of any omelette and count the layers with her. There is one.

> *Did you know?* Sushi masters once judged an apprentice on his tamagoyaki
> before letting him near the fish.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Two new years in one book is a useful idea.**
> Azlyn has no working sense of a year. January 1 meant nothing to her beyond
> the noise, and December is not a place she can picture. What she can hold is
> a thing that comes round again. Marking a second new year this spring, with
> the Persian *Nowruz* behind us, the Thai and Cambodian new years in the
> middle of this month, and the blossom outside, gives her a second run at the
> same idea while the evidence is on the trees. Repeat the ritual and she gets
> time as a circle before she ever gets it as a number. Six painted eggs on
> the dinner table do that work for you all week.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** You boil the eggs tonight while Kreston is up. At 9 months he
> pulls to stand on anything at knee height, including the oven door, so he
> stays out of the kitchen the whole time the pan is on the stovetop. A chunk
> of hard-boiled egg is the exact size that blocks his airway. Count the eggs
> onto the tray and count them back. The painted eggs stand on the table all
> week as decoration, so nobody eats one.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Squeezing the Egg

**🧰 You need:** 1 raw egg · 1 large mixing bowl · soap and a towel at the sink.

1. Hold the egg down in the bowl and squeeze it in your whole fist, hard, no fingernails and no thumb on one spot. It holds.
2. Her turn. She will not break it, and will not believe that until she has tried three times.
3. Now tap the same egg once on the rim. Ask her why one hand could not do what one tap did, and leave her answer until 9:15. Soap and the towel at the sink first.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Books on the Eggshells

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4 empty half eggshells with the rims trimmed level
- 1 flat piece of thick card or a chopping board
- 10–15 books of similar size
- 1 tray to work on
- Masking tape
- Paper and a marker for the count

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Stand the four shells dome side up on the tray in a rectangle the size of the board, each stuck down with a curl of masking tape.
2. Lay the board flat across all four. Press the middle with one finger and let her feel that nothing moves.
3. First book on, flat and central. She places every one from here. Write **1** on the paper.
4. One book at a time, counting out loud and writing each number as it lands. Past eight she will start whispering.
5. When a shell goes, it goes with a crack and no warning. Circle the number that broke it.
6. Turn the surviving shells the other way up, dome down, and press one with a thumb. It caves at once.

> 💡 **Tip:** The dome sends the weight down the curve to the rim instead of into one spot. Say it after she has watched it happen.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Blossom Walk

Early April is the two weeks the blossom is out and the wind is waiting for
it. Stand under the loudest tree on your street. Cherry is pink and frilled,
crabapple deeper and a week or two behind it, redbud purple straight off the
bare wood, and all of them snow when the wind gets up. Let her catch petals,
then collect five off the ground, one from under each different tree.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and pulls to stand on anything
> that holds him. Give him two books off the pile at floor level and let him
> haul himself up on the sofa. The eggshells and the tray stay on the table.
> Under the blossom, hold him up to a low branch.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Permission to Smash

A dozen of the cheapest eggs in the store and one instruction: break them. She
has spent three months hearing you say be careful.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 12 eggs, the cheapest box
- 2 large mixing bowls
- 1 whisk and 1 fork
- 1 old towel on the floor
- 1 apron or an old shirt
- 1 shallow bowl for shells
- Warm soapy water and a cloth

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Towel under the table, apron on her, both mixing bowls and the shallow bowl in her reach.
2. Hand her the box. Eggs into the first bowl any way she likes, and say nothing about technique for the first eight.
3. Shells go into the shallow bowl as she goes. That is the one rule.
4. Keep the last four back. Crack each one and tip the yolk from half shell to half shell, letting the white run into the second bowl. Give her the fourth.
5. Whisk in her hand, second bowl in your lap. Clear, then cloudy, then white, then a foam that holds the whisk's shape.
6. Dip the fork in and lift it. A peak stands up on the tines and stays there.
7. Warm soapy water and the cloth. She does the table, you do the floor, everybody does hands.

> 💡 **Tip:** Eight eggs make a large omelette or tomorrow's pancakes. Say that out loud at the start.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Six eggs instead of twelve, straight into the pan.
- Whisk dishwater bubbles in the sink and skip the eggs.
- Crack them outside on the step, into a bucket.
- Meringue, if the foam has come out well enough to bake.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum**
- **The museum**, first Saturday of the month
- Whichever room has bones, eggs or birds in it, and skip the rest
- Indoor playground if the line is out of the door
- The park bench by the blossom tree from this morning
- The garden center, for the bird feeders and the seedlings

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes to the museum in the carrier. At 9
> months a big echoing room is a lot of work, so twenty minutes up high facing
> out, then a carpeted corner where he can pull up on a bench. Let Azlyn pick
> the room he sees.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sanctioned rule-breaking is good for a rule-following child.**
> Azlyn has spent the winter learning what she must not do with the good
> plates, the wall and the eggs. Handing her twelve eggs and permission to
> destroy them does not undo that, because the permission comes with a
> boundary she can see: this box, this bowl, this table. She gets to run the
> destructive impulse inside a frame you built. Children who get sanctioned
> outlets for the wild end of themselves push less at the edges of everything
> else, and she learns that a rule has a shape and an inside. Say the yes out
> loud and mean it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Raw egg carries salmonella and it will be on her hands, the
> table and the floor. Soap and warm water before anyone touches Kreston, the
> snack or a tap handle. Wipe drips as they land, because a wet floor is a
> fall for Kreston hauling himself upright on furniture. Broken shell has an
> edge on it, and he now picks up single small things and puts them in his
> mouth, so the shell bowl stays on the table.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: No Hands Allowed

**🧰 You need:** masking tape · 1 rolled pair of socks.

1. Run a strip of masking tape down the hall floor, three or four meters.
2. Walk the line together, feet turned out, arms flat at your sides. No arms from here on.
3. Balance the rolled socks on the tops of her feet and let her shuffle the line without dropping them. See how far she gets before they land.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Penguin Shuffle

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3 hard-boiled eggs
- Masking tape for the course line
- 1 folded towel as the landing pad
- A stopwatch or the phone timer
- Paper and a marker for the drop count

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. This morning's tape line is the course. A fresh strip of masking tape across the far end is the finish, and the folded towel down the middle is the landing pad.
2. Egg on the tops of her feet, ankles together, hands off. She shuffles the line without lifting a foot off the floor.
3. Every drop gets a stroke on the paper in marker. Do not comment on them.
4. Time how long she can hold one egg standing still. A male emperor penguin does it for two months in the dark at forty below, without eating.
5. The hand-off: she shuffles the egg onto your feet and you shuffle it back, hands behind your backs. Real penguins lose eggs here too.
6. Run the course with all three eggs at once if she is still in it. Count the survivors.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will want to use her hands, so give them a job. Have her hold her own elbows.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Waddle to the Corner

Walk to the end of the road the way the birds do. Penguin: feet out, arms
flat, tiny steps. Duck: same feet, lower. Heron: one slow leg at a time, knees
high. Pigeon: head forward and back with every step, which she does better
than you. Let her call the changes.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 9 months and waves at anything with a
> face. Sit him on a cushion past the finish line so Azlyn shuffles toward him
> and gets a wave each time she arrives. The eggs go back in the box between
> runs, because loose on the floor they are the size he chokes on.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Four Kinds of Beak

Four tools and four kinds of dinner. Every beak in the yard handles one and
fails at the other three.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 clothespins
- 1 teaspoon
- 1 drinking straw
- Kitchen tongs, or a second clothespin
- Dried pasta and uncooked rice
- 1 shallow bowl of water with torn lettuce floating in it
- String cut into short worms, buried in a tray of flour
- 4 small bowls

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Four stations along the table: dried pasta in one bowl, rice in a second, the shallow bowl of water with the lettuce on top, and the flour tray with the string worms buried in it.
2. The last two small bowls are the stomachs, hers and yours. Everything caught goes in.
3. Lay the beaks out: a clothespin each, the teaspoon, the straw, the tongs. She tries one on all four foods before swapping.
4. The clothespin cracks pasta out of the bowl like a finch, the tongs pull worms out of the flour like a robin, the teaspoon skims lettuce like a duck.
5. The straw looks useless until she sucks on it, caps the top with a finger and lifts one grain of rice. That is a hummingbird.
6. Ask her which beak she would want, then what a bird with tongs for a mouth does about the rice.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her thirty seconds a go and count out loud. A time limit turns it into a game.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Clothespins and pasta alone. One tool, one food, twenty minutes.
- Feed the birds outside instead and watch which beak turns up.
- Bury the worms in dry rice rather than flour and skip the mess.
- Draw four beaks on paper and match them to birds in her book.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Feeding the ducks**, with oats or defrosted peas rather than bread
- The pond edge, counting how many ducks tip up and how many dabble
- A long walk with the stroller and no destination
- The playground, for the tunnel and a run
- The riverside path, looking for a heron standing still

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes to the water in the carrier or the
> stroller and stays in one or the other the whole time you are near the edge.
> At 9 months ducks are the best moving thing he has seen all week. Hand Azlyn
> the food to show him.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Trying and failing at something an animal does easily builds real respect.**
> Azlyn dropped the egg off her feet eleven times this morning. A penguin
> holds one there for two months. She learned more about that bird in ten
> minutes of failing at its job than she would from a photograph and a fact,
> because the difficulty went through her own ankles. Attempting an animal's
> movement gives a child a body-level measure of what the animal is doing, and
> the respect that comes out of it holds in a way that admiration does not.
> She will tell someone about the penguins this week, and the thing she tells
> them will be how hard it was.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Dried pasta, uncooked rice and chunks of hard-boiled egg all
> end up on the floor today, and every one is a choking size for a 9-month-old
> who picks up single small things and mouths them. Sweep between activities
> rather than at the end, keep the bowls at the far side, and put him down on
> a floor you have looked at. Azlyn sucks in on the straw, so sit level with
> her and keep the rice bowl low. If she is a big inhaler, swap the rice for
> puffed cereal or drop the straw station. Count the string worms into the
> flour and count them back out, because a short length of string goes down
> him faster than the pasta does.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Rinsing Off the Shell

**🧰 You need:** the jar of vinegar eggs · 1 bowl of cool water · paper towels.

1. Lift both eggs out over the bowl. They are heavier than she expects and the shell has gone. A day and a half in vinegar ate it.
2. Rub the last white grit off under the water with your thumb. Let her do the second, flat hands, no fingers pushing.
3. Roll them dry on paper towels and let her hold one in two cupped palms. Ask what happened to the shell and leave her answer until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Egg With No Shell

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 raw eggs soaked 36 hours in a jar of white vinegar
- 2 clean jars
- Plain water
- Corn syrup, or 6 tablespoons of salt stirred into water
- String and 1 pair of scissors (**adult only**)
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 sheet of card to tape the measured strings to
- Masking tape
- 1 flashlight

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Curtains shut. Hold the flashlight under one egg in her cupped hands. It lights up orange, the yolk a dark ball in the middle.
2. Bounce one from an inch above your open palm and let it land back in it. It gives and comes back. Two inches, no more: it is raw inside and will burst.
3. Wrap string round the fattest part of each egg, mark where it meets and cut there. You do the cutting. Tape both lengths to the card and write **MONDAY** beside them.
4. Fill one jar with plain water and the other with corn syrup. Label them with the marker and lower an egg into each.
5. Ask her which one will get bigger and write her answer on the card under the strings.
6. Both jars go on a high shelf where she can see them. She checks at 4:15, and you measure again with fresh string tomorrow.

> 💡 **Tip:** Water walks into the egg through its skin and syrup pulls it back out, so by tomorrow one is a water balloon and the other is wrinkled.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Gatepost

Walk the New Year's Day route again and stop at the gatepost you have stopped
at all winter. The first trees are breaking bud and most of the street is
still bare. Put her hand flat on the same post and ask what has changed since
the frost walk. Count the ones with green on them today, because in three
weeks the count runs the other way.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** **Kreston turns 10 months today.** He cruises the
> sofa sideways, hand over hand, and points at what he wants instead of
> grabbing. On the walk, stop when he points and name the thing. Say happy ten
> months out loud, because nobody else will.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The April Handprint

January's handprint sheet has been on the wall since Day 1. April's goes up
next to it, and Kreston gets his first line on the door frame today.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Thick card, 2 sheets
- Washable non-toxic poster paint
- 1 wide soft brush
- 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
- 1 pencil and 1 measuring tape
- 1 permanent marker
- Poster putty, for putting both cards up
- January's handprint sheet, for the comparison

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Paint her palm with the wide brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat on the first card, count to three, lift straight up. Write **April** and **3** in marker.
2. Kreston next on the second card, while he is calm and the washcloth is in your hand. Write **April** and **10 months**.
3. Both of them against the door frame. Mark with the pencil, run the measuring tape from the floor and write the number and date on the wall. His first line lands four below hers.
4. Lay January's sheet next to April's and let her put her hand on both prints. She will do it twice.
5. Find January's pencil mark on the door frame and put her thumb on the gap. Three months, about the width of two fingers.
6. Both cards go up on poster putty somewhere she passes, not into a drawer.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do her print first while your hands are clean, and keep the wet washcloth in the bowl beside you the whole time you are doing Kreston's.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Handprints and nothing else. The wall marks can wait a day.
- Draw round her whole hand in pencil instead of painting it.
- Draw round her feet and compare those to January.
- Measure everyone in the house, including the tallest and the teddy.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The field walk**, out to where the grass has come up since March
- The footpath along the hedge, checking for nests in the low branches
- The neighborhood park, for the swings and the run home
- The lane, if there are lambs in anybody's field this week

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He cruises the sofa and the coffee table now, so
> both egg jars come off any low surface once the measuring is done. At 10
> months he understands **no** and stops, then checks your face. Put a low box
> of his own things where he cruises past.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Children can't perceive their own growth, and showing it matters.**
> Azlyn cannot feel herself getting bigger. From the inside she has always
> been this size, so the January handprint under her April one is the first
> evidence she has ever had. Children build a sense of themselves through time
> out of external markers, and a three-year-old needs the marker to be
> physical: a hand that no longer fits, a pencil line she has passed, a coat
> from the winter. She will ask to check it, over and over. Keeping the sheets
> where she can reach them turns a craft activity into the thing she uses to
> answer her own question about growing up.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The shell-less egg is raw inside and bursts if she grips it,
> so hands get washed with soap after every hold. Both jars go up high,
> because Kreston cruises furniture this month and pulls down whatever his
> hand lands on. The scissors stay with you.

**📅 Tuesday, April 6, 2027**
**Theme:** Egg-cellent Science

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Measure the two egg jars again before bed and tape the new strings up beside yesterday's. Put six sheets of paper, the ruler and one hen egg on the table, and the swimming bag by the door.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Six Eggs on One Sheet

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 pencil · 1 hen egg.

1. Stand the hen egg on the paper and draw round it. That shape is the one she knows.
2. Ask her to draw the smallest egg she can imagine next to it, then the biggest that will still fit on the sheet.
3. Ask which bird lays each one. Take her answers and put the sheet aside. She finds out how close she got at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: From Hummingbird to Ostrich

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper, 6 sheets
- 1 pencil and 1 pair of child-safe scissors
- Crayons
- 1 real hen egg to trace
- 1 quail egg, or a large dried lima bean as the stand-in
- Masking tape or poster putty
- 1 ruler

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Six sheets, one egg on each, drawn at true size with the ruler and the pencil: hummingbird 1 cm, robin 2 cm, quail 3 cm, hen 6 cm, goose 9 cm, ostrich 15 cm.
2. Trace the hen egg for the fourth and stand the quail egg (or the bean) on the third while you draw it.
3. She cuts out the four biggest with her child-safe scissors. You do the hummingbird and the robin, which are fiddly cuts.
4. Crayons, and she draws the bird beside each egg. Sizes out loud: a hummingbird sits in your palm, an ostrich is taller than Dad.
5. Lay all six along the hall floor smallest to biggest and tape them down against the baseboard.
6. Walk the line with her, the hummingbird end to the ostrich end and back. She will do it on her own nine more times before bed.

> 💡 **Tip:** One ostrich egg is worth around twenty-four hen eggs, and it takes an hour and a half to hard-boil.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Birds From One Bench

Pick a bench near a hedge, sit down and stay there for fifteen minutes. Count
how many different birds land and name Sunday's tools by their beaks: the
sparrow has a clothespin, the robin has tongs. Bring a handful of oats, let
her put them out, then sit back down.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and has started pointing at
> what he wants you to look at. On the bench he points at movement before you
> spot it. Name whatever he picks out, right or wrong, then wait. He often
> points again to check you got the same one.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Feathers, Scales and Six Legs

Her animal toys come out of the box and she sorts them by what the animal has
on the outside.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Her animal toys, 15–20
- An old magazine or supermarket catalog
- 1 glue stick and 1 pair of child-safe scissors
- 4 sheets of paper or 4 paper plates
- 1 marker to draw the four headings

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Four sheets across the floor. Draw a heading on each with the marker: a feather, a patch of fur, a scale, a six-legged bug. Say the words and let her repeat them.
2. Tip the animals out. One at a time, she decides which sheet each one belongs beside.
3. Take the hard ones at face value. A penguin has feathers and does not fly. A whale has neither fur nor scales, and if she puts it with the fish, ask what it breathes.
4. When she gets stuck, hand her the animal and ask what her hand finds.
5. Magazine next. She cuts out any animal she can find with her child-safe scissors while you tear out the fiddly ones.
6. Glue each cutting onto the sheet she picks. Wrong ones stay where she put them.
7. Count each pile out loud and see which family won. Leave all four sheets out beside the toy box.

> 💡 **Tip:** Feathers and fur cut clean across color, so a brown bird and a brown dog land on different sheets.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Two headings instead of four. Feathers and everything else.
- Sort the toys by how many legs and stop there.
- Find one of each family in her books rather than her toy box.
- Sort the paper eggs from this morning by size again, then by bird.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one, and try her floating on her front with your hand under her chin
- Indoor playground if the pool is closed for a school session
- The library, a day early
- A café with wet hair and something warm
- The park on the way home, for twenty minutes of dry land

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes to the pool, and twenty minutes in the
> water is plenty at 10 months. Hold him under the arms and walk him along the
> bottom. Dress him before yourself.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sorting into families is a more advanced move than sorting by color.**
> Color sits on the surface and Azlyn has been sorting by it since she was
> two. Feathers, fur and scales ask her to hold a rule the object does not
> show at a glance and apply it to a brown bird and a brown dog with different
> answers. That move, grouping by a property she has decided matters and
> ignoring the loud one, is the beginning of category thinking, and it runs
> underneath reading, number work and science. Her wrong answers are worth
> more than her right ones today, because a wrong one means she is using a
> rule rather than a memory.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The quail egg, or the dried lima bean standing in for it,
> sits in a bowl on the far side of the table and goes away the moment the
> drawing is done. Both are a choking size for a 10-month-old, so neither goes
> on the floor and neither is left within Kreston's reach. The child-safe
> scissors stay at the table and come back to your hand between cuts. Poolside
> tile is wet, and Kreston pulls up on the steps and the rail without any idea
> of the drop, so one hand stays on him the whole time.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Invisible Drawing

**🧰 You need:** 1 white wax crayon · paper, 2 sheets · 1 dark crayon with the paper peeled off.

1. White crayon on white paper, pressing hard. She draws and the drawing vanishes as she makes it.
2. Lay the dark crayon on its side and rub it flat across the whole sheet. Her lines come back through the color.
3. Second sheet: she leaves you a message you cannot see, and you find it. Say nothing about why it works until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Lines the Dye Can't Cross

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 hard-boiled eggs, cooled
- 1 white wax crayon and a stub of white candle
- Food coloring in 4 colors
- White vinegar, 4 teaspoons
- 4 mugs of hand-warm water
- 1 slotted spoon
- Paper towels and 1 empty egg carton for drying

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Four mugs of hand-warm water, a teaspoon of vinegar in each, ten drops of a different color per mug. Stir with the slotted spoon handle.
2. She draws hard on the cold eggs with the white crayon. Nothing shows, so she works blind. Two get the candle stub, which lays a fatter line.
3. Lower two eggs into two different mugs with the slotted spoon. Three minutes for pale, six or seven for deep.
4. Lift the first out and roll it on paper towels. Every line she drew comes up white.
5. Dye the rest. Try one egg half in one mug and half in another, and one dipped, dried, crayoned again and dipped a second time.
6. Stand all six in the carton to dry, then on the table beside Friday's painted ones.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cold eggs take color slower and hold it better. If a mug comes out weak, another teaspoon of vinegar beats another ten drops of color.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Water That Won't Soak In

April gives you a wet sidewalk most days this week, so go out in it. Water
beads and rolls off her coat, the hood of a car and the waxy top of an ivy
leaf, and sinks into her jeans, the path and a paper bag. Let her tip a puddle
onto a leaf and watch the drop sit up like a bead.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and cruises the furniture,
> which puts his hands at table height. The dye mugs stay at the far side of
> the table for the whole hour. Give him a plastic cup and a dry pastry brush
> at floor level, and he copies the brushing.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Jar That Won't Mix

Wax kept the dye off the shell this morning. Oil does the same to water, and
this one she can shake.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 clean jars with lids
- Cooking oil, 1 cup plus 3 tablespoons
- Water
- Food coloring
- 1 teaspoon
- Dish soap
- Vinegar, oil and a pinch of salt for the dinner dressing
- 1 small bottle or jar with a tight lid

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Half fill both jars with water, then half a cup of oil into each. The oil climbs to the top.
2. Lids on tight. She shakes the first jar hard and sets it down. Count while it comes apart again, about twenty seconds.
3. Two drops of food coloring into the first jar. The color falls through the oil and dyes the water underneath.
4. One teaspoon of dish soap into the second jar. Lid on, shake, and this one stays cloudy. Check both again after ten minutes.
5. The dressing next. Into the small bottle: three spoons of oil, one of vinegar, a pinch of salt. She shakes it until it goes thick and pale.
6. Put it in the fridge. At 4:00 it will have separated and she shakes it again for the table.
7. Ask her which jar the dressing is like.

> 💡 **Tip:** Dish soap works because one end of it grabs oil and the other grabs water. That is also why it gets the pan clean.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One jar, no dish soap. Shake it and watch it split.
- Drop cooking oil into a bowl of water and chase it with a spoon.
- Wax crayon on paper and a watery paint wash over the top.
- Float pepper on water and touch it with a soapy finger.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Church hall playgroup**, and take two dyed eggs to hand over
- Indoor playground, if the hall is shut this week
- The park with the shelter, for rain that has not stopped
- The store, and let her carry one thing on the list
- Home early with the eggs, if the morning has been enough

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At playgroup he is a cruiser among crawlers and
> heads for the furniture rather than the mat, so find him a low bench to work
> along. He understands **no** this month and stops on it, which is worth
> saving for the door and the steps.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Resist techniques teach a real idea: some things repel others.**
> The white crayon on the egg and the oil in the jar are the same fact twice.
> Wax and oil push water away, and Azlyn has now watched that happen on a
> shell, on paper, on her coat in the rain and in a jar she shook herself. A
> three-year-old builds a concept out of repeated instances in different
> materials rather than an explanation, and four in one day is a strong run at
> it. She will not have the word for it. She will have the expectation that
> water beads on some things and sinks into others, and the habit of checking
> which.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Four mugs of hand-warm dye water sit at table-edge height
> today with a 10-month-old cruising the furniture and pulling down whatever
> his hand finds. Keep them past the middle of the table and empty them the
> moment the last egg is out. Vinegar stings in eyes, so wash her hands before
> she rubs her face, and food coloring stains everything it lands on.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Two Bowls, Two Forks

**🧰 You need:** 6 eggs · 2 bowls · 2 forks · soap at the sink.

1. Three eggs into her bowl, three into yours. She has cracked a dozen since Saturday and is better at it.
2. A fork each, and beat until the yolk and the white are one color. Hers will have lumps and cook fine.
3. Both bowls into the fridge, both pairs of hands washed with soap. The pans come out at 9:15 and she gets her own.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Tamagoyaki, Twice

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 eggs
- Milk or water, 1 tablespoon
- Soy sauce, 1 teaspoon
- Sugar, 1 pinch
- Cooking oil
- 2 small non-stick frying pans, or one pan and take turns
- 2 bowls and 2 forks
- 1 spatula
- 1 chopping board and 2 plates
- 1 knife (**adult only**)

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Both bowls out of the fridge, three eggs in each. A tablespoon of milk between them, half a teaspoon of soy each, the pinch of sugar split. She stirs hers with her fork.
2. Both pans on a low heat with a smear of oil. She stands beside you at the stovetop, your body between her and the burner, and you hold her pan handle throughout.
3. She pours a thin layer into her pan, enough to coat the bottom. Wait until the top stops looking wet.
4. Spatula in her hand with yours over it. Roll the sheet from the far edge toward you, push the roll back, oil the gap, pour the next layer in and lift the roll so the raw egg runs underneath.
5. Three or four layers each. Yours will be neater. Hers is a rolled omelette either way.
6. Tip both onto the board, let them sit a minute, then cut into thick slices onto the two plates. Count the layers in her slice.

> 💡 **Tip:** Low heat is the whole technique. A hot pan browns the layers so they stop sticking to each other, and the roll falls apart on the board.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Chalk Eggs on the Path

Take the chalk out to the path and draw Tuesday's six eggs again at sidewalk
scale. The ostrich egg comes out as big as she is, and she can lie inside the
outline. Draw the hummingbird one beside her thumb. Let her fill them in and
leave the lot for the rain.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and copies what he sees hands
> doing. Sit him on the path with one fat piece of chalk and he bangs it,
> drags it, then looks at the mark. Keep it out of his mouth. Put him in the
> middle of the drawing.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Book of What Happened

Seven days of eggs, and she has forgotten Friday. A stapled paper book puts
the week back in order, and you make one too.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper, 12 sheets
- 1 stapler
- Crayons and 1 pencil
- Your phone, for the week's photos
- 1 glue stick, for anything she wants stuck in

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Six sheets folded in half for each book, three staples down each spine. Let her push the stapler with your hand over hers. One book each.
2. Scroll the week's photos in order and name the days: painted eggs, books on shells, the penguin shuffle, the egg with no shell, six paper eggs, the dyeing, the pans.
3. One page per day. She draws first, and you write her sentence along the bottom in pencil, word for word.
4. Fill your own book at the same table and keep your hands off hers. She will look over.
5. Glue stick for anything she wants stuck in: a torn corner of yesterday's crayon sheet, one of Tuesday's small paper eggs.
6. Last page each. She names her favorite day and you write it down. Write yours in yours.
7. Swap books and read each other's back, out loud, cover to cover.

> 💡 **Tip:** Her sentence goes down as she says it. "The egg went bouncy" is the whole caption.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One page, not seven. The best day of the week and nothing else.
- Print six photos and let her put them in order on the floor.
- Tell the week back to a grandparent on the phone instead.
- Draw the whole week as one long picture across the back of a cereal box.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The thrift store**, with two dollars of her own to spend on a book
- The bookstore window and the bakery next door, if the store is closed
- The park, for a run before the store
- The library, to hand back what came home last week
- The bird feeder aisle at the garden center, after the week you have had

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Take him into the thrift store in the carrier
> facing out. At 10 months he points at things across a room, so follow his
> finger. Let Azlyn choose a board book for him and carry it to the register.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Doing your own version beside her beats helping with hers.**
> You cooked your own omelette this morning and made your own book this
> afternoon, and both times you left hers alone. That arrangement gives Azlyn
> a model she can watch without a correction attached to it. Children copy
> what they see competent adults doing and ignore most of what those adults
> tell them to do, so working next to her puts the whole demonstration on
> offer while the decisions stay hers. She also gets to see you make a mess of
> a layer and carry on, which is a harder thing to teach on purpose than any
> of the science this week.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A hot pan and hot oil at stovetop height with a 10-month-old
> cruising toward the oven door. He stays out of the kitchen for the cooking
> hour, in the highchair or behind a gate, and every pan handle turns inward.
> The knife is yours for the slicing and goes back out of reach the moment the
> board is clear. Raw egg goes on her hands, the forks and the board, so soap
> and warm water before either child touches anything else.
