## 🌟 Day 120: Petals and Perfume 🌟
**📅 Friday, April 30, 2027**
**Theme:** Bugs & Blooms

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand any past-it flowers in a pitcher on the table, with three clean jam jars, the sieve and a wooden spoon beside them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Taking a Flower to Pieces
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Perfume in a Jam Jar (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Filling the Petal Bag (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Bashing the Color Out of the Petals (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Flower Press
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: A Petal in the Bath
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Taking a Flower to Pieces

**🧰 You need:** 3 flowers past their best · 1 white plate · 1 damp cloth.

1. Hand her a whole flower and let her pull it apart onto the plate. Three piles: petals, leaves, and the middle with the pollen on it.
2. Name the parts while her hands are on them: petal, stem, leaf, pollen. Rub a fingertip through the pollen and look at the yellow on it. You smell it and tell her what it smells of.
3. Tell her the petal pile becomes perfume at 9:15. Wipe her hands with the damp cloth before they reach her face.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Perfume in a Jam Jar

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3 clean jam jars with lids
- 1 bunch of past-it flowers, or petals off the garden
- 1 sprig of mint or rosemary
- Half a lemon
- Warm water in a pitcher
- 1 wooden spoon
- 1 sieve
- 1 small funnel, or a cone folded from paper
- Sticky labels and 1 pencil

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Petals into the first jar, hers from this morning and the rest off the bunch, until it is half full. Press them down with the spoon.
2. Tear the mint or rosemary and drop it in. Squeeze the half lemon over the top, pips and all.
3. Pour warm water from the pitcher over the petals until the jar is two thirds full. Warm, not hot.
4. Give her the wooden spoon and let her mash. It takes ten minutes. The water turns the color of the flowers.
5. Lid on, one good shake, then hold the sieve over the second jar and pour it through. Press the pulp with the spoon, tip it away and rinse the first jar.
6. Stand the funnel in the third jar and let her share the perfume between all three. Labels, pencil, and she says whose is whose. Three jars and four people, so somebody doubles up.

> 💡 **Tip:** Warm water pulls more smell out than cold, and the lot turns in two or three days, so use it today. Kreston's jar gets sniffed and never worn.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Filling the Petal Bag

Everything this afternoon needs comes off this walk, so hand her the paper bag
at the door. Work low: the flowerbed by the wall where the tulips have blown
open and dropped, the violets in the grass strip, a flat leaf off anything
with a strong vein down the middle. Leave whatever is still standing on a stem
in somebody's front yard. Ask her which colors will print, take her guess as
it comes, and write it on the bag in pencil so you can read it back at one
o'clock.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and points at whatever he
> wants named. Walk him along the flowerbed at your hip and answer every
> point, including the fourth one. Back at the table, give him his own wooden
> spoon on the high chair tray. He picks it up with finger and thumb, drops it
> over the side and wants it back, and it goes in his mouth where a petal must
> not.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Bashing the Color Out of the Petals

The color in a petal comes out under a wooden spoon and prints straight onto
cloth.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 old white pillowcase or T-shirt, or 4 sheets of thick paper
- Fresh petals and flat leaves
- Baking paper
- 1 wooden spoon or a rolling pin
- 1 chopping board
- Masking tape
- Paper towels

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the chopping board on the table and spread the pillowcase over it, one layer thick. Tape the corners down so it cannot shift.
2. She lays petals face down with gaps between them. Pull the stems and fat middles off first, since thick things smear.
3. Add two or three flat leaves. A leaf prints its veins.
4. Cover the lot with a sheet of baking paper and tape two corners of that down as well.
5. Hand her the wooden spoon and let her tap. Steady taps over every petal until the color comes through the baking paper.
6. Peel the paper back and lift the flattened petals off with paper towels. Look at what stayed behind.
7. Slide the cloth along, tape it on a clean patch and start again. Leave it flat over a chair back to dry.

> 💡 **Tip:** Dark petals print hardest and yellow tends to give nothing at all. Let her waste four or five finding that out for herself.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Petals in a tray of water with a spoon, and nothing else.
- Glue the flattened petals onto card instead of printing them.
- Sort this morning's petals by color into an egg box.
- Draw round the leaves and color inside the outlines.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Playgroup**, with the printed pillowcase in the bag to show
- A friend's garden, where the flowers are different from yours
- The park, for the blossom lying under the big trees
- A walk to post a jar of perfume through somebody's door
- The corner store for lemons, since she used yours

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 10 months and cruising, so he arrives
> at the table edge the moment the spoon starts banging. Give him his own end
> of it: a sheet of baking paper taped flat to his tray. He flattens it with
> both palms while she hammers.

### 🌍 Around the World: Bugs Everywhere 🐛

About two billion people eat insects as everyday food. Market stalls in Oaxaca
sell **chapulines**, grasshoppers toasted with lime and chili, by the bagful.
Cambodian cooks fry crickets with garlic. In Botswana and Zimbabwe, dried
**mopane worms** sell like beans and carry more protein by weight than beef.

> **✨ Try it:** Honey on toast, and tell her which insect made it. Kreston
> gets none of it, because honey is off limits under one year old.

> *Did you know?* One honeybee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in
> her whole life.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Smell is wired directly to memory in a way the other senses aren't.**
> Everything Azlyn sees and hears goes through a relay station in the middle
> of her brain before it reaches memory and feeling. Smell skips the relay.
> The nerves in her nose run to the olfactory bulb, which sits next door to
> the hippocampus and the amygdala, so a smell arrives with a memory and a
> feeling attached. That is why one can knock the wind out of you thirty years
> on. The smells she meets at three are the ones she will recognize at forty,
> and a jar of mashed petals files itself somewhere permanent. Name what she
> is smelling while her nose is still in it, because the word files itself
> alongside.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Daffodil sap, foxglove and lily are toxic if chewed, and she
> has garden flowers in her hands all day. Nothing goes near a mouth, hers or
> Kreston's, and both get their hands washed before snack. Kreston is 10
> months and cruises to whatever sits at his height, so the glass jars stay at
> the back of the table. The perfume gets a label, and it is not a drink.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Cutting the Fair Shares

**🧰 You need:** 1 soft banana and 1 soft apple · 1 table knife · 2 plates.

1. Ask her how many people live in the house. Four. Then ask who else in the yard eats fruit.
2. Give her the table knife and the banana and let her cut the shares. You do the apple. The pieces will be uneven and the count off. Leave both.
3. One plate for the people, one for the bugs. The family plate goes back for snack, the bug plate goes out at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Butterfly Plate

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 saucer or a plastic tub lid
- Overripe banana, apple or orange
- 2 tsp sugar
- Warm water
- 1 small sponge or 1 cotton ball
- 1 shallow dish
- A handful of pebbles
- Chalk to mark the spot

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip the bug share onto the saucer and let her squash it flat with her thumb.
2. Tip the sugar into the shallow dish, add a splash of warm water and let her stir with a finger until the grains vanish.
3. Soak the sponge in it, squeeze it once, and set it on the saucer next to the fruit.
4. Rinse the dish, fill it a thumb deep and stand the pebbles in it. Bees drown in open water and need a stone to land on.
5. Pick the spot together: full sun, up on a wall, clear of the door, the stroller and anywhere you eat. Saucer down, dish beside it, chalk a ring round it.
6. Check it at 11:00, after lunch and before dinner. Flies and ants come first, so tell her that now.

> 💡 **Tip:** Butterflies want it rotten, so a banana gone black beats a fresh one. The plate does its best work tomorrow.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Ant Trail

Ants are out in force by the first of May. Find a line along a paving joint
and follow it until it goes underground. Put a crumb from her snack half an
inch off the trail and sit back. The first ant to find it comes back with
company.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and got a share this morning
> because Azlyn counted him in. Put his banana on his tray while she carries
> the bug plate out. Outside, sit him facing the ant line. He tracks small
> moving things and points at them to show you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: A Butterfly for Every Person

Color bleeding through wet paper towels takes four seconds and she cannot
predict any of it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper towels or coffee filters, 6 sheets
- Washable markers
- 1 small bowl of water and 1 teaspoon
- 5–6 clothespins
- String or pipe cleaners
- 1 tray
- Tape and 1 length of string to hang them

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay a sheet of paper towels flat on the tray. Fat blobs and thick stripes of marker, no pictures, white gaps between.
2. Dip the teaspoon in the bowl and dribble water over the color. The lines spread and run together.
3. Lift the sheet with two hands, because it tears when wet, and lay it somewhere warm. Color the next while that one dries.
4. Gather a dry sheet along its middle into a concertina and clip a clothespin over the pinch. Wings both sides, clothespin as the body.
5. Twist a pipe cleaner round the top of the clothespin for antennae, or tie on a short length of string.
6. One butterfly per person. She hands them out and says who gets which.
7. Tape the length of string across the window frame and let her clip the butterflies along it.

> 💡 **Tip:** Washable markers bleed and permanent ones sit there doing nothing. Test one on a corner first.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- A folded coffee filter dipped corner-first in the water.
- Clothespins and paper, no water, and color the wings in dry.
- Cut butterfly shapes from yesterday's printed cloth.
- Count what flies past the window in ten minutes.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum**
- **The museum**, first Saturday of the month, and the bug case first
- The garden center greenhouse, warm and full of things flying
- A bus into town, if the museum line has beaten you
- The park with the big flowerbeds, and count what is on them
- Straight home to the window butterflies, if the morning was enough

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 10 months and the museum is ceiling
> from where he sits. Take him out in the biggest, quietest room and let him
> cruise a bench with your hand at his back. He points at whatever is high up
> and lit, so follow the point and name it. Forty minutes, then the stroller.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Fairness is the strongest moral instinct a three-year-old has.**
> Azlyn will hand a cookie to a child she has never met and refuse Kreston a
> crayon inside the same minute, and both come off the same instinct. Three
> year olds track who got what with an accuracy that outstrips their counting.
> Put four grapes and two children in front of her and she splits them two and
> two long before she can tell you what two and two makes. Sharing with a
> butterfly she has never seen stretches the same muscle, and it costs her
> something real, which is the part that works. Let her set the size of the
> bug share.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Sugar water and rotting fruit pull in wasps as well as
> butterflies. Site the plate well away from the door, the stroller and
> anywhere you eat, and neither child stands over it. Nobody swats anything.
> If a wasp comes to her, stand still with her and let it leave.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: One Sheet, Eight Pages

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of letter paper · 1 pair of adult scissors · 1 pencil.

1. Fold the sheet in three thirty times, letting her press each crease with her thumb. Open it flat and count the eight boxes.
2. Fold it back in half the long way and cut along the center crease to the middle. You cut, she holds. Push the ends together and it opens into a book.
3. She writes her name on the front in pencil. Everything this week goes in here.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Four Sticks and a Piece of String

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4 sticks or craft sticks
- 2 m string
- 4 clothespins
- The folded notebook from 8:00
- Crayons and 1 pencil
- Clear tape
- 1 jam jar of water, used as a magnifier

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Let her choose the square: somewhere she can kneel, that nobody is mowing, and that she can see from the door.
2. Push the four sticks into the ground in a square, an arm's length a side. Tape round the top of each so they show from the house.
3. Run the string round all four and hold it with a clothespin at each stick.
4. Both of you down on your fronts. Count out loud what is in there: flowers, different leaves, anything moving. Stand the jam jar of water in front of something small and look through the glass.
5. Page one of the notebook. She draws what is inside with the crayons, you write the date and her words underneath in pencil.
6. Nothing else goes on page one. She draws the same square on Tuesday and Thursday, on pages two and three.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not move the string when the first page comes out thin. Three dandelions and a pill bug is the measurement.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Sidewalk Crack Flowers

Walk the street with your eyes down. Dandelions, chickweed, moss and the odd
violet come up through cracks in the sidewalk and out of the joint where the
wall meets the path. Ask her how a flower gets into a crack with no soil in
it. Count how many you pass before the corner, and pick none of them.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and understands *no*, which
> he shows by stopping for a second and then carrying on. The square of grass
> is the one thing he cannot crawl through today, so put him down the far side
> of you with a stick of his own, sanded blunt and longer than his forearm. He
> turns it over and works the grain with his thumb.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Flower That Opens on the Water

Paper takes on water and swells along its fibers, enough to push a folded
petal open with nobody touching it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper, 6–8 sheets
- Scissors (adult)
- Crayons or markers
- 1 dishpan or a baking tray
- Water
- 1 towel

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Draw a flower on a sheet with a crayon: a middle and six fat petals. Cut it out with the adult scissors while she holds the sheet.
2. She colors it, both sides. The more crayon goes on, the longer the paper takes to soak.
3. Fold each petal in to the middle, one lapping over the next, until it makes a bud in her palm.
4. Fill the bowl with two inches of water and stand it in the middle of the table.
5. Lay the bud on the surface, folds up, and take her hands away. Count out loud. It opens on its own inside thirty seconds.
6. Do the rest, changing one thing each time: more crayon, tighter folds, a bigger flower. Ask her which will be slowest.
7. Tip the water out the moment she is finished and dry the table with the towel.

> 💡 **Tip:** The last one can sit on the water while she watches it go to mush, and then it comes out with the water. Nothing stays on the table.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Fold and float paper boats in the same bowl instead.
- Draw the square of grass again from memory, indoors.
- Tear paper petals and stick them on a card flower.
- Cups and a sieve in the sink, no plan at all.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The sunset walk**, and it stays light past eight this month, so take the long loop
- Feeding the ducks with the last of the soft bread
- A new playground two streets past your usual one
- The long way round, past the square she clipped out this morning
- A scooter run to the mailbox and back

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 10 months and stands at the sofa arm
> for whole minutes. Once the bowl is emptied, hand him the wet towel. He
> drags it and drapes it over his head, a game he found this month.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A record makes slow change perceptible.**
> Azlyn cannot see a plant grow. The change runs slower than a three year
> old's memory can hold, and last week for her is a fog with a few bright
> things in it. A drawing fixes one day in a form she can hold up against
> another one. Thursday's page beside Sunday's page does the work her memory
> cannot: two dandelions become five, the bare patch fills in, something has
> legs that was not there before. She is using a notebook the way a scientist
> uses one, for the same reason. Keep the wrong drawings, because the
> comparison needs both ends.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A bowl of water at floor height and a 10 month old who pulls
> up on furniture. Two inches is enough to drown in. The bowl goes on the
> table or stays within your arm's reach, and it gets tipped out the moment
> she is finished. The scissors stay with you.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Sieving the Soil

**🧰 You need:** 2 cups garden soil or compost · 1 sieve · 1 large bowl · newspaper.

1. Spread the newspaper over the table and stand the bowl in the middle of it.
2. Hand her the sieve and let her shake soil through by the handful. Stones and roots stay on top.
3. Look at what stayed in the sieve before you tip it back outside. Hands away from her face until they are washed.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Seed Balls for the Bare Patch

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 cups compost or garden soil
- 1 cup all-purpose flour
- Water in a pitcher
- 1 packet wildflower or herb seed (substitute: seed shaken out of a dandelion head, or seeds scooped from a supermarket tomato)
- 1 large bowl
- 1 sieve
- 1 baking tray
- Newspaper to work on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Newspaper still down, sieved soil in the bowl. Sieve another scoop if there is less than two cups in there.
2. Add the cup of flour on top and let her mix the two dry with both hands until the color is even.
3. Water from the pitcher, a splash at a time. Stop when a squeezed handful holds its shape. Too wet, and a handful more soil brings it back.
4. Tip the seed in and fold it through with her hands so it runs all the way through.
5. Roll balls the size of a walnut between her palms and line them up on the baking tray. Aim for twenty.
6. Carry five out to the bare corner by the door and press them in with her thumb while they are soft. The rest dry on the tray, somewhere warm and out of reach.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not bury them. A seed ball sits on the surface and waits for rain.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Following One Bumblebee

Bumblebees are heavy, loud and slow enough to follow on foot. The first week
of May is the best of the year for it, because the dandelions are at their
peak and the queens are out working them. Pick one working the dandelions and
walk with it. Count the flowers it lands on before it goes over a fence, and
watch the yellow build up on its back legs. Stay an arm's length back the
whole time.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and will put soil in his
> mouth given four seconds alone with it. Sit him the far side of the
> newspaper with his own bowl of dry flour. He points at everything Azlyn
> does, so name it back: rolling, pressing, filling.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Carrying the Pollen

Pollen moves because it sticks to a fuzzy body. The whole business runs on one
cotton ball and two spoons of flour.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 paper cupcake cases or paper cups
- 2 tbsp all-purpose flour, or cocoa, as the pollen
- 1 cotton ball taped to a clothespin, as the bee
- 1 small paintbrush
- 1 tray
- Tape and crayons

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Open the six cupcake cases out and let her color the insides with the crayons, one color each.
2. Tape each case down onto the tray, spread apart, so they stay put when she lands on them.
3. Tape the cotton ball to the clothespin. She holds the clothespin, and the cotton ball is the fuzzy back of the bee.
4. Brush a pinch of flour into two of the six cases with the small paintbrush. The other four stay clean, and she checks that.
5. Fly the bee into a floury flower and press it down. Look at the cotton ball, then fly to a clean flower and press again.
6. Keep going, flower to flower. After twenty trips, count how many of the six have flour in them.
7. Pull the cases off the tray, stand them a meter apart round the room, and let her run it again.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cocoa shows up better than flour and it smells of something. Either way the sleeve of her top gets pollinated.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Cotton ball bee on a string, flown by hand, no flowers.
- Paint flowers on paper and stop there.
- Sort the leftover seed by size on a dark plate.
- Blow flour off a spoon outside and follow it.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The neighborhood park**, and find the tree the bees are on
- The grass strip at the end of the road, thick with dandelions
- A walk past the front yard she likes the look of
- The green with a ball, if she has had enough of looking
- The community garden, to see what other people are putting in

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 10 months and cruising, and grass is
> harder work than carpet. Stand him at the park bench and let him work along
> it, then set him down on the grass. He will hate the feel of it and then
> pull it up in fistfuls. Watch his hands, because grass goes in the mouth
> like everything else.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Keep environmental talk local and hopeful at this age.**
> Azlyn cannot picture a rainforest or a decade. She can picture the bare
> corner by your door, and she can picture bees on it. Children who meet the
> big environmental story before they have any power over it end up holding
> the worry with none of the agency, and three is early for that. Give her the
> version she can act on: this patch had nothing on it, we put seeds there,
> look at it in July. Caring for one square meter she can reach builds the
> same instinct, and it leaves her feeling useful. The wide version of the
> story keeps until she is old enough to do something with it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Hands washed after soil and before food, both children.
> Compost and garden soil carry bacteria and neither of them should be
> mouthing it. Bees get watched and never touched or trapped, and nobody
> swings at one.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="day-124"></a>

## 🌟 Day 124: The Snails Get Names 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, May 4, 2027**
**Theme:** Bugs & Blooms

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Save six to eight cardboard tubes, cut four strips off a corrugated box, and put the shoebox and the packing tape on the table.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Rolling the Little Rooms
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Bug Hotel by the Fence (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Turning Over the Stones (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Two Snails and a Wet Tray (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Page Two of the Square
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Snail Book
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Rolling the Little Rooms

**🧰 You need:** 3 strips of corrugated card · 3 cardboard tubes · packing tape.

1. Roll one strip into a spiral so the ridges make tunnels, then let her roll the other two. Hers come out loose, which is better.
2. Push a spiral into each tube. If one springs out, wrap tape round the roll first and try again.
3. Hold a tube up to her eye and let her look down it. The gaps are the rooms.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Bug Hotel by the Fence

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 shoebox or small sturdy box
- 6–8 cardboard tubes
- Corrugated card, 4 strips
- Dry grass, straw or dead leaves
- A handful of short sticks
- Packing tape or string
- Scissors (adult only)
- 1 brick or heavy stone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Take the lid off the shoebox and stand the box on its long side so the opening faces you. The lid goes underneath.
2. Cut the tubes down with the scissors so they finish flush with the front. You cut, she holds each one against the box.
3. Pack the tubes in on their sides until nothing rattles. Roll the fourth strip of card into a spiral and wedge it in a corner.
4. Push short sticks in on end to fill the gaps, then press dry grass into what is left. Nothing should fall out when she tips it.
5. Run packing tape round the box twice, or tie string round it both ways, so it holds once it has been rained on.
6. Wedge it against the fence, opening away from the weather and off the wet ground if you can. Brick on top.

> 💡 **Tip:** Nothing moves in today and she will look anyway. Tell her first: pill bugs within days, spiders after that, bees by the end of summer.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Turning Over the Stones

Every flat stone, log and upturned pot has a colony under it. Lift, look, and
put it back the same way up, because it is somebody's roof. Pill bugs, worms,
centipedes, and on a damp May morning, snails. Take two or three snails and a
leaf indoors in a tub for this afternoon, and chalk a cross on the stone each
one came off.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months, and short sticks, small
> stones and snails are all mouth-sized for him. Keep the build up on the
> table and give him a spare tube, too long to fit in his mouth, down on the
> floor. He bangs it, finds it makes a different noise on carpet, and does it
> fourteen more times.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Two Snails and a Wet Tray

Two snails from the morning hunt get an afternoon as guests.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 baking tray or a large plastic lid
- Water and a cloth
- 2–3 snails or pill bugs from the morning hunt
- 1 lettuce or dandelion leaf
- Chalk
- Paper and crayons
- 1 soft paintbrush for lifting them

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Wet the tray all over with the cloth. A dry surface is no good to a snail.
2. Lift each snail on with the soft paintbrush, under the foot and never by the shell. Never pull a snail off a surface it has gripped.
3. She names them. Write the names on the paper and let her draw each shell in crayon, spiral and all.
4. Set the leaf at one end and sit back while they find it. It takes longer than she expects.
5. Outside, chalk a start and a finish line on a paving slab, a hand's width apart, and wipe the slab damp.
6. Lift two snails to the start with the brush, put the leaf past the finish, hands off. The winner wins nothing.
7. Back on the wet tray, then back to their own chalked stones before dinner. Wash hands, and leave the notebook and the crayons out, because she draws page two of the clipped square at 4:15.

> 💡 **Tip:** A snail pulled into its shell wants leaving alone, and comes out in a few minutes on wet ground.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Pill bugs instead, which are faster and easier to hold.
- Draw a snail's spiral on paper, round and round, ten times.
- Build a snail run out of the leftover tubes.
- Wet a paving slab and see what comes out from under the pot.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one, and the pool is quiet on a Tuesday
- The park on the way home, if the pool session is short
- Indoor playground, if the pool is shut for maintenance
- A splash in the yard with the tray and the hose instead
- The library, a day early, for a snail book

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 10 months and holds the rail in the
> shallow end while his legs work. Give him the edge to cruise with your hands
> either side. He understands *no* now, though never lean on it: your hands
> stay on him. Twenty minutes and out before he goes cold.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Giving something a face changes how a child treats it.**
> The minute a snail has a name, Azlyn stops carrying it by the shell and
> starts talking to it. Naming does something you can watch happen: she gives
> it wants, a home to get back to and a preference between two leaves, then
> handles it as though all of that is true. Treating an animal as a person is
> a step toward taking someone else's view rather than a mistake to correct.
> She practices on a snail because a snail is safe to be wrong about. The same
> machinery goes to work on Kreston. Use her names out loud all day, and take
> her word for what the snail wants.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Snails and slugs carry parasites and soil bacteria. Hands
> scrubbed after handling and before any food, and nothing goes near a face.
> Snails, small stones and short sticks are all mouth-sized for Kreston at 10
> months, so the tray stays up on the table. The scissors stay with you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 125: The Big Bug Count 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, May 5, 2027**
**Theme:** Bugs & Blooms

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Cut a piece of stiff card off a cereal box and leave it out with the ruler, two sharp pencils, the crayons and the masking tape.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Six Boxes and a Picture Each
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Big Bug Count (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Count on the Green (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Turning the Marks into a Picture (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Wiping the Table
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Sticker Columns
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Bug Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Six Boxes and a Picture Each

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 piece of stiff card · 1 ruler · 1 pencil · crayons · masking tape.

1. Tape the sheet of paper along its top edge onto the stiff card. That is her clipboard.
2. Rule five lines down the page so it comes out in six columns. Her hand on the ruler, yours on the pencil.
3. She draws one creature at the top of each column in crayon: ant, pill bug, snail, bee, spider, worm.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Big Bug Count

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The tally clipboard from 8:00
- 2 pencils
- 1 clear cup with a paper lid, as a bug pot
- 1 jam jar of water as a magnifier
- 1 soft paintbrush
- 1 sun hat

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sun hat on, clipboard under her arm, one pencil in her hand and the spare in your pocket, because the first gets dropped.
2. Show her the mark once. One line for one creature, in the column under its picture.
3. Start at the front step and work round the house in one direction. Under stones, up the wall, in the long grass.
4. For anything worth a longer look, put the clear cup over it and slide the paper lid underneath. Stand the jam jar of water beside it and look through both.
5. Anything that needs moving gets moved with the soft paintbrush. Fingers stay off, and whatever came out of a stone goes back under it.
6. Come in when the page is full or she is finished, and leave every mark as she made it.

> 💡 **Tip:** Count the same pill bug twice if she finds it twice. Arguing the point costs you the rest of the hour and gains her nothing.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Count on the Green

Take the clipboard and the spare pencil to the green at the end of the road
and run the count again on ground nobody looks after. Different grass,
different bugs. The numbers are in the long stuff, so wade in with her rather
than working from the path.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** **Kreston turns 11 months today.** He lets go of
> the furniture and stands on his own for a second or two before sitting down
> hard, and he runs that experiment all morning. Put him on grass for it. A
> first word comes out as half a word, so listen on the walk and say it back
> to him whole.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Turning the Marks into a Picture

Her tally sheet answers a question she cannot read off it yet. Stuck up in
columns, the answer is the tallest one.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large sheet of paper
- 1 ruler or a strip of straight card
- Sticky labels, or paper torn into squares
- 1 glue stick
- Crayons
- The tally sheet from this morning

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Big sheet on the table the long way round. Rule a line along the bottom with the ruler and mark six spaces, one per bug.
2. She draws the same six creatures along the bottom in crayon, copying her own pictures off the morning sheet.
3. Take the first column of tallies. Count the marks out loud and let her stick that many labels in a stack going up from her drawing.
4. Do the other five the same way. She sticks, you count and hand them over, and every square sits on top of the last.
5. Stand back and look at it from the door. The tallest stack is the winner.
6. Ask which one she thought would win before she started, and write her answer along the top.
7. Glue the morning's tally sheet into the bottom corner so both live on one page, and put it on the wall at her height.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep the squares the same size and touching, or the tallest stack stops meaning the biggest number.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Sort the six drawings into things that fly and things that do not.
- Stack coins or buttons in columns instead of sticking paper.
- Count what is on one flower for ten minutes and nothing else.
- Draw the morning's biggest bug at life size.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Indoor playground**, the between-week one, and go for the quiet late session
- The library, if you would rather have books than noise
- The park, since it stays light and warm until dinner now
- A friend's house, with the graph rolled up under her arm
- The green again, to check the count in the afternoon heat

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 11 months and indoor playground is where
> standing on his own costs nothing when it fails. Put him in the toddler pen
> and let him haul up on the padded blocks. He lets go, stands, wobbles and
> drops, over and over. Keep him out of the big-kid runs.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Tally marks are her first taste of representing data.**
> One line for one pill bug is an idea with a lot packed into it. The mark on
> the page is not the pill bug. It stands in for the pill bug, and it holds
> still while the pill bug walks off. Azlyn cannot count past a handful with
> any reliability and she does not need to, because the marks do the
> remembering for her. This afternoon takes it a step on: the tallest stack
> answers the question with no counting at all. Reading a chart at nine rests
> on this, and it starts with a pencil line she made in the grass.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Long grass in May means ticks, so check both children's
> hairlines, necks and behind the knees when you come in. Nettles are up and
> sting on contact. Bees and wasps get looked at through the jar and never
> picked up.

## 🌟 Day 126: A Garden in a Jar 🌟
**📅 Thursday, May 6, 2027**
**Theme:** Bugs & Blooms

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Pull a clump of moss off a wall on your way in and leave it in a saucer of water by the sink, with the big jar.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Scrubbing the Pebbles
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Jar That Waters Itself (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Moss Hunt (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Scrubbing the Pebbles

**🧰 You need:** a handful of pebbles or gravel · 1 bowl of warm water · 1 old toothbrush · 1 dish towel.

1. Pebbles into the bowl and let her scrub them with the toothbrush. The water goes brown fast.
2. Line the clean ones up on the dish towel to dry, biggest to smallest if she wants an order.
3. Tell her what they are for: spare water sits in the bottom of the jar and not in the roots.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Jar That Waters Itself

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large clear jar with a lid (a pasta sauce or pickle jar)
- A handful of pebbles or gravel
- 2 cups soil or compost
- 1 clump of moss (off the wall last night)
- 1 small plant or 3 cuttings (a supermarket mint pot works)
- 1 spoon
- 1 pitcher of water
- 1 cloth
- 1 label and a marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip the scrubbed pebbles into the jar, two fingers deep, and let her shake it flat.
2. Spoon in two cups of soil and press it down with the back of the spoon.
3. Dig a hole with the spoon and stand the plant or the cuttings in it. She firms the soil round the stems with her thumbs.
4. Press the moss down over the bare soil like a carpet, green side up, out to the glass.
5. Two spoonfuls of water from the pitcher and no more. Damp, not wet. Wipe the inside of the glass with the cloth so she can see in.
6. Lid on tight. She writes the date on the label in marker and it goes on the front. Stand it at the back of a bright sill, out of direct sun.

> 💡 **Tip:** It fogs up by tomorrow. If water runs down the glass all day, take the lid off for an hour. If it never fogs, one more spoonful.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Moss Hunt

Moss grows where nothing else gets a hold: north-facing walls, the shady side
of the shed, the joint between two paving slabs. Take a spoon and a tub and
collect three kinds. One will be flat, one will look like a forest half an
inch high, and one comes up in cushions.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and pulls up on anything that
> holds still. Give him his own saucer of wet moss on the floor with you
> sitting right there. He will squeeze it and try to eat it, so this is a
> both-hands-on job or it does not happen.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Flowers Between Two Pieces of Tape

Sealed between two strips of tape, a flower keeps its color and the light
comes through it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The pressed flowers from Friday, or fresh flat petals put under a heavy book at breakfast
- Clear packing tape, 1 roll
- Scissors (adult)
- Thin card for the frames
- String
- 1 pencil

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Pull an arm's length of packing tape off the roll and lay it sticky side up. Two short tabs off the roll hold the ends down.
2. She lays the pressed flowers along it face down and spaced out. Anything with a lump in it will not seal.
3. Lay a second strip of tape over the top, sticky side down, and press the air out from the middle with her thumb.
4. Peel the whole strip up off the table. Hold it against the window and look at what the light does.
5. Fold thin card in half, pencil a window on the front, and cut through both layers with the adult scissors.
6. Tape the strip inside the fold so it shows through, and let her write on the frame in pencil.
7. Tape a loop of string to the back and hang it against the glass. Leave the notebook by the back door for 4:15: she draws page three kneeling at the clipped square, then the three pages go side by side on the table with Sunday's on the left.

> 💡 **Tip:** Press the tape down hard along every edge. Air left in there goes cloudy in a week, and the ones she seals flat still look right at Christmas.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Tape flowers straight onto the window with no frame at all.
- Press more flowers under books for next week.
- Draw round the frames and color the windows in.
- Sort the pressed flowers by which kept their color.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The hardware store**, for a bag of gravel and a second jar
- The garden center, to see what is flowering this week
- The park, to check whether the bumblebee tree is still busy
- A walk to deliver a taped flower frame to a neighbor
- The corner store, and she carries the bag home

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 11 months and the hardware store is a
> wall of nameable things. Keep him in the cart seat or the carrier, because
> everything at his height is small, sharp or heavy. Say the word for what he
> points at and wait a beat.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A closed system is a big idea in a small jar.**
> Water goes up through the soil into the plant, out through its leaves, onto
> the cold glass and back down as rain, and the lid means none of it leaves.
> Azlyn finds the fog inside the jar tomorrow morning and it lands as magic.
> Let it. The version she can hold at three is that the water goes round and
> comes back, which is the water cycle in one sentence and the reason the sea
> does not run out. She has a rainstorm on the windowsill she can check before
> breakfast for a year. Look at it with her when she asks, and let her tell
> you what changed overnight.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A big glass jar full of wet soil is heavy, and Kreston is 11
> months and standing. It lives at the back of a high sill, never on a low
> table or a sill he can pull up to. Hands washed after the soil, both
> children. The scissors stay with you.

<a id="backup-apr"></a>

# 🌧️ April — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

April hands you two kinds of ruined day. On one the weather takes the morning:
showers coming through every hour, wind that leans on the house all day, or a
cold snap overnight that takes back everything last week gave you. The week's
pages want a garden, a walk or a dry path you no longer have. On the other
somebody is ill and the whole day shrinks to the size of the sofa. These five
pages cover both, and the last one is for the morning you open this book with
ten minutes and no plan. Everything here comes out of your own cupboards and
the recycling, because on a day like this nobody is going to the store either.

---

<a id="apr-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — The Walk That Stayed Indoors

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Leave the masking tape, a marker, three slips of paper and a stack of plain paper on the kitchen table, stand six empty bottles or cans from the recycling inside the hall closet, and put her boots by the front door where she will see them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Counting Out the Route
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Three Hundred Steps to the Duck Pond (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Six Windows and the Open Door (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Paper Road (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎳 Rainy Hour: Bottle Bowling Down the Hall (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Tape Still Down
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: A Hot Bath With the Rain on the Glass
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Counting Out the Route

**🧰 You need:** masking tape · 1 marker · 3 slips of paper · her boots by the door.

1. Ask her where you would have gone today. Take the first answer, even the pond you went to on Sunday, and say out loud that the rain has it.
2. Count her steps from the front door to the kitchen door with her, out loud, and let her hear how few of them there are. Then tell her the pond is three hundred.
3. Write **100** on each of the three slips and put all three in her pocket. She hands you one back every time the count gets there.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Three Hundred Steps to the Duck Pond

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 roll masking tape
- The 3 paper slips marked 100
- 1 chair, 1 coat rack and 2 teddies, as the three stops
- 1 envelope with something in it
- 2 rolled pairs of socks

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape a route through the downstairs: out of the hall, around the table, past the sofa, back to the front door. That loop is the walk, and she picks which way it runs.
2. Set the three stops on the loop. The coat rack is the big tree, the chair by the door is the mailbox, the two teddies at the far end are the ducks on the water.
3. Boots on, both of you, and walk it counting from one. Say the numbers yourself and let her join in where she can. She hands over a slip at every hundred.
4. Every lap she does the three jobs: a flat hand on the tree, the envelope posted at the mailbox and fished out again, the socks thrown to the ducks and carried back.
5. Keep going until the last slip is out of her pocket. Three hundred comes in at around six laps and takes longer than either of you expects.
6. Sit down on the floor at the end with the three slips in front of her and ask how far the pond is. Her answer is the whole point of the morning.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do the counting out loud yourself. She loses the thread somewhere in the thirties and picks it back up off your voice, and the walk keeps going.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Six Windows and the Open Door

Go window to window and look out of each one for a minute. Mid-April changes
the view faster than any other month, so most of them have something new in
them: the grass gone shaggy, buds broken on the tree, water standing where none
stood on Tuesday. Finish at the front door. Open it, stand together on the mat,
and let her hold a hand out into the rain until it runs off her fingers.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months and cruises the furniture, so
> run the taped route past the sofa and the low table and he walks a stretch of
> it hand over hand while she counts. He points at the rain on the glass and
> waits for a word, so give him one at every window. At the open door he goes
> still and listens. Keep the envelope, the slips and the tape ends off the
> floor while he is down there.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Paper Road

Her legs did three hundred steps this morning. The same walk goes onto the
table this afternoon, small enough to cross with two fingers.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 long strip of paper, or 4 sheets taped end to end
- Masking tape
- Crayons and 1 marker
- 2–3 small figures or animals
- 1 toy car
- The three paper slips from this morning

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape the strip down the middle of the table, both ends stuck flat so it cannot roll itself back up.
2. Start at the left-hand end with your front door and let her draw it. She decides how big it goes.
3. Work along the paper in her order: the tree, the mailbox, the pond, and whatever else she remembers passing. Take her order even where it is wrong.
4. Write what she calls each one underneath in her own words. **The pond with the mean duck** goes down as she says it.
5. Stand the spare figures at the pond and walk one of them along the road with two fingers, stopping where she stopped this morning, and count his steps out loud. He gets there in about twenty.
6. Lay the three slips beside him. Three hundred of hers, twenty of his, and the same pond at the end of both.
7. Leave the road taped down through dinner and let her drive the car up and down it.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her draw the pond bigger than the house. Size on her map is about how much a place matters, and tidying the proportions costs you the drawing.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Draw the whole road on the back of a cereal box and stop there.
- Lay the crayons end to end down the table and count how many make a road.
- Mail the three slips under her bedroom door and go in and get them.
- Skip the paper and drive a toy car around the taped route on the floor.

### 👶 Kreston's Afternoon

Sit him at the far end of the table in the high chair with a sheet of his own
and one fat crayon. At 10 months he holds it in his fist, bangs more than he
draws, and looks surprised at the mark. He points at what her hand is doing, so
name it back: drawing, taping, the car. Press every tape end flat before he
goes down on the floor, because a lifted strip is the first thing he takes.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Big numbers mean nothing until she's walked them.**
> Azlyn can say three hundred. The word sits in her mouth with nothing behind
> it, the same as a thousand or a hundred and six. Numbers get their weight from
> something she has done with her body, and three hundred steps through her own
> hallway leaves one in her legs by lunchtime. Children build a rough sense of
> quantity long before they can count with any accuracy, and it grows out of
> amounts they have carried, poured or walked. She will not be able to tell you
> what three hundred is. She will know the pond is a long way and that the
> mailbox comes first, and the counting she learns at five lands on top of that.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Press every end of the tape route flat to the floor and check
> it each time you pass. A lifted strip is a trip at a run for Azlyn and goes
> straight into Kreston's mouth. Shut and latch the front door the moment the
> two minutes on the mat are up, and never leave it standing open with him
> loose in the hall. Socks and an envelope are the only things thrown today.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="apr-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Wind That Never Lets Up

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand two clean jars the same size and a bag of dried beans on the counter, empty the laundry basket, and put a roll of masking tape beside them. Everything else today is already in the house, and the heat goes on before you come down.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Choosing the Six Games
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Six Games, Two Jars (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Warmest Place in the House (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Shop That Takes Beans (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎵 Loud Hour: Every Fast Song in the House (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Shop, Still Open
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath, and Pajamas Warm Out of the Dryer
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Choosing the Six Games

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the two jars and the beans.

1. Fold the sheet into six boxes and open it flat. Six games today, and she picks them.
2. Walk the downstairs together and take six things two people can do indoors: throw, jump, balance, carry, roll, stand still. She draws one in each box, however it comes out.
3. Stand the two jars on the table with the beans between them. One bean is one point, one jar is one person, and tell her that now so the rules arrive before the noise does.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Six Games, Two Jars

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 clean jars, the same size
- Dried beans or dried pasta, a large handful
- 1 roll masking tape for the lines
- 1 laundry basket
- 2 rolled pairs of socks
- 1 hardcover book
- 1 tablespoon and 1 orange, or an onion or a potato if the fruit bowl is empty
- 1 ball, bigger than her fist
- The sheet of six games

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape a line across the floor at one end of the longest room and stand the basket four of your paces away from it. That line starts every game, and her sheet of six goes down beside it so you both know what is left.
2. Game one is the socks into the basket, three throws each from the line. One bean into your own jar for every one that lands.
3. Game two is the standing jump. Both of you go from the line and mark the back of your heels with a strip of tape. The further mark takes the bean.
4. Run the other four the same way: the book carried across the room on her head, the orange walked there and back on the spoon, the ball rolled nearest the far wall, the one-leg stand counted out loud.
5. Play your own turns at your real speed on two of the six, and let her watch you drop whatever is on the spoon.
6. Tip both jars out at the end and lay the beans in pairs, hers against yours, until one line runs out. The longer line won and nobody counted a thing.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her win the ones she wins and lose the ones she loses. A three-year-old will argue with you about the last four throws and will not argue with a jar.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Warmest Place in the House

Go around the house with her hand as the thermometer. A palm flat on the window
glass, on the floor by the front door, on the vent, on the inside of the closet
wall, on the fridge, on the rug where the sun lands. She calls each one warm or
cold before you say a word. April turns cold overnight and the house takes a
day to catch up, so half of these have changed since Sunday. Rank them together,
carry a blanket to the winner, and stay there for five minutes while the wind
works on the windows.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 10 months, and a dried bean is the exact
> size that blocks his airway, so he spends the games hour in the high chair
> beside the action or behind a gate with two plastic beakers and a wooden
> spoon. He rides the warm-and-cold lap on your hip with a palm on the glass,
> and he goes still when a gust hits the window the way he does at running
> water. He understands **no** this month and will look at your face and reach
> for the jar anyway.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Shop That Takes Beans

The beans stop being points and turn into money. This one runs at a table with
everybody sitting down, which is what the afternoon needs after that morning.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The beans, in one bowl
- 8–10 things off the shelves: a can, a box of pasta, a roll of tape, two socks, a book
- Sticky labels, or scraps of paper and masking tape
- 1 marker
- 2 paper bags
- 1 tray as the counter
- 2 cups, one for each purse

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Clear one end of the table for the counter, stand her chair behind it and line the goods up along the tray.
2. Price everything at one, two or three beans and no higher. You write the number, she sticks the label on and says it out loud as it goes down.
3. Count twelve beans into each cup and give each of you a paper bag. You shop first, one thing at a time into your bag, and she checks every payment before it goes in the register.
4. Swap over. She shops with the other bag, you keep the counter, and you refuse the sale when she puts two beans down for a three-bean can. Wait while she fixes it.
5. Sell her out. Once the shelf is bare, restock it together and let her set the new prices, which will be higher than yours.
6. Run one round where she gets three beans and wants five things, and let that sit there without solving it.
7. Count every bean back into the bag at the end, and the jars go up on the shelf with them.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep every price at three or under. A price she can count on one hand keeps the shop open for an hour, and a five-bean can shuts it inside four minutes.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One shelf, three things, three prices, and stop there.
- Deliver the shopping to every door in the house in the laundry basket.
- Sort the goods into what you eat and what you wear.
- Play the whole shop with words and no beans, and see whether she notices.

### 👶 Kreston's Afternoon

He is the customer who clears the bottom shelf, which at 10 months is a real
job and worth handing him on purpose. Put three of the goods low down where he
cruises past and let him take them off and pass them over. He points at what he
wants named, so name the can, the box and the sock every time. Sweep the
floor and count the beans back into the bag before he goes down there.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Scorekeeping turns a chaotic game into a calm one.**
> Two people and one basket ends in a fight about who threw what. A bean dropped
> in a jar settles the same question without either of you having to remember
> anything, and Azlyn holds almost nothing in working memory at three, so an
> argument about the last four throws is one she cannot win on the facts. The
> jar puts the fact outside her head where you can both see it. She also gets
> the shape of a game out of it: rules first, turns in order, an ending that
> arrives whether she likes it or not. Keeping score is what lets her lose a
> round and stay in the game, and that is the piece worth having by five.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Dried beans are a choking size for a 10-month-old with a
> working pincer grip. Kreston stays in the high chair or behind a gate the
> whole time any of them are out of the jars, and you count them out and count
> them back before he goes on the floor. Point the throwing line away from the
> window and the television. Nothing gets thrown or rolled while he is down.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="apr-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Day the Fever Runs It

This is the day she is hot, floppy and wants you in the room. There is no
schedule on this page, because a fever runs the day and you follow it. Nothing
here has to be finished, nothing needs cutting, baking or clearing up, and every
one of these can be abandoned halfway with nothing lost. Your job today is
fluids, a lap and the same face every time she opens her eyes.

### 🕗 The Shape of Today

- **Whenever she wakes:** downstairs in her pajamas with her own blanket. Build the corner before anything else happens.
- **After the first long sleep:** one small thing, ten minutes at most, and only if she asks for it.
- **When she asks for food:** give her whatever she names, in a small amount, and take the no without comment.
- **Before the afternoon dip:** the rest block, and the rest of the day bends around it.
- **When the light goes flat:** one story, an early bath if she wants one, and bed a good hour before her usual.

### 🛋️ The Corner She Stays In

Take one end of the sofa and make it hers for the day. Her own blanket, one
pillow, the toy she has slept with all winter, and a bowl on the floor within
reach of her head. Pull the curtain half across so the room goes dim without
going dark. Put her cup on a low table where she can get it herself and refill
it every time you walk past. She will not move off that end of the sofa all
day, and it saves her deciding anything.

### 💧 A Sip Every Time the Song Ends

Fluids matter more than food today, and asking her to drink gets you a no every
time. Put a song on instead and hand her the cup at the end of each one. Small
sips beat a full cup, and cold water, watered juice, a popsicle or a spoonful
of ice cream all count as fluid. Keep her cup and her spoon separate from
everybody else's from the first hour, because that is the part you will be
glad of on Thursday.

### 😴 The Rest Block: Sleep Is the Activity

Sleep is the middle of this day and the point of it. Lie her down under the
blanket at whatever hour she starts to go quiet, put the lights out and lie down
yourself if Kreston will allow it. She may sleep two hours, which is the best
thing that happens today. If she surfaces and cannot go back under, leave her
lying there with an audio story or the radio on low and no expectation that she
does anything with it. Getting up is what starts the crying.

### 🤲 Counting in Squeezes

She keeps one hand in yours and everything else stays where it is. Squeeze her
hand three times and wait. She squeezes three back, then sends you a number of
her own and you send it back. Go up to five and no higher, and let her catch
you getting it wrong. This costs her nothing, asks for one hand and no eyes at
all, and it runs as long as she wants it. It stops the second she lets go, and
it is the one thing on this page that works while she is crying.

### 🪟 The One Thing That Changed Outside

Once each time she surfaces, go to the window yourself and bring one thing back
to her in words. April gives you something new every single day, so there is
always an answer: the grass longer, the tree further on, a bird carrying
something, water standing on the path. Let her guess first and give her three
tries. She never lifts her head off the cushion, and on a day like this it
counts as having been out.

### 📖 The Story She Hears With Her Eyes Shut

Keep the lights off and the book out of it, because holding one up is work and
looking at a page is more work. Use a story she knows and put her in it, walking
to the pond, feeding the ducks, meeting the neighbor's cat. Go slow and repeat
whole lines. She will correct you when you get a detail wrong, which is the best
sign of the day and worth getting wrong on purpose once or twice.

### 👶 Keeping Kreston Out of It Today

He is 10 months, he cruises, and he will head straight for her face and her cup.
Keep him off both. He needs floor space away from the sofa, so gate one end of
the room and put a box of his own things in it, and take her cup up out of
reach every time you stand. Wash your hands between the two of them, more often
than feels necessary. If anybody can take him out for an hour this afternoon,
say yes to it, because his day gets thin today and a walk in the stroller with
somebody else fixes it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Fluids in, and pee out. No wet diaper or no trip to the
> bathroom in eight hours means you call the doctor today. Call today, and do
> not wait for tomorrow, for a fever over 102°F that will not come down, a
> stiff neck, a rash that stays visible when you press a glass against it,
> breathing that sucks in under her ribs, or a child you cannot wake. Never
> give aspirin to a child. Kreston is under one, so he gets nothing off her
> cup, her spoon or her hands.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Telling a story with no pictures forces her to say what she means.**
> With her eyes shut there is nothing to point at, so the story runs on words
> alone. A picture does half the work for her, since she can put a finger on
> it and say "that one." A story in the dark makes her name the pond and the
> ducks. Getting a detail wrong on purpose pulls those words out of her: she
> hears the mistake, holds the right version in her head, and has to find
> language for it before you can put it back. All of it happens with the
> lights off and her eyes closed, and that is why it still works today.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="apr-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — The In-Between Day

She woke up better and she is not better. The fever has gone, the appetite is
half back, and by nine o'clock she is bored, whiny and following you room to
room. Going out is still off, and a full day would put her back on the sofa
tomorrow. Everything on this page happens sitting down, needs one hand, and can
stop dead the moment she has had enough.

### 🕗 The Shape of Today

- **Whenever she wakes:** dressed, but in soft clothes, and breakfast wherever she wants to eat it.
- **Through the morning:** one thing at a time with a gap after it, and no second thing until she asks.
- **When she asks for food:** a proper meal if she wants one, and half of it back in the fridge if she does not.
- **Before the afternoon dip:** the rest block, and hold this one even though she will fight it.
- **Late afternoon:** the phone call, then a bath and bed at the usual time.

### 🦷 What the Teeth Are For

Sit her on your lap with a mirror and let her look at her own teeth first. Run
a finger along them with her: flat slabs at the back for grinding, points at the
front for tearing off a bite. Then open any animal book you own and go through
it asking one question at each picture, which is what that animal eats. Take her
answer, then look at the mouth together and find the evidence. A rabbit, a dog,
a horse, a bird with no teeth at all. Nothing gets set up and nothing gets
cleared away, and she can stop after four pages.

### 🧦 Pairing the Socks From a Lap

Bring the clean laundry basket to the sofa and tip the socks onto the cushion
beside her. She pairs them, one at a time, at whatever speed she has today, and
you take the pairs as she finishes them. A recovering child wants a job with a
visible end and no standing up in it, and this one has both. She will find the
odd one and want to know where it went, so let that be the interesting part.

### 😴 The Rest Block: The Lie-Down She Argues About

She is well enough to refuse this and not well enough to skip it. Take the
argument out of it: the lie-down happens on the sofa with the curtains half
shut, she keeps her socks on, and she does not have to sleep. Put an audio
story on, lie down at the other end yourself, and say nothing for forty minutes.
About half the time she goes under. The other half she lies there and comes out
of it steadier than she went in, which was the point either way.

### ☎️ Telling It Down the Phone

Call a grandparent, or Joseph, and hand her the phone. She tells them what she
has got, how many days she has had it and what she threw up on. This is the
best twenty minutes of her day and it costs you nothing but the call. Stay
beside her and stay out of it. Whatever she says is the version of the week
that has stuck, and it will not be the one you would have given.

### 🍲 The List of What She Wants Tomorrow

Sit with a scrap of paper and ask what she wants to eat when she is better. Write
every answer down word for word, including the ones nobody is cooking. She draws
one of them at the bottom. Stick the list on the fridge, and buy or cook one
thing off it tomorrow so the list turns out to have been real.

### 👶 Kreston at the Other End of the Sofa

She wants to be near him today and he wants everything she is holding. Sit him
on the floor at the far end of the sofa with the sock basket between them, give
him two socks of his own to pull apart, and keep her hands out of his mouth
until she is a day clear. He is 10 months and cruises the length of the
cushions, so he arrives at her end on his own feet whether or not you planned
it. Her best twenty minutes with him is reading him a board book from where she
is lying, which serves both of them and costs her nothing.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Twenty-four hours clear of a fever and of throwing up before
> she goes near other children, and the clock starts at the last one and not at
> bedtime. Keep the fluids going even though she looks fine, because the day
> after is when the tank runs low. Call the doctor if the fever comes back
> after a clear day, if a cough is still there in two weeks, or if she goes
> quiet and floppy again after a morning of being herself.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Teeth are evidence, and reading evidence is the whole of paleontology.**
> Azlyn looked in a mirror this morning and found flat slabs at the back of her
> mouth and points at the front. Every animal in that book carries the same
> story in its jaw, and she can read it off a picture: points and gaps for meat,
> broad grinding surfaces for grass. A scientist with a jawbone in a drawer
> works the same way, with the animal itself gone for sixty million years.
> Naming what she sees and then saying what it means is a two-step move she can
> make at three, on a sofa, with one hand. The dinosaur skulls she meets at
> seven are the same puzzle with more of the pieces missing.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="apr-extras"></a>

## 🎲 April — Extra Ideas

For the morning you have ten minutes, no plan and a wet garden. No steps, no
shopping, and nothing here takes longer to set up than it takes to do.

### 🎲 Alternative Activities

- **Naming the Puddles:** every puddle between your door and the corner gets a name and a size word.
- **The Two-Minute Rain Run:** out in whatever she has on, once around the house, back in, towel over her head.
- **Barefoot on Four Floors:** carpet, tile, wood and doormat, named with her eyes shut.
- **The Shoe Line, Biggest to Smallest:** every shoe in the house laid along the hall in one order.
- **A Ribbon Out the Window:** tied to the latch at breakfast and checked again at every meal.
- **The Stairs, Counted Both Ways:** counting up on the way up, counting back down on the way down.
- **One Thing in a Sock:** one object dropped into a long sock, named by hand before it comes out.
- **Everything Green She Can Carry:** one pile in the middle of the floor, then all of it back where it came from.
- **The Windowsill Cafe:** two cups, two chairs at the glass, and whatever goes past.
- **The Drawer of Spoons:** tipped onto a dish towel and sorted back into families.
- **Warm Hands on Cold Glass:** hands in warm water, then flat on the window, and the print that comes up.

### 🎨 Alternative Arts & Crafts

- **Blowing the Paint Across the Page:** a puddle of watery paint, a drinking straw, and how far she can push it.
- **A Nest for the Ones Outside:** yarn scraps, dryer lint and short bits of string on a saucer by the step.
- **Printing With the Bottom of a Boot:** paint on the sole, then walk it across a long sheet of paper.
- **The Longest Snake in the House:** playdough rolled thin until it runs off the end of the table.
- **Two Tubes and a Piece of String:** binoculars for the street, colored in before they get used.
- **The Drawing You Both Work On:** one sheet, a crayon each, and nobody says what it is going to be.
- **Newspaper Hats for Everybody:** one fold each, and a name on every brim.
- **Foil Pressed Flat:** a smooth sheet and a blunt pencil, and every mark she makes stays there.
- **Blue and White and Nothing Else:** one painting with two colors and no others on the table.
- **The Card That Goes in the Mailbox:** her drawing, your words underneath, walked to the box and posted.
- **A Picture With No Brush:** a sponge, a cotton ball and both thumbs.

### 👶 Kreston's Turn

- **The Cruising Lane:** two chairs pushed together, backs out, so he sidesteps the whole run with a hand on each.
- **In and Out of the Big Pot:** a saucepan and four things too big to swallow, taken out and put back for as long as it holds him.
- **The Point-and-Name Lap:** carried around the room, with a word for whatever his finger lands on, including the fourth time.
- **Paper He Is Allowed to Wreck:** one whole newspaper page, too big to get in his mouth, and the noise is the whole point.

# 📘 May
## ☀️ *The Big Book of Little Days* ☀️
### Booklet 5 of 12 · Days 127–154
**May 7 – June 3, 2027**

*For Azlyn & Kreston · Made by Joseph for Brooklyn*

---

## This Month

- [**Week 19** · Mother's Day & Family Love](#week-19) — *Days 127–133*
- [**Week 20** · Backyard Science Lab](#week-20) — *Days 134–140*
- [**Week 21** · Superheroes & Helpers](#week-21) — *Days 141–147*
- [**Week 22** · Memorial Day & Community Heroes](#week-22) — *Days 148–154*
- [🌧️ **Backup Days & Extra Ideas**](#backup-may)

> 👶 **Kreston this month:** He is 11 months for all 28 days, turning **1 on
> June 5**, two days after the booklet closes. He lets go of the furniture and
> stands alone for a few seconds before he sits back down. He hands you things
> on purpose and waits for you to take them, and he follows a one-step
> instruction like *drink* before he can say it back. A first word is close.

> 🧒 **Azlyn this month:** She is three all month. She stays three until
> December 20.

---

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Small parts**: the button tin on Day 130, the tray of things smaller than her thumb on Day 137, the pasta shapes on Day 138, the loose oats and raisins on Day 150. Kreston pulls to stand at table height, so work high and count everything back into its box before he is on the floor.
- **String, wool and cord**: the lifting machine on Day 142, the seven wool medal loops on Day 143 and the camera strap on Day 127 all use them. Nothing goes around a neck, Kreston's medal tapes flat to his high-chair tray, and the string comes down the moment the activity ends.
- **Standing water**: the bubble tray on Day 134, the bucket and Kreston's pouring tray on Day 139, the dishpan flood on Day 142, the pool on the four swimming afternoons. Kreston can drown in a few inches of water and he does it in silence, so tip every container out when you finish.
- **Roadside plants are up now**: poison hemlock on the Day 129, Day 151 and Day 153 walks, waist-high, lacy white heads on a purple-blotched stem, and wild parsnip on the Day 129 walk, flat yellow heads and sap that burns skin in sunlight. Pick nothing tall, white and lacy on any walk this month, and wash both pairs of hands before anybody eats.
- **Adult-only tools**: the pan of hot oil on Day 131, the screwdriver on Day 136, the heavy scissors on Day 141, the craft knife on Day 148. Day 136 also opens a dead flashlight, so the batteries go into a sealed bag on a high shelf first, because a swallowed button battery burns a child from the inside within hours.
- **The darning needle on Day 131**: she pulls it through from her side while you push it from yours, so it stays hand to hand and never on the table. It goes back in the tin the second you stop.
- **Late spring sun**: the foil oven and its metal tray run hot on Day 135, and Day 137's glass magnifying lens focuses sunlight hot enough to scorch paper and skin, so the lens stays indoors on the table with you. Sunscreen before you go out and again after lunch, hats, shade, water, and check the back of Kreston's neck because he overheats before he can say so.

## Week 19: Mother's Day & Family Love 💐
**📅 May 7 – May 13, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

This week points Azlyn at the four people in her own house. She photographs
them, feeds them, makes a toy for Kreston, mends what belongs to them and puts
clean sheets on their beds. A family is a set of people you do things for, and
she is old enough now to be one of the ones doing.

Mother's Day lands on Sunday. Saturday builds toward it, she lays the table
for five and guards the plate in the fridge, and Monday winds back down out of
it into the button tin and a shoebox of things nobody throws away. The
handprint card she paints on Sunday is May's, fifth of this year's twelve, so
hold April's sheet up beside it and put both back on the wall.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **What a frame leaves out.** She lines up every shot through a cardboard window first, so choosing one thing means dropping another.
- **What it takes for two things to be the same.** A tin of odds and ends hunted for exact twins, and every near miss argued out with a reason she has to say out loud.
- **Making something for a particular person.** The plate, the card, the cake and Kreston's rattle all get judged on whether they land with the person they were for.
- **Hand strength with a point to it.** Cracking an egg, beating batter until it holds on the fork, pushing wool through a needle eye, pulling a stitch through from her side.
- **Carrying her own share of the work.** A wet laundry basket across the grass, two full watering cans, a pillow shoved into its case.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Tools shape what a child notices
- One of the oldest child-centered teaching rituals we still have
- Rituals that repeat annually do something one-off events can't
- "Same" is a harder word than it looks
- "Waste" is a concept, and it's teachable through objects
- Abundance of choice produces better work than the perfect kit
- Heavy work is the most reliable regulation tool you have

---
