### 🌅 Opening Activity: Spreading Out the Photographs

**🧰 You need:** every printed photograph in the house · the kitchen table, cleared.

1. Spread them face up across the whole table. If they all live on your phone, pick ten and go one at a time.
2. She names who she can. You name the rest, and say the relationship with the name: that is Joseph's mom, so she is your grandma.
3. Count the people the family has. She will land on a different number every time, so take the last one and tell her they each get a card at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Who Belongs to Who

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Card or cereal-box panels cut into 10–12 rectangles
- Crayons
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 roll masking tape
- Printed photos if you have any, otherwise she draws each face
- A door or a blank stretch of wall

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Start at the bottom, at her eye height. Azlyn and Kreston, one card each. She draws the faces, you write the names in marker.
2. Row above: you and Joseph. Say it while you tape. I am your mom, Joseph is your dad, and we are Kreston's mom and dad as well.
3. Row above that: grandparents. Tape a photograph onto the card where you have one, and she draws the ones you do not.
4. Run a strip of masking tape from each parent down to each of their children, so the lines are there to point at.
5. Aunts, uncles and cousins go out to the sides at the height that matches their row. Give the dog a card if she asks.
6. Stand back and ask questions the wall can answer. Who is Kreston's dad. Who is grandma's daughter. Leave it up all week.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say the relationship every time you say a name today, even when it sounds laboured. She hears grandma as a name, the way she hears Kreston.

### 🌳 Get Outside: A Daisy for Each Person

Late May and the daisies are thick on any grass that has not been cut this
week. Give her one job: one daisy for every person on the door. She will lose
count and start again twice. Sit down when the bunch looks about right, count
it against the names, and split the chain-making between you on the way home.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and a first word is possible
> from here. The words that arrive first are the people. Hold his own card up
> and say his name, then Azlyn's, and watch him reach for the face he knows.
> Out on the grass, sit him in the daisies and let him pull to standing off
> your knee to get at them.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Finding Everybody Again

The cards come off the door after lunch and go round the house, and she has to
earn every one of them back.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The 10–12 cards from this morning
- 1 roll masking tape
- A basket or a paper bag for carrying finds
- A cushion for Kreston's spot on the floor

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Send her upstairs to count to twenty. Hide the cards one per room, at her height, nothing above her reach.
2. Hand her the basket with one rule: she names who it is and who they belong to before it goes in.
3. When she stalls, give her the relationship instead of the name. This one is Joseph's mom. She gets there from that.
4. Sit Kreston on the cushion where he can watch, and lay the full basket out in rows on the table, above his reach.
5. She tapes them back up herself, in whatever order she wants, which will not be this morning's.
6. Play the swap. She shuts her eyes, you take one card down, and she works out who is missing from the gap.
7. Last round is hers. She hides them, you hunt, and you name the wrong person on purpose at least twice.

> 💡 **Tip:** Naming who is missing is harder than naming who is there, so hold step six back until she has won a few of the easy rounds.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Hide three cards instead of twelve and stop when she has them.
- Sort the cards into who lives in this house and who does not.
- Mail the cards through the doors on yesterday's street map.
- Draw one more card for somebody she has thought of since breakfast.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A bus ride** to nowhere in particular, upstairs at the front, home on the next one
- The park, if the bus feels like too much organizing
- A walk to the mailbox with a card she has drawn for somebody on the wall
- Any bench with a view of a busy road
- Grandparents, if anyone on the door is close enough to call in on

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Take him on the bus in the sling and stand him on
> your knee at the window. At 11 months he tracks what moves past him and
> turns back to check your face, which is him asking whether the truck was
> worth reacting to. Answer him, and let Azlyn ring the bell.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Family structure is confusing at three, and worth being explicit about.**
> Azlyn hears grandma as a name, the way she hears Kreston. Understanding that
> one person carries several labels at once, that Joseph is your dad and also
> Kreston's dad and also somebody's son, takes relational thinking that
> arrives closer to five or six. Until then she files people one label deep.
> Saying the relationship whenever you say a name, and putting the cards in
> rows where the lines between them show, hands her the structure in a form
> she can point at. She will get it wrong for another two years. The version
> she builds now is the one that gets corrected, and it has to exist first.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The cards and the masking tape stay off the floor while
> Kreston is down. He is 11 months, pulls up on the table edge and mouths
> whatever he lands on, and a cereal-box card is the right size to go in a
> mouth. Hide the cards at her height and nowhere she has to climb for.

## 🌟 Day 150: The Secret She Can't Keep 🌟
**📅 Sunday, May 30, 2027**
**Theme:** Memorial Day & Community Heroes

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the washed jar on the table with the flour, both sugars, the oats and the raisins, and decide tonight which person tomorrow's shelf is for.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Picking the Person

- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Jar That Bakes Later (60 min)

- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Picking the Person

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · crayons · 1 marker.

1. Ask her who outside this house has been kind to her this week. Offer names if she stalls: the neighbor, the woman in the store, whoever brings the mail.
2. She draws them. You write the name across the top.
3. Say the rule once. It is a surprise until we hand it over. Then let her practice telling you what is in it.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Jar That Bakes Later

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 clean jar with a lid, big enough for three cups of dry ingredients
- All-purpose flour, 1 1/4 cups
- White sugar and brown sugar, 1/3 cup each
- Rolled oats, 1/2 cup
- Raisins or chocolate chips, 1/3 cup
- 1 tablespoon and 1 teaspoon
- A funnel folded from paper
- 1 card label, string, 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Jar on the table, funnel in the neck. Flour first, tablespoon for the bulk and teaspoon for the last of it. She taps it flat with the back of the spoon.
2. White sugar next, then brown sugar pressed down hard so the line between them stays sharp.
3. Oats after that, tapped down the same way. Raisins or chocolate chips last, up to the neck of the jar so nothing shifts on the walk over.
4. Lid on tight, and the jar goes high on a shelf while she does the label.
5. She draws on one side of the card. On the other you write the method: tip into a bowl, add a stick of soft butter and one egg, roll into balls, twelve minutes at 350 degrees. Sign it from Azlyn.
6. Tie the string twice round the neck, tuck the label under it, and let her pull the knot tight with you.

> 💡 **Tip:** Flat layers make it a gift instead of a bag of groceries. Let her do the tapping and accept the mess.

### 🌳 Get Outside: First Barefoot Grass

Pick the warmest part of the day and take everybody's shoes off on grass for
the first time this year. She will stand on the spot before she trusts it.
Walk her across the whole patch: the cold strip in the shade of the hedge, the
dry prickle where the sun has had it all morning, the give underneath after a
wet week.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a second
> or two on a flat floor. Set him down barefoot on grass and he will hold one
> foot up, curl his toes and object at the texture before he agrees to weight
> it. Hold his hands and wait him out.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Delivering It Without Telling

The jar goes across the road this afternoon, wrapped in paper she has covered
herself.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The filled jar
- Brown paper, or a paper bag cut open flat
- Crayons
- 1 roll masking tape
- String
- 1 card for the message
- 1 permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread the brown paper on the floor and give her the crayons. Whole sheet, ten solid minutes.
2. Move to the table for the jar. Paper up round the glass, tape wherever she is holding it. Lumpy is the correct result.
3. Message card: she draws, and underneath you write what she dictates, word for word.
4. String round the parcel, card tucked under the string, knot pulled tight by both of you.
5. Rehearse on the way over. Give her one sentence for the door and let her change it.
6. She carries it with both hands and she knocks. Stand a pace back.
7. She will announce what is inside before the door is halfway open. Let her, and let the neighbor do the surprised face.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not prompt her on the doorstep. A three-year-old fed her line in front of a stranger goes silent.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Wrap it in a paper bag with one drawing taped on and go.
- Mail the message card today and hand the jar over tomorrow.
- Fill a second jar for somebody in this house instead.
- Draw the neighbor's front door and add it to Friday's street map.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A playground you have never been to**, two streets past the usual one
- The long way home from the delivery, on the other side of the road
- Feeding the ducks, if the new playground is too far
- A field, a ball and nothing organized
- The same barefoot grass again, with a blanket and a book

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** New playground, new bars to pull up on. At 11
> months he wants the equipment the big children are on, so let him watch the
> baby swing from your arms first, then put him in it. Push him facing Azlyn,
> because he checks where she is every twenty seconds.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Secrets are cognitively demanding, and she will probably fail.**
> Holding a surprise asks two hard things of her at once. She has to track
> what somebody else does not know, which is theory of mind and still under
> construction at three, and she has to stop herself saying the most exciting
> thing in her head, which is inhibitory control and thinner now than it ever
> will be. Most three-year-olds leak the surprise inside a minute of meeting
> the person. Set the day up so the telling is the gift: she carries the
> parcel, she knocks, she announces what is in it on the doorstep. Nobody has
> to pretend, and she gets the practice without the failure.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A glass jar at floor level with an 11-month-old who stands
> and cruises. Fill it and wrap it on the table, never on the floor, and put
> it high the moment the lid is on. Loose oats, raisins and chocolate chips
> are all choking-sized for Kreston, so sweep before he goes down. You carry
> the jar over the road and hand it to her on the far curb, so the crossing
> happens with your hands on the glass.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 151: Before Azlyn 🌟
**📅 Monday, May 31, 2027**
**Theme:** Memorial Day & Community Heroes

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put the two or three oldest photographs in the house out of her reach with one small thing that belonged to the person you chose, and count the small water bottles for Tuesday.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Older Than Her
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Three Stories from Before (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: A Bunch for the Photograph (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Remembering Shelf (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Filling the Water Pitcher
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Photographs on the Rug
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Story She Asks For Again
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Older Than Her

**🧰 You need:** 3 things older than Azlyn, one of them the oldest thing in the house · the kitchen table.

1. Line the three up on the table and let her handle all of them.
2. Ask which is oldest. Take her guess, then tell her the real age of each one and where it came from.
3. Every object on this table was here before she was. Say that out loud, and tell her three stories from then are coming at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Three Stories from Before

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3 sheets of paper
- Crayons
- 1 marker, for you to write the caption she gives each drawing
- 2–3 old photographs
- 1 roll masking tape

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Paper and crayons down in front of her, then start talking. She draws while you talk.
2. Story one is yours, from before she was born. Keep it small and true: the job you hated, the apartment with the broken window, the first time you met Joseph.
3. Story two is Joseph's. Pick one he tells at the table, or ring him and let him tell it himself.
4. Story three is the person who is gone, with the old photograph out. Say the name, say how you are related, and say one thing they did that you can still see them doing.
5. Ask her what each story was about as she finishes each drawing and write her answer on it. She will get it wrong, and the wrong version is worth keeping.
6. Tape the three drawings in a row above the windowsill you are clearing at 1:00.

> 💡 **Tip:** Story three does its work with no ceremony attached. Tell the sad one the way you told the funny one. She reads your face first, and a warm flat delivery lets her ask questions.

### 🌳 Get Outside: A Bunch for the Photograph

Go out with one purpose: enough flowers for a jam jar on a windowsill. Late
May puts them everywhere, buttercups and clover on the green, wild mustard
along the roadside, whatever has escaped a garden wall. She picks and she
decides. If your town has a memorial, walk past it. There will be flowers on
it today, put there by somebody this morning.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and has started handing
> things over on purpose. Give him one sturdy stalk and hold your hand out for
> it. He gives it, takes it back and gives it again, twenty times over. Keep
> the picked flowers out of his mouth walking home.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Remembering Shelf

One windowsill becomes a place for one person this afternoon, and it stays
that way well past this week.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- A windowsill or a low shelf, cleared
- 1 small jar or glass of water
- The flowers from the walk
- 1–2 photographs
- One object that belonged to the person
- Card and a marker for the name
- A cloth for wiping the sill

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She clears the sill herself and wipes it with the cloth. Everything that used to live there goes elsewhere.
2. Fill the jar at the tap and let her carry it the whole way, both hands, at whatever speed she manages.
3. She snaps the stems short with her fingers and puts the flowers in. Crowded and lopsided is fine.
4. The photograph goes at the back, propped against the glass. She picks which one faces into the room.
5. The object goes in front. Tell her whose hands used it and what for, and let her hold it before it goes down.
6. Name card last. She draws on it, you write the name in letters readable from the door, and it props against the jar.
7. Sit down in front of the lot before you tidy anything. Ask her to tell one of the three stories back. Take whatever version comes.

> 💡 **Tip:** Leave the shelf up. She will walk past it for weeks and ask about it at odd moments.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One photograph and one jar of flowers, and stop there.
- Draw the person from the photograph and tape it above the sill.
- Ring the oldest person in the family and let her ask one question.
- Go through a whole album on the floor and stop there.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A field walk**, the long edge of one, out and back, grass high enough to run a hand through
- The riverside path, if the field is still wet from last week
- A quiet stretch of the churchyard, walked slow
- The green space with a ball, busier than usual with everybody off for Memorial Day
- The playground, and let her run the whole hour off

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Put him down where the grass is short and let him
> crawl. At 11 months he will sit and pull at one stalk for two minutes. Keep
> him off the roadside itself and carry him the last stretch.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Children can't yet imagine their parents as separate people.**
> To Azlyn, you began when she did. She has no working model of you as a
> person with a childhood, a job you hated, an apartment with a broken window.
> Parents turn up in a three-year-old's mind as roles rather than histories,
> and the idea that you existed for years without her is close to unthinkable.
> One small true story from before she was born is the first evidence against
> that. She will not grasp it today. The shape is what stays: people were here
> before, some are gone, and the ones still here carry the stories. That is as
> much as a remembering day asks.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** You check every stem before she picks it. Poison hemlock
> grows along these roadsides, lacy white heads on a purple-blotched stem, and
> it is deadly. Nothing tall, white and lacy gets picked, nothing goes near a
> mouth, and hands get washed the moment you are in. The jar on the sill is
> glass. Stand it at the back of the sill, out of Kreston's reach, because he
> is 11 months and pulls up on anything at chest height.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 152: Azlyn Runs the Morning 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, June 1, 2027**
**Theme:** Memorial Day & Community Heroes

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Clear Kreston's clothes drawer down to what he can wear, stand the shoebox and the water bottles by the front door, and text whoever you are ringing tomorrow for a photograph of their room.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Jobs Done Before She Woke Up
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Azlyn Does Kreston's Morning (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Watering Somebody Else's Flowers (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Cold Water Box by the Door (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Kreston's Cup
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Kreston's Basket
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Books She Picked for Kreston
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Jobs Done Before She Woke Up

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the downstairs as you left it.

1. Walk her round and hunt for what has already happened this morning. Kettle, dishwasher, curtains, bins out, Kreston fed and changed.
2. Write each one down as she spots it and let her mark it off.
3. Ask who did all of it. Then tell her Kreston's next hour is hers, and you are there for the lifting.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Azlyn Does Kreston's Morning

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Kreston's clothes drawer, open
- 1 bib and 1 washcloth
- His cup, for her to fill
- Banana or cucumber cut into strips he can hold
- A basket for his three chosen toys
- 1 board book

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Clothes first. She picks the whole outfit out of the drawer and you put it on him without editing one item.
2. Bib next, and she does the fastening at the back of his neck. He wriggles.
3. Cup: she fills it at the tap, carries it over and hands it to him.
4. Snack: three strips onto his tray from her hand, and more when those have gone.
5. Washcloth over his face and hands at the end. He will object, she does it anyway.
6. Three toys into the basket, chosen by her, and that is his lot until lunch. Then she reads him the board book. He will crawl off halfway, and it counts as read.

> 💡 **Tip:** Sit on your hands unless he is about to fall. Every choice you correct tells her the job was never hers.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Watering Somebody Else's Flowers

June and the first dry spell, so take a full watering can up the road and
water somebody else's pots. The neighbor who is at work, the tubs outside the
store, the planter at the end of the street that nobody owns. She is doing a
job for people who will never know it happened.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and follows more one-step
> instructions than he can answer. Hand him his cup and say drink, and watch
> him do it. He has spent the morning being served by his sister rather than
> by you. He will look for her when he wants something.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Cold Water Box by the Door

A box goes out by the front door this afternoon, stocked for whoever turns up.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 shoebox or small basket
- 4–6 small bottles of water
- Wrapped snacks, 4–6
- Card and crayons for the sign
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 roll masking tape
- A trash bag or plastic bag to keep the rain off

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sit on the doorstep and count who comes to this door in a day and gets nothing out of it. The mail, deliveries, the trash collectors.
2. She loads the box: bottles along the bottom, snacks on top, in whatever order she decides.
3. Sign next. She draws on the card and you write underneath in marker what she dictates, big enough to read from the gate.
4. Tape the sign to the front of the box so it faces the path rather than the house.
5. Lay the trash bag over the top and tape the corners down at the back, so a shower does not turn the sign to mush.
6. She carries it out and picks the spot. Wherever she picks is where it goes.
7. Check it together at five and count what is left.

> 💡 **Tip:** Refill it before she is up and say nothing. Let her find it fuller than she left it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One bottle and one note taped to the door.
- Draw the sign only, and load the box tomorrow.
- A second box for the sidewalk outside the store.
- Do the whole thing for the trash collectors, out on trash day.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one, and warm enough now to walk home with wet hair
- The splash pad or the kiddie pool, if the session is full
- A shallow bit of the river or the lake, feet only
- The park with a picnic, if nobody can face changing rooms
- The garden with a dishpan of water and two cups

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes in with you. At 11 months he stands
> alone on land and has no idea that does not carry into water, so he stays in
> your hands. Walk him along the wall under the arms so he can pat it. Twenty
> minutes, then out.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Acts of service are the hardest gift for a young child to conceive of.**
> Handing over a wrapped object is easy for her to understand. The thing was
> hers, then it was theirs, and she watched it happen. Doing something for a
> person who is not in the room asks her to hold a stranger in her head and
> picture them thirsty, a bigger act of imagination than most adults credit at
> three. Making the service concrete closes the gap: a box she can see, things
> she can count, a spot she chose, and two bottles missing from it by teatime.
> She takes generosity from the evidence, and the evidence today is the empty
> space in the box.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Swimming with two children and one adult. Kreston is 11
> months, stands alone for a moment and lunges at water, so he is in your
> hands the whole time and Azlyn stays inside arm's reach. On a hot day get
> him out at twenty minutes. Nothing goes in the water box that Kreston can
> reach if he is out on the step with you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 153: The People Who Are Far Away 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, June 2, 2027**
**Theme:** Memorial Day & Community Heroes

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fix the call for mid-morning, charge the phone, check their photograph has arrived, and put May's drawings and pressed flowers in one pile for tomorrow.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Who Isn't Here
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Call with Jobs In It (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Finding the Elderflower (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Their Room and Ours (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Two Rooms
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Elderflower on the Sill
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Who Isn't Here

**🧰 You need:** the family cards from Saturday, still on the door · 1 sheet of paper · crayons.

1. Go along the rows and ask which of these people she has not seen for a long time. Take her first answer.
2. Take that card off the door and let her carry it about.
3. She draws them a picture. Tell her it goes up on the screen at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Call with Jobs In It

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- A phone or tablet
- A mug and a book to prop it up at her height
- One of the family cards from Saturday
- A drawing to hold up
- A flashlight
- Kreston

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Give her the running order before you dial. Say hello, show the drawing, take them round the house, fetch Kreston, finish with the flashlight.
2. Prop the phone against the book with the mug behind it, down at her height, so nobody has to hold it up for ten minutes.
3. Hello and the drawing first, close enough to fill the screen. She will hold it upside down and explain it anyway.
4. Then the tour. She carries the phone round and shows them her bed, the window, and their own card on the door.
5. Fetch Kreston into shot and let her introduce him. She will lift his hand and wave it for him.
6. Finish with the flashlight. Big light off, flashlight under her chin, and the person on the screen does it back if they can find one.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let the silences run. The temptation is to fill every gap for both ends, and the call gets better once she works out nobody is going to talk over her.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Finding the Elderflower

Early June is the two weeks the elderberry is out, flat white plates of flower
on a scruffy shrub along ditches, fence lines and the edge of any damp scrub.
Walk until she finds one, check it yourself, then hold the head down for her
to smell. It smells of honey with something sharper under it. Snap one head
off for the sill and carry it yourself. If nothing is open yet, the black
locust hanging in white chains over the road does the same job for her nose.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and knows voices with no face
> attached. Hold him in shot and watch him check behind the phone for the
> person. Hand him a board book once he has had his turn.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Their Room and Ours

Two shoeboxes go down on the floor a hand's width apart, standing in for two
rooms and the distance between them.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 shoeboxes
- 2 heavy books, to hold the boxes still
- Scraps of card and an old dish towel for furniture
- 1 roll masking tape
- Crayons and 1 marker
- 2 small dolls, or 2 clothespins with faces drawn on
- 2 short cardboard tubes as the phones
- A photo of their room on your phone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay both boxes on their sides, open faces toward each other, and weight each one with a book so they hold still.
2. The left box is theirs. Look at the photograph and copy it: wall color in crayon, a bed folded out of card, the dish towel as the blanket, a window drawn on the back panel.
3. The right box is hers, and she does it on her own. Hands off unless she asks.
4. Two clothespins or two dolls, faces drawn on in marker. One into each room, and she says which is which.
5. A cardboard tube in each room as the phone. Hold yours to your ear, she holds hers, and talk across the gap.
6. Run this morning's call again through the tubes. Hello, the drawing, the tour, then Kreston.
7. Lift the book off her box and slide it across the room, as far from theirs as the floor allows, then do the tube call from there.

> 💡 **Tip:** Copy their room down to the boring details, the lamp and the wrong-colored curtains.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One box, their room only, and hers stays real.
- Draw both rooms flat on one big sheet instead.
- Record a video message and let her direct it.
- Post a real letter with this morning's drawing folded inside.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The church hall playgroup**, and let her take one thing to show
- Indoor playground, if the hall is shut for the holiday
- The park with whoever is going
- A walk to the mailbox with the letter
- The garden center café, for a bun and a sit down

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Playgroup at 11 months is a room of children who
> move faster than he does, and he will sit in the middle and watch. Put him
> down near the ride-on toys rather than the baby mat. He pulls up on anything
> at chest height.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Video calls are hard for young children, and that's not rudeness.**
> Researchers call it the video deficit. Children under about three take in
> less from a screen than from the same person in the room, and the gap closes
> when the person on screen responds to them in real time. A face saying hello
> sweetheart on a loop gives her nothing to work with. A person who asks to
> see her bed, then waits while she carries the phone there, is running a live
> back-and-forth, and that she can use. Her wandering off mid-call is her
> going to find something to do. Build the call out of jobs and you answer
> that before it starts.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Nothing picked on this walk goes near a mouth. Elderberry
> grows in the same rough ground as poison hemlock and water hemlock, both
> deadly and both carrying lacy white flower heads at this time of year, so
> you identify every plant before she touches it. Kreston is 11 months and
> mouths whatever reaches his hand, so he carries nothing and she hands
> everything to you. Wash both pairs of hands when you get in.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 154: What We Keep 🌟
**📅 Thursday, June 3, 2027**
**Theme:** Memorial Day & Community Heroes

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Scroll your phone back to Friday so this week's photographs are in order, and stand the paint, the brush, the card and a washcloth by the sink.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Telling the Week Back
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)

- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch

- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Telling the Week Back

**🧰 You need:** your phone, with this week's photographs · the sofa.

1. Sit down together and go through the week from Friday forward, in order, saying nothing.
2. She tells you what each one was. Let the order come out wrong and leave it wrong.
3. Count the days off on her fingers. Seven. Tell her each one gets its own card at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Week in Seven Pictures

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 7 pieces of card
- Crayons
- 1 marker, for writing her words down exactly as she says them
- 1 roll masking tape
- This week's photos on your phone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the seven cards in a row across the table. Put a finger on the first and say Friday.
2. Show her Friday's photo, then take the phone away before she picks up a crayon.
3. Ask what it is when she stops. Write her answer underneath in marker, word for word, wrong words and all.
4. Work along the row. Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Today goes last, and she decides what today has been.
5. Tape the seven up in a line at her height, beside the family cards on the door.
6. Walk the line and read her own words back in order. She will correct you on at least one, and her correction goes on the card.

> 💡 **Tip:** If four of the seven come out the same scribble, tape all four up. The words underneath are what you read next year.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Walk, All Green

Walk the route you walked on the first day of January, when the trees were
bare. It has closed over. Stop where January's photograph was taken, look up
at a ceiling of leaves where there was sky in winter, and take the summer one
from the same spot. Do four of these across the year, and keep them together.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and did this walk in January
> facing out of the carrier. Put him down at the flat stretch and let him walk
> it holding one finger. He turns twelve months on Saturday, so say happy
> nearly-one to him out there.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Sealing Up May

May gets sealed into an envelope this afternoon, and June opens with fresh
handprints.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large envelope, or a cereal box flattened and folded into one
- The month's drawings and pressed flowers
- Washable non-toxic poster paint
- 1 wide soft brush
- 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
- Thick card, 1 sheet, for the handprints
- 1 pencil and 1 marker
- The growth chart wall

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread May's drawings and pressed flowers over the floor. She keeps three out for the wall and the rest go in the envelope.
2. Write MAY and the year across the front, hand her the marker for the rest of it, then fold the flap over and press it down.
3. Handprints, and Kreston goes first while he is calm, washcloth already in your other hand. Paint his palm with the brush rather than dipping his hand, press flat on the card, lift straight up and wipe him down.
4. Azlyn next, her palm on the same sheet beside his. Same brush, press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write June beside the pair of them.
5. Wash both pairs of hands and stand the card flat somewhere high to dry.
6. Growth chart: both of them against the door frame. Mark with the pencil, write the name and the date, and do the adults too.
7. Stand her next to May's mark and let her find the gap with her own finger. Ask what she thinks July will be and put a pencil dot there.

> 💡 **Tip:** Her guess will be near the ceiling. Put the dot where she says and leave it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Handprints only, and seal the envelope tomorrow.
- Draw round both their hands in pencil instead.
- Sort May's drawings into keep and send, and post two of them.
- Measure everybody with string and tape the strings up.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The thrift store**, where she has a dollar and full authority over it
- The park on the way back, to try whatever she came home with
- The library, if the thrift store is shut by three
- A bench outside the bakery, one bun, split four ways
- The green space and a ball, if the store lasted four minutes

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Thrift stores are the right size for an
> 11-month-old. Keep him in the sling and put him down in the book corner if
> there is one. Let Azlyn pick something for him and pay for it at the
> register. Nothing with a loose eye or a small wheel.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Children don't have autobiographical memory the way we assume.**
> Azlyn will keep almost nothing from this week on her own. Autobiographical
> memory, the kind with a when and a who in it, assembles between three and
> five, and how well a child builds it tracks how the adults around her talk
> about the past with her. Parents who ask open questions and add detail,
> rather than checking the facts, tend to get children who tell fuller stories
> about their own lives years later. Seven cards on a wall with her own wrong
> words under them give that conversation a handle. Read them back, let her
> correct you, and the week gets filed.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Washable non-toxic paint only. Kreston is 11 months and will
> have a painted palm in his mouth before you have finished pressing it, so
> his print goes first, while he is calm, with the washcloth in your hand
> before you start. Keep the pencil off the floor when he is down.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>
<a id="backup-may"></a>

# 🌧️ May — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

May is the month that promises and then goes back on it. You get a warm
morning, a black sky by eleven, thunder over lunch and sun again in time for a
long light evening. These pages are for the days the plan stops working: two
full days for when the weather shuts you in, two for when one of them wakes up
ill, and a page of ten-minute ideas for the mornings you open this book with
nothing left in the tank. Nothing here needs a store trip, because on those
days you are not going to one.

---

<a id="may-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — Thunder and Nowhere to Run

For the day the storm sits over the house. Warm air, rain hitting the glass
sideways, thunder near enough to feel, and a three-year-old with a full tank
and no yard to empty it into. The whole plan below is built to burn that fuel
indoors and then bring her down again after lunch.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the paper recycling in a pile by the sofa, put the masking tape and a marker on top of it, and empty the laundry basket. If the storm is forecast, tell her at bedtime that tomorrow is an inside day, so the news is old by breakfast.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Fifty Paper Balls
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Sticky Doorway (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Loudest Window in the House (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Rain Down the Paper (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🤸 The Jumping Line Down the Hallway (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Paper Balls Back in the Basket
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Painted Sheets, Now Dry
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Warm Washcloths and Pajamas Early
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Fifty Paper Balls

**🧰 You need:** the paper recycling, newspaper and junk mail · 1 laundry basket · 1 marker · masking tape.

1. Sit on the floor with the pile between you and show her one ball: a sheet crushed in two hands until it stops making noise. Loose ones fly wrong, so squeeze yours hard where she can see it.
2. Count them into the basket out loud as she goes. Fifty is the target and thirty is a working morning.
3. Write the number on a strip of tape and stick it to the basket. She will beat it before lunch and want the number changed.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Sticky Doorway

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 roll masking tape or packing tape
- 1 doorway with nothing breakable through it
- The basket of paper balls
- 1 marker
- 2 strips of tape for the throw line

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Run four strips of tape across the doorway, sticky side facing her, at heights between her knees and the top of her head. Press the ends to the frame and press them hard. Keep the lowest strip above Kreston's standing reach.
2. Stand her one long step back and put a tape line on the floor there. Give her ten balls and let her throw. Some stick, most drop, and the sound of the ones that stick is the whole appeal.
3. Count what stuck. Write the number on the door frame in marker or on a strip of tape beside it.
4. Now hand her the roll and let her change something. More strips, a wider gap, the line moved back, tighter balls. One change at a time is the rule, and you say it once rather than enforcing it.
5. Throw the same ten again and compare the counts. She will want to argue about which change did it. Let her, and write both numbers up.
6. Take a turn yourself from the back of the room. Losing to her is worth more than coaching her.

> 💡 **Tip:** Tape that has gone dusty stops catching. Peel that strip off, throw it away and run a fresh one, rather than letting her decide she has broken it.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Loudest Window in the House

Nobody is going out in this. Take the movement anyway. Go around the house
window by window, stand a step back from each one for a count of ten, and rank
them by how loud the rain is. Run between them rather than walking. The windows
stay shut and the front door stays closed while you can hear thunder, and both
of you keep off the glass and the frames. Finish at the loudest one and count
the seconds between the flash and the rumble together. A long count puts the
storm a long way off, and a count that grows each time means it is leaving.
The open door waits for the end of the day. Twenty minutes after the last
thunder, step onto the mat with her and let her smell what May rain does to hot
ground, because that smell is one she will recognize for the rest of her life.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and thunder will wake him from
> the morning nap. Bring him down rather than settling him back up there on his
> own. Wet paper turns to a plug in a baby's throat, so the ball basket lives on
> the table between throws and the floor gets swept before he goes down on it.
> Give him a second basket with a folded blanket and three books in the bottom,
> because an empty one tips the moment he pulls up on the rim. He hauls himself
> up on the weighted one, holds the stand for a second or two, and drops back
> onto his bottom, which is the work his legs need this month. At the windows,
> hold him a step back from the glass and say **rain** every time. One word said
> the same way twenty times is how a first word arrives.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Rain Down the Paper

The morning was loud and fast. This one is slow, sitting down, and it makes
something that stays on the wall.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Washable poster paint in two or three colors
- 3 small cups or a muffin tin
- Water, and 1 teaspoon per color
- Thick paper or cut-open cereal boxes, 4 sheets
- 1 baking sheet or a large tray
- Masking tape
- 1 old dish towel

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Mix each color in its own cup with enough water that it runs off a spoon in a thread. Too thick and it sits still, which is the one way this fails.
2. Tape a sheet of paper to the baking sheet at all four corners. Rest one end of the sheet on a rolled dish towel so the paper sits at a slope.
3. Spoon one blob of paint along the top edge and stop. Both of you watch it decide to move.
4. Her turn with the spoon, one color at a time, along the top edge only. The rule she has to hold is that the brush stays out of it. Gravity does the work.
5. Lift the tray higher and let her see the runs go faster and thinner, then lower it and watch them stall and pool. Ask her which one looks more like the window.
6. Second sheet, and let her break the rule she learned an hour ago. Tilt it sideways, tip it end over end, blow one run off course.
7. Lay the finished sheets flat on the kitchen counter to dry, up out of Kreston's reach, and leave them there. She will go back to them at 4:15 and find the pools have dried with hard edges.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do your own sheet on the other side of the tray. She works longer next to somebody working than next to somebody watching.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Skip the paint and race two real drops down the window glass, best of five, from a step back.
- Flatten the morning's paper balls back out and draw on the creases.
- Tape a sheet to the fridge and do the same runs standing up.
- Give her a cup of water and a dry brush and let her paint the front door with it.

### 🤸 The Jumping Line Down the Hallway

The paint held her still for ninety minutes and the storm is still going, so
the hour after it belongs to her legs. Lay one strip of tape across the hallway
floor for the takeoff and let her jump from it. Mark where she lands with a
second strip and write the number of the jump beside it. She goes again, aiming
past her own mark, and the marks pile up down the hall. Two-footed, one-footed,
backward, from a run-up: the variation is hers to invent and yours to lose at.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Watered-down paint goes in his mouth the moment
> your back turns, so he needs his own thing at the same table height. Two inches
> of warm water in a roasting pan on a towel, one cup and one spoon, and he will
> stay with it for twenty minutes. He tips it over himself at the end. That is
> the point at which you move him, not before.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A system she can change one piece of beats a toy that already works.**
> A toy that works gives her one move, which is to switch it on. The doorway
> you taped up this morning gave her ten. She moved the throw line, packed the
> balls tighter, aimed at the low strip because it caught more, and every change
> she made showed up in the count. That loop is engineering at three, and she can
> run it on tape and old newspaper. Watch for the moment she starts changing one
> thing at a time instead of everything at once. It shows up around now, and it
> is worth more than any score on the door frame. Leave the tape up an extra day
> if she is still testing it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Tape strung across a doorway at head height is a hazard for a
> baby who is pulling up on furniture. Kreston does not go through that doorway
> while it is up, so gate it, shut it, or keep him in the room with you. Every
> strip comes down and goes in the trash the moment the game ends, and the floor
> gets swept before he crawls on it. Wet paper balls and torn tape both choke.
> During a thunderstorm keep both children off the corded phone, out of the bath
> and away from the sink until the thunder has been gone twenty minutes or more.
> Fill the paint cups, the roasting pan and the washcloth bowl in one trip, and
> let the dishes wait.
> The day ends with warm washcloths and pajamas early instead of a bath. No open
> windows and no open front door while you can still hear it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="may-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Rain That Sets In

May does this too. Gray from breakfast to bedtime, eight degrees colder than the
forecast said, and rain that never gets going enough to be interesting. The cold
snap buys you a day indoors, so spend it on the job the warm weather has been
waiting on, which is getting the summer clothes out and the too-small ones
gone.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Pull the bag or box of hand-me-downs and next-size clothes out of the closet and stand it by her bedroom door. Two empty laundry baskets, a marker, and the full-length mirror uncovered if you have one.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Three Piles on the Bed
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Show Down the Hallway (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Test Run in the New Clothes (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Kreston in Her Old Clothes (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🤸 The Fastest Outfit in the House (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Hangers Back on the Closet Rail
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Empty Bed and the Hand-Me-Down Bag
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Pajamas She Chose
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Three Piles on the Bed

**🧰 You need:** her drawers and hanging clothes · 1 bed or a cleared floor · 2 laundry baskets.

1. Empty every drawer she owns onto the bed while she watches, then bring what hangs in her closet down on top of it. The size of the heap is half the fun and she needs to see it all at once.
2. Three piles, named out loud as you start: **fits me** stays on the bed, **too small** goes in one laundry basket and **not yet** in the other. She rules on each item and you hold your tongue on the strange calls.
3. Anything she cannot decide stays in the middle of the bed for 9:15. Aim for a middle pile of eight or so, because that is an hour.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Show Down the Hallway

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The undecided pile from the bed
- The bag of next-size hand-me-downs
- 1 full-length mirror, or the bathroom mirror
- Masking tape for the runway line
- 1 marker and 4 strips of paper
- Your phone for photos

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Run a line of masking tape down the hallway floor and tell her it is the runway. The rest of the house watches from the kitchen doorway.
2. She puts on one thing from the undecided pile. Getting dressed on her own is most of the work here, so sit on the floor and wait rather than helping. Help arrives when she asks for it.
3. Down the runway and back, then a look in the mirror. She gives the verdict, keep or pass on, and you write it on a strip of paper and put the item on the matching pile.
4. Two rules that make it honest: arms up over her head, and squat down to the floor. Anything that pulls tight in either of those has gone too small, and she can feel that for herself.
5. Work through the whole pile, then open the hand-me-down bag and do the same with what is in there. Photograph the outfits she loves, because these are the clothes she will wear in every picture this summer.
6. Give her the drawer at the end and one instruction: what fits goes in, and it has to shut.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will want to keep something that has not fit her since March. Let her keep it. One item costs you nothing and it buys you agreement on the other twenty.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Test Run in the New Clothes

She stays in whatever she chose. Take the movement break in it and call it the
test. Ten laps of the downstairs, a stair climb, a crawl under the table, arms
up high enough to touch the door frame. Anything that rides up, drops down or
stops her doing something gets pulled out of the drawer and put back in the bag.
Open the front door and stand on the mat to watch the rain for a minute at the
end. Cool air on bare arms is information too, and she can tell you herself that
today is not the day for it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 11 months and a bed covered in soft
> piles is the best thing he has seen all week. Put him on it with you and let
> him pull the heaps over. He stands himself up against the mattress edge, holds
> it for a second or two and sits back down, over and over. Say the word for each
> thing you hand him, one word, the same one: **sock**, **hat**, **shoe**. Keep
> drawstrings, plastic bags and any string longer than his forearm off the bed
> and in the closet.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Kreston in Her Old Clothes

The morning was about her body getting bigger. The afternoon hands the evidence
to somebody smaller, which is the part she has been waiting for.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The **too small** pile
- 1 clean towel or blanket on the floor
- 1 laundry basket or a bag for what he cannot use yet
- 1 marker and masking tape for labels
- Your phone, with old photos of Azlyn on it
- Kreston, in a good mood, after a nap

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread the too-small pile out on the towel and let her pick five things for Kreston. Her choices, including the ones that will swamp him.
2. Find a photo on your phone of Azlyn wearing one of them and show her before you start. She will not believe it was her.
3. Dress him in one, with her doing the arms and you doing the head. Say the plan out loud to him each time, because eleven months is old enough to hold an arm out for a sleeve when he knows what is coming.
4. Photograph each one on the same spot on the towel. Two of the five will fit him now and the rest go in the basket with a tape label she scribbles on.
5. Let her tell him what he looks like. He will hand her something back and wait for her to take it, which is his newest trick and worth stopping for.
6. Load the rest of the too-small pile into the bag and write the size on it big enough for her to point at.
7. Stand the bag by the door for whoever is getting it, and let her be the one to put it there.

> 💡 **Tip:** Stop at five, even when she wants to keep going. He will run out of patience before she does, and the afternoon is better ended on a good one.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Try on your own clothes instead and let her rule on those.
- Line up every pair of shoes in the house, smallest to biggest, and count.
- Sort the whole pile by color instead of by size and photograph the rows.
- Wash the four things she loves most by hand in the sink so they are dry by morning.

### 🤸 The Fastest Outfit in the House

She has been sitting down since breakfast and the yard is out, so give the hour
to her legs and to the drawer she filled this morning. She picks a whole outfit,
lays it on the floor in the shape of a person, and stands at the end of the
hallway. You count out loud. She gets the outfit on, runs the hall and back, and
you tell her the number she landed on. Three rounds, a different outfit each
time, and the socks are what will beat her. Take a turn yourself in something of
your own and let her count you down.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him a drawer of his own on the floor, filled
> with the things from the bag he cannot wear yet. Pulling soft items out of a
> container one at a time and dropping them holds an 11-month-old longer than any
> toy in the house. Sit him next to Azlyn's pile rather than in it, so she keeps
> her order and he keeps his job.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **She'll defend a category harder than she'll defend a fact.**
> Ask her whether a shirt still fits and you get an answer. Put that shirt on
> the **fits me** pile and the answer hardens into a position she will hold
> against the evidence of her own arms. Sorting does that at three, and it is
> the reason the arms-up test earns its place: it moves the argument off her
> word and onto her body, so she can change her mind without losing. Let her
> name the piles and let her be wrong in one or two of them. She will re-sort
> half of it herself over the next week, on her own time with nobody watching,
> and that version is the one that holds.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Sort the drawstrings out today while everything is in front of
> you. Cords and ties at the neck of a hood strangle a crawling baby on furniture
> and playground equipment, so cut them out of anything going to Kreston. The
> plastic storage bags go straight back to the closet the moment they are empty.
> Old shoes stay out of the hand-me-down bag: a walker needs a sole that has not
> already been worn into somebody else's shape.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="may-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — Flat All Day

The day she does not get off the sofa. Fever, a throat, a stomach bug, it makes
no difference to the shape below. There are no times on this page on purpose.
She sleeps when she sleeps and eats when she asks, and the whole job is to keep
the day small and let the illness run. Nothing here needs setting up, cutting or
cleaning after, and every piece of it can be dropped mid-sentence when she
turns her face into the cushion.

### 🌙 Before She Wakes
> Strip the sofa of anything that cannot be washed and build the nest: her pillow, two blankets, the bucket, a pile of washcloths, a full cup with a straw in it. Put a towel under the whole thing. Clear the coffee table down to nothing but the cup, and cancel today out loud to yourself before she comes down, because the plan you had is over.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes** — down to the nest in whatever she slept in
- **Before she asks** — the first drink, small and cold, on the table beside her
- **The first long stretch** — 🛋️ Nothing But the Nest
- **When she surfaces** — 🪟 The Window From Where She Is
- **When she asks for food** — dry, plain and half of what you think
- **The long middle** — 😴 The Rest Block
- **After the sleep** — 🧼 The Warm Cloth and the Cold Cloth
- **The flattest hour, late afternoon** — 📖 The Story of Kreston's Morning
- **Before dinner she may not eat** — 🎵 Two Songs and a Phone Call
- **Early, and without the usual routine** — bed

### 🛋️ Nothing But the Nest

The first stretch is the one where you do the least. She lies down, you sit at
her feet with your hand on her leg, and the television goes on if that is what
gets you both through it. Guilt about the screen costs you energy you need for
the rest of the day. Keep the room dim, keep the house quiet, and keep the cup
where her arm reaches without her sitting up. Say once that she is allowed to
stay there all day, and then prove it by not asking her to move.

### 🪟 The Window From Where She Is

**🧰 You need:** the sofa turned or her head at the window end.

1. Turn her so she can see out without lifting her head. That one move is worth more than any activity on a bad day.
2. Give her a job with no effort in it: tell me when a car goes past, tell me when the tree moves. May weather does the rest, and a gray sky that breaks into sun over an hour is a whole show.
3. Answer her with a word. She wants company at this end of the day and a sentence is more than she can hold.

### 😴 The Rest Block

This is the middle of the day and the point of the day. Two hours, curtains
half drawn, no screen, no talking, no visitors. She sleeps or lies there, and
both count. Lie down yourself if Kreston is settled or somebody else has him,
because you will be up in the night with her and this is the only chance you
get. If she fights it, sit beside her with your hand flat on her back and say
nothing at all. A silent adult is what tips a wired sick child over the edge
into sleep.

### 🧼 The Warm Cloth and the Cold Cloth

**🧰 You need:** 2 washcloths · 1 bowl of warm water · 1 bowl of cool water.

1. Warm cloth first, over her face, hands and the back of her neck. Slow, and the same order every time, because the order is the comfort.
2. Cool one folded on her forehead after, if she is hot. She will hold it there herself and that is the first thing her hands have done all day.
3. Fresh pajamas at this point if she can face it. A clean top on a sick child buys an hour of better mood.

### 📖 The Story of Kreston's Morning

**🧰 You need:** your voice, and her eyes shut.

1. Tell her what her brother did while she was lying there, in order and out loud: he woke at six, he banged the spoon on the tray, he ate half the cereal and dropped the rest, he cried at the vacuum.
2. Get one thing wrong on purpose in every stretch. She corrects you from the cushion without opening her eyes, and the correcting is the whole activity.
3. Keep going after she stops answering. She is still listening for a good while after she stops talking.

### 🎵 Two Songs and a Phone Call

Put on the two songs she asks for and leave them on repeat. Then call somebody
who loves her, put it on speaker, and hold the phone near her without making
her perform. A grandparent talking to a silent child for four minutes gives her
the feeling of being visited and costs her nothing. End it before she has to be
polite.

> 👶 **Kreston Today:** He is 11 months, cruising, and he will head for her
> face, her cup and her bucket in that order. He needs somewhere else to be for
> most of today. Call whoever can take him for the afternoon, and if nobody can,
> gate one room, put the sofa out of reach and run the day from there. Everything
> she has touched is his next: her cup goes in the dishwasher after every use,
> her cloths go in a bag, and you wash your hands between the two of them all
> day. He will get it anyway, four days behind her. Feed him and settle him
> somewhere Azlyn cannot hear the two of you.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Illness is a good time to be the one with the ideas rather than the hands.**
> A sick day strips out everything she does with her body. Her legs are no use
> to her, her hands last four minutes, and the part of her still running at full
> speed is the part that thinks. Give that part the work. Ask what happens next
> in the story, which song, which blanket, what the cup should have in it, and
> then do the moving for her. She gets to run an afternoon from a cushion and
> you get a child who feels like herself instead of a patient. Talk less than
> usual while you do it. One question every few minutes is plenty and the
> silence in between is part of the rest.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Fluids beat food by a mile, so keep small cold drinks going all
> day and count her wet diapers or trips to the bathroom. Call the doctor the
> same day for: no wet diaper in eight hours, a dry mouth with no tears, a fever
> over 102°F that will not come down, or a child too sleepy to wake for a drink.
> Call an ambulance for a stiff neck, a fit, hard fast breathing with the skin
> pulling in between her ribs, blue or gray lips, or a rash of small dark spots
> that stays visible when you press a glass against it. Medicine goes back on the
> high shelf between doses, and you write down the time of every one, because the
> day blurs and you will not remember.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="may-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Done Lying Still

Day three, or day four. The fever has gone, she is done lying still, and she is
not well enough for anything real. This is the hardest day of the illness for
you, and the answer is small jobs with a visible end rather than free play she
has not got the fuel for. Still no times, still no going out, and the rest block
in the middle stays even though she will tell you she does not need it.

### 🌙 Before She Wakes
> Move the nest from the sofa to the floor by the window, which changes the room enough to buy an hour. Fill the cup, put a banana and some crackers where she can reach them, and pick three of the jobs below to have ready. Not four.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes** — breakfast on the floor by the window, whatever she wants
- **The good hour, and it comes early** — 📚 The Books in a Line
- **When she flags** — back on the cushions with no comment from you
- **When she asks for food** — 🍊 The Peel That Doesn't Break
- **The long middle** — 😴 The Rest Block, Shorter and Still Not Optional
- **The slump after** — 🧺 Ten Things in the Wrong Room
- **When she starts talking about tomorrow** — ✏️ The Five Drawings for Next Week
- **Late, when nothing else is left** — the bath, long and early
- **Bedtime** — the usual routine, back in place, on time

### 📚 The Books in a Line

**🧰 You need:** every book in the house she can reach.

1. Bring the lot to her in armfuls and dump them where she is sitting. She does not fetch today.
2. One rule, chosen by her: tallest to smallest, or the ones she loves at one end and the rest at the other. Her rule, and she has to say it out loud before she starts.
3. Leave her to it and go do something in the same room. Come back when the line is done and walk its whole length while she tells you the order.

### 🍊 The Peel That Doesn't Break

**🧰 You need:** 1 orange or a tangerine · 1 plate.

1. Start the peel with your thumbnail and hand it over. The whole job is getting it off in one piece.
2. She will break it. Start a second one and tell her that two out of three is a good result at this.
3. Lay the peels on the plate and let her build the fruit back up out of them. Eating some of it is a bonus on a day like this.

### 😴 The Rest Block, Shorter and Still Not Optional

An hour, in the afternoon, in her bed rather than on the floor. She will argue
harder today than she did yesterday, and the argument is proof she needs it,
because a child on the mend who skips this crashes at four and takes the evening
with her. Books in with her, no screen, curtains half shut. Sleep is a bonus and
lying down is the whole requirement.

### 🧺 Ten Things in the Wrong Room

**🧰 You need:** 1 laundry basket · your legs.

1. Walk the downstairs with the basket and collect ten things that live somewhere else. She picks them from where she sits, pointing.
2. Tip the basket out in front of her. She sorts them into piles by the room each one belongs to.
3. You do the walking and she does the counting. Ten back where they belong, and the empty basket is the finish line she can see.

### ✏️ The Five Drawings for Next Week

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the fridge.

1. Ask her for five things she wants to do the week she is better, and take them one at a time.
2. Draw each one on the sheet yourself, stick figures, numbered one to five. Hold the sheet up after every drawing so she can tell you what you left out.
3. Tape it to the fridge at her height. She crosses one off with the marker each day next week, and the swimming or the park goes first.

> 👶 **Kreston Today:** He is 11 months and he has spent two days shut out of a
> room he can hear her in. Bring him back in this afternoon, on the floor, with a
> border of cushions between the two of them and a basket of his own things.
> Azlyn will want him closer than is wise, so give her a job that involves him
> from a distance: she names what he picks up and you hand it to him. Keep the
> cups separate and keep her hands off his face. He may be starting his own
> version of this in a day or two, and a rested adult handles that better than a
> spotless kitchen does.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A job with a visible end is what a recovering child wants.**
> Boredom on the third day is a sign the illness is loosening, and it turns up
> before her stamina does. Open play needs energy she has not got back yet, so it
> falls apart into whining within minutes and you both end up worse off. A job
> with edges holds. Twelve books to line up, one orange to peel, ten things to
> send back to their rooms: she can see the finish from the start, and reaching
> it hands her the thing this week has taken away, which is evidence that she can
> still do something. Keep them small enough to finish in one sitting. A job she
> abandons costs her more than no job at all.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A child on the mend goes back to preschool or a friend's house
> 24 hours after the last vomiting, diarrhea or fever, with no medicine holding
> the fever down. Going back early spreads it and buys you a relapse. Watch for
> the second wave: a fever that clears and returns two days later, a cough that
> gets worse rather than better, or a child who goes quiet again after a good
> morning. Call the doctor for any of those. Kreston's cups, spoons and pacifiers
> stay separate from hers for the rest of the week.

## 🎲 May — Extra Ideas

For the morning you open this book with ten minutes and no plan. One line each,
no steps, nothing that needs buying.

### 🎲 Alternative Activities

- **The Storm Tally** — one mark on the door frame paper per rumble, read out at dinner.
- **Dandelion Clocks** — one puff each, then count what is left on the stalk.
- **After-Dinner Walk** — the long May light spent on a slow lap of the block in pajamas.
- **Barefoot on Three Floors** — grass, tile and carpet, and her verdict on each one.
- **Maple Helicopters** — two dropped off the step at once and she calls the winner.
- **The Hose With Her Thumb On It** — ten minutes of watering, and her thumb doing the work.
- **Ants at the Crack** — one crumb left on the path and checked every half hour.
- **The Sound Under the Umbrella** — standing still in the rain to listen to it hit.
- **The Wet Grass Sprint** — shoes off, fence to door and back twice, feet dried on the mat.
- **The Stairs Counted Two Ways** — numbers going up, the same numbers backward coming down.
- **The Cupboard Lunch** — one shelf, and she picks the whole meal off it.

### 🎨 Alternative Arts & Crafts

- **The Dandelion Rub** — yellow heads rubbed hard on paper until the color comes off.
- **The Grass Brush** — a fistful of grass taped to a stick and used as a paintbrush.
- **Tape Resist Letters** — her initial taped on paper, painted over, the tape peeled off last.
- **The Egg Carton Caterpillar** — six cups, twelve legs and a name she picks.
- **Petal Prints** — petals folded inside paper and tapped with the back of a spoon.
- **Cardboard Sunglasses** — cut from a cereal box with colored plastic wrap for lenses.
- **String Painting** — a paint-soaked string dragged out from between two folded sheets.
- **The Foil Flower** — foil pressed around a bottle cap and bent out into petals.
- **The Junk Mail Collage** — flyers and envelopes torn up and glued into one shape.
- **Handprint Wings** — two hands printed either side of her name down the middle.
- **Wax Rain** — white crayon lines pressed hard, then blue paint washed over the top.

### 👶 Kreston's Turn

- **The Low Shelf He Can Empty** — one shelf cleared and refilled with things he may pull out and drop.
- **Cruising for a Cracker** — the snack set at the far end of the sofa, with the furniture in between.
- **One Word All Day** — a single object named the same way every time it comes near him.
- **The Roasting Pan of Warm Water** — two inches of water on a towel, one cup, and you within arm's reach.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Standing water**: the dishpans of color on Day 160, the kiddie pool through all of Week 24, the tub under the sheet on Day 178. Kreston climbs into a pool at one year and cannot climb back out, so tip every container out when you finish.
- **Small round things**: the bottle caps on Day 162, the beans on Day 167, the map markers on Day 171, the rice in the shaker on Day 176. Each one matches Kreston's airway at twelve months, and you quarter Day 170's cherry tomatoes lengthwise before they reach his tray.
- **Balloons**: three come out for the smash cake on Day 156 and two more for the static tests on Day 161. You inflate them, they stay above head height, and you pick a burst one up whole before he is back on the floor.
- **String and cord**: the wind line on Day 161, the throw line on Day 165, the family line on Day 170, the bunting on Day 181. All of it goes up out of reach or comes down when the activity ends, because a loop at Kreston's height is a strangulation risk.
- **Adult-only steps**: the oven and the candle on Day 156, the table knife on Day 170, the scissors on most days from Day 155 on. "The scissors stay with you" runs through the month, because he is on his feet now and a table edge sits at his eye level.
- **Late June heat**: hats and sunscreen on both of them before you open the door, then again after any water. Put your own hand flat on paving, dark plastic and metal first, and shade the stroller by parking it rather than draping a cloth over the top, which traps the heat.

<a id="week-23"></a>

## Week 23: Colors of Summer ☀️
**📅 June 4 – June 10, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

Color is the one thing Azlyn has all the words for, so this week takes it
apart. She mixes red into five pinks a dot of white at a time, freezes color
and drags it across paper, drops it onto wet paper and gets a circle every
time, leaves it out in the sun until it fades, and pours it bowl to bowl until
all three go brown. Every day she guesses first and looks second, and you
write down both.

Kreston turns 1 on Saturday. Day 156 gives him a banana cake he is allowed to
wreck, one candle for ten seconds, June handprints, a pencil line on the door
frame, and the museum after lunch. Azlyn chooses his icing color at breakfast
and then has to keep her hands off the cake, which is the hardest thing anyone
does all week.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Color is something you make.** Red walks to pink in five steps, one dot of white at a time.
- **Guess first, look second.** She calls what the cabbage water will do before the lemon goes in, and both answers go on the paper in the same pen.
- **Do it twice.** The same red ice cube down a second sheet, to find out whether the world repeats itself when nobody changes anything.
- **Counting with a reason.** Five blue and two red, dropped in with a teaspoon and spooned back out, gives her a color she can build again from her own card.
- **Things move without being touched.** The sun pulling color out of paper over four hours, a balloon lifting paper it never reaches.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Appreciation is different from praise, and children need more of the first
- Things that break the rules are the best teachers
- Repeating an experiment is what makes it an experiment
- "Why is it always round?" is a question worth leaving open
- Same object, different result, and the variable is time
- Being wrong in public is a skill, and it's built cheaply here
- Invisible forces are a big conceptual step

---

**Theme:** Colors of Summer

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
