## 🌟 Day 177: Fireworks Without the Bang 🌟
**📅 Saturday, June 26, 2027**
**Theme:** Red, White & Blue Countdown

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Cut one end of two cardboard tubes into a fringe with the kitchen scissors, and stand the dark paper, the three paints and a washcloth by the sink.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Black Paper Sky
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Fireworks Made With a Fork (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Flowers Shaped Like Fireworks (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Bang She Controls (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Napkins
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Looking at the Dry Paintings
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and Two Quiet Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Black Paper Sky

**🧰 You need:** dark blue or black paper, 4 sheets · newspaper · 1 white crayon or a stub of chalk.

1. Newspaper across the table, then the four dark sheets on top, one at each side so she can walk round them.
2. Give her the white crayon and ask for the bottom of the sky: rooftops, a fence, trees, whatever she says lives there.
3. Everything above her line stays empty. Say it is for later and leave all four sheets until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Fireworks Made With a Fork

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Dark blue or black paper, 4 sheets (substitute: a cereal box painted dark)
- Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, white and blue
- 1 fork
- 1 whisk
- 2 cardboard tubes, one end cut into a fringe
- 2 shallow plates for the paint
- Newspaper for the table
- 1 wet washcloth in a bowl

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Newspaper back down. Red and white onto one shallow plate, blue onto the other, wet washcloth in its bowl at her elbow.
2. Press the back of the fork into the paint, then straight down onto the dark paper and straight up again. Turn a quarter, press again round the same middle. Four presses make one burst.
3. Whisk next. Dip the round underside, press, hold for a count of two. It prints fatter than the fork.
4. Fringed tube last. Dip the cut end, press, twist a quarter turn before lifting.
5. Let her fill all four sheets and go on filling them. Hands into the washcloth between colors or the sky turns purple.
6. Lay them flat on the floor out of Kreston's line to dry. She comes back at 4:15.

> 💡 **Tip:** Load the fork light. A fork thick with paint prints a blob, and a fork with almost nothing on it prints thin lines that read as a firework.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Flowers Shaped Like Fireworks

Late June is the two weeks for this. Look for flowers that burst out of one
point: alliums on their tall stalks, the domed head on a milkweed, Queen
Anne's lace on the roadside, a dandelion clock gone to seed. Get her to trace
one from the middle out to the tip, then bring a clock home and blow it on the
doorstep. Leave the milkweed stem unbroken, because the white sap inside it
stings eyes.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and everything in his hand
> travels to his mouth. Sit him at the far end of the table with the wet
> washcloth and let him press it onto the newspaper, where it leaves a dark
> mark that fades while he watches. He will do that twenty times. On the walk
> he pushes the stroller along one flat stretch.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Bang She Controls

A firework goes off whether or not she is ready. Every loud noise this
afternoon starts with her hands, and she counts it down first.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 paper lunch bags
- 1 saucepan and lid
- Bubble wrap, a sheet
- 1 wooden spoon
- 2 cushions
- 1 folded towel to muffle the floor

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Set up at the far end of the room from Kreston, or hand him over and take this hour with her alone. Everything happens on the folded towel.
2. Bags first. She blows one up, twists the neck, and you both count backwards from three before she claps it flat. Six bags, six goes, all hers.
3. Pop the second bag under a cushion so she hears how much it takes away. The other cushion is hers, for her ears.
4. Saucepan on the towel, lid in her hands. Lid on pan, lid on towel, wooden spoon on pan. Three sounds, and she names each one.
5. Bubble wrap flat on the towel. Stamp along it, then roll it up and squeeze with both arms.
6. Second round is hers to order. She says what is coming, you both count, and she does it.
7. Finish on the floor with the towel over the bubble wrap. Ask her which was loudest.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say the noise out loud before it arrives, every time, in the same words. *Ready. Three, two, one, bang.* She will start doing the countdown herself.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Bubble wrap only, on the hall floor, in socks.
- Drum on upturned pans in the yard where the sound has somewhere to go.
- Blow the bags up and let them go without popping any.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The botanical garden**, still hunting flowers built like fireworks
- The park, with the shadiest bench you know
- A quiet walk with the stroller if the afternoon has been loud enough
- The garden center, cool inside and full of the same flower shapes

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Take him round the botanical garden on foot. At
> 12 months he stops at every edge, every step and every change of surface,
> and gravel to grass to path is the whole outing to him. Let him drink from
> his cup on a bench in the shade.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Children take their fear reading from your face first.**
> A loud unexpected noise sends Azlyn's eyes to you before she decides
> anything about it. Psychologists call the habit social referencing, and it
> is running hard in both of them this year. Your face is the fastest
> information available and she trusts it over her own ears. This is why the
> countdown works: she gets the warning, she watches you stay unbothered, and
> the bang arrives inside a frame she already has. Firework night in eight
> days will be easier for the same reason. Name the noise before it comes,
> keep your shoulders down, and she borrows your reading of it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A saucepan lid banged near Kreston's head is loud enough to
> hurt him at 12 months. Keep every bang at the far end of the room from him,
> or take him out for the ten loudest minutes. Washable non-toxic paint only
> this morning, and expect him to put a painted hand in his mouth.

## 🌟 Day 178: Red, White and Frozen 🌟
**📅 Sunday, June 27, 2027**
**Theme:** Red, White & Blue Countdown

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Clear a flat shelf in the freezer wide enough for eight paper cups standing up, and move the yogurt, the juice and the fruit to the front of the fridge.

- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch

- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Water Pitchers
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Empty Ice Cups
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Cool Bath, Curtains Shut
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Mashing the Blueberries

**🧰 You need:** the punnet of blueberries · 1 fork · 1 pitcher.

1. Tip the punnet into the pitcher and hand her the fork. Mashing blueberries takes longer than she expects, which is why it belongs at 8:00.
2. Stand the pitcher in the fridge. This is the top layer and it waits until late morning.
3. Give her the last few whole ones to eat.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Three-Layer Ice Pops

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Blueberries, one pint, or grape juice
- Plain yogurt, 1 small pot
- Apple or orange juice, 300 ml
- Strawberries or red fruit punch
- 8 paper cups
- 8 craft sticks or plastic spoons for the handles
- 1 teaspoon or plastic spoon for the yogurt
- Kitchen foil
- 1 fork and 1 pitcher

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Hull the strawberries, two or three into each of the eight paper cups. She squashes them with the fork and pours about 100 ml of juice between the eight.
2. Stand the cups in the corner of the freezer shelf where they cannot tip. They want an hour.
3. At the 10:15 snack they come out. She spoons yogurt over the frozen red with a plastic spoon, a heaped load per cup.
4. Tear eight squares of kitchen foil. Press one over each cup and push a craft stick through the middle into the yogurt, which holds it standing.
5. Before lunch, stir the last 200 ml of juice into the mashed blueberries. Lift each foil square, pour the blue on top and press the foil back down.
6. At 3:30, run one cup under the warm tap for three seconds and peel the paper off in one piece.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will want one at eleven. Take her to the freezer, let her look at the half-frozen cups and put them back herself.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Coolest Spot on the Street

Go out hunting shade and be home before the sun is overhead. Name what makes
each patch of it: the north side of a wall, the big tree, a parked van, a deep
doorway. Ask her which of them will still be shaded when you come past on the
way home this afternoon, and chalk a mark on the sidewalk at the two she
picks. Then stand in the deepest one for a minute with your eyes shut and let
her tell you what she can hear.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and drinks from a cup, so his
> water goes everywhere you go today and he gets offered it whether or not he
> asks. He walks the shaded stretches and rides the sunny ones. A hat stays on
> him for about four minutes, so take the stroller with the hood up.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Tub Under the Sheet

One old sheet over the clothesline makes a room with shade in it, and the tub
goes underneath.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 dishpan or storage tub
- 1 old sheet
- 6 clothespins
- The clothesline, or two chairs and a broom handle
- 2 pitchers and 4 cups
- 1 sieve
- 1 sponge
- 2 towels
- Drinking water for both children

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Clip the old sheet along the clothesline with the six clothespins, one edge low, so the shade falls where you sit. Two chairs and the broom handle across their backs do the same job.
2. Set the dishpan in that shade and fill it a hand's depth with cold water. No deeper, today or any other day.
3. Spread one towel where she kneels and keep the second folded within reach.
4. In go the two pitchers, the four cups, the sieve and the sponge. Show her one thing, pouring from high so it splashes, then stop.
5. The sieve holds her longest, because water leaves it and she cannot see where it went.
6. The sponge goes in last: fill, lift, squeeze over her own knees, and half the tub ends up on the grass.
7. Drinking water stands in the shade beside you and both of them drink at the top of every hour. When she has finished, tip the bowl out and turn it over.

> 💡 **Tip:** Refill the bowl twice rather than filling it deep. Shallow water warms up, which she prefers, and the depth never changes.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Wash the dolls in the bowl and clip them on the line to dry.
- One pitcher and the doorstep, no tub at all.
- Paint the fence with water and a decorating brush.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Feeding the ducks**, late enough that the water has the shade
- The kiddie pool at the park if the town has one
- A shaded woodland path where the temperature drops as you walk in
- The library, for the air conditioning as much as the books

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He sits beside the bowl, never in it and never on
> his own. At 12 months he tips a cup over on purpose to watch what comes out,
> so give him one of his own on the towel away from the tub. Watch his feet on
> hot paving now that he walks barefoot.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Heat, hunger, and tiredness account for most "bad behavior."**
> A late June afternoon does more to Azlyn's mood than anything you say to
> her. Small bodies heat up faster than yours and cool down slower, and a
> three-year-old cannot read the signal or name it. She gets a meltdown over a
> cup instead. Before you deal with the behavior, run the three: has she drunk
> anything in the last hour, has she eaten since lunch, has she been out in
> the sun without a hat. Fix whichever one is missing and most of the trouble
> goes with it. The afternoons that need managing are the afternoons that
> needed a glass of water an hour earlier.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A 12-month-old drowns in the depth of water that is in that
> tub. Kreston never sits beside it unwatched, and you tip it out the moment
> you go in, not later. Late June sun: hats, sunscreen on both of them before
> you go out and again after lunch, shade by 11:00, and check the tub water
> and any metal or dark plastic with your own hand before either child touches
> it.

## 🌟 Day 179: Roll, Then Tell 🌟
**📅 Monday, June 28, 2027**
**Theme:** Red, White & Blue Countdown

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Find a small square box, a tissue box or a cube-shaped parcel box, and stand it on the table with the permanent marker and the masking tape.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Drawing on All Six Sides
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Story the Dice Tells (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Whatever Happens at the Next Corner (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Six Pages and a Cover (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks and the Spoons
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Reading Her Book to Kreston
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Her Own Book, Twice
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Drawing on All Six Sides

**🧰 You need:** the small square box · 1 permanent marker · 1 roll masking tape.

1. Tape the box shut on every open edge so it holds its shape when it lands.
2. Ask her for six things: a person, an animal, a place, a weather, a food, and one of her own choosing. Draw each on a face while she watches. Yours will not be good and she will tell you so.
3. Roll it across the floor once. Whatever lands on top, name it out loud. Then it sits in the middle of the table until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Story the Dice Tells

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 small square box, a tissue box or a cube-shaped parcel box
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 roll masking tape
- Paper, 4 sheets
- 1 pen

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sit on the floor with the paper and the pen beside you. Write *Once there was* at the top of the first sheet and let her finish the sentence out loud.
2. She rolls the cube. Whatever is on top is the next thing that happens in the story, and she says how.
3. Write her words down as they come. No tidying, no fixing the grammar, no better version of what she meant.
4. Roll again. Six or seven rolls is a whole story, and the same picture landing twice means it comes back.
5. If a face has stopped working for her, tape a fresh square of paper over it and draw something new with the permanent marker. She chooses what.
6. Read the finished thing back to her, out loud, at full commitment, in her exact words.

> 💡 **Tip:** A three-year-old's plot has a dog, then a cake, then the dog again, and you read it back with a straight face.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Whatever Happens at the Next Corner

At every corner she calls left or right and you go that way without comment.
Between corners, narrate what you pass as if it were the story: the cat on the
wall wanted something, the parked van has been there since Friday. Late June
mornings are warm by eleven, so take the shady side home.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and follows a one-step
> instruction. Roll the cube toward him and say *bring it*, and about half the
> time he will. Carrying an object across a room to another person is what he
> practices hardest this month, and the box is light enough for both hands.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Six Pages and a Cover

Her story exists on four loose sheets in your handwriting. This afternoon it
becomes a book.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Plain paper, 4 sheets, folded in half
- 1 roll masking tape for the spine
- Crayons
- 1 permanent marker
- The written-down story

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Fold the four sheets in half, stack them one inside another, and run masking tape down the outside of the fold. That is a cover and six pages, with a couple spare.
2. Read the story back and stop at each thing that happens. One thing, one page. Number them with the permanent marker while she watches.
3. Crayons out. She draws page one, and you say nothing about what it looks like and add nothing to it.
4. Write her sentence for that page underneath the drawing, word for word, the same as this morning.
5. Keep going. Six pages if she stays, three pages if she does not, and three pages is a book.
6. Cover last. She chooses the title and you write it, then she does her own name however her name comes out.
7. Sit Kreston down and let her read it to him. She will not read the words, and it does not matter.

> 💡 **Tip:** Put the date on the back cover in permanent marker before it goes on the shelf. In two years the handwriting will be the interesting part and neither of you will remember which June this was.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One page, one drawing, and call it finished.
- Act the story out with teddies instead of drawing it.
- Draw the story on one long strip of paper end to end.
- Tell a second story with the cube and write nothing down.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The neighborhood park**, with the cube in your pocket for a story on the bench
- The same corner-by-corner walk, going the other way this time
- The green space with a ball
- A shaded bit of woodland, with her book to read under a tree
- The playground with the big slide, late enough that the metal has cooled

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At 12 months he listens to Azlyn read for about
> ninety seconds and then wants the book itself. Let him have it once she has
> finished, and expect a bent corner. At the park he walks the flat path and
> pulls himself up the first step of the climbing frame. Stay a hand's width
> behind him.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Storytelling with prompts is easier than storytelling from nothing.**
> Ask Azlyn to tell you a story and she freezes or recites a movie. Hand her a
> picture that has already landed and she is away. The hard part of
> storytelling at three is the choosing: settling on what comes next out of
> everything that could come next, while also finding the words for it. The
> cube does the choosing and leaves her the connecting. A prompt gets longer
> sentences out of her than a blank start does, and more complicated ones.
> Writing her words down without editing them tells her the sentences were
> worth keeping, and she notices that.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The permanent marker and its cap go back on the table out of
> Kreston's reach the moment you stop writing, at 8:00 and again over the
> book. Everything else on the floor is his: check the cube for loose tape
> before you roll it to him, and pick the masking tape and the offcuts up as
> you go. On the corner walk you take the curb side. The turn is hers and the
> road is yours, at every corner, including the ones where she has already set
> off.

## 🌟 Day 180: The Flag on the Floor 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, June 29, 2027**
**Theme:** Red, White & Blue Countdown

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Empty the laundry basket and stand it by the stairs, and put a white sheet or a big bath towel on the arm of the sofa.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Every Red Thing She Can Carry
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Flag Made of Things From the House (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Flat on Our Backs in the Grass (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Fifty Stars Is a Lot (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Putting the Red Things Back
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Star Pile
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Long Story
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Every Red Thing She Can Carry

**🧰 You need:** 1 laundry basket · her · one room at a time.

1. Give her the basket and one word: **red**. Start in her bedroom and do not help her choose.
2. Follow her round. Name each thing as it goes in, and let the arguable ones in; orange counts if she says it counts.
3. Stop when the basket is heavy enough that she has to drag it. Tip nothing out; it comes to the front room at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Flag Made of Things From the House

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 white sheet or bath towel as the base
- Red, white and blue objects from around the house
- 1 laundry basket for carrying
- Your phone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Spread the sheet on the floor in the room with the best light and smooth the creases with her.
2. The red things from 8:00 go down first, in a long line across the bottom edge. Leave a stripe of bare sheet, then another red line above it. Four or five stripes with white sheet between them.
3. Send her out for blue, one room at a time. Blue fills a square in the top left corner, packed as solid as she can get it.
4. White goes last, on the blue, one white thing for each star. Buttons are out, so think socks, paper, a plastic spoon, a hair clip too big to swallow.
5. Hold the phone as high over it as your arm reaches and take the photograph. Let her take one at her height, and keep both.
6. Everything goes back in the basket the way it came out, her job at 4:00.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not straighten her stripes. She carries a wonky flag she laid herself back to every room this afternoon, telling you where each thing lives.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Flat on Our Backs in the Grass

Take a rug to the shadiest grass you can reach and lie on your backs, all
three of you. Late June skies at eleven are full of movement: swifts, a plane,
a seed head, one cloud with an edge on it. Say what you can see, let her say
what she can see, and stay down longer than feels reasonable.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and walking, which makes the
> flag on the floor a road. Give him three white things of his own on the far
> side of the sheet, each one too big for his mouth: a folded pillowcase, a
> plastic mixing bowl, a paper plate. Let him walk to them. Lying on his back
> in the grass is a harder ask now that he can stand, so put him beside Azlyn
> and let him crawl off when he has had enough.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Fifty Stars Is a Lot

The flag has fifty stars and Azlyn cuts every one she can face. Stopping at
eleven is fine.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Blue card or paper, 2 sheets (substitute: white paper colored in)
- White paper, 5 sheets
- 1 glue stick, or flour-and-water paste in a saucer
- Child scissors
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Draw ten stars on each sheet of white paper with the marker. Big ones, fat points, room between them.
2. Hand her the child scissors and let her cut them out. They will not come out as stars. Every one goes on the flag anyway.
3. Lay the two blue sheets side by side. With no blue in the house she colors two white sheets in with the marker, ten minutes she enjoys.
4. Glue stick, or a spoonful of flour-and-water paste in the saucer that she spreads with one finger. The paste is slower and she will pick it.
5. She sticks them down and counts out loud as she goes. Count with her, then count again when she has finished, because the two numbers will not match.
6. Write the real number on the back with the marker and the date beside it.
7. Cutting is tiring. When she puts the scissors down, that is the end of it.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut two or three yourself at the start so she has something to compare against, then stop. Fifteen minutes in she is cutting to cut and the stars have stopped mattering.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Tear the stars instead of cutting them.
- Stick the stars on the window with tape instead of on card.
- Count fifty of anything: pasta, socks, steps up the road.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one, and the pool is the coolest room in town this week
- The splash pad if the pool is packed with the holiday crowd
- A shaded park and a bottle of water each
- Indoor playground with the air conditioning on

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He goes in the water too. At 12 months he can
> stand in the shallow end holding both your hands and take steps against the
> drag, which is hard work and he loves it. Twenty-five minutes is plenty. Get
> him out while he is enjoying it and feed him within the half hour.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Continuity of ownership matters during illness.**
> Putting the red things back is Azlyn's job today, and the pull on a sick day
> is to take it off her and do it yourself. Take a job off her and she reads
> it as evidence she is not capable, which is the last thing she needs while
> she already feels wrong in her own body. Cancel the plan, as on any sick
> day, then keep her jobs hers and shrink them instead. Two forks instead of
> six, the basket carried to the door rather than up the stairs. Illness takes
> away a lot of what she controls, and the small fixed things she owns are
> worth defending through it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** She is collecting small objects from every room and laying
> them at floor height while Kreston walks around them. Coins, magnets,
> buttons and anything holding a button battery go straight back in the
> basket, not on the sheet. Sweep the line she works along before you put him
> down. Late June sun reaches her on a shaded rug, so hats and sunscreen on
> both of them before you go out. The child scissors live on the table and go
> back in the drawer the moment she leaves it.

## 🌟 Day 181: The Whole Day Outside 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, June 30, 2027**
**Theme:** Red, White & Blue Countdown

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill two pitchers with water and put them in the fridge, and pile by the back door what the day needs: the old sheet, the markers, the string, the clothespins, the chalk, a shallow dish for the birds.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Everything Goes Out the Back Door
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Twenty Flags on a String (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Water Out for the Birds (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Course She Sets Out Herself (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Watering the Pots
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Under the Bunting
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Cool Feet and Two Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Everything Goes Out the Back Door

**🧰 You need:** the pile by the back door · 1 laundry basket · 1 rug or picnic blanket.

1. Tell her the plan before she asks: today the table is outside and it stays out until dinner.
2. Load the basket together and let her carry it out in as many trips as she wants. Trips are the activity.
3. Spread the rug in the shade the house casts at 8:00, and say the shade will move and so will the rug.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Twenty Flags on a String

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 old sheet, or 6 paper grocery bags
- Scissors (**adult only**)
- Red and blue markers, or washable paint and a brush
- String, 4 meters
- 12 clothespins
- 1 permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cut twenty triangles from the old sheet or the paper bags, a hand span along the top edge. You cut, she counts them into a pile and says when there are twenty.
2. Red and blue markers, or the paint and brush if you want it wetter. She covers as many as she wants and leaves the rest plain.
3. Write on four with the permanent marker: her name, Kreston's, yours, Joseph's. She says which flag belongs to whom.
4. Tie the string between two fixed points, four meters of it, high enough that she walks under it with a hand up.
5. Fold the top edge of each triangle over the string and clip it. One clothespin pinches two neighbors together, so twelve of them hold twenty flags.
6. Stand at one end and count along the line with her, out loud, to twenty.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut all twenty before she starts coloring. A three-year-old colors four flags with enormous care and the last sixteen in a single stroke each.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Water Out for the Birds

The last day of June is hot and every bird on the street is hunting for water.
Set a shallow dish in the shade of the wall, no deeper than her thumb, with
one stone standing proud in the middle so a bee can land on it and climb out
again. She fills it from the pitcher and marks the level on the outside with
chalk. Walk the block while it settles, counting the birds you hear rather
than the ones you see, and check the mark against the water when you get back.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and a new walker, so a change
> of surface stops him dead while he works out what his feet are standing on.
> Give him his own cup of water to carry as far as the dish, which is one
> instruction and a job he can finish. Most of it lands on his feet, and he
> will go back for the rest.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Course She Sets Out Herself

Ninety minutes of running about in the heat needs shape or it turns into
whining. Azlyn draws the shape herself and you follow it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Chalk, 1 box
- 2 buckets
- 1 plank or a long strip of flattened cardboard
- 3 cushions
- 3 of the morning's flags as station markers
- 1 pitcher of water and cups

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Hand her the chalk and two fixed points: the course starts at the back door and ends wherever she says.
2. She draws the line. Walk behind her and mark nothing yourself, including the bit that goes through the flower bed.
3. Set the stations where her line passes them. Two buckets to step in and out of, the plank to walk along, three cushions spaced for jumping between.
4. Tuck one of the morning's flags under each of the three stations so she sees them from the start line.
5. Run it together, counting out loud, and tell her the number at the end. She will want to beat it.
6. The pitcher of water and the cups live at the middle station. She drinks a full cup every time she passes it, and so does Kreston.
7. She changes the course whenever she likes. A wet foot rubs the chalk out and she redraws it somewhere worse.

> 💡 **Tip:** Move the course into shade after one o'clock rather than shortening it. Chalk redraws in two minutes and the cushions carry.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One plank and one bucket, and nothing else.
- Chalk a hopscotch grid on the paving instead.
- Draw round all three of you on the paving and color the outlines in.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Indoor playground**, indoors and cool, on the hottest afternoon of the week
- The shaded end of the park, later than usual
- The splash pad or the kiddie pool
- A cool store with wide aisles, and let her push the basket

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Indoor playground is a different building for him now
> that he walks. At 12 months he goes into the baby area and out of it under
> his own steam, and the ball pit is work rather than fun because the floor
> moves. Ten minutes of the padded slope on his feet, holding your hands.
> Water and a sit-down after twenty minutes.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Outdoor play is the highest-return activity available, and June is when it gets easy.**
> A day like this buys you more than any indoor plan. Outdoors, Azlyn runs
> faster, talks more, argues less and sleeps better that night, and the space
> does the work you would be doing with instructions. Daylight sets her body
> clock, and you collect that at bedtime. Uneven ground builds balance no flat
> floor can teach her. Her eyes spend the whole day focusing at distance, and
> the research linking outdoor hours to lower rates of nearsightedness is
> strong enough to act on. From here to September the barrier is low: open the
> door, carry the water out, and let the garden run the day.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A whole day outdoors at the end of June is a heat day. Water
> at every station and not only when she asks, hats on, sunscreen on both of
> them before you open the door and again after lunch, and the middle of the
> day spent in shade. Test the plank, the buckets and any dark surface with
> your own hand first, and watch Kreston's feet on hot paving now that he is
> walking. The scissors stay with you.

## 🌟 Day 182: Someone Else's Birthday 🌟
**📅 Thursday, July 1, 2027**
**Theme:** Red, White & Blue Countdown

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Flatten a large cardboard box down one side so it opens out, stand it by the back door with the packing tape, and gather the week's makes into one pile.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Three Links Left
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Setting the Table Four Days Early (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Every Flag Between Here and the Corner (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Box That Waits Until Sunday (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Carrying In the Shopping
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Photographs of the Week

- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Three Links Left

**🧰 You need:** the paper chain · 1 permanent marker.

1. She tears off today's link and holds the chain up. Three left, and she can see all three at once now.
2. Count them with her: Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Say what happens on each, in order, the same way every morning from here.
3. Write **3** on the bottom link and hang it back up. Leave the question of whose birthday it is for the Morning Meeting.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Setting the Table Four Days Early

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper plates and cups, one per person
- The week's flags and bunting
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 pitcher of water
- A tablecloth or an old sheet

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. The tablecloth or the old sheet goes on first and she smooths it flat with both arms.
2. Tape a length of the week's bunting along the front edge so it hangs where she can see it from her chair, and lay the flags down the middle.
3. Count the people in the house out loud on fingers. One paper plate and one paper cup each, and she carries them over one at a time.
4. Write each name on a cup with the permanent marker. She tells you whose is whose, then adds her own marks to each one.
5. She decides who sits where. Take her seating plan as final, including the part where Kreston sits next to her.
6. Fill the cups from the pitcher of water and eat the 10:15 snack sitting at it, in the right seats, four days early.

> 💡 **Tip:** Leave it set. She will walk past a table that stays laid and rearrange it eleven times before Sunday.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Every Flag Between Here and the Corner

The flags go up on houses this week, so walk the street and count them. Front
porches, cars, a sticker in a window, bunting over a driveway. She counts and
you keep the running total. Go as far as the corner and decide together
whether the next street has more.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and sits at the table in his
> own seat with a paper cup he can lift himself. Half of it goes down his
> front and the other half gets drunk, and both count as practice. Give him a
> paper plate of his own at the snack. At the table he watches Azlyn hard, and
> copying her does more for him than anything you demonstrate.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Box That Waits Until Sunday

Most of what the week made goes into one box this afternoon. She paints it,
prints her hand on the side, and it is shut until Sunday.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large cardboard box
- Packing tape
- Washable non-toxic paint in red, white and blue
- 1 wide brush
- 1 wet washcloth in a bowl
- 1 permanent marker
- The week's makes: the instruments, the star field, her book
- Your phone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Box out on the grass, paint beside it, and she goes at the outside with the wide brush. No plan, no design, all four sides and the flaps.
2. Handprint next. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand, press it flat on the front, count to three and lift straight up. Do Kreston's beside hers if he will hold his fingers open for a second. Write **JULY** and **3** beside the two of them.
3. Wet washcloth straight away, both sets of hands, before either of them gets to a face or the door handle.
4. Load it while the paint dries: the instruments, the star field, her book. The chain stays on the wall, because there are two more links to tear before the box opens, and the flags and the bunting stay on the table she laid this morning. Photograph each thing as it goes in, because the box gets emptied in a hurry on Sunday.
5. She puts the last thing in and closes the flaps herself.
6. Packing tape across the seam. You write **OPEN JULY 4** on the top in permanent marker and she goes over your letters with her own hand on the marker.
7. Up on top of the closet now, not at bedtime.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep her book out if she asks for it. Three days is a long time to a three-year-old.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Paint the box and leave it empty until Saturday.
- Skip the paint and let her cover the box in stickers and marker.
- Make a birthday card for the country and post it on the fridge.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The hardware store**, for a packet of flag stakes or a length of rope for Sunday
- The grocery store, and she picks one thing for the Fourth
- The park on the shaded side, with the cube in your pocket
- The bakery, for something to eat at the table she laid

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The hardware store at 12 months is a corridor of
> things at his own height. Put him in the cart seat for the aisles and let
> him walk the wide empty bit by the registers. Give him one thing too big for
> his mouth to hold the whole way round, and he will keep it.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A sibling's birthday is hard, and preparation helps more than correction.**
> Sunday is a party for somebody who is not Azlyn, and a three-year-old does
> not separate a country's birthday from her own the way you do. She will ask
> where her cake is. Telling her on the day that it is not about her lands as
> a correction, and she has done nothing wrong. Telling her four days early,
> at a table she laid herself, gives her a job inside the celebration instead.
> The same thing works for Kreston's next birthday: a role, a task, something
> of her own to carry. Preparation gets you a helper, and correction gets you
> a scene.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The box fills up with the rice shaker and the drum beater at
> exactly Kreston's height, and at 12 months he helps himself to open boxes.
> Tape it shut and put it up high the moment you finish, not at bedtime.
> Washable non-toxic paint only, and wipe his hands before he touches his
> face.

# 🌧️ June — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

These pages are for the mornings the plan does not survive. Two of them are
for weather that keeps everybody in, which in June means heat as often as
rain, and both are written for a day when going out is off the table. Two
more are for the days somebody is sick, and those run on a different clock,
because a sick day has no nine fifteen in it. The last page is a list to read
standing up, for the ten minutes when you want one idea rather than a whole
day.

---

<a id="jun-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — Too Hot to Go Out

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill two pitchers with water and stand them in the fridge, and dig out a small screwdriver and two dead ballpoint pens.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Shutting the House Against the Sun
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Taking-Apart Table (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Coldest Floor in the House (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Rope She Twists Herself (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🧊 The Cold Hour: A Bowl of Ice and Two Spoons (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Cold Drinks Round
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Parts Tray
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: A Cool Bath and the Dark Room
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Shutting the House Against the Sun

**🧰 You need:** every curtain and blind on the sunny side · 1 baking tray · her.

1. Walk the house with her and shut everything on the side the sun is on. Tell her the plan out loud: the house stays dark and shut all morning, and the two of you stay in it.
2. Send her hunting for six things that look like they come apart. She comes back with a pen, a clothespin, an old flashlight, a whisk.
3. Lay the six in a row on the tray and put it in the middle of the table. Nothing gets opened until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Taking-Apart Table

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 dead ballpoint pens, the kind that unscrew
- 1 wooden clothespin
- 1 old flashlight, batteries out
- 1 whisk, 1 tape dispenser, or anything else off the tray
- 1 small screwdriver (**adult only**)
- 1 baking tray, to hold every part
- 1 sheet of paper, 1 pencil, 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Pen first. Unscrew it over the tray and lay the parts out in the order they came off: cap, barrel, ink tube, spring, tip.
2. Hand her the name of each part as it lands, then say it again when she picks it up. **Spring** is the one she keeps.
3. Second pen, and this one is hers to open on her own. Sit on your hands, and let her turn it the wrong way for a while.
4. Clothespin next. Two wooden legs and a spring, and the word she learned five minutes ago turns up inside something else. Then the flashlight, which is yours to open with the small screwdriver while she holds each piece and says its name back to you.
5. Draw around every part on the paper with the pencil and write its name beside the outline in marker. That sheet is how she gets the pen back together.
6. Rebuild one pen together, then let her pick one more thing off the tray, the whisk or the tape dispenser, and pull that one apart last. The rest stay in pieces on the tray until 4:15.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her the words and stop there. She wants the name of the small coiled thing more than she wants to know what it does, and the explanation keeps for a year or two.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Coldest Floor in the House

Shoes and socks off, and walk the house barefoot hunting for cold. The tile by
the back door, the bathroom floor, the strip of hall the sun has never reached,
the inside of the cupboard under the stairs. She reports on each one and you
put a hand down beside her feet. Let her pick the coolest room in the house,
and move the afternoon into it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and puts a hand out for
> whatever is on the table, so the tray of springs and pen tips stays pushed to
> the far side and never comes down to him. Give him a metal bowl and a wooden
> spoon at the other end, which is his version of finding out what a thing
> does. Strip him to a diaper and offer his cup every time you pass him. He
> drinks from it without help now, and at a year he heats up faster than she
> does.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Rope She Twists Herself

The morning pulled things to pieces. This afternoon she starts with a flat
sheet and finishes holding something that did not exist at lunchtime.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 old bedsheet or a worn t-shirt, or 6 plastic grocery bags
- 1 pair of adult scissors (**adult only**)
- Thick wool or garden twine, 2 yards, if you would rather not cut up a sheet
- 1 door handle or a chair back, to anchor the strands
- 1 marker
- 1 shopping bag loaded with books, as the weight to test it against

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cut the sheet into strips two fingers wide, as long as the sheet will give you. You cut, she counts them into a pile and says when there are six.
2. Knot two strips together at one end and hook the knot over a door handle. She takes one strand, you take the other, and you both stand back until the pair pulls straight.
3. Twist. Both of you turn the same way until each strand is tight enough to want to curl back on itself. Say the direction out loud every few turns.
4. Walk your two hands together and let go of the middle. The strands wrap around each other on their own, and her face does the rest.
5. Knot the loose end, take it off the handle, and let her pull on it with both hands as hard as she can.
6. Hang the bag off it and add one book at a time until it fails or she runs out of books.
7. Measure the rope against her and mark her height on it with the marker, then coil it and hang it high, and tell her why it goes up there.

> 💡 **Tip:** Both of you twist the same way. One strand turned backwards cancels the other and the cord falls apart in her hands, which is worth doing on purpose once she has a good one.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Twist one short cord out of garden twine and stop there.
- Braid three strips flat on the floor instead of twisting two.
- Tie the finished rope between two chairs and hang socks off it.
- Pull the sheet into strips by hand along a snipped edge, no cutting at all.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Long strips of fabric stay off the floor while he
> is on it, so give him three folded washcloths and a big plastic bowl to post
> them into and tip back out. At 12 months a one-step instruction lands, so
> hold your hand out and ask him for one washcloth at a time from where he
> sits. Cup of water on the hour, and he plays on the coolest floor in the
> house.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Making a material from scratch is rarer than making a thing.**
> Azlyn makes things most days of her life. A rope is a different order of
> object: she started with a flat sheet and ended up holding something with a
> property the sheet never had. Materials reach her finished, and the making of
> them sits behind a door she has no picture of. Twisting two strands and
> watching them lock together puts one whole step of that in her own hands. She
> meets the same idea in paper, in cloth, in flour. Hang the rope where she can
> reach it and leave it up for a week, because the strength she built into it
> is the part she will keep testing.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Check the flashlight for a coin-shaped button battery before
> she opens anything, and take every one of them out of the room. A swallowed
> button battery burns through the throat inside a couple of hours and is an
> emergency room trip that hour, not a wait and see. Springs, pen tips, ink
> tubes and screws stay on the tray, the tray stays on the table, and you count
> the parts back before Kreston is on the floor. Drinks go around every hour
> whether or not anybody asks. The scissors stay with you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Storm That Sits Over the House

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand a heavy bowl, the rolling pin, the sieve and a bag of rolled oats on the counter, and put an old towel by the kitchen table.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Three Bowls of Grain
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Grinding the Oats by Hand (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Counting to the Thunder (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Laundry Done by Hand (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🧺 Hanging It Up Around the House (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Sweeping Under the Table
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Sieve and the Bowl
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Rain on the Window, Two Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Three Bowls of Grain

**🧰 You need:** 3 small bowls · rolled oats · rice · all-purpose flour.

1. One thing per bowl, laid out in front of her, and a finger into each before anybody says a word.
2. Ask her which two are the same thing and let her argue it out. She will pair the oats with the rice, because both of them rattle.
3. Tell her the flour started as something with a rattle in it, and leave that where it lands until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Grinding the Oats by Hand

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Rolled oats, 1 cup
- 1 heavy bowl with high sides, a deep mixing bowl or a mortar
- 1 rolling pin, or the end of a wooden spoon, or a jam jar with a heavy base
- 1 sieve and 1 more bowl
- The bag of all-purpose flour from the Opening Activity
- 1 tablespoon
- 1 kitchen timer, or the one on your phone
- Paper and 1 pen for the count

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Half a cup of oats into the heavy bowl. She pushes and turns with the end of the rolling pin, and the first thing she learns is that oats jump.
2. Set the timer for two minutes and let her work until it goes. Then both of you stop and look at what is in there.
3. Sieve the lot over a second bowl. The flour drops through and the rest stays behind. Tip what stayed behind back into the heavy bowl.
4. Run that loop four times, adding each sieving to the same bowl and marking a line on the paper for every round.
5. Hold the finished flour up in the tablespoon. Half a cup of oats gives her about two spoonfuls, and the gap between those two amounts is the whole morning.
6. Open the bag of all-purpose flour beside it. A finger in each, and a straight question: which one took longer?

> 💡 **Tip:** Use a bowl with real sides. A flat plate sends oats across the kitchen in four seconds and the activity becomes sweeping.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Counting to the Thunder

Set two chairs a body's length back from the window and sit there with her.
Count out loud from the flash and stop counting when the rumble arrives. Five
seconds is about a mile, so write each number on a scrap of paper and lay them
in a row on the floor. The numbers shrink while the storm comes on and grow
while it leaves, and she can see that on the paper before she can feel it in
the sky. Once the count holds above ten the storm has moved off, and the two of
you can carry the chairs up to the glass and watch the rest of it go.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 12 months and takes his reading of a
> bang off your face before he decides anything about it. Sit him on your knee
> back from the glass and stay loose in the shoulders through the loud ones.
> Give him a spoonful of cooked oatmeal on his tray at the table while Azlyn
> grinds, and his own metal bowl and spoon at the far end, well clear of the
> rolling pin.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Laundry Done by Hand

Grinding was work with a hard result. The afternoon runs the same argument
through warm water, and she gets to see the dirt come out.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 dishpans or big mixing bowls, on the table
- Warm water for both bowls, drawn before the storm sits overhead, and 1 squirt of dish soap
- 8–10 small things worth washing: socks, washcloths, dish towels, her own t-shirt
- 1 old towel under the bowls and a second one folded beside her
- String across the kitchen, a drying rack, or two chair backs
- 8 clothespins

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Fill both bowls in a lull or before the storm settles overhead, one warm and soapy, one warm and clean for rinsing, and carry them to the table with the towel underneath. The sink is finished with for the afternoon. She kneels on a chair to reach.
2. One sock to start. In, squeeze, rub the toe against itself, and up out of the water twenty times.
3. Into the rinse bowl next. Hold it up between the two of you and watch the soap leave it.
4. Wringing takes more grip than she has, so she twists one end while you twist the other over the folded towel and count the drips.
5. She pegs each one along the line and decides the order. Hang the heavy things at the ends where the string sags least.
6. Keep going until she stops. Six things washed by a three-year-old is a full afternoon.
7. Tip both bowls out once the storm has moved off, stand them upside down and count what is hanging. Count it again at bedtime and see what has dried.

> 💡 **Tip:** Warm water, not hot. Her hands are in it for an hour, and she will tell you it has gone cold long before it has.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One sock, one bowl, and stop when the sock is clean.
- Wash one window from the inside with a cloth and a bowl of warm water.
- Hang everything on the backs of the dining chairs and skip the line.
- Scrub the muddiest pair of shoes in the house with an old toothbrush.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** No bowl of his own on the floor today. Give him a
> wrung-out washcloth on his tray and one instruction, *wipe*, which he can
> follow at 12 months and will run twenty times over. Later he gets the empty
> clothespin bag to fill and empty where he sits. Hand him one clothespin at a
> time and take it back before it goes in his mouth.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Grinding grain by hand is how she finds out that food used to be work.**
> Flour arrives in this house in a bag, and the bag is where the story stops.
> Half a cup of oats and twenty minutes of pushing gives Azlyn two spoonfuls
> and an ache in her wrist, and the ratio between those two things is the
> lesson. For most of human history somebody spent a good part of every day
> doing what she did before ten o'clock, and most of them were women and girls.
> She has no use for the history yet. She has use for the arm. Effort is how a
> three-year-old works out what a thing is worth, and she eats what she ground
> with an attention no store loaf has ever earned.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Stay in until half an hour after the last rumble, and settle
> the question of going out to look before she asks it. A strike travels
> indoors through plumbing and wiring, so the bath waits and nobody stands at
> the faucet while the storm is overhead. Fill the laundry bowls in a lull or
> before it settles in, then leave the sink alone until it has moved off. Keep
> both children a body's length back from the glass while the flash-to-rumble
> count sits under five, and do the counting from a chair or the doorway. The
> rolling pin lives on the table and goes back to the table between grinds,
> because Kreston is 12 months old and the table edge sits at his eye level.
> The laundry bowls stay up on the table too, never on the floor.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jun-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Day She Stays Down

Nothing on this page has a time on it. She is flat, the plan is canceled, and
the only two jobs today are fluids and company. Everything below can be
abandoned in the middle without anybody minding.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Nothing to set up. If she went to bed hot, put a pitcher of water, a stack of washcloths and a spare blanket on the arm of the sofa before you go up.

### ⏰ The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes**, blanket to the sofa, no getting dressed, something to drink within her reach.
- **The first stretch**, nothing asked of her at all. Sit down yourself while you can.
- **When she asks for food**, dry toast or nothing, and neither answer is a problem.
- **The long middle**, the rest block, and the rest of the day bends around it.
- **After the first long sleep**, the naming game, run from where she is lying.
- **Before the afternoon dip**, one book she picks, read twice.
- **The end of the afternoon**, drawing on her back with the lights low.
- **Bed early**, the same books in the same order, nothing new in the room.

### 🛋️ The Rest Block

The rest block is the day, and everything else is what happens around its
edges. Make one place on the sofa and keep her in it: her pillow from
upstairs, a blanket she can push off, a cup on the floor where her hand
reaches, and the curtains half shut against a bright June morning. She will
sleep in stretches at hours that make no sense. Let every one of them run to
its own end. Sit in the room while she sleeps if you can manage it, because
she surfaces, checks that you are still there, and goes back down faster when
the answer is yes. The television is allowed and it is not the plan, so put it
on for a stretch and take it off again, or the afternoon has nothing left in
it.

### 🔦 Naming What She Can See From There

She stays flat and the two of you take one ordinary object to pieces with
words. Start with the lamp: shade, bulb, cord, switch, the collar that holds
the shade on. Then her own hand: palm, knuckle, wrist, the crease at the
bottom of her thumb. Then a shoe, a door, the window. Give her the word, let
her say it back or ignore it, and move on. Ten minutes of this is plenty, and
the only material is your voice.

### 📚 The Pile She Chooses From

Bring eight books down and put them on the floor beside her within arm's
reach, then read whatever she hands up. She will pick the same one four times.
Read it four times. A book she has memorized asks nothing of a sick brain and
gives her the one thing she can control today, which is what happens next.

### 🖐️ Drawing on Her Back

Sit behind her and draw a shape on her back with one finger: a circle, a line
down, a big letter A, a rain shower with your fingertips. She guesses. Then
she does one on your arm and you guess, and you get it wrong on purpose more
often than you get it right. It costs nothing, it works lying down, and it
carries the touch she wants without either of you having to talk.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

A sick sibling changes his day more than hers. If there is anybody who can
take him for a few hours, today is the day to ask, and take the offer without
apologizing for it. If he stays, keep him off her: his floor is the far end of
the room with the door gate up, his own cup and his own washcloth, and nothing
of hers goes near his mouth. At 12 months he comes over to see her every few
minutes, walking or on all fours, so set something up at his end that holds
him. A stack of plastic containers to pull apart and press back together will
run a long time, and it keeps him near her without landing on her.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Naming the parts of something ordinary makes it interesting again.**
> Azlyn has looked at that lamp her whole life without once looking at it.
> Handing her the words breaks it open: shade, bulb, cord, switch, the collar
> under the shade. A named part turns into something she can hunt for in other
> objects, and she starts finding switches and cords around the room without
> being asked. Naming carries attention with it. Most of the vocabulary she
> owns at three arrived this way, an adult putting a word on a thing while she
> was already looking at it. On a day when she cannot get off the sofa, the
> lamp and the window and her own hand are the whole available world, and every
> one of them has parts.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Write the time of every dose on a piece of paper on the fridge
> along with what you gave. On a long day with two adults going in and out, the
> dose given at eleven gets given again at twelve from memory. Medicine goes
> back up on a high shelf between doses, because Kreston is up on his feet at
> the furniture now and a bottle on the arm of the sofa sits at his eye level.
> Call the doctor rather
> than sitting on it if she will not drink, if she has not peed since the
> morning, if a fever holds past what you expected, or if she looks wrong to
> you in a way you cannot name. Nobody has ever been told off for calling.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jun-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Bored, and Not Better Yet

This is the harder of the two days. She has enough in her to want something
and not enough to do it, and she will ask for the garden about forty times.
Everything here happens on a sofa or a lap, and the answer about the garden
stays no.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Nothing to set up. If there is heavy cream in the fridge, stand it at the front and put a clean jam jar with a tight lid beside it.

### ⏰ The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes**, downstairs in pajamas, and say out loud that today is another indoor day so it stops being a negotiation.
- **The first stretch**, the jar, which takes as long as it takes.
- **When she asks for food**, more than yesterday and less than she thinks.
- **The long middle**, the rest block, shorter today and still the center of it.
- **After the rest**, the bag of things she has not seen since March.
- **Before the afternoon dip**, the list, dictated from where she is sitting.
- **The end of the afternoon**, a window open, a blanket, and a look at the street from indoors.
- **Bed at the usual time**, because tomorrow is the day she goes back out.

### 🛋️ The Rest Block

She will tell you she does not need it. Put it in the middle of the day
anyway, and drop the word rest: pull the curtains, lie down beside her with a
book, and let the room go quiet for forty minutes. A child on the mend runs at
full speed for an hour and then falls apart at four o'clock, and the block in
the middle is what buys you a calm evening. If she sleeps, she needed it. If
she lies there and talks at you for the whole forty minutes, that counts too.

### 🫙 The Jar That Changes While She Holds It

Half fill the jam jar with heavy cream, screw the lid down hard, and give it
to her. You do most of the shaking today. She takes it back when she wants it
and hands it over the second her arms give out, and neither of you keeps count.
Nothing happens for a long stretch, and then it happens inside about four
seconds: the sloshing stops, a lump appears, and the jar goes quiet. Open the
lid, let her look in, and stop there. The butter keeps in the fridge until she
is well enough to want it on toast. An empty fridge runs the same activity on
staples, a jar half full of dry rice shaken until the sound changes, or an inch
of water and a squeeze of dish soap shaken up to a head of foam. She may have
done the cream in February. She will remember none of the numbers and all of
the moment it turned.

### 🧺 The Bag of Things She Has Not Seen Since March

Go through the closet and the back of the toy box and fill a bag with anything
she has not laid eyes on for three months. Tip it out on the sofa beside her
and leave it there. Old things come back as new things, and she can play with
them at half power without needing you to explain anything. Anything she
ignores goes back in the bag for the next sick day.

### 📋 The List of What She Will Do When She Is Better

Give her a pen and take the writing yourself. Ask what she wants to do the day
she goes back out, and put down every answer word for word, in her order,
including the ones that make no sense. Read the list back to her twice. Tape
it low on the fridge where she passes it, and cross each line off with her
over the next week, because a list she dictated on a bad day and completed on
a good one is worth more than either half on its own.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

He is either coming down with it or he is climbing on her, and neither one
suits her today. Keep their cups apart, wash your hands between the two of
them, and expect to lose. Give him his own version of what she is doing: a
plastic bottle with two spoons of water in it and the lid taped down with a
strip of packing tape, to shake beside her while she works the cream, a
folded blanket of his own on the floor by the sofa, and his cup within reach.
At 12 months a one-step instruction lands about half the time, so *give it to
Azlyn* is worth saying, and it gets him near her with
something in his hands instead of on top of her.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Waiting for cream to turn into butter is a bet she'll want to see through.**
> Nothing happens in that jar for a long stretch, and then it all happens at
> once. Azlyn shakes it, hands it back, asks twice, and stays with it anyway,
> because she has put something in and wants to see what comes out. Waiting has
> a floor and a ceiling at three. She cannot hold out for a week, and she can
> hold out for eleven minutes when the thing she is waiting on sits in her lap
> where she can hear it changing. Being ill strips away most of what she gets
> to affect. The jar hands one thing back, and she gets to call the moment it
> turned.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Standing water waits for a whole ordinary day. A child on the
> mend is unsteady and off her food, and the kiddie pool and the dishpan both
> stay empty and turned over until she has had one full day back to herself.
> The jar lid comes off the floor before Kreston is down on it, because a
> screw-top lid is a choking size at 12 months. Hand washing after every trip
> to her and before you touch his food buys you a day or two of stagger rather
> than both of them at once.

## 🎲 June — Extra Ideas

### 🎲 **Alternative Activities**

- **Barefoot on Six Surfaces**, grass, paving, doormat, tile, carpet and gravel, named as she crosses each one.
- **One Hand Cold, One Hand Warm**, two bowls and a third in the middle that both hands go into at the end.
- **Melting an Ice Cube in Her Fist**, one cube each, and the first hand to come up empty wins.
- **The Hallway Bowling Alley**, six empty bottles at one end and a soft ball at the other.
- **The Upside-Down Afternoon**, dinner food at four and pajamas straight after it.
- **Hide the Timer**, wound up, hidden in one room, and found by the ticking.
- **The Great Shoe Sort**, every pair in the house paired up and lined out by size along the hall.
- **Counting the Steps to the Corner**, walked out at eight in the morning before the heat arrives.
- **The Watering Can Round**, every pot in the yard done before the sun gets on them.
- **The Fridge Inventory**, she names everything on one shelf out loud while you write it down.
- **Grandma on Speakerphone**, she does the talking and you stay out of it.

### 🎨 **Alternative Arts & Crafts**

- **The Paper Bag Cut Flat**, a bigger sheet than any she owns and crayons in the middle of it.
- **Chalk on the Shady Wall**, one wall she is allowed to draw on and a bucket of water to take it off.
- **Painting the Path With Water**, one wide brush and a bucket, and the whole thing gone by lunch.
- **The Sticker Made of Tape**, a small drawing on a strip of masking tape, stuck where she says.
- **A Crown From a Cereal Box**, cut to fit her head and taped at the back.
- **Fingerprint Bugs**, one thumb, washable paint, and two legs drawn on each.
- **The Straw Necklace**, drinking straws cut into lengths and threaded onto wool, up out of reach when she finishes.
- **A Cover for the Book She Loves**, brown paper, her title, her name.
- **The Picture Torn, Not Cut**, ripped into six and glued back down in the wrong order.
- **Painting the Window From Inside**, washable paint on the glass and a cloth to clear it after.
- **Tape Roads on the Floor**, masking tape from room to room and every wheeled toy in the house on them.

### 👶 **Kreston's Turn**

- **Carrying One Thing to One Person**, handed over, taken back, and run again twenty times.
- **The Cup With Two Swallows In It**, offered on the hour and refilled small, because he holds it himself now.
- **Washcloths Into the Big Bowl**, posted in, tipped out, and nothing in the game small enough to swallow.
- **The Laundry Basket He Pushes**, upturned on the grass to lean on, where a landing is soft.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Standing water**: the bucket under Day 193's water wall, the wash bowls on Day 194, the paddling pool on Days 196, 200 and 208, the camp dishpans on Day 214. Kreston walks now and drowns in the depth of a dishpan without a sound, so stay within arm's reach and tip it out the moment they finish.
- **Two children at the water**: swimming every Tuesday, the paddling pool and the real pool on the same day on Day 208, the lake on Day 212. One adult cannot watch two in water and water wings do not stand in for a second pair of hands, so bring a second adult or take them one at a time.
- **Small parts, and he picks things up now**: ice cubes on Day 187, the watermelon seeds on Day 188, the coins in the market purse on Day 189, cotton balls and the ping-pong ball on Day 192, the pebbles on Day 206, the raisins and cereal hoops on Day 216. Count them out and count them back in before he is on the floor.
- **String and cord**: the drying line on Day 194, the octopus and dolphin strings down the stairs on Day 205, the hanging jellyfish on Day 208, the clothesline holding the tent sheet from Day 211, the flag line on Day 215. Run a line at knee height and take it down when the activity ends, because a line at her chest sits at Kreston's neck.
- **Adult-only steps**: the matches and the sparklers on Day 185, the big knife and the boiling corn pan on Day 188, the craft knife on Day 198's shop hatch, the oven and the hot foil parcels on Day 212. Scissors go back on a high shelf between cuts rather than onto the arm of the sofa.
- **Summer specific**: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, on every day in this booklet, and watch Kreston for a hot dry neck and a sudden flop, because he cannot tell you he is overheating. Test the paving with the back of your hand before her bare feet go on it on Days 191, 208 and 213, and the drain cover as well on Day 213.

## Week 27: Independence Day Celebration 🎆
**📅 July 2 – July 8, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

Everything a party takes, Azlyn makes. A cake out of a cereal box on Friday,
streamers on the scooter for Saturday, a real cake iced on Sunday morning and a
bag packed for after dark. Monday onward the week runs on what July hands you:
a paper vest she wears out of the house, ice melting on the path in six
places, lunch she cuts herself, three dollar bills at the market.

Independence Day is Sunday and it gets the full day, from the parade round the
block to the first fireworks either child has seen. Tuesday carries the other
marker. The book is six months old, so January's handprint comes off the wall,
and April's with it, and a July one goes up beside them, with the same four
questions underneath and her old answers read back to her. Kreston turns 13
months on Monday.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Cutting her own food.** A butter knife through cucumber, tomato and cheese, and the different way each one gives.
- **Saying what she thinks will happen.** Which ice cube goes first, how many seeds are in the watermelon, written down before anyone checks.
- **Counting past what she can hold.** Flags on the street, candles onto a plate, watermelon seeds into a jar in tens.
- **Testing what she made and mending the part that failed.** Three paper pockets, four objects, one stone that stayed in.
- **Three rules she can recite.** She dictates the game rules for the fridge and the market rules in the car, then holds you to both.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- One-year-olds don't understand birthdays, and that's fine
- Discovery requires an incomplete set
- Pointing and giving are the foundations of conversation
- Making something she wears is a different order of pride
- Repeating an activity across seasons produces a comparison she can make herself
- Involvement predicts eating better than persuasion does
- Three rules, repeated forever, beats twenty rules said once

---
