# 🌧️ July — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

These five pages are for the mornings when the day on the printed page has
already fallen over. Two of them are full days for weather that keeps everybody
in, which in July means thunder all morning or an afternoon too hot to stand
in. Two are for the days somebody is sick, and those ask less of you than an
ordinary page does. The last one is a list to open at eight in the
morning when you have ten minutes and no plan.

---

<a id="jul-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — Lightning Keeps Everybody In

A July storm parks over the house for hours, takes the light out of the rooms
and makes going out a bad idea. Nobody is leaving today, and the plan runs on
that. Nothing on this page sends anybody to a store.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight

> Find the whistle and the flashlight and stand them on the kitchen counter, and leave the biggest empty box you own flat behind the sofa.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule

- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: What the Whistle Will Mean
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Hour With No Words (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Watching It Come Down (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Boat That Fits the Whole Toy Box (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🤸 Indoor Energy Burn: Cushions From One End to the Other (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Inside the Boat
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Pajamas Early, Three Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: What the Whistle Will Mean

**🧰 You need:** 1 whistle, or a saucepan lid and a wooden spoon · 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · 1 roll masking tape.

1. Blow it once at the table, then twice, and ask her which one sounds like *come here*.
2. Settle two meanings and no more. She picks which is which, and you draw both on the paper: one blast, two blasts.
3. Tape the paper to the fridge at her height and run three practice rounds before the bowls are cleared. She signals, you obey.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Hour With No Words

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 whistle (a saucepan lid and a wooden spoon does the same job)
- The signal sheet from this morning, taped to the fridge
- 1 kitchen timer, or the timer on your phone
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Say the rule out loud one last time, because it is the last thing anybody says: from the timer starting, nobody in the house speaks.
2. Set it for ten minutes to begin with. Ten is a long stretch with no talking and she will break it inside four, so restart the timer instead of calling it a failure.
3. Run a real job inside the silence. Get the snack out, lay four places, carry the recycling to the door. She reads where you are looking and what your hand is doing, and the whistle covers the rest.
4. Swap over. She takes the whistle and hands out the jobs, and you do what her signals mean rather than what you can see she wants.
5. Halfway through, let her invent a third signal and give it a meaning. Add it to the sheet on the fridge in marker while she watches, then use it wrong on purpose twice and let her correct you both times.
6. Finish with one round where the winner is whoever hears something nobody else did: the gutter, the fridge, a car going through the water outside, thunder a long way off.

> 💡 **Tip:** Blow it soft. A whistle at full strength in a closed house ends the game inside a minute and wakes whoever is asleep upstairs.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Watching It Come Down

Pull two chairs up to the window that faces the weather and stand them a
stride back from the glass. Say the one rule before you sit down: nobody
touches the window or the frame while the thunder is overhead. Put her hand
flat on the wall beside the window instead, and let her feel the big ones come
through the house. Watch where the water goes: down the gutter, along the
curb, into the drain, standing in the low corner of the street. Pick one
puddle and one leaf, then come back at lunch to see what both of them did.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 13 months and turns his whole body toward a sound he cannot place, which is most of what a whistle is for at his age. He cannot blow one, and it is the exact width of his throat, so it hangs around your neck or it goes on a high shelf. Give him the wooden spoon and an upturned plastic bowl for his own signal. He walks and carries at the same time now, so the recycling job in the silent hour is his: one item, from your hand to the box by the door.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Boat That Fits the Whole Toy Box

The street outside is under an inch of water. Everything in this house that
matters to her is getting on board, and she decides who that is.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large cardboard box, big enough for her to sit in
- 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (**adult only**)
- 1 roll masking tape and 1 roll packing tape
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 flattened box offcut for the ramp
- 1 blue sheet, blue trash bags, or any blanket that will do as water
- Paper and 1 pen for the passenger list
- Every soft toy and plastic animal in the house

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape every seam of the box shut and stand it up, then let her mark the doorway with tape where she wants it. Cut on her marks with her standing back, and say why she is standing back.
2. Tape the offcut on as a ramp from the floor to the doorway. It has to hold a teddy and it will not hold her, so say that once and mean it.
3. Write the boat's name on the side in marker. She chooses it and she gets the whole side to spell it across.
4. She dictates the passenger list and you write it down, one name per line, including the ones that are not animals. Kreston goes on it.
5. Spread the sheet around the boat as water. Nothing walks across it, so everything that boards comes up the ramp, and Kreston is the one who ferries them over.
6. Roll call. You read the list, she answers for each passenger and marks a check beside the name once it is aboard. She will find two missing and send you for them.
7. Sit in it with her while the rain keeps going, and let the water rise every time the thunder rolls.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut the doorway smaller than looks right. A box with three walls still standing is a boat until Thursday, and a box cut into flaps is a pile of cardboard by four o'clock.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One box, one blanket, no list. Get in and stay there.
- Draw the boat on a flattened box instead and leave the toys out of it.
- Line every animal up along the hall in size order and count them.
- Build a raft for two teddies out of the recycling and float it in the sink.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Carrying a thing to a place is the job of his month, and the ramp gives him a destination he can see. Hand him one animal at a time and let him work out the walk. He will drop half of them on the way and go back for them without being asked. Keep the tape and the marker up on the table between steps, and let him have a small box of his own so the boat is not the only thing on the floor.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A game with a whistle and rules teaches listening better than being told to listen.**
> Telling her to listen is a sentence she has heard four hundred times, and it
> names no action she can take. A whistle with two agreed meanings names one.
> She has to hold both rules in her head, wait for a sound that arrives with no
> warning, and act on it in the middle of doing something else, which is the
> whole of what adults mean by the word. Rules she helped set are the ones she
> defends. Expect her to police your obedience harder than her own, and expect
> the signals to outlast the day. One blast at the back door still works in
> September.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Nobody goes out while the thunder is going, and that includes
> the yard, the porch and the doorstep. Wait thirty minutes after the last
> rumble before anyone opens the back door. Both chairs at the window stay a
> stride back from the glass, and nobody puts a hand on the window or the frame
> while the storm is overhead. Baths and showers wait too, because
> plumbing runs the length of the house, so tonight's bath comes after the storm
> has moved off or gets skipped for a washcloth. Keep both children off the
> corded phone and away from the open back door. The whistle is the size Kreston
> chokes on and it never goes on the floor. The craft knife is adult-only, cuts
> the boat once and goes straight back out of reach. If the power drops, use
> flashlights and no candles, because a walking 13-month-old and an open flame
> at his eye level do not share a room.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jul-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Afternoon That Belongs to the Shade

The other kind of July weather. The sun is on the front of the house by nine,
the sidewalk is too hot for bare feet, and taking two children out into it
between ten and four buys you nothing. Drop the blinds on the sunny side and
run the whole day out of the coolest room you have. The kitchen already holds
everything this one needs.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight

> Open every window once the sun is off the house and leave them open overnight, drop the blinds on the sunny side before you go up, and stand the masking tape and a marker by the sink.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule

- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Lining Up Everything That Holds Cold Water
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Pitcher That Has to Be Empty by Dinner (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Wrists Under the Cold Tap (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Coolest Clothes in the House (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🧊 Cool-Down Hour: The Frozen Bottles in a Dish Towel (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Refilling the Pitcher for Dinner
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Clothes Pile and the Mirror
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Wet Hair, Cool Sheets, Two Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Lining Up Everything That Holds Cold Water

**🧰 You need:** every pitcher, bottle, jar and lidded cup in the kitchen · her two hands.

1. Open the cabinet doors and let her pull out everything that holds water. She lines them up along the counter, biggest to smallest, and she gets to argue the order with you.
2. She picks the one that holds the most, and that one is the pitcher for the day. Two of the small bottles go in the freezer for two thirty, each one wrapped in a dish towel when it comes out, and the rest go back in the cabinet.
3. Give her the last job: work out which room is going to be coolest at two o'clock. That room is where the afternoon happens.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Pitcher That Has to Be Empty by Dinner

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large pitcher
- 1 roll masking tape and 1 permanent marker
- 3 clear glasses
- 1 lemon, or any fruit in the bowl, or a spoonful of jam out of the pantry
- 1 cup per person, and a lidded cup for Kreston
- 1 tray
- The kitchen clock

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Three glasses on the table: water from the tap, water from the fridge, water with the fruit squashed into it or the jam stirred through. She tastes all three and picks what goes in the pitcher today.
2. Run a strip of masking tape from the top of the pitcher to the bottom. She draws a line across it for every hour between now and dinner, and the lines come out crooked and uneven, which changes nothing.
3. Fill it to the top line, the fruit or the jam in, and stand it on the tray in the room she picked at eight, with everybody's cup around it.
4. First round is hers. She pours for every person in the house, carries the cups, and then reads which line the water has dropped to.
5. From there, every time the clock hand comes around she checks the level against the lines and says out loud whether the house is behind. Say nothing about drinking yourself. The pitcher is doing the asking.
6. Empty by six is the target. Refill and start again if she gets there early, and put a mark on the tape for how far past the last line the house got.

> 💡 **Tip:** Hand her the pouring and let the tray take the spills. A pitcher she is allowed to lift is one she comes back to twelve times.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Wrists Under the Cold Tap

Stand her on a chair at the kitchen sink and run the cold tap over the inside
of both wrists for a slow count of twenty. She will tell you where she feels it
first. Do the backs of her knees and her neck with a cold washcloth, then do
her feet in a bowl on a towel while she stays on the chair. Let her do yours
after, and let her get you wetter than is necessary. Fill the cups from the
pitcher before anybody dries their hands.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 13 months and heats up faster than either of you, with less to say about it. He gets his lidded cup topped up every half hour whether he asks or not, and the back of your hand on his neck is how you check him: hot and dry means he comes to the coolest room now. Sit him on the towel with his own washcloth and a shallow bowl with an inch in it, within arm's reach of you the whole time. He will chew the cloth, which is fine, and carry it around the kitchen, which is what he does with everything this month.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Coolest Clothes in the House

An hour of rummaging on the coolest floor in the house, and it ends with her
wearing the answer.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The clothes drawers and the closet, hers and yours
- 1 old sheet, a scarf and a dish towel
- 1 mirror, or the biggest one you can carry into the room
- 1 laundry basket
- Sun hats, both of them
- Your phone, for the photographs

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip a basket of clothes onto the floor of the coolest room, hers on top and a few of yours underneath. Sit down in the middle of it with her.
2. Two rules and no more: nothing that needs ironing, and everything goes back in the basket at the end.
3. She feels her way through the pile and makes two heaps, hot clothes and cool clothes. Jeans, fleece and anything tight land in one, cotton and loose things in the other. Take her sorting as it comes, and put your hand on the fabrics she asks about.
4. She builds an outfit for every person in the house out of the cool heap, yours included, and everybody puts theirs on. The sheet is a robe, the scarf is a headwrap, the dish towel goes over the back of a neck.
5. Stand the mirror against the wall and let everybody look before the camera comes out. One photograph each in the doorway, and let her direct where people stand.
6. Last job is tomorrow's. She picks what she will wear in the heat in the morning and lays it flat on the end of her bed with the hat on top of it.
7. Everything else back in the basket, carried between the two of you, and the basket stays in that room with the mirror for four o'clock.

> 💡 **Tip:** Wear what she picks for you. An outfit she chose that gets refused stops the game, and the whole hour runs on her being the one who decides.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One outfit each, five minutes, then books on the floor.
- Try on every hat in the house and rank them for shade.
- Sort a drawer of her clothes into fits and does-not-fit.
- Lay out four days of hot-weather outfits and stack them in order.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Strip him to a diaper and a t-shirt for the rest of the day and leave him that way. At 13 months he climbs anything with a lip on it, so the basket of clothes is a thing he will try to stand in, and a full one will go over with him. Keep it half empty and beside you. Give him one sun hat to carry from the pile to the door and back, which is a trip he will make six times. He wants a cup every half hour, sitting down.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A measurement she takes every day teaches more than a fact does.**
> *Drink your water* is a fact she hears from you and drops on the floor. A line
> on the side of a pitcher is a thing she reads herself, and reading it belongs
> to her. Repeated measuring gives a three-year-old what one explanation never
> does: a number that moves, a reason to go and look, and a stake in what it
> says. She finds out where the water went by watching the level fall past marks
> she drew. Use the same pitcher and the same tape tomorrow and the day after,
> because a measurement earns its keep next to the one she took yesterday.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Heat is the whole hazard today. Water into both of them every
> half hour whether either asks or not, and watch for the quiet flushed child
> with a hot dry neck, which is the one to carry to the coolest room and cool
> down before anything else happens. Neither child goes into a parked car today,
> for any length of time, for any reason, including a two-minute errand: the
> inside of a car in July reaches lethal heat within minutes and the windows
> make no difference. Upstairs rooms hold the day's heat until late, so keep
> both of them downstairs until the sun is off the house. A bottle straight out
> of the freezer sticks to skin, so it stays in the dish towel for both of them.
> A floor fan tips over and a 13-month-old puts fingers through a grille, so
> stand it high and out of his reach or leave it off while he is loose in the
> room.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jul-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — Fever in a Hot House

This is the flat day. She is hot, heavy-limbed and on the sofa, the plan for
today is gone, and the only thing on the page is a shape for the hours. Nothing
here has to happen, and everything here can be abandoned halfway through
without spoiling anything.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day

- **Whenever she wakes.** Straight to the sofa in what she slept in. No table, no getting dressed, no schedule.
- **Before the first long sleep.** One quiet thing on your lap, twenty minutes at most.
- **The rest block.** The middle of the day, and the part everything else bends around.
- **When she asks for food.** Anything she names, in a small amount, on a small plate.
- **The afternoon dip.** The worst hour. Expect tears over nothing and hold the bar on the floor.
- **The long end of the day.** Lights low from five, and bedtime an hour early with nobody in a hurry.

### 🧺 What to Set Up Before She Comes Down

Five minutes of work buys the whole day. Sofa cushions flat, one folded blanket
even in July because a fever runs cold and hot in the same hour, a bowl of cool
water and three washcloths on the floor beside her, her cup with a straw in it
on a low chair she can reach without sitting up, a small trash can within arm's
reach, and the curtains half drawn on the sunny side.

### 🛋️ The Rest Block

The center of the day is a long stretch of nothing, and the job is protecting
it. Lie down with her. Phone face down and out of your hand for the first
twenty minutes of it, because she reads the top of your head as an instruction
to hold on and ask for things. Let her sleep if sleep arrives, and let her lie
awake and quiet if it does not. Two hours of this is a good day's work for both
of you, and the hours after it are easier for having had it.

### 📖 Three Things She Can Do Lying Down

**The Animals That Sleep All Winter.** Her eyes stay shut and you talk, with no
book open and nothing for her to do. A bear in a hole, a bat under a roof, a
hedgehog in a pile of leaves. Ask her what each one needs before it can sleep
that long, and take the answers slow. She is under a blanket in July with the
curtains drawn, which is the same arrangement, and she will get there herself.

**One Thing Out of the Window.** From where she is lying she can see one strip
of window. Name a thing in it, then let her name one, and go slow enough that
the gaps get long. A bird, a car, the light moving off the wall.

**A Sip a Page.** Her cup, a straw and a stack of books. One sip at the end of
every page, counted by her. Small sips going in all day beat a full cup she
refuses at four o'clock, and this turns the drinking into something she runs.

> 👶 **Where Kreston Goes:** A sick sister and a walking 13-month-old cannot share a sofa. He will climb on her, pull her blanket and take the cup, and today she has nothing to meet that with. Give him the floor at the far end of the room behind a gate or a pushed-back armchair, with a box of things he has not seen for a couple of weeks, and put yourself between them. His cup, his spoon and his washcloth stay his, and hers stay hers. If there is a second adult in the house or a grandparent who can take him out for two hours, today is the day to ask.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Thinking about what an animal needs in winter is easier than thinking about herself.**
> Ask a three-year-old with a fever how she feels and you get nothing, or you
> get an answer she has borrowed off your face. Her own state sits too close to
> look at, and the words for it arrive years later. A bear in a hole is far
> enough away to think about. She can tell you the bear needs the dark, a full
> stomach and nobody bothering it, and every one of those is a thing she wants
> and cannot ask for. Take her answers as a list of requests. Sick days go
> better when she works the whole question out on something that is not her.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Fluids matter more than food today, so small sips often, and
> count wet diapers or trips to the toilet rather than guessing. Call the doctor
> the same day for any of these: no pee for eight hours, a fever with a stiff
> neck or a headache she keeps holding, breathing that is fast or looks like
> hard work, a rash that stays visible when you press a glass against it, a
> child too sleepy to wake up to you, or a fever in a child who is getting worse
> after three days. Trust yourself over the list; being worried is a reason to
> call. Keep her cool with a washcloth and light bedding, never a cold bath,
> because shivering drives her temperature back up. Write down the time of every
> dose of whatever medicine your doctor has told you to give, because by the
> afternoon you will not remember.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

---

<a id="jul-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — The Day She Sends You for Things

The fever has broken and she is still not right. She is grouchy, quick to take
offense, tired by anything that lasts ten minutes, and bored out of her mind.
Today has more in it than yesterday and less than a normal day, and the shape
that works is her running things for other people from where she is sitting.

### 🕰️ The Shape of the Day

- **Whenever she wakes.** Dressed if she wants to be, pajamas if she does not. Both are fine.
- **The first stretch.** One thing with an end to it, done on a lap or a sofa.
- **When she asks for food.** She is hungry again today, and small and often still beats a plate.
- **The rest block.** Shorter than yesterday and it still happens, whatever she says about it.
- **After the rest.** The one hour in the day with any energy in it. Spend it on the round.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** Everything winds down from three, because she has half a tank.
- **The end of the day.** Early bath, early bed, and no negotiating over either.

### 🛋️ The Rest Block

She will fight it today, which is the difference between this day and
yesterday. Lay it out as a fact rather than an offer: after lunch everybody lies
down, and she can look at books instead of sleeping. Half of the sleep on a mend
day happens in the twenty minutes after she has announced she is not tired. Stay
in the room. Getting up too early into a full afternoon costs you the evening.

### 🔔 The Round She Runs

Give her the household to run for an hour from the sofa. Set it up as three
jobs, in this order, and keep a warm soapy cloth on the arm of the sofa for the
two that touch food.

**The Drinks Order.** She asks every person in the house what they want, holds
the answers, and sends you for them. She hands each cup over herself and takes
the empties back. Two rounds of this is not too many.

**Her Own Plate of Fruit.** Wash her hands with the warm cloth first, both
sides. You load a plate with four or five pieces out of the fruit bowl and hand
it to her on a towel, and that plate belongs to her. She wipes each piece, sets
them out in an order she likes and eats her way through them. Nothing on the
plate goes back in the bowl for anybody else.

**Kreston's Snack, Handed Over By Her.** Wash both sets of hands again, hers
and yours, before the plate comes anywhere near him. She holds it, he comes to
the sofa for one piece at a time, and she is the one who gives it to him. Three
days of him being kept away from her ends with her deciding when he comes
close, and that order matters to her more than it does to him.

### 📖 Two Things For the Flat Stretch

**The Catalog She Marks Up.** Any junk mail catalog, a pen, and she circles what
she would buy for each person in the house. She will spend twenty minutes on it
and she will explain every choice.

**The Photograph Round.** Your phone, the pictures from last month, and she
names who is in each one and what they were doing. Let her scroll and let her go
back to the same one four times.

> 👶 **Where Kreston Goes:** He has had a strange three days and he wants his sister back, so let them be close in short bursts with you sitting between them. He can carry things to her, which is the job of his month and the perfect job for today: her cup, a book, one shoe, whatever she sends him for. She will manage ten minutes of it and then be finished, so take him off to the other end of the room before she has to say so herself. Cups and washcloths still stay separate for a few more days.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Serving other people is a role she'll take more seriously than being served.**
> Three days of being carried, wiped and handed things puts her at the bottom of
> the house, and a child who has been done to for that long comes back grumpy
> and clinging. Handing her the drinks order turns it over. She has to hold what
> each person said, remember who is still waiting and get it to them, which is
> more thinking than any toy asks of her and it comes with a person saying thank
> you at the end. Being useful is the fastest route back to feeling herself,
> and it costs you nothing beyond fetching what she asks for.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** She is still passing this on. Her cup, her towel and her
> washcloth stay hers for a few more days. Wash her hands and your own before
> she touches any food anybody else will eat, before she hands Kreston his
> snack, and after every diaper and every nose. Swimming, playgroup and
> anybody's house wait until she has been fever-free for a full twenty-four
> hours with no medicine in her. Give a
> mend day the coolest part of the house and keep her out of the July afternoon
> altogether, because a child who has been running a temperature dehydrates
> faster in the heat than she did last week. Keep the fluids going at the same
> rate as yesterday. You are the one who loads Kreston's plate before she hands
> it over, because at 13 months his pieces have to be soft and no wider than his
> finger, and she has no way of judging that. A fever that comes back after a day
> clear is worth a phone call rather than a wait.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="jul-extras"></a>

## 🎲 July — Extra Ideas

For the morning you open the book with ten minutes, a hot house and no plan.
Nothing here needs a shopping trip and nothing takes longer to set up than it
takes to run.

### 🎲 **Alternative Activities**

- **One Cube in Each Hand.** Two ice cubes, one per fist, and the first hand to come up empty wins.
- **The Coldest Thing in the Fridge.** The back of her hand on every shelf and every jar, ranked coldest to warmest.
- **The Full Cup Down the Hall.** A cup filled to the brim carried the length of the hall and back without a drop.
- **The Smell She Has to Find.** One open jar hidden in the kitchen, and she walks toward it with her eyes shut.
- **The Shadow Marked Every Hour.** A strip of tape laid where the sunlight edge falls, once an hour, and the strips counted at dinner.
- **Ten Things That Fit in a Shoe.** She hunts them down and then argues for the eleventh.
- **The Tape Trail.** Masking tape stuck down as a path around the furniture, walked heel to toe.
- **The Paper Strip at the Doorway.** A torn strip of newspaper held up in every doorway to find where the air is moving.
- **Everybody Swaps Places.** Lunch eaten in somebody else's seat, yours included.
- **The Rice Tray on the Floor.** Two cups, a spoon and a funnel on a towel, in the shade, swept up after.
- **The Photograph She Explains.** One old picture and ten questions about who is in it and where they were.
- **Reading in the Empty Bathtub.** Cushion in, water off, two books and the coolest seat in the house.

### 🎨 **Alternative Arts & Crafts**

- **Crayon Shavings in the Window.** Shavings on paper on a sunny sill, watched until they slump.
- **The Paper That Fades.** Keys and a spoon laid on colored paper in the sun for a day, then lifted off.
- **Foil From One Square.** One square of foil, one animal, no tape and no scissors.
- **The Cardboard Fan.** A cereal box cut into a paddle, drawn on by her, waved at whoever is hottest.
- **Newspaper Hats.** One each, then a row of small ones for the animals.
- **Junk Mail Confetti.** Torn small, shaken in a jar, poured out on a dark plate and sorted by color.
- **The Envelope Zoo.** Old envelope corners cut into mouths, drawn on, fed paper scraps.
- **The Long Strip Family.** Everyone in the house drawn end to end on a strip as long as the table.
- **Bottle Cap Printing.** Caps dipped in paint, printed in rows, counted when they dry.
- **Paper Plate on Her Head.** She draws a face on a plate held on top of her head, then looks at what she made.
- **Chalk on Dark Paper.** A flattened cereal box colored dark, chalk over the top, smudged with a thumb.
- **The Flip Book.** Ten pages of a stick figure on the corner of an old notepad, thumbed through fast.

### 👶 **Kreston's Turn**

- **The Basket That Goes to the Other Room.** Three soft things in, carried through, tipped out, carried back.
- **One Step, Then Down Again.** The bottom stair or a firm cushion, up and down with one hand held, twenty times.
- **Posting the Big Lids.** Palm-sized lids through a slot cut in a shoebox, and nothing smaller than his fist.
- **The Wet Sponge and the Empty Bowl.** An inch of water in one bowl, a sponge, an empty bowl to fill, and you within arm's reach of both.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Small parts**: the whistle and the pea inside it, ten bottle caps at the flicking game, six paperclips on the paper planes, the bottle-cap coins at the market stall, the rice and pasta in the guessing tubs. Count them out and count them back in, then stand the tin up high.
- **Standing water**: the bottle canal and the paddling-pool lagoon, the duck-hooking bowl, his own inch in a baking tray. Kreston drowns in an inch of it without a sound, so stay within arm's reach and tip every container onto the grass the moment you stop using it.
- **At head height**: hang the bunting line across the yard high and tight, and take it and the string across the museum table down the same day. Tape the broom-handle gate barrier at one end only, because the far end has to drop when Kreston leans his whole weight on it.
- **Button batteries**: the flashlight dancing and the sound hunt both run on them, and they are the worst thing a 14-month-old can swallow. Check the battery door on every flashlight before he is in the room, and never leave a loose one on the floor.
- **Adult-only steps**: the craft knife for the ticket press, the sharp knife for the oranges and the bottle channels, the stapler and the table knife for the passport, the dry pan for the tortillas. Look for the adult-only mark in each activity, and the scissors stay with you.
- **August heat**: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, every day in this booklet. Paving burns bare feet by mid-morning, so shoes on for the chalk work, shade for anything past noon, and both children indoors the moment either goes red-faced.

## Week 32: Sports & Team Play ⚽
**📅 August 6 – August 12, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

This week Azlyn builds a sport out of its parts. A ball wound from grocery
bags on Friday, a numbered shirt on Saturday, a whistle and three signals on
Sunday, five events chalked onto the path on Monday, a long jump measured in
string on Tuesday, half-time drinks she mixes to her own recipe on Wednesday.
The question sitting under all of it: **what does a game need before anybody
can play it?** On Thursday she answers it by making up a game of her own and
running the whole thing end to end.

Nothing lands in this week but the heat, and it shapes every day. The outdoor
hour goes before eleven, and the afternoon event sits indoors at a table, on
the floor or on a tray. Four things get built to be used later: Friday's wound
ball, Saturday's numbered shirts, Sunday's peg scoreboard and Monday's five
chalked stations all come back out on Thursday. Keep the first three somewhere
she can see them, because the week ends with a trophy and she needs to know
what it is for.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Sorting by what a thing does.** Balls go in the HIGH basket or the LOW one, and only dropping them settles which.
- **Stopping on a signal.** One whistle blast freezes her mid-stride, two turn her round, three put everybody on the floor.
- **Measuring with string.** A cut length holds a jump, so three jumps lie side by side on the wall and she sorts them longest to shortest.
- **Keeping a score.** One point, one peg, one space along the line, counted out loud.
- **Writing rules and mending them.** She invents a game, plays it until something breaks, and says what the new rule should be.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Sorting by an invisible property is a step up
- Oil and water is the same lesson as the wax crayon and the sticker resist
- Freezing on cue is one of the best self-control exercises there is
- Choosing what to leave out is harder than choosing what to include
- Sand is one of the best materials there is, and it's the resistance that makes it good
- "Too much" and "not enough" is a real concept, and it's rarely taught
- Asking for her rule is better than checking her answer

---

## 🌟 Day 218: The Bounce Test 🌟
**📅 Friday, August 6, 2027**
**Theme:** Sports & Team Play

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Send a laundry basket round the house tonight for every ball in it, and leave an orange, clean socks and a sheet of foil beside it.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Rounding Up the Balls
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: High Bouncer, Low Bouncer (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Where the Ball Bounces Best (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Ball Made of Bags and String (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks and the Water Pitcher
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Sorting the Balls Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Cool Bath and the Soccer Book
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Rounding Up the Balls

**🧰 You need:** 1 laundry basket · every ball in the house · 1 orange · 1 pair of clean socks · 1 sheet of kitchen foil.

1. Hand her the basket and send her round the house. Under the beds, the closet, the shed shelf. Eight is enough, twelve is better.
2. Add three things that are not balls. Roll the socks into one, scrunch the foil into another, put the orange on top.
3. Line them up in the order she thinks they bounce, best to worst. You test that order at quarter past nine.

### 🎨 The Main Event: High Bouncer, Low Bouncer

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Every ball in the house, 8–12 (soccer ball, tennis ball, ping-pong ball, the sock ball, the orange, this morning's foil ball)
- 2 laundry baskets or empty boxes
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 permanent marker
- 4 sheets of paper for her predictions
- A clear stretch of hard floor and a wall

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape a strip to the wall at your shoulder height and write **DROP HERE** on it. Every ball starts against that tape and gets let go, never thrown.
2. Stand the two baskets a stride back on either side. Tape a label on each, **HIGH** and **LOW**.
3. Drop the first ball. Watch where the top of the bounce reaches on her, knee or waist or shoulder. She calls it.
4. Before each new ball she squeezes it and says which basket it lands in. Write the prediction down and tick it after the drop.
5. Work through the lot on hard floor. The orange divides opinion and the foil ball disappoints her.
6. Count each basket and read the prediction sheet back, ticks and all. Ask what the high ones have in common and write her answer word for word.

> 💡 **Tip:** The squeeze is doing the work. Hard and springy comes back, soft and dead does not.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Where the Ball Bounces Best

Take the tennis ball and a piece of chalk to the front and bounce it on
everything hard enough to bounce on. The paving, the drain cover, the driveway,
the grass baked flat since June. Chalk an **H** or an **L** on each as she calls
it, and finish on the shaded lawn, which still has give in it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and walks into the middle of
> whatever is happening. Give him the soccer ball, the one ball too big to fit
> in his mouth, and sit a few feet off with your legs open. Roll it across and
> wait. He shoves it back with both hands.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Ball Made of Bags and String

Children in half the world make their own soccer balls, and this is how.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4–6 plastic grocery bags
- 1 ball of string or thick wool
- Packing tape and masking tape
- 1 old sock
- Newspaper, 4 sheets
- 1 pair of adult scissors (**adult only**)
- The taped mark on the wall from this morning

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Scrunch two sheets of newspaper into the tightest ball she can manage. Squeeze, do not fold. That lump sets the size of everything after it.
2. Push the core into the old sock, knot it tight above, and cut the tail off with your scissors.
3. Wrap a grocery bag round the sock and twist the handles down flat. Then the next over the twist from a different side, four to six in all.
4. Hold the bundle while she winds the string. Round, then across, then round again. Twenty turns leaves an egg. Fifty looks like a ball.
5. Tie the string off, cover the knot with packing tape, and run masking tape over any bag still showing.
6. Take it to the taped mark on the wall. She calls high or low, then drops it, and finds she was right about a sock ball.
7. Out on the grass, kick it. It flies heavy and dead and will not roll far, which is what makes it good on a dry lawn.

> 💡 **Tip:** Wind the string tighter than feels reasonable. A loose ball goes egg-shaped on the second kick, and the fix is another fifty turns.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Sock ball only. Roll two socks into each other and stop there.
- Wind string round a tennis ball you own and compare the two.
- Sort the morning's balls by size instead of bounce.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A café with a window seat**, cake and an hour of watching people go past
- The shady half of the park, once the paving is off the boil
- The playing field at the end of the road, with the new ball
- Home and the hose, if the heat has beaten everyone

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him a sheet of the newspaper to scrunch and
> tear while you wind, and keep the grocery bags up on the table. At 14 months
> the noise is half the appeal. Hand him the finished ball first. It takes both
> arms.

### 🌍 Around the World: The World's Game ⚽

More people play soccer than any other game on earth, and most of them never
owned a store-bought ball. In Ghana, Brazil and the Philippines children wind
grocery bags, rags and string into one the same way Azlyn did this afternoon,
and no two of them come out alike.

> **✨ Try it:** Half-time oranges, the way teams everywhere have taken them for
> a hundred years. Cut two into six wedges each and hand them round at the
> halfway point of whatever game she plays this week.

> *Did you know?* In Brazil a ball wound out of rags is a *bola de meia*, which
> means sock ball.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sorting by an invisible property is a step up.**
> Azlyn has sorted by color, shape and size since she was two, and all three
> sit on the surface of the object. Bounce hides until you drop it. To put a
> ball in the right basket she has to hold a category the ball's appearance does
> not hand her, then find the evidence herself. Researchers watch for this shift
> around three, sorting by what a thing does rather than what it looks like. The
> squeeze test is the bigger move, because she is predicting an outcome from a
> feel. She will be wrong about the orange. Being wrong out loud and then
> watching is what makes the rule stick.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Ping-pong balls and anything smaller than a tennis ball fit
> down Kreston's throat, and at 14 months he walks into the middle of things to
> get at them. Count the small ones into the basket at the end and stand it up
> high. The bouncing out front stops at the curb: hold his hand from the curb
> onward, keep the drain cover on your side of him, and any ball that gets away
> is yours to fetch, never hers. August sun burns faster than it feels, so hat
> on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

**📅 Saturday, August 7, 2027**
**Theme:** Sports & Team Play

### 🌙 Prep Tonight

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Oil, Water and a Good Shake

**🧰 You need:** 1 clear jar with a lid · water · 2 tablespoons cooking oil · 1 tablespoon · a drop of food coloring or watered paint.

1. Half fill the jar with water and let her stir a drop of color through it.
2. Pour in two tablespoons of oil, lid on tight, and let her shake it as hard as she can.
3. Stand it on the table and watch. The oil climbs back to the top every time. Tell her a crayon does the same trick at quarter past nine.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Number the Paint Runs Off

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 white wax crayon or a white candle stub
- Thick paper, 6 sheets
- Washable poster paint in two colors, watered down in jam jars
- 1 wide soft brush
- 1 jar of clean water
- 1 old towel
- 1 permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She picks the team's two colors out of the jars and names the team. Write the name on the back of one sheet in marker.
2. Give her the white crayon and a sheet of thick paper. She draws a big number, pressing hard. It comes out close to invisible.
3. Load the wide brush with the first watery color and wash it edge to edge in one direction. The number rises up through it.
4. Rinse the brush in the jar of clean water and dry it on the towel before the second color, or you get mud.
5. Do a second sheet in the other color, and a third with a stripe of each meeting in the middle.
6. Hand her the last three sheets to do on her own. Write a squad number on the back of each and lay them out of the sun to dry.

> 💡 **Tip:** Press hard with the crayon and water the paint down further than looks sensible. Thick paint covers the wax instead of sliding off it.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Ten Kicks Against the Shed Wall

Chalk a rectangle on the shed door at her height and get out before ten, while
the wall still has shade. Ten kicks each, counted out loud, and a chalk tally on
the paving for every one that lands inside the box. Leave the tally where it is.
Tomorrow needs a scoreboard.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and scribbling, so hand him a
> fat piece of chalk and let him work the paving beside the tally marks. He
> holds it in his fist and drags it, and every line on there is his. He will
> walk into the goal about six times.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Numbers on Real Shirts

The wax trick works on cloth too, and this one she wears to the museum.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3–4 old white t-shirts (pillowcases work if you have no spare shirts)
- 1 roll masking tape
- Washable poster paint or fabric paint
- 1 sponge or 1 stiff brush
- Flattened cardboard, one piece per shirt
- 6 clothespins and the clothesline

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Slide a piece of cardboard inside each shirt, up to the shoulders. Paint goes through cotton in seconds and the card is the only thing stopping it.
2. Tear the masking tape into strips and build a number on the back of the first shirt. Straight lines only. A 1 is one strip, a 7 is two, a 4 is three. Press every edge down hard.
3. Let her build the next number herself. Crooked is correct. If she wants a 12, both digits go on.
4. Load the sponge and press it straight down over the tape rather than brushing across. Brushing lifts the edges and the paint creeps underneath.
5. Cover the whole back panel, tape and all, and stop while the paint is wet.
6. Peel the tape off there and then, corner first, pulling it back on itself. The number underneath stays white.
7. Clip the shirts on the line in the sun. August dries a t-shirt inside an hour.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do a spare pillowcase first if you have one. The first number teaches you how much paint a sponge holds.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Paper numbers only, taped to her front.
- Handprints in the team colors instead of a number.
- Paint the numbers on freehand and skip the tape.
- Sort the morning's painted sheets into two piles by color.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum**
- **The museum**, first Saturday of the month, and cool inside on the hottest afternoon of the week
- The shady side of the park with Friday's ball
- A friend's garden, shirts on
- The library, for anything with a team in it
- The paddling pool at home, if the line is out of the door

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He walks the museum at 14 months, which means one
> gallery rather than four. Put him down where the floor is open and let him
> cover it on his own feet, then get him back in the stroller. Give him the smallest
> shirt to hold on the way in.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Oil and water is the same lesson as the wax crayon and the sticker resist.**
> Azlyn met one idea three times today in three materials. Oil sitting back up
> on top of the water, wax turning the paint away, tape holding a white number
> under a loaded sponge. The rule underneath all three is that some things
> refuse to mix, and the one doing the refusing wins. A three-year-old does not
> carry a rule from a single demonstration over to a new material on her own.
> She needs it in enough different clothes to strip out whatever was incidental
> about the first one. That is why the jar at breakfast earns its five minutes,
> and why the shirts matter.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Use a plastic bottle for the shake rather than a glass jar, or
> keep your hand round the jar while she shakes it. The wax crayon and the
> candle stub are both choking size, so count them into a tin and stand it up
> high the moment the painting is done. Washable non-toxic paint only, because a
> 14-month-old gets a hand in it. Both children go out to the shed wall covered:
> hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Pegs go back on the line at the
> end rather than down on the paving.

## 🌟 Day 220: Somebody Has to Say Go 🌟
**📅 Sunday, August 8, 2027**
**Theme:** Sports & Team Play

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Hang the whistle on the back of the kitchen door, clear the hallway, and cut two arm-lengths of string for this afternoon.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: One Blast, Two Blasts, Three
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Statues on the Whistle (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Stop and Go Through the Sprinkler (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Peg Scoreboard (90 min)

### 🌅 Opening Activity: One Blast, Two Blasts, Three

**🧰 You need:** 1 whistle · 2 cushions · the hallway.

1. Sit her at the table with the whistle between you. Blow it once. Then twice. Then three times.
2. Set the meanings out loud. One blast stop, two turn round, three everybody down on the floor. Have her say them back in order.
3. Practice sitting down. One blast and she freezes in her chair, three and she slides onto the floor. Then drop a cushion at each end of the hall.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Statues on the Whistle

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 whistle (a saucepan lid and a wooden spoon, or your own voice, does the same job)
- Music on your phone
- 1 roll masking tape for the start and finish lines
- 2 cushions as the turning markers
- A clear hallway, or the coolest room in the house

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape a start line and a finish line at each end of the hallway and stand a cushion past each. Those are the turns.
2. Music on, and send her line to line however she wants to travel. Running, crawling, sideways, hopping.
3. One blast. She holds whatever shape she is in, mid-stride, until the next blast. Count three out loud while she wobbles, then let her go.
4. Add the second signal. Two blasts, she turns at the nearest cushion and comes back. Give her four or five before the third arrives.
5. Three blasts, everybody on the floor including you. Getting down there yourself is what makes her drop fast.
6. Hand her the whistle for the last ten minutes and run when she says run. She holds the stop for an unreasonable length of time.

> 💡 **Tip:** Blow the stop when she is going flat out, not when she is slowing down anyway.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Stop and Go Through the Sprinkler

Set the sprinkler on the grass and run the same three signals through it. One
blast and she freezes in the spray. Two and she goes back through it the other
way. Get out before eleven while the grass is cool underfoot, and take the
whistle with you.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and will not freeze for
> anybody, so give him the edge of the spray rather than the middle. Sit him
> where the water arrives as mist and let him decide whether to walk in. He will
> work out that the water comes round again.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Peg Scoreboard

The rest of the week needs somewhere to put its points. It gets built once,
sitting down, and used on three more days.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 sheet of thick card, or a flattened box
- String or thick wool, 2 arm-lengths, cut last night
- 10–12 clothespins
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 roll masking tape
- Stickers or bottle caps for the point markers

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the card flat and rule a line down the middle. Two teams. She names both and writes what she can of the names at the top.
2. Tape one string across the upper half, the other across the lower half. Pull each tight before the second tape goes down, or the clothespins sag instead of sliding.
3. Mark ten spaces under each string. Nought at the left, then a line for every point up to ten. She does the marks under the second string.
4. Clip a peg to the left end of each string. That is nought all, and a point moves a peg one space right.
5. Stick a sticker at the five and the ten on both strings, or tape a bottle cap there, so she finds halfway without counting.
6. Test it. Three points to you, four to her, one space at a time and counting out loud, then slide both back.
7. Stand it against the wall where it lives all week, spare pegs clipped along the top edge.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her move both pegs, yours as well as hers, counting out loud.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Two paper cups and dry pasta. One piece in for every point.
- Chalk the score on the paving and start again each game.
- Pegs along the clothesline, no card at all.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Feeding the ducks**, late enough that the pond has gone into shade
- A long walk with the stroller and the whistle, one blast for stop at every curb
- The playground, once the equipment has cooled enough to touch
- A sunset walk after dinner instead, and skip this hour

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Clip two of the spare pegs to the edge of the card
> for him and let him pull them off. At 14 months that pinch grip is work. At the
> pond he goes in the stroller or on your hip.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Freezing on cue is one of the best self-control exercises there is.**
> Stopping a body that is already moving is one of the hardest things a
> three-year-old brain does. Azlyn has to hold a rule, catch a signal, and shut
> down a movement her legs have committed to. Researchers who study executive
> function use games close to this one as a measure, and how children handle
> them at four tracks with how they settle into a classroom later. The
> two-blast turn is a step up again, because it swaps one rule for another
> mid-run. She will fail the first few, and those are the ones doing the work.
> Every failed stop is practice, and the laughing is what keeps her doing
> thirty of them.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A whistle is the exact size Kreston chokes on, and the pea
> inside it comes loose. It goes round your neck or in a high drawer, never on
> the floor. Keep him out of the running lane. At 14 months he walks straight
> into the path of a sprinting three-year-old. Wet skin burns quicker than dry,
> so both of them go into the sprinkler covered: hat on, cream at eight, cream
> again at eleven.

## 🌟 Day 221: The Pitch on the Path 🌟
**📅 Monday, August 9, 2027**
**Theme:** Sports & Team Play

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Flatten a cereal box and cut a dozen cards out of it, and stand the chalk, the crayons and an empty shoebox on the table beside them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Walking the Edges
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Five That Made It (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Chalking the Five Stations Onto the Path (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Same Course, Teddy Sized (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Cold Water Pitcher for Dinner
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Teddies Round the Little Course
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Cool Bath, Then the Course Cards Again
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Walking the Edges

**🧰 You need:** her shoes · 1 piece of chalk · the path or the drive.

1. Shoes on, out before the paving warms, and walk the path end to end counting steps out loud.
2. Walk it again down one edge and back down the other.
3. Chalk a cross at each end. That is the pitch, and everything she picks at nine has to fit between the two crosses.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Five That Made It

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 10–12 cards cut from a cereal box
- 1 permanent marker
- Crayons for her to draw each event
- 1 shoebox with a lid, for the ones that do not make it
- 1 roll masking tape
- This morning's two chalk crosses on the path

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Sit down with the cards and ask what she wants in her games. Running, jumping, throwing, hopping, the dog joining in. Write each on its own card in her words.
2. She colors each card while you write the next. Ten or twelve, then stop, even if she has more.
3. Take the cards and the tape out to the path. Lay them between this morning's two crosses, one per station, with running room between them.
4. They will not all fit. Five is what the path holds. Say it straight and hand the decision to her. Five stay, the rest go in the shoebox.
5. Do not rescue the ones she cuts. She drops them in herself, and you write **RESERVES** on the lid so nothing is gone for good.
6. Tape the five survivors down in order and read them out end to end. That is her program.

> 💡 **Tip:** Resist steering her five towards the ones that will work. Her list will include something impossible, and the path tells her so.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Chalking the Five Stations Onto the Path

Straight on from the table with the chalk. Draw a station round every taped
card: a start line, a box to jump out of, a circle to throw into. Work the
shaded end first and move down as the sun comes round. Shoes stay on, and the
water bottle stands in the shade.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and scribbling, so give him a
> fat piece of chalk at the shaded end and his own square of paving. He drags
> it, drops it and eats some of the dust, which is why it is chalk and not
> marker. Sit him where he can watch Azlyn run the line.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Same Course, Teddy Sized

The path is too hot to kneel on by one o'clock, so the course comes indoors at
teddy scale. Everything shrinks except the number of stations.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 large tray, or a flattened box, as the base
- Paper cups, 5–6
- Drinking straws and cardboard scraps
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 foil ball or 1 ping-pong ball (no marbles)
- 3–4 teddies or small toys
- Her five event cards from this morning

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Peel the five cards off the path on the way in and lay them along one edge of the tray in order. The tray is the pitch now.
2. Draw the lines onto the tray with the marker. A start, a finish, and whatever the middle three need.
3. Build the equipment from what is on the table. Two cups on their sides make a goal, two straws taped across two upright cups make a hurdle, a cardboard scrap folded double stands up as a wall.
4. Tape every piece down.
5. Put the ball at the start line and check it fits through the cup goal. Squash the foil ball smaller if it will not go, or swap it for something that fits.
6. Run the first teddy through all five stations with her holding it, in card order.
7. Leave her to run the other teddies on her own, and let her decide what the winner gets.

> 💡 **Tip:** Animate the teddy rather than sliding it. She narrates a toy that moves its own legs.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One cup, one ball, and a teddy that shoots from further back each time.
- Draw the course on paper instead of building it.
- Run the five stations indoors at her own size, down the hallway.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The hill walk**, up at half past two under the trees, with a stop at the top
- The riverside path, shaded all afternoon
- The paddling pool, if the hill is more than either of you has in you
- The green space with Friday's ball

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him one teddy and one paper cup of his own on
> the floor beside the tray. At 14 months he puts a thing into a container and
> takes it out again. On the hill he walks the flat bit at the top.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Choosing what to leave out is harder than choosing what to include.**
> Azlyn can name ten things she wants in forty seconds. Asking which five to
> drop is a different job, because every card that goes in the box is something
> she gives up while holding the reason in her head. Three-year-olds manage the
> dropping far better when the limit comes from the world instead of from you.
> The path is five stations long, a fact she can walk the length of, so the
> argument is with the path. The reserve box matters as much as the limit does,
> because nothing she drops is thrown away. She is ordering the cards rather
> than destroying any of them, and that is what keeps her deciding instead of
> digging in.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** August paving gets hot enough to burn bare feet by mid-morning.
> Shoes on, chalk at the shaded end, and a water bottle out there with you. Hat
> on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, because an hour of chalking on an
> open path is an hour of full sun. Both children come in the moment either goes
> red-faced. The foil ball and the ping-pong ball are both small enough for
> Kreston to swallow, so whichever one she uses stays on the tray and off the
> floor.

## 🌟 Day 222: Jumping Into Sand 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, August 10, 2027**
**Theme:** Sports & Team Play

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Tip the play sand into the large shallow tub tonight, stand a pitcher of water beside it, and put the swimming bag by the front door.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Raking the Sand Flat
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Where Her Heels Land (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Jumping the Widening River (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Everybody's Jump on the Wall (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Cups and Forks Before Swimming
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Sand Tray on the Back Step
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Rinsing the Chlorine Out
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Raking the Sand Flat

**🧰 You need:** the tray of sand · 1 pitcher of water · her two hands.

1. Walk her fingers through the dry sand, then pour half the pitcher over one end while she stirs.
2. Press your flat hand into the damp end, then the dry end. Damp sand keeps the print and dry sand fills it in.
3. Sweep the tray level with the side of her forearm and smooth it with her palms. She resets it after every jump.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Where Her Heels Land

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 bag of washed play sand in a large shallow storage tub or the paddling pool (a tray of potting soil does the same job)
- Chalk
- String or thick wool, 1 ball
- 1 pair of adult scissors (**adult only**)
- Craft sticks or clothespins, 3, to mark each landing
- 1 pitcher of water for damping the sand
- 1 permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Chalk a take-off line on the paving at the edge of the tray. Her toes go behind it.
2. First jump: arms at her sides, no run-up. Push a craft stick in behind the dent her heels leave.
3. Cut a string from the chalk line to the stick. Write **ONE** on the stick and tie the string round it.
4. Smooth the sand, damp it from the pitcher if it has gone crumbly, and jump again with her arms swinging. Mark it, cut a second string, label that stick **TWO**.
5. Hold the two strings side by side. The arms one is longer.
6. Last jump: she wades to the far end through the sand and goes from in there. Her legs will not do what they did on the paving. Cut a third string, label it **THREE**, and lay all three in order.

> 💡 **Tip:** Measure to the heels and say so out loud every time. Three-year-olds measure to whichever bit went furthest.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Jumping the Widening River

Chalk two lines on the paving a hand's width apart and call the gap a river. She
jumps it, you widen it by a hand, she jumps again. Keep going until she lands in
the water, then go back two hands and let her clear it three times.
Work the shaded side of the house, and let her watch you miss it too.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and nowhere near jumping,
> since both feet leaving the ground is closer to two. He has bend and spring,
> so hold both his hands and let him bounce on the spot at the edge of the
> chalk.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Everybody's Jump on the Wall

Indoors the floor is cool and the measuring carries on, with everybody in the
house on the line.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 roll masking tape
- String or thick wool, 1 ball
- 1 pair of adult scissors (**adult only**)
- 1 permanent marker
- A clear wall, or the back of a door
- Everyone who is home

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape a take-off line across the hall floor. Everyone jumps from behind it, standing start, no run-up.
2. Azlyn goes first. Mark where her heels land with tape and write her name on it.
3. Take your turn, then anyone else home, each with a taped and named mark.
4. Cut a string for every jump, floor line to landing mark, and wrap tape round one end as a label with the name on it.
5. Hang the strings on the wall side by side, all from the same height, and let her sort them longest to shortest before you tape anything down.
6. Ask her who went furthest and why. Take the answer as it comes. Legs turn up in it somewhere.
7. Leave them up. Anybody who visits gets a jump and a string.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not shorten your own jump to keep it close to hers. She reads a wall of strings as a fact about grown legs.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Tape marks on the floor only. Skip the strings and the wall.
- Jump off the bottom stair and compare it with the standing jump.
- Frog, rabbit and kangaroo jumps down the hall, no measuring.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly hour and the best place in town in August
- The splash pad, if the session is booked out
- The paddling pool with the sprinkler going
- A shaded walk and a popsicle, if nobody can face chlorine

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He comes to the pool. At 14 months he walks the
> shallow end holding both your hands, so let him wade rather than float.
> Twenty-five minutes, then out and warm before he goes quiet on you.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sand is one of the best materials there is, and it's the resistance that makes it good.**
> Sand answers back in proportion. Press hard and it holds the print, press soft
> and it does nothing, wade through it and her legs have to find more than they
> needed on the paving. It also has no correct outcome, so she cannot get it
> wrong and cannot finish it, and she stays with a tray of it long after she
> abandons a puzzle. Damp sand and dry sand behave like two different
> substances, and moving between them is her first real handle on why water
> changes things. Sand is patient with a three-year-old's hands and still makes
> her work for what she wants, which is why twenty minutes in it outlasts
> twenty minutes at almost anything else.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Use washed play sand, not construction sand. Kreston will put
> it in his mouth and rub it into his eyes at 14 months, so he gets a
> dishwashing bowl of his own sand, set well clear of the landing end, and you
> stay close enough to touch him. Azlyn comes down heels first into the big
> tray, so keep him out of it. Tip any standing water out of the tray before
> either child gets near it. He stays within arm's reach at the pool as well.
> A morning on open paving is a morning in full sun: hat on, cream at eight,
> cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 223: Half Time 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, August 11, 2027**
**Theme:** Sports & Team Play

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill the ice tray, stand the thawed juice concentrate and six clear cups by the water pitcher, and rinse ten bottle caps to dry.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule

- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Carrying the Cold Drinks to the Shady Bench (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Bottle Cap Cup (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Filling the Ice Tray for Dinner
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Cap Box and the Lid
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: A Cold Washcloth and One Long Book
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Oranges Cut Into Smiles

**🧰 You need:** 2 oranges · 1 board · 1 sharp knife (**adult only**) · 1 plate.

1. Cut both oranges into six wedges on the board, then put the knife away before she sits down.
2. Show her the trick. Bite the flesh out from inside and the peel left in your mouth is a wide orange grin. Do yours first.
3. Two wedges each now. The rest go on the plate in the fridge for half time, and she carries them out.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Too Strong, Too Weak, Just Right

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Frozen juice concentrate, thawed, or lemon juice and sugar
- 1 pitcher of cold water
- 6 clear cups or glasses
- 1 tablespoon and 1 teaspoon
- Ice
- 1 card and 1 permanent marker
- 1 tray to carry it all out on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Line three of the clear cups up. She pours the same amount of cold water into each from the pitcher.
2. Cup one gets four tablespoons of concentrate. Cup two gets one teaspoon. Say the numbers out loud as they go in and let her stir both.
3. She tastes cup one, then cup two. Take the face she makes as the result and give her the words. Too strong. Too weak.
4. Cup three is hers. She adds concentrate a teaspoon at a time, tastes after every one, and stops when she says stop. Count the spoons out loud and let her number stand.
5. Write her recipe on the card in her own measurements. Her spoons, that cup, that much water.
6. Make the last three cups to her card, drop the ice in and load the tray.

> 💡 **Tip:** No concentrate in the house works fine. Lemon juice and a spoon of sugar give her two things to adjust instead of one.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Carrying the Cold Drinks to the Shady Bench

She carries the tray. Pick the bench you can see from the gate and walk it at her
pace with the cups sliding about. Drink them out there rather than at the table.
The green stripes in the grass show where the shade sits.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and drinks from an open cup
> with two hands if you fill it a third full. Give him a little of the juice he
> watched her mix and let him hold it himself. On the walk he would rather push
> the stroller than ride in it, so allow ten spare minutes.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Bottle Cap Cup

A whole tournament fits on a table top, with everybody sitting down.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 10 plastic bottle caps
- 1 shoebox lid, or a sheet of thick card
- 1 paper cup, or a matchbox, as the goal
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 small box with a lid, for counting the caps back into
- The peg scoreboard from Sunday

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape the shoebox lid flat to the table, open side up.
2. Lay the paper cup on its side at the far end and tape it down. That is the goal.
3. Mark every cap. Five for her team, five for yours, and she decides what the two marks mean.
4. Show her the flick. One finger held back against the thumb and let go, not a push and not a throw. The first ten go on the floor.
5. Take turns. A cap in the cup is a point, a cap off the lid loses the turn.
6. After every point she walks to the peg scoreboard from Sunday and moves the peg one space.
7. Play to five, swap ends and play again. Count the caps into the small box at the end.

> 💡 **Tip:** Start her a hand's width from the goal rather than at the far end. A three-year-old who scores in the first two minutes stays at the table for twenty.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Flick the caps at a chalk target instead of into a goal.
- Sort the caps by color and by size and stop there.
- Build a tower of caps and count how many before it goes over.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Indoor playground**, the quiet session, and the coolest hour available indoors
- The library on the way home, for anything with a ball on the cover
- A friend's house with the paddling pool out
- The garden and the hose, if leaving is beyond everybody

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He is not at this table. Bottle caps go in the
> mouth inside four seconds at 14 months, so set him up on the floor with the
> empty pitcher and the tablespoon. At indoor playground he gets the under-twos area on his
> own feet.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **"Too much" and "not enough" is a real concept, and it's rarely taught.**
> Azlyn knows more and less. Both are easy, because you can see them. Too much
> needs a target, and that target sits in her own mouth rather than in the cup.
> Taste, add a spoon, taste again is the whole method for cooking, for mixing
> paint, for how hard to throw a ball, and she gets almost no practice at it. She
> adjusts, checks, adjusts again and lands on an answer nobody handed her. Her
> number will come out sweeter than yours, and the card is a record of what she
> decided rather than what you would have poured. Write it as it stands.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Bottle caps are the classic choking size and there will be ten
> of them on a table Kreston can reach standing up. Play where he cannot get to
> them, count them into the box at the end, and put the box up high. He never
> gets one to hold, however hard he asks; a jar lid too wide for his mouth is
> the swap. The walk to the bench runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight,
> cream again at eleven. The orange knife goes back in the drawer before either
> child is at the table.
