# 🌧️ August — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

These five pages are for the days August takes off you. Two of them are
weather days, which in this month means a storm that sets in before breakfast
or heat that makes the front step a bad idea by ten. Two are sick days, one
for the worst of it and one for the long bored middle, and neither has a clock
in it. The last page is a list of one-line ideas for the morning you open the
book with ten minutes and no plan.

---

<a id="aug-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — The Storm That Sat Still

August storms tend to blow through in twenty minutes. This one has not. The
sky went dark before breakfast, the rain is coming straight down, the yard is
under an inch of water and the gutter has given up. Nobody is going out today,
so the whole day is built around the one thing a dark house is good for. Week
35 gave her that flashlight and a wall of shadows. Today the same flashlight
hands her color, and she will recognize the setup the moment the curtains go
across.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand every clear glass, jar and plastic lid you own on the kitchen table with a flashlight, a hand mirror and a stack of white paper, set the cornstarch and the food coloring beside them for the afternoon, and check the flashlight batteries before you go up.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Every Clear Thing in the House
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Rainbow She Can Turn Off (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Crossing the Room on Cushions (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Puddle That Goes Hard When She Hits It (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🛋️ The Storm Hour: Blankets, Books and the Big Light Off (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Putting the Cups Out for Everyone
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Jars on the Windowsill
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Warm Bath While It Hammers on the Roof
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Every Clear Thing in the House

**🧰 You need:** 1 laundry basket · every clear glass, jar, plastic lid and bottle you own · 1 old CD or DVD · 1 hand mirror.

1. Send her around the house with the basket for anything she can see through. Take the ones you would rather she did not carry out of her hands at the door of each room and carry those yourself.
2. Line them up along the table in front of the window, tallest to shortest, and let her look through each one at the rain.
3. Put the CD and the mirror at the end of the row and tell her both of those have a color hidden in them. Leave the claim sitting there until quarter past nine.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Rainbow She Can Turn Off

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 flashlight with fresh batteries
- 1 tall straight glass, filled to the brim with water
- White paper, 4 sheets
- 1 hand mirror and 1 shallow bowl of water
- 1 old CD or DVD
- 1 roll masking tape
- A room you can get dark

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Curtains across, big light off. Stand the full glass at the edge of the table with a sheet of white paper on the floor underneath it.
2. Shine the flashlight through the glass from low down and off to one side, and walk the beam around until a band of color lands on the paper. She holds the flashlight for this and finds it herself, which takes longer than you want it to.
3. Once she has it, tape the glass down and tape the paper where it lies. Now she switches the flashlight off. The colors go. She switches it back on and they come back in the same place. Let her run that switch as long as she wants.
4. Move the flashlight nearer and further while she watches the band stretch and shrink, then hand the job over and sit where you can see her face.
5. Tilt the CD under the beam. Same light, a different rainbow, and this one slides about the ceiling when her wrist moves.
6. Last one: mirror leaning against the inside of the bowl of water, beam down onto the wet half of it, and the band comes out on the ceiling above her.

> 💡 **Tip:** The angle is the whole trick. A flashlight held straight on gives her a white blob, so start it low and to the side and let her hunt from there.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Crossing the Room on Cushions

Legs still need spending. Pull every cushion in the house onto the living room
floor and lay them in a path from the door to the window, close enough that
she can step between them. The floor is the water. She crosses, and each time
she gets over you take one cushion away and she works out a new route. Give
her the last two and let her set the crossing for you, then follow her route
to the letter, including the bit where you have to jump.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and walks straight into the
> middle of a dark room. Sit him in the color while it is on the paper, so the
> band lands across his hands, and give him a clear plastic tub to look through
> and carry off. He is at the stage of moving a thing rather than keeping it
> still, and he will bring it back. On the cushions he gets his own two, flat
> on the carpet at the edge, to climb on and off.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Puddle That Goes Hard When She Hits It

Morning was dark and still and about looking. This afternoon her hands go into
something that behaves like nothing else in the house.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Cornstarch, 1 box, with a cup of it held back in the box
- Water, about half as much as the cornstarch
- 1 large shallow tray or a roasting pan
- 1 old towel under the tray
- Food coloring, 1 color, or a spoon of any drink mix in the cupboard
- 1 spoon and 1 small pitcher
- 3 or 4 small plastic toys
- 1 bowl of warm water and a washcloth, standing by

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Towel down, tray on it, most of the box tipped in and a cup of it left in reserve. Let her run her hands through the dry powder first, because the change is the point and she needs the before.
2. Pour the water in a little at a time from the pitcher while she stirs with both hands. Stop when a spoon dragged through it leaves a line that takes a moment to close behind it. Add powder if it turns to soup.
3. Show her the two things it does. Slap it flat with your palm and it goes hard as a plate. Rest your fingers on it and they sink to the bottom.
4. Roll a lump between her hands. It holds while she works it and runs off her wrist the second she stops.
5. Drip food coloring on the surface and watch the color sit there in a line rather than spreading. She stirs it in, and the whole tray turns.
6. Sink the small toys and let her fish them out. Slow hands get them, fast hands get nothing.
7. Finish with hands in the warm bowl and the washcloth, and leave the tray to dry out rather than washing it into the sink.

> 💡 **Tip:** Half the water you think. Too wet is a tray of milk and the way back is more powder, so the cup you held back stays in the box until the mix reads right.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One cup of cornstarch in a cereal bowl, on her lap, and stop there.
- Flour and water instead, thick, and let her make a paste to stick paper with.
- Skip the tray and build the biggest cushion pile the room allows.
- Sort the clear jars from this morning by how much water each one holds.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Cornstarch powder is not for him at 14 months, so
> he is not at this tray. Give him a baking tray with an inch of warm water in
> it on a towel at the other end of the room, two jar lids too wide for his
> mouth, and stay within arm's reach of it. Tip it out the moment he is done.
> Once the tray of goo is drying, let him press one flat hand into what is left
> in the bowl and wash it straight off.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A rainbow with a switch on it puts the cause in her hand.**
> A rainbow in the sky arrives whole, belongs to nobody, and gives her no way
> in. The one on your floor answers to her thumb. She switches the flashlight
> off and the colors go, switches it on and they come back in the same place,
> and the cause sits in her own hand. Three-year-olds sort the world into
> things that happen and things they do, and moving an event from the first
> pile to the second is worth more to her than any account of white light. She
> will not carry away the word refraction. She carries away that the colors
> were in the flashlight the whole time and the water let them out.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A hand mirror on the floor with a walking 14-month-old in the
> room is a sheet of glass waiting to be stood on. It stays on the table, it
> goes back in the drawer the moment step six is done, and Kreston is on your
> hip or out of the room while it is out. Check the battery door on the
> flashlight is screwed or clipped shut before it goes near him, because button
> batteries are the worst thing he can swallow. Never pour cornstarch down the
> sink; it sets in the trap. Let the tray dry and throw the powder away. Keep
> the cornstarch box up high and out of his hands, since a lungful of loose
> powder makes a 14-month-old cough hard. An August storm this size carries
> lightning, so hold the five o'clock bath until the thunder has been gone
> twenty minutes.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="aug-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — Too Hot to Open the Door

The other August bad day. No rain, no wind, no excuse she can see out of the
window, and a heat index that makes an hour on the path a bad idea for a
three-year-old and a worse one for a 14-month-old. The blinds stay down,
the house stays shut on the sun side, and the whole day runs indoors on cold
water and moving air.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Fill both ice trays and a lidded tub, close the blinds on the west side of the house before bed, and stand four clear jars, the shaving foam and the food coloring on the kitchen table.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Cold Water in Four Jars
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Foam Cloud That Rains (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Sky From the Coolest Window (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Everything the Fan Can Lift (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🧊 Cool-Down Hour: Wet Washcloths on the Coolest Floor (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Bowls Down the Table
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Jar of Ice She Watches Go
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: A Cool Bath and the Curtains Still Shut
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Cold Water in Four Jars

**🧰 You need:** 4 clear jars or tall glasses · cold water · 2 small cups · food coloring · 1 teaspoon.

1. She fills all four jars two-thirds full of cold water at the sink and stands them on a tray in the middle of the table.
2. Two small cups of water beside them, four drops of coloring stirred into each. That is the rain, and it waits on the table until quarter past nine.
3. Walk the house together while it sits. Flat hand on every window, blinds down on the hot ones, and the two shaded windows opened wide for a draft through the hall. She calls hot or cold at each one and you follow her call.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Foam Cloud That Rains

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The 4 filled jars, on a tray
- 1 can of shaving foam, or a wad of cotton balls teased flat
- The 2 cups of colored water
- 1 teaspoon
- 1 dish towel under the tray
- 1 permanent marker and a strip of masking tape for each jar

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Dish towel under the tray. Heap shaving foam onto the water in the first jar to about a finger's depth and flatten the top with the back of the teaspoon. That is the cloud, and she says out loud what is underneath it.
2. Spoon the colored water on top a teaspoon at a time. She counts each spoon as it goes on. For a good while nothing happens at all.
3. Keep going past the point where she says it is broken. The cloud holds the color until it cannot, then a thread of it drops through and spreads down the jar in slow ropes.
4. Second jar gets a thin cloud, third gets a cloud twice as thick. Tape a strip on each and write her guess at how many spoons it will take before the rain comes. Test them one at a time and write the real number underneath.
5. Read the three numbers back with her hand on the jars. Thicker held more, and she got there before you said it.
6. The fourth jar is hers to wreck. Let her stir it, pile it, tip the whole thing into the sink and start again with whatever cloud is left.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep her spoon out of the first jar. Stirring gets her the color in four seconds and costs her the only interesting part, which is the wait.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: The Sky From the Coolest Window

Take the coolest window in the house, the one with the blind still up on the
shaded side, and pull two chairs to it with a pitcher of water. Give her three
names for what is up there: the thin high streaks, the flat cotton ones with
gray undersides, and the tall piles that build all afternoon and turn into the
evening storm. She draws one of each on a card while she looks. Come back to
the same window after lunch and again at four, cards in hand, and see which
kind has taken over. On a humid August day the tall ones win by five o'clock.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and hot children get quiet
> before they get loud. Wring a washcloth out in cold water and hand it to him
> to chew and wave about, and give him a second one for the back of his neck.
> He has three to five words, so name the fan and the sky every time you pass
> either. At the window he will stop dead when the room darkens under a cloud,
> which is worth watching for.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Everything the Fan Can Lift

The morning made weather in a jar. The afternoon makes wind in the hallway,
and she gets to decide what it carries.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 fan, standing on a table or a chest of drawers, never on the floor
- Paper napkins or tissue paper, 6
- Printer paper, 6 sheets
- 1 roll masking tape
- 1 cotton ball, 1 coin, 1 metal spoon, 1 plastic lid, 1 sock
- 1 pencil
- String, 4 short lengths, and 1 clothespin

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Stand the fan up on a table pointing down the hall and tape a masking tape line on the floor a long stride in front of it. One rule that does not bend all afternoon: nobody's hands go past that line, hers or yours.
2. Lay the test pile out behind the line. She sorts it into LIFTS and STAYS before a single thing is tested, and you write both lists on a sheet.
3. Drop each one into the moving air from behind the line, one at a time. The cotton ball and the napkin go up the hall, the coin drops straight down, and the sock divides the house.
4. Tear a napkin into long strips and tape them to the pencil. She holds it out at arm's length and watches every strip point the same way.
5. Tape six paper strips along the top of the doorway so the whole doorway moves, then walk her through it.
6. Parachute: one napkin, a short string taped to each corner, all four knotted onto the clothespin. She drops it from standing on a chair with you holding her arm, and it beats the same peg dropped bare.
7. Fan off. Everybody lies on the floor under the strips and watches them come to a stop.

> 💡 **Tip:** Run the fan on its lowest setting. Full blast blows the whole test pile off the floor at once and she never sees one thing at a time.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One paper fan each, folded from a sheet, and no electric fan at all.
- Blow the cotton ball across the table with a straw and race two of them.
- Tape strips to the back of a chair and pull it up and down the hall.
- Cold cloths, the darkest room, and a long book instead of any of it.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The fan is the hazard of the day and he is 14
> months, so he does not share the hall while it is on. Give him the far room
> or your hip. Once the fan goes off, lay him under the paper strips and pull
> one across his face with your hand for the last ten minutes. He will carry a
> strip off, and it is paper, so let him.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Naming clouds is the first time the sky has parts.**
> The sky reads to Azlyn as one object, a lid over the day that is blue or is
> not. Hand her three names and it comes apart into pieces she can point at:
> the thin streaks up high, the cotton ones with gray undersides, the tall
> piles that grow all afternoon and turn into tonight's storm. Naming is how a
> three-year-old cuts anything into parts, and the sky is the largest thing
> anybody has offered her names for. She will use them wrong for weeks. Keep
> using yours, take hers as they come, and by the end of the summer she is
> telling you what the weather plans to do before you have looked up.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A box fan on the floor sits at Kreston's exact height and the
> gaps in the guard take a 14-month-old's fingers. Stand it up on a table or a
> dresser, tape the cable flat along its whole run so nobody trips it or hauls
> it down, and keep him out of that room while it is turning. Shaving foam
> stings hard in eyes and is not for his hands or hers to rub a face with, so
> wash both pairs of hands before anyone touches their eyes and keep the can up
> high. Heat is the real hazard today. Water in front of both of them every
> hour whether they ask or not, and a hot, flushed, quiet child who stops
> sweating needs cooling and a call, not a nap.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="aug-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — Flat on the Sofa

This is the bad one. She has a fever, she is not eating, and she has not
lifted her head off the cushion since seven. There is no schedule on this page
because a clock is no use to you today. The day has a rest block in the middle
of it and everything else bends around that. Nothing here needs cutting,
baking or cleaning up, and all of it can be abandoned halfway through without
anybody minding.

### 🌙 Before She Comes Down
> Make the sofa up before she gets to it: a folded towel over the arm, a cool room with the blinds down, a pitcher of water and a cup with a straw, a bowl within reach in case, and a stack of books on the floor beside her rather than in her hands.

### 🕗 The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes.** Straight to the made-up sofa, a drink in front of her, and no questions past the one on the envelope.
- **Once she has settled.** The faces go on the envelope, and you ask her the first time.
- **When she asks for food.** Take what she asks for and hold everything else back. Dry toast, a popsicle, cold fruit, nothing on a schedule.
- **The long middle.** The rest block, and it takes as much of the day as it wants.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** One slow story on your lap, then drinks again.
- **The last stretch.** Lights low, the fan across the room, and bed early with the door open.

### 🙂 Once She Has Settled: The Five Faces on the Envelope

**🧰 You need:** 1 envelope or the back of a cereal box · 1 marker.

Draw five faces in a row along the envelope, left to right. The first one is
grinning, the last one is crying, and the three in between move between them.
Number them one to five underneath and give her nothing else to do with it
than point.

Ask her once, then leave the envelope propped on the arm of the sofa where her
hand falls. Ask again after the rest block and once more before dinner, and
write the number and the time along the bottom edge each time. She points at
the crying face for the first three hours and that is your answer, not an
exaggeration. Anything she says on top of the pointing goes on the envelope
too, in her words.

### 😴 The Rest Block: The Hours That Do the Work

This is the center of the day and the only part of it that matters. Blinds
down, big light off, fan on low pointing across the room rather than at her,
one thin blanket within reach so she can push it off. Sit where she can see
you, with your hand on her back if she wants it there and off her if she does
not.

She may sleep for three hours. She may lie there awake and blank for two.
Both count, and neither one needs improving. Keep the drink topped up and
within reach, and resist filling the quiet with anything at all. A sick
three-year-old asleep on a sofa in a cool room is the entire plan working.

### 📚 Before the Afternoon Dip: The Slow Story She Finishes

Pick the book she has heard four hundred times, sit her across your lap, and
read it at half speed. Stop before the last word of every line and wait. She
supplies it with her eyes shut, which costs her nothing and gives her
something to be good at on a day when she has been good at nothing.

If she has no voice left in her, read the whole thing yourself and let the
waiting go. Two books like that, then the drink again.

### 🎯 Four Things That Work Lying Down
- Naming everything she can see from where her head is, ceiling first.
- One hand in a bowl of cool water on a towel on your lap.
- Your phone on the arm of the sofa, playing the songs she picks.
- A cold washcloth over her forehead, taken off and put back by her.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

He is 14 months, he walks, and he will climb onto the sofa and onto her within
the first ten minutes. If there is anybody who can take him for a few hours,
today is the day to ask, and ask early rather than at two o'clock when you are
out of road.

If he stays, give him the far end of the room with a laundry basket of safe
things to fill and tip out, and rotate him through the yard door for short
stretches while she sleeps. Keep her cup, her spoon and her washcloth separate
from his and wash your hands between them. He will come and pat her, and one
pat is fine. Standing on her is not, and he cannot tell the difference, so
that one is on you.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A scale with pictures lets her rate something she can't measure.**
> Ask a three-year-old how she feels and you get *bad*, or nothing, or a word
> she once heard you use about yourself. She has the sensation and no way to
> size it. Five faces on an envelope hand her a ruler she can point at, and
> pointing costs her nothing on a day when talking is work. You get something
> you can compare: the face at eleven against the face at three tells you which
> way the morning went, and it beats your own read of her. Hospitals give
> children the same tool for the same reason. Ask three times, write the number
> down, and she starts reaching for the envelope herself.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** August dehydration moves fast in a child who is not drinking.
> Call your doctor the same day if she has not passed urine in eight hours, has
> no tears when she cries, has a dry mouth or sunken eyes, or is hard to rouse.
> Call straight away for a rash that does not fade when you press a glass
> against it, breathing that is fast or labored, a stiff neck, a fever in
> anyone under three months, a fever over three days, or a seizure. Small
> frequent sips beat a full cup she refuses. Cool the room rather than the
> child; no cold baths and no rubbing alcohol. Check the ingredients on any two
> medicines before you give both, because doubling the same one is the common
> accident.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="aug-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Better and Bored

The mend day, and the harder one. The fever broke overnight, she has decided
she is fine, and she is wrong. She has no stamina, no patience and a whole day
to spend. Everything on this page is done on a lap, on a sofa or with one
hand, and it can all be walked away from. There is still a rest block, and
today it is the part she argues about.

### 🌙 Before She Comes Down
> Freeze a cup of water solid overnight, so the ice comes out as one block too big to fit in a mouth. Stand a tray, a shallow bowl and a dish towel by the sofa, and put the fan on the far side of the room.

### 🕗 The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes.** Bigger breakfast than yesterday, and let her ask for it rather than offering it.
- **The first good hour.** Take it. The ice tray on her lap, and the whole morning can be that.
- **When she starts wandering.** She is done, whatever she says. Wind it down before she falls apart.
- **After lunch.** The rest block, and it happens whether she believes in it or not.
- **The long afternoon.** The window list, drinks, and one thing she chooses.
- **Before dinner.** Bath, early bed, and tomorrow still counts as a recovery day.

### 🧊 Whenever She Wakes: The Ice That Melts in Her Hand

**🧰 You need:** 1 block of ice turned out of a cup · 1 shallow bowl · 1 tray · 1 dish towel · 1 teaspoon of salt · 2 drops of food coloring · 1 small pitcher of warm water.

Dish towel on the tray, tray on her lap, bowl in the middle, ice block in the
bowl. That is the whole setup and it is done in a minute.

She holds it until her fingers say stop, then puts it down and picks it back
up. Sprinkle a little salt on the top and leave it. Salt eats channels into
the surface, and the drops of coloring run down those channels and show her
where the block is going first. Give her the pitcher of warm water last and
let her pour it over the top, a little at a time, until there is nothing left
to hold.

If she loses interest after four minutes, that is four minutes and it cost you
one cup of water frozen overnight. Leave the tray there. She comes back to it.

### 😴 The Rest Block: The Afternoon Nobody Skips

She will tell you she is not tired. Put her on the sofa anyway with the blinds
down and the fan across the room, and set the terms low: she does not have to
sleep, she has to lie down. Take one book, read it at half speed, and stop
reading before she stops listening.

Most mend days she is asleep inside fifteen minutes. The ones where she is
not, she lies there for an hour looking at the ceiling and gets up steadier
than she went down. A day back too early buys you two more days on the sofa
later in the week, so hold this hour even when she has spent the morning
looking well.

### 🪟 The Long Afternoon: The List of Everything Out the Window

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen · the sofa nearest a window.

She lies down where she can see out. You sit with the paper. She calls out
what she can see and you write every one of them down in her words, numbered
as they come. Cars, a bird on the wire, next door's flag, the man with the
dog, a cloud shaped like something.

Read the list back at twenty. Then start a second list of what has changed
since the first one, which she will find funnier than it is. Pin both to the
fridge, because tomorrow she will want to check whether the man with the dog
comes past at the same time.

### 🎯 Four Things She Can Do From the Sofa
- Sorting a bowl of clean socks into pairs on her stomach.
- A flashlight and the ceiling, with the blinds down.
- Telling you what to draw while you hold the paper up.
- One tray of dry crackers she is allowed to eat crumb by crumb.

### 👶 Where Kreston Goes

He is 14 months and next in line for this by the look of it, so today is
about keeping the two of them apart without leaving either one alone. Set him
up on the floor within sight of the sofa rather than on it: he stacks two
blocks, he tips out anything you fill, and a basket and six safe things buys
twenty minutes at a stretch.

Cups, spoons and towels stay separate and go straight in the wash. He will
want on that sofa and he will want whatever she is holding, so give him his
own version of it, a dry bowl and a spoon while she has the ice, and keep the
melt tray up on the table between turns. He gets his own quiet hour at the
same time as hers, and you get twenty minutes.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Cold is easier to investigate than hot, because she can hold it.**
> Heat comes to Azlyn as a rule rather than a material. The stove is hot, the
> concrete is hot, and every sentence she has heard about either one ends in *do
> not touch*. Cold she gets to hold. A block of ice in a bowl on her lap
> answers her, changes while she works on it, numbs her fingers until she puts
> it down, and asks nothing of her. She can push it, drip warm water over it
> and watch salt cut a channel through it. Half her idea of temperature gets
> built out of the half she is allowed to handle, which is why a bowl of ice on
> a bad afternoon does more than a talk about hot.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Freeze the ice in a cup so it turns out as one block too big
> to fit in a mouth. Loose cubes are a choking hazard for both of them, and
> Kreston at 14 months will take one off a tray at his own height in seconds,
> so the tray goes up on the table the moment she puts it down. Salted ice gets
> cold enough to hurt bare skin held against it, so let her put it down when
> she wants to and keep the block off her stomach and out of her mouth. Keep
> pushing fluids today; a child who feels better and stops drinking is the one
> who ends up back on the sofa. Send her back to normal food and normal running
> about a day later than she asks.

## 🎲 August — Extra Ideas

> *One line each, no steps. For the morning you open the book with ten minutes
> and no plan, or the afternoon the heat took the whole thing apart.*

### 🎲 Alternative Activities

- **The Cicada Shell Hunt**, along tree trunks and fence posts at her head height, lined up on a plate at the end.
- **The Fridge Picnic**, everything cold in there on one tray, eaten sitting on the kitchen floor.
- **Half a Lemon Each**, squeezed by hand into cold water with as much sugar as she argues for.
- **The Bug Under the Glass**, a clean jar set over something on the path, a good look, then a lift and a wave.
- **Breakfast Outside at Seven**, the table carried out while the concrete is still cool and nobody has dressed.
- **The Basket of Warm Laundry**, tipped onto the floor for her to find every pair in it.
- **Reading in the Bathtub**, an inch of cool water, no soap, two books that can take a splash.
- **The Nap Under the Table**, pillows pushed underneath and the fan pointed at the gap.
- **Counting the Cars by Color**, from the shaded step, one tally mark each on the back of an envelope.
- **The Long Grass Barefoot**, shoes off on the shaded lawn at six, naming what her feet find.
- **The Cold Bag Race**, unpacking the groceries with the freezer things put away first and fast.

### 🎨 Alternative Arts & Crafts

- **Sun Prints on Colored Paper**, leaves laid out on a sunny sill and lifted two days later to find their shadows.
- **The Paper Bag Sun Hat**, folded, taped to fit her head and drawn all over.
- **Sidewalk Paint**, cornstarch, water and food coloring in muffin cups, brushed on thick and hosed off at five.
- **The Corn Husk Doll**, husks off the cobs from dinner, twisted and tied with yarn.
- **The Torn Paper Sunset**, magazine strips torn along their length and glued down in bands.
- **Seed Mosaic on a Paper Plate**, melon and sunflower seeds saved from the week and glued in rings.
- **The Pressed Flower Card**, whatever is out in the yard flattened under the heaviest book in the house.
- **Flyswatter Painting**, a spoonful of paint on a tray, one clean swatter and a sheet taped to the fence.
- **The Foil Sun Catcher**, a strip of foil scrunched and smoothed again, hung where the light hits it.
- **Chalk Dust on Wet Paper**, a sheet soaked in the sink and chalk dragged across it while it drips.
- **The Cicada Shells on a Card**, the morning's finds glued in a row with a word from her under each one.

### 👶 Kreston's Turn

- **Two Blocks and a Wait**, one stack built for him, the second block handed over, and nothing said.
- **The Fat Crayon and the Taped Sheet**, a big page taped flat to the floor so his whole arm can work.
- **Six Cold Things in a Basket**, wide jar lids and metal spoons out of the fridge, handed to him one at a time.
- **His Three Words Back**, whichever ones he uses today repeated to him inside a whole sentence.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Standing and open water**: the Labor Day dishpans, the mud bucket on the 11th, the water run buckets on the 14th, the chalk bucket on the 23rd, the fence bucket on the 30th, the pond on the 19th and the 27th. Kreston can drown in two inches, so tip each container out as the activity ends and hold him at the pond and the pool.
- **Small parts**: the six wrapped parcels on the 3rd, the six objects buried in soil on the 11th, the dyed pasta on the 22nd, the buckeyes on the 23rd and the 26th, the letter cards on the 29th. He runs now and mouths what he reaches, so count them out and count them back in.
- **String and cord**: the mail bag strap on the 3rd, the lantern handle on the 5th, the pasta necklace on the 22nd, the jump rope curved into letters on the 25th, the three tied parcels on the 30th. A loop at his height is a strangulation risk, so take it down the moment the activity ends.
- **Curbs and traffic**: the driveway crossing on the 4th, the three curbside stops on the 15th, the chalk name path on the 24th, the street sign hunt on the 29th. Keep yourself between both children and the road, with Kreston on a hand or in the stroller with the brake on.
- **Adult-only steps**: the knife that carves the potato stamps on the 8th and the 22nd, the stapler on the finds book on the 15th, the sharp knife on the eating tile on the 20th, the craft knife on the throwing box on the 26th, adult scissors on most days, the oven on the 30th. Each one goes back to your hand or a high shelf between uses.
- **September specific**: the first two weeks run hot, so hat on and cream before the door opens, again at eleven. Wasps come for anything sweet outdoors on the 14th, and after the equinox on the 23rd the park light goes at seven.

## Week 36: Community Helpers 🚚
**📅 September 3 – September 9, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

Every day this week hands Azlyn a job that somebody in your town does for a
living. She carries a mail route in a bag on her shoulder, draws the street
from above and walks the map she drew, works a half-hour night shift by
flashlight, and runs a lending library off the bottom shelf. Each job turns up
with its own kit (a bag, a sign, a badge, a stamp), and the kit is what makes
her believe in the work. Friday's bag comes back off the hook on Thursday,
loaded with six cards for the six helpers she marked on Saturday's map.

Labor Day lands on Monday and gets a light touch. The morning washes the
summer off the buckets and shuts them in a crate for the year, then Azlyn
makes a picnic for the people who work in this house, serves it, and no adult
gets up for an hour. Tuesday comes in hot, so that day bends around the heat:
cold experiments in the morning, swimming at half past two, the middle of the
day indoors.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **Carrying a load and adjusting it.** Six parcels bend her sideways, and she takes one out at a time until she can walk the whole hall upright.
- **Matching a number to a place.** Every parcel gets a number from 1 to 6, and one of the six houses down the hallway is the one that takes it.
- **Reading a map she drew herself.** Six helpers placed in relation to home, then copied onto one sheet small enough to carry and walked with a crayon in her hand.
- **Sorting into categories she names.** Every book in the house into four piles, labeled, shelved, and issued to you on a card she stamps.
- **Testing one thing at a time.** Frozen washcloth, cold bowl, card fan, shade, cold drink, run one after another so she can tell you which one worked.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Carrying her own pack changes the walk
- A map is a shift from being *in* a space to seeing it from above
- Breaking the routine deliberately makes a memory
- Endings need marking, and packing up does it
- In serious heat, the physical problem comes before the behavior problem
- Cozy is a real regulatory state rather than a mood
- Being ill in summer is worse psychologically, and that's worth acknowledging

---

## 🌟 Day 246: The Bag on Her Shoulder 🌟
**📅 Friday, September 3, 2027**
**Theme:** Community Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put the grocery bag, the old belt, newspaper, packing tape and the marker on the kitchen table, and clear a space beside them for the six things she picks in the morning.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: What Goes Out Today
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Bag That Holds the Whole Round (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Card That Arrives After She Does (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Depot in the Hallway (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Delivering the Bread to the Table
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Parcels, Unwrapped Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath, Then the Bag Packed for Tomorrow
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: What Goes Out Today

**🧰 You need:** newspaper · packing tape · 1 permanent marker · the 6 small things from the table.

1. Six things on the table, each small enough for one hand: soap, a spoon, a hairbrush, a ball of socks. She picks them.
2. She wraps each one in a sheet of newspaper while you hold the tape. Lumpy is the correct shape for a parcel.
3. Number them **1** to **6** in marker, big enough to read from standing. All six have to be somewhere else by tonight.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Bag That Holds the Whole Round

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 sturdy paper grocery bag with handles, or a cloth tote
- 1 old belt, a bathrobe cord or 3 feet of thick string
- Packing tape
- 1 permanent marker
- The six wrapped parcels from 8:00
- Newspaper, 4 or 5 sheets
- Kitchen scales, if you have them

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape the bag's base inside and out, and a strip round the top edge. Six parcels tear a paper bag out of its own bottom.
2. Thread the belt through both handles and buckle it, or knot the cord. Shorten it until the bag sits at her hip, then tape the crossing so it stops sliding.
3. She writes **MAIL** and her name on the side in marker.
4. Load all six and send her down the hall and back. Watch the shoulder drop and the lean come on.
5. Take one out and go again, until she walks the whole hall upright without stopping. Count what is left in.
6. Scrunch newspaper into the gap so the load stops swinging, weigh the bag on the scales, and write the number on the tape.

> 💡 **Tip:** She will stagger and refuse to take anything out. Let the walk fail twice before you suggest it. The number she reaches herself is the one she believes.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Card That Arrives After She Does

Draw a card and address it to Azlyn at your own house, her name in full, then
walk it to the blue collection box. September mornings still take bare arms and
the hedges are full of blackberries, so allow a stop. Read her the collection
times off the little door. The card lands on your own doorstep on Tuesday,
because Monday is a day off for the people who carry it, and she has to wait for
it.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and carries things while he
> walks, which is most of what he wants to do. Roll a dish towel, tape it into a
> parcel too big for his mouth, and hold your hand out for it. He brings it, you
> take it, he brings it again. Say **mail** each time it lands in your palm.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Depot in the Hallway

Six houses go down the hallway after lunch, and every parcel carries a number
that has to match one of them.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 shoeboxes or box lids
- 1 laundry basket
- 3 feet of string to pull the basket
- 1 roll masking tape for the roads
- Chalk
- 1 permanent marker
- The wrapped parcels
- A few of her toys as extra cargo

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Two strips of masking tape down the hall, a basket's width apart. That is the road, and the basket stays inside it.
2. Set the six boxes along one side, open ends to the road. She chalks a number on each, and you leave her backwards sixes alone.
3. Tie the string to the basket handle, knotted short so nothing trails. The basket is the truck and she drives it.
4. She reads the number on a parcel, drives to the house wearing it, posts it through. Wrong house happens. Let the householder complain.
5. Her toys go on as second-round cargo, each with a numbered strip of tape stuck to it in marker.
6. Run the round backwards: empty basket down the hall, collecting from every house with something to send.
7. Park the truck. She counts what came home.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her one depot rule and hold to it. Nothing leaves without a number on it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Three houses and three parcels, on the kitchen floor.
- Drop everything through the real mail slot from outside.
- Sort the parcels by size, then by weight, and stop there.
- Load the stroller and do the round around the yard.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A friend's house**, and the bag goes with her, loaded with something for whoever lives there
- The café with the window seat, watching for anybody working outside
- A walk past the collection box to see whether the pickup has been
- Grandparents, and she delivers the parcels a second time
- The road crew at the end of the street, and ten minutes watching over the fence

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He wants the basket. At 14 months in and out is
> the whole game, so give him a box of his own at the far end of the hall and
> two rolled dish towels to fill it with. He empties it and fills it again. The
> six numbered parcels stay on her round.

### 🌍 Around the World: Feeding the Workers Everywhere 🍱

Getting a hot lunch to somebody at work is a job in itself. In Mumbai,
**dabbawalas** collect stacked tin lunchboxes from home kitchens each morning
and carry them across the city by bicycle and train. Sweden stops work twice a
day for **fika**, coffee and a bun with everyone at the same table. A Japanese
**bento** packs a whole meal into compartments small enough to carry onto a
building site.

> **✨ Try it:** Stack her lunch instead of plating it. Two lidded tubs, one on
> the other, pasta below and something on top, tied in a dish towel and carried
> to whoever is working today.

> *Did you know?* Mumbai's dabbawalas move around 200,000 lunches a day and
> lose almost none of them.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Carrying her own pack changes the walk.**
> Azlyn will ask to be carried on an empty walk and cover half a mile with a
> loaded bag on her shoulder. A load hands her a job, and a job keeps a
> three-year-old moving, because the walk now has a point that belongs to her.
> Weight through her shoulders and back sends steady information about where
> her body is, and that settles her more than talk does. Keep the bag under a
> tenth of what she weighs, about three pounds, and let her load it herself.
> Parcels going to somebody else beat a bag of her own toys, every time.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The bag strap. Keep it short enough that it cannot go over
> Kreston's head at 14 months, and take it off her before she climbs anything.
> The six numbered parcels are choke-size for him and they look like food, so
> they stay in her bag or in your hand and get counted back in before he is down
> on the floor. What he carries is a rolled dish towel, wider than his fist, and
> it comes back to your hand every time. Untie the string from the basket the
> moment the round finishes.
> September sun still burns on a walk with no shade: hat on, cream at eight,
> cream again at eleven.

## 🌟 Day 247: The Street From Above 🌟
**📅 Saturday, September 4, 2027**
**Theme:** Community Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Trim two or three boxes square and leave them flat on the living room floor with the masking tape beside them, and cut one big circle from a spare box lid using a dinner plate as a guide.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Looking Down From the Top Step
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Town Seen From Above (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Map on the Clipboard (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Crossing She Runs Herself (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Putting the Shopping Where It Lives
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Driving the Map
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Map Spread on the Floor
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Looking Down From the Top Step

**🧰 You need:** the stairs · 2 toy cars · paper · crayons.

1. Park the two cars at the bottom of the stairs and lie down beside them with her.
2. Go up and sit on the top step together. Same cars, and now she sees their roofs.
3. Hand her paper and a crayon up there and ask her to draw the cars from where she sits. Two rectangles is a right answer.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Town Seen From Above

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The 2–3 trimmed cardboard sheets from last night, or 6 feet of butcher paper
- 1 roll masking tape
- Crayons and 2 thick markers
- 1 sheet of paper for the walking copy
- 1 clipboard, or a hardback book to lean on
- Small toy cars
- Sticky labels, or card scraps and tape
- 1 pair of scissors (**adult only**)

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape the sheets into one big sheet she can sit in the middle of. She holds each seam flat while you run the tape along it.
2. Ask where our house goes. She draws it there in marker, then tape the roads on: the road outside, a strip running to the store, junctions where she says there are junctions.
3. Mark the helpers: mailbox, store, fire station, doctor, the garbage truck stop by the house, the school crossing. A sticky label or a taped card scrap each, her drawing, your writing.
4. Crayon the garbage truck's route along the roads it takes past the house, with a cross at every stop.
5. Copy the six helpers onto the sheet of paper with the house in the middle. That is the walking copy, it goes on the clipboard, and the big one stays on the floor.
6. Hand her the cars. She drives the big map and tells you where she is going.

> 💡 **Tip:** The distances will be wrong and the store will end up beside the fire station. Leave it. She places things in relation to home.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Map on the Clipboard

Take the walking copy out and walk the streets it covers, warm enough on the
first Saturday in September to go slow. It sits on the clipboard and she holds
it herself. At every place she marked, stand in front of the real one and let
her put a crayon cross on the paper. Turn the clipboard with her at the
corners.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 14 months and scribbles with a whole
> fist. Give him one crayon and the far corner of the map, and let whatever he
> puts there stay on it. He works flat on his belly longer than he works
> sitting up. Azlyn will name his marks as something within a day.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Crossing She Runs Herself

The crossing goes on the driveway after lunch and she works it. Everybody else
does as they are told.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Thick chalk
- 1 large cardboard circle, cut last night
- 1 wrapping paper tube, or a wooden spoon
- Red, yellow and green paper, or paint
- Packing tape
- Toy cars
- The stroller or a ride-on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Chalk the crossing across the top of the driveway, well in from the street: six fat bars, her width apart, with a waiting box at each end. She draws, you keep the line straight.
2. Tape red paper to one face of the circle, green to the other, then tape the circle to the tube, right round the join. Finger paint it instead if you would rather.
3. Tape a small yellow circle to the tube below the sign. Yellow means get ready, and she decides what counts as ready.
4. Push the toy cars along a chalked road towards the crossing and let her stop them with the red face.
5. Then real traffic: you with the stroller, Kreston on a hand, anybody else in the house. She holds it up and everybody obeys.
6. Swap. You take the sign, she takes the stroller, and now she watches for the color instead of showing it.
7. Sign indoors at the end, and the crossing goes onto the big map. She crayons six fat bars across the road beside the label she made this morning, so it is on the map as well as the driveway.

> 💡 **Tip:** Obey her the first ten times with no commentary. A sign held up by a small person still stops a grown-up.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Chalk the crossing and skip the sign.
- Drive the toy cars over the morning's map instead.
- Chalk a parking lot and park everything with wheels in it.
- Chalk round her shadow at the crossing, and again before dinner.

### 🌳 Out Again: **The Museum**
- **The museum**, first Saturday of the month, hunting anything seen from above: a model village, an aerial photograph, a floor plan
- The upstairs window of the library, if yours has one over the street
- A footbridge over a road or a railroad
- The park, and up whatever she can climb to look down from
- The top floor of a parking garage, and the streets laid out below

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Twenty minutes on his own feet in the museum
> beats an hour in the carrier. At 14 months he stacks two blocks and he will
> find the one interactive drawer on the ground floor and open it forty times.
> Carry him past anything roped off.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A map is a shift from being *in* a space to seeing it from above.**
> Azlyn has spent three years inside the street at knee height, learning it as
> a sequence of things she goes past. A map asks her to float above the lot and
> see it at once, and that change is one of the harder pieces of thinking
> available to her this year. She gets the landmarks long before the layout. The
> mailbox goes on the map because she remembers posting something, while the
> distances stay wrong for years yet. Hold the paper the way you are walking and
> turn it as you turn corners, and she keeps the two versions of the street
> attached.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The crossing goes on the driveway, the path or the yard, never
> on a road, and say that out loud before the chalk comes out. A three-year-old
> carries the game to wherever she last played it. Work the top end of the
> driveway, keep yourself between both children and the street, and put Kreston
> on a hand or in the stroller with the brake on from the moment the door opens,
> because a car reversing out of a driveway sees neither of them. The sign sits
> at Kreston's face height, so keep a hand on the tube while she waves it. The
> walking map takes you out at eleven with no shade on the route: hat on, cream
> at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

## 🌟 Day 248: The Night Shift 🌟
**📅 Sunday, September 5, 2027**
**Theme:** Community Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put fresh batteries in both flashlights and test them, fold two or three blankets by the window, and stand the basket of unmatched socks beside them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Who Is Awake While She Sleeps
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Working by Flashlight (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Every Streetlight on the Way to the Corner (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Jar Lantern for After Dinner (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Water Pitcher on the Table
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Lantern Beside Her on the Floor
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Pajamas On, Then Out the Door
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Who Is Awake While She Sleeps

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · crayons.

1. Tell her the true version of three in the morning here: everyone asleep, street empty, one car going past. Then ask who was awake somewhere else.
2. Write her list down the page word for word. Bakers, nurses, the man who drives the big truck, a cat.
3. She draws one of them at the bottom. The list stays on the table, because you need it at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Working by Flashlight

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 flashlights with fresh batteries
- 2–3 blankets or towels for the windows
- 1 basket of unmatched socks
- Silverware for the table
- 1 lidded cup of water for Kreston
- 1 alarm clock or a kitchen timer
- Her list from 8:00

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Blankets over the curtain rail or wedged into the frame, every light off, doors shut. Half past nine, and the room needs a flashlight.
2. Set the alarm clock for thirty minutes. That is the shift, and it ends when the bell goes.
3. One flashlight each. She can point hers anywhere she likes for the first two minutes.
4. Four jobs off her list by flashlight: match the sock basket, lay the silverware, find one red thing, carry Kreston's water through.
5. Sock matching is the hard one in the dark. Let two pairs go wrong and let her find out when the blankets come down.
6. At the bell, pull the blankets off together. Ask which job the dark made harder.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say the shift ends at the bell, then hold to it even if she is enjoying herself.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Every Streetlight on the Way to the Corner

Walk to the corner and back counting streetlights, stopping at each one long
enough for her to touch the post. They are all off in warm September daylight.
Ask who switches them on and let her theory stand. Count the row again on the
way home, because you walk this stretch after dinner with a lantern.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** **Kreston turns 15 months today.** In the dark room
> this morning, put your flashlight spot on the wall and move it slow. He points
> at pictures in books at this age, and he will point at the spot and chase it.
> Say happy fifteen months out loud, because nobody else will.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Jar Lantern for After Dinner

The lantern has to be dry and lit by seven, so it gets built at one and left in
a warm window while you are out.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 clean glass jar, no lid
- Tissue paper or parchment paper
- Flour-and-water paste, 3 tbsp of each
- 1 small bowl for the paste
- 1 brush
- 20 inches of string
- 1 battery tealight (a small flashlight does the same job)
- 1 small bag for the late walk
- 1 lidded cup and a drink for the walk

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Mix the flour and water in the small bowl until it looks like thin custard. She stirs, and it wants to be smooth.
2. She tears the tissue into palm-sized pieces. A torn edge lies flatter on the curve than a cut one.
3. Paste the jar with the brush, press the pieces on, then paste over the top. Two overlapping layers, and leave the rim bare.
4. Tie the string round the neck under the rim, both ends knotted into a short handle. Test the knot over the table.
5. Stand it on a warm windowsill and leave it there while you are out.
6. After dinner, drop the battery tealight in and turn the kitchen light off.
7. Pack the small bag for the walk: the second flashlight and something to drink. She carries the bag, an adult carries the lantern.

> 💡 **Tip:** Pajamas, shoes and out of the front door at seven is the part she tells people about. The whole thing takes fifteen minutes.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Flashlight under a blanket with two books and nothing else.
- A paper bag lantern with a flashlight inside, no paste.
- Draw the night shift: a nurse, a baker and a driver.
- Shadow puppets on the wall with the flashlight and her two hands.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The sunset walk, scouted early**, the route you take again at dusk, so she knows what is coming
- The duck pond, counting how many are settling for the night
- A slow walk with the stroller while Kreston runs the flat bits
- The playground while the light is still high
- The scooter along the flat stretch, so her legs are used before the late walk

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He is 15 months today and he runs, so the late
> walk has him in the stroller or on a hand from the front door onward. Give him
> his own flashlight in the stroller and let him switch it on and off the whole
> way. He will sleep on the way home.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Breaking the routine deliberately makes a memory.**
> Azlyn's days run on a shape she knows by heart, and a day that matches
> yesterday leaves nothing behind. Blankets over the windows at half past nine,
> dinner before a walk, out of the front door in pajamas: her brain marks the
> events that break the pattern and files them whole, while the ordinary ones
> blur into one average day. She will bring this Sunday up in November and
> remember none of last Tuesday. You need three or four of these a year, no
> more, and this one costs a flashlight, two blankets and one rule broken in
> front of her.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** No candle and no flame in the jar at any point, battery light
> or flashlight only. Azlyn wears something pale on the late walk and holds a
> hand at every curb, with you on the road side of her and Kreston in the
> stroller or on a hand from the front door onward. The jar stays on the floor,
> not in her
> hand on the stairs, and the string handle comes off it before it goes near
> Kreston. The streetlight walk runs in open September sun: hat on, cream at
> eight, cream again at eleven.

## 🌟 Day 249: Packing Up the Summer 🌟
**📅 Monday, September 6, 2027**
**Theme:** Community Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the empty crate by the back door with the nail brush and the dish soap, and put two old towels where you can reach them without crossing the house wet.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Everything That Lived Outside All Summer
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Washing the Summer Off Everything (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Emptying the Pool Onto the Flower Bed (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Day Off Picnic (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Shaking Out the Picnic Blanket
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Last of the Chalk
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Warm Bath After a Wet Day
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Everything That Lived Outside All Summer

**🧰 You need:** the yard · 1 empty crate or big box · her.

1. Send her round the yard for everything that has been out there since June. Buckets, spades, water pistols, the chalk tub, one shoe.
2. Pile it on the patio in front of the crate. Say out loud that this is the last day it lives outside.
3. Ask which one she used most. That one goes on top, because it gets washed first at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Washing the Summer Off Everything

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 dishpans
- Warm water and dish soap
- 2 old towels
- 1 nail brush or sponge
- 1 lidded crate or a big box
- 1 permanent marker for the label
- The summer pile from 8:00

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Two bowls on the patio, a stride apart. One warm and soapy, one plain for rinsing. She fills the second and carries it.
2. She washes with the nail brush and you take anything with mud welded on.
3. Rinse in the second bowl and stand each thing upside down on the first towel in the sun to drain.
4. Dry with the second towel and load the crate. She decides the order, and the biggest thing will go in last.
5. Write **SUMMER** and the year on the lid in marker. She adds her own mark beside it.
6. Tip both bowls over the grass the moment the last thing is dry, and let her carry them back in empty.

> 💡 **Tip:** Warm water, not hot, and give her twenty minutes of it before you press on with the crate.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Emptying the Pool Onto the Flower Bed

The kiddie pool goes today. Tip it a little at a time so she can see where
the water runs, then aim the rest at the flower bed and the pot by the door,
because it has been dry since August. She scrubs the inside with the same nail
brush, and it gets folded onto the crate. Say goodbye to it out loud. She will
want to.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 15 months and runs, and the words that
> hold him are the ones he is doing: **wet**, **wash**, **gone**. Give him his
> own small bowl with two inches of water and a spade in it, on the grass
> beside you. He tips it over himself within four minutes.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Day Off Picnic

Labor Day gives the people who work a day off. Azlyn makes lunch for the
workers in this house, and then nobody does a job for an hour.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Bread, butter and 2–3 fillings
- 1 butter knife
- Plates and a tray
- 1 blanket
- 1 pitcher of juice and cups
- Paper and crayons for the menu
- Fruit she can cut herself

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tell her what today is in one sentence: everybody who works gets a day off, and that includes this house.
2. Menu first. She draws what is on offer and you write the words underneath in her order, spelling and all.
3. She butters the bread with the butter knife. Torn slices go on her own plate, which she will decide is fair.
4. Fillings on, tops on, and she cuts each round into halves. Aim for a wonky diagonal and praise it.
5. Fruit next: banana, strawberries, a soft pear, all of it cut by her with the same knife.
6. Load the tray. Plates, the pitcher of juice, a cup for everybody eating.
7. Blanket down on the grass or the living room floor. She serves, everybody sits, and no adult gets up for an hour. She will check.

> 💡 **Tip:** Take the hour as written. Lie down on the blanket and leave the phone in the house.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Menu only, and a picnic of whatever is in the fridge.
- Eat lunch on the floor with no plates at all.
- Deliver a sandwich to a neighbor who is working today.
- Blanket, cushions and a pile of books, and call that the day off.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The green space with a ball**, busier than usual with everybody off for Labor Day
- The riverside path, counting the people out who would be at work
- The playground, late enough that the heat has come off it
- A slow walk with the stroller and nothing to achieve
- The yard with the sprinkler on for the last time this year

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At 15 months he spoons food into his own mouth
> and gets about half of it there. A picnic blanket is the best floor for that.
> Give him his own plate and a spoon and let the rate of loss go unremarked.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Endings need marking, and packing up does it.**
> Summer ends for Azlyn the moment somebody tells her it has, and a sentence is
> thin evidence. Washing the buckets, drying them and shutting the lid hands
> her the ending in a form she can hold: the things went away, she put them
> there, the season is behind the lid. Three-year-olds run on episodes rather
> than calendars, and a small ceremony at the close of one lets her file it.
> She may want the crate open again on Thursday. Open it. The marking has done
> its work either way, and next March she will remember the day it came back
> out.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Standing water. Kreston is 15 months and runs, and a dishpan on
> the ground holds enough to drown in. Tip the bowls and the pool out the moment
> you are done with them, and stay within arm's reach of him the whole time
> water is out. A wet patio is slick under her feet, so the
> carrying happens at a walk. The morning runs outdoors start to finish, so hat
> on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

## 🌟 Day 250: Working in the Heat 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, September 7, 2027**
**Theme:** Community Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Soak two washcloths, wring them out, fold them flat and put them in the freezer, and fill an ice cube tray. Swim bag by the door.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Washcloths in the Freezer
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Which One Cools Her Down Fastest (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Hand on the Path, Hand on the Grass (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Jacket You Can See From a Long Way Off (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Ice in Everybody's Glass
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Setting the Cones Out Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Coolest Room in the House, With Books
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Washcloths in the Freezer

**🧰 You need:** the 2 frozen washcloths · 1 plate.

1. Open the freezer and let her take both washcloths out. Stiff as boards, and she has not met that before.
2. One on a plate on the table to thaw where she can watch it, one back in for 9:15.
3. Ask her to name every way she knows of getting cooler. Take the list as it comes, then open the windows on the shady side.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Which One Cools Her Down Fastest

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 washcloth, still frozen from last night
- 1 dishpan of cold water
- Ice cubes
- 2 pieces of thick card for fans
- 1 pitcher of water and cups
- Paper and a marker for the chart
- Chalk

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Chart first. Five rows down the paper, and she draws at the head of each: washcloth, bowl, fan, fence, cup.
2. The frozen washcloth on the back of her neck for a count of twenty, then one foot, then the other. One washcloth, three places, and she says which one she felt first.
3. Bowl of cold water on the patio with a handful of ice cubes in. Both feet in, twenty seconds, out.
4. A piece of card each. She fans your face and you fan hers.
5. Out to the shade by the fence with nothing in her hands. Chalk round the edge of the shade while she stands in it.
6. Back into the sun for the last one, a cold cup out of the pitcher, drunk where the sun is. Then to the chart, and she marks her winner in marker, any shape she likes.

> 💡 **Tip:** Run these one at a time with a gap between. Do them together and she cannot tell which one worked.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Hand on the Path, Hand on the Grass

Out before eleven and back before the heat sets in. Flat palm on the paving
slab in the sun, then on the grass a step away, then the metal gate and the
wooden fence. Same sunshine, four answers, and she will not believe the gate
until she touches it. Walk the shadiest route home and let her pick the shade
at every corner.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 15 months and runs, which makes him
> hotter than her and less able to say so. Hat on, water offered every fifteen
> minutes whether or not he asks, and no bare feet on the paving. Hand him the
> thawing washcloth off the plate for two seconds, cool rather than stinging,
> and watch his face do the whole report.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Jacket You Can See From a Long Way Off

Every helper she has watched this week wears one. Hers comes out of a carrier
bag, and the whole job happens at the table and on the hall floor, because the
hall is the coolest strip of the house at one o'clock.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 yellow or orange grocery bag, or an old adult t-shirt
- Kitchen foil, or silver packing tape
- 1 pair of scissors (**adult only**)
- Masking tape
- 6 paper cups for cones
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 piece of card for the sign
- The stroller or a ride-on

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the bag flat on the table, cut the base seam open, then cut a slit down the middle of one face so it does up like a jacket.
2. Cut an armhole out of each side, high up. Hold it against her shoulders first and cut small.
3. She tries it on, and masking tape takes in the shoulders wherever it gapes. It comes straight back off, because sealed plastic holds heat.
4. Tear the foil into four strips as long as her arm. Two across the chest, two across the back, taped at both ends.
5. She draws on the card, you write **STOP** in letters she can copy, and it stays in her hand.
6. Six paper cups upside down along the hallway are the cones. She draws a stripe round each one in marker and sets them out in a line.
7. Jacket on, and she closes a lane on the hall floor. Everybody who comes past gets stopped, held and waved on, and the stroller goes through the gap she leaves. The cones go out onto the path at quarter past four, when the heat has come off it.

> 💡 **Tip:** A grocery bag holds heat like a greenhouse, so the jacket goes on for the lane and comes off between jobs. Foil beats a drawn silver stripe because it flashes when she moves, and dusk is when she gets to see that.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Cones only, six cups down the hall and the ride-on round them.
- Tape foil strips to a t-shirt she owns and skip the cutting.
- Badge and sign only, and she works the kitchen doorway.
- Write **STOP** in outline and let her fill the letters in with crayon.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one, and the best place to be at half past two in September heat
- The shallow end and nothing else, if the pool is packed
- A splash pad or the kiddie pool at home, if the pool is shut
- The shady half of the park, and home before four
- A cold drink somewhere with air conditioning, if she is done in by three

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Twenty minutes in the water is plenty at 15
> months, and he will be cold before he looks it. He runs on the poolside now,
> so keep a hand on him out there. Hold him facing you for the first minute in,
> then let him kick.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **In serious heat, the physical problem comes before the behavior problem.**
> A hot afternoon produces a version of Azlyn nobody can reason with, and the
> heat arrives before the tantrum does. Small bodies carry more skin for their
> size, start sweating later than yours, and warm up three to five times
> faster. Watch for the flushed, floppy, gone-quiet child rather than the loud
> one, because quiet is the one that matters. Fluid goes in before she asks for
> it, since thirst turns up once she is already short. Meet the body first with
> a cold drink, a wet washcloth and shade, then find out what the argument was
> about. Half of it will have gone.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** September heat. Cream on both of them before the door opens,
> and again before the pool: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.
> Paving, metal slides and buckle clasps burn small hands at these temperatures,
> so test each one with the back of your hand first, and if you cannot hold it
> there it comes off bare feet and bare hands. Fluid into both of them early,
> and keep the middle of the day indoors. The
> jacket is sealed plastic and holds heat against her, so it comes off between
> jobs and never goes on outdoors before four. The scissors stay with you.
