### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Well in the Flour

**🧰 You need:** the measured flour · 3 eggs · a clear table or a big board.

1. Tip the flour into one heap in the middle of the table and let her flatten the top with her palm.
2. She pushes a fist down through the middle, then walks her fingers round the inside until the walls stand up on their own.
3. Crack the eggs into her well one at a time while she watches for a leak. Leave it standing there until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Hand-Cut Noodles

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 1/3 cups all-purpose flour (300 g)
- 3 eggs, or 2/3 cup warm water (150 ml)
- Extra flour for the board
- 1 rolling pin, or a clean bottle
- 1 butter knife
- 1 clean chair back or a coat hanger for drying
- 2 dish towels
- 1 baking tray

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She breaks the yolks with two fingers and pulls flour in from the walls until the middle turns to paste and then to a lump.
2. Knead in turns for ten minutes: heel of the hand, push, fold, quarter turn. Hers is a squash rather than a push. Rest the ball under a dish towel.
3. Flour the board hard and roll it out with the rolling pin or the bottle, thin enough to see her fingers through.
4. Flour the top, fold the sheet over three times, and let her cut across the folds with the butter knife. Fat ones, thin ones, one enormous one.
5. Shake the strips loose. Half go over the chair back or the coat hanger, the rest coil into nests on the second dish towel on the baking tray.
6. Leave them to dry until 1:00 and keep her out of them.

> 💡 **Tip:** Flour anything sticky, add water by the teaspoon to anything cracking, and let her decide which it needs.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Where the Steam Comes Out

Cold air makes every warm thing on the street visible. Walk the block hunting
steam: furnace vents on house walls, a dryer vent, the bakery door. She
breathes out hard and finds her own. Hold her hand near a vent so she feels
wet warm air, then say the word steam once and leave it with her.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and wants whatever Azlyn has,
> so give him a fistful of all-purpose flour and a spoon on his tray while the
> kneading goes on. None of the egg dough goes near him. He drags one finger
> through the flour forty times.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: A Bowl Each, Built to Order

Six bowls go down the middle of the table and everybody builds their own
dinner.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Her dried noodles
- 1 large pan of water
- 1 colander
- 1 ladle
- 1 carrot
- 1 vegetable peeler (**adult**)
- Green onion or chives
- Cooked chicken or ham
- 4 eggs
- Soy sauce
- A splash of oil
- 6 small bowls
- 4 dinner bowls
- Forks and chopsticks

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Six small bowls in a row down the middle of the table. She fills every one and nobody else touches them.
2. You peel the carrot into ribbons with the vegetable peeler and she coils them into the first bowl.
3. She tears the green onion or chives into the second and pulls the cooked chicken or ham into shreds for the third.
4. Boil the 4 eggs eight minutes, cool them under the tap, and she picks the shells off into the fourth. Soy sauce in the fifth. The sixth waits.
5. Bring the large pan of water to a rolling boil. Her noodles go in for three minutes, then you drain them into the colander with her well back.
6. Turn the noodles through a splash of oil, ladle cooking water into the sixth bowl for anyone wanting broth, and share them between the 4 dinner bowls.
7. Everybody builds their own on top of the noodles she cut. Forks, or chopsticks for whoever fancies the fight.

> 💡 **Tip:** Fresh noodles cook in the time it takes to lay the table. Fish one out at two minutes and let her bite it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Store-bought noodles, and she runs the whole topping bar.
- Toppings only, over rice or toast.
- Freeze the spare noodles in nests for the week.
- Lay the table for four, one job at a time.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A train ride**, two stops out and two back
- Indoor playground, for a Saturday spent standing still
- The park in the last of the light
- A café, and she orders her own

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and eats what everyone else
> eats, so chop a few noodles short for him and add carrot ribbons and egg to
> his tray. Nothing hot goes down in front of him. On the train he wants the
> window and the word for it, and *train go* may arrive today.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Laying the track is planning, and it's harder than driving on it.**
> Everything Azlyn did this morning paid off at one o'clock. Nothing about
> rolling and cutting fed her at the time, and a three-year-old lives close to
> the present, so holding a plan across four hours is real work for her. She
> manages it here because the plan hangs over a chair back where she can see
> it. Children this age keep an intention alive through a physical reminder
> long before they can hold one in their heads. Say at breakfast what one
> o'clock is for, point at the drying nests when she asks about lunch, and the
> waiting teaches on its own.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** A full pan of boiling water and the steam coming off the
> colander. Steam scalds worse than the water does, so she stands back for the
> drain and Kreston is out of the kitchen entirely while the pan moves. Raw egg
> dough goes in the trash, not in a mouth.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 332: Beating Air Into It 🌟
**📅 Sunday, November 28, 2027**
**Theme:** Kitchen Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand four eggs out so they reach room temperature, and mix a jar of bubbles: warm water, a squeeze of dish soap, a spoon of sugar.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Separating the Yolks
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Whisking Until It Stands Up (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Bubbles in the Cold Air (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Pancakes That Puff (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Filling the Water Glasses
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Whisk and the Empty Bowl
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Sunday Book Pile
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Separating the Yolks

**🧰 You need:** 4 eggs · 2 large bowls, one metal or glass · 1 fork.

1. She cracks each egg on the flat of the table, never the bowl rim, and opens it into her cupped hand over the metal bowl.
2. The white runs between her fingers and the yolk stays in her palm. It goes into the second bowl. A broken one joins the yolks and you crack another.
3. Beat the yolks smooth with the fork. Tell her the other bowl is the hard one and leave it until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Whisking Until It Stands Up

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4 eggs
- 2 large bowls, one metal or glass
- 1 balloon whisk
- 1 fork
- A pinch of salt
- 1 tablespoon sugar
- 1 jam jar with a lid, the substitute if there is no whisk
- 1 clean dish towel

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Beat the yolks smooth with the fork, cover that bowl with the dish towel and stand it in the fridge. Two of them go into the batter at 1:00.
2. Pinch of salt over the whites. She whisks while you count sixty, then you take sixty, then her again. With no whisk in the house, the whites go in the jam jar with the lid on and she shakes.
3. Stop at the loose foam stage. Lift the whisk out and show her the trail it leaves in the surface, then hand it straight back.
4. Once the foam turns white and holds a mark, rain the tablespoon of sugar in while somebody keeps whisking.
5. Pull the whisk up and look at the peak. A tip that flops needs more. A tip that stands is done, and it takes longer than either of you expects.
6. Hold the bowl upside down over her head. Nothing lands on her, and she will ask for that eleven times.

> 💡 **Tip:** Any grease kills it. Wipe both bowls dry and keep every scrap of yolk out of the whites. Ten minutes with no thickening means starting again.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Bubbles in the Cold Air

Bubbles are strange at the end of November. Cold air makes them slow and
heavy, so they sink and sit on the grass instead of sailing off. Blow a few
low over the frost and see how long one lasts on a cold leaf. She chases them.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and tracks a bubble right
> across the yard now, head and eyes together. Give him his own bowl and a
> spoon on the kitchen floor for the whisking hour. He is two-word building, so
> feed him *more bubble* outside, over and over, and wait for him to have a go
> at it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Pancakes That Puff

The bowl of whites goes into batter, and what comes out of the pan stands
twice as tall.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 1/4 cups all-purpose flour (150 g)
- 1 tsp baking powder
- Generous 3/4 cup milk (200 ml)
- The 2 egg yolks
- The whisked egg whites
- A pinch of salt
- 1 large mixing bowl
- 1 nonstick skillet
- Butter or oil
- 1 ladle
- 1 spatula
- Honey or jam
- 4 plates

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Flour, baking powder and the pinch of salt into the large mixing bowl. She stirs the dry lot together with her hand.
2. Well in the middle, same as yesterday. The 2 egg yolks in, then the milk in a thin stream while she stirs outward.
3. One ladle of the whisked egg whites in first, stirred through hard to loosen the batter.
4. The rest go in with a lift and a fold, under and over, no stirring. Show her once. She will stir anyway, so let her flatten half of it.
5. Butter or oil in the nonstick skillet over medium heat. She ladles the batter in from the side with your hand over hers.
6. Once the bubbles on top open and stay open, you turn each one with the spatula. She counts them out loud.
7. Stack them on the 4 plates with honey or jam, holding one up sideways so she sees the depth.

> 💡 **Tip:** Use as few strokes as you can manage. Every extra stir knocks out air she spent an hour putting in.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Ordinary pancakes, and she does the ladling.
- Whisk cream instead and watch it go past soft into butter.
- Fold the whites into the batter and bake the lot as one tray pancake.
- Keep the whites cold and make them tomorrow.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A sunset walk**, out at three, because the light goes at half past four
- The duck pond, then home before it goes dark
- A friend's house with a plate of pancakes
- Round the block on the scooter

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and feeds himself a wedge of
> pancake, so tear one into strips and leave the honey off his. On the sunset
> walk he wants to be down and walking, which is slow, so allow twice the time
> and take the stroller for the way home.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Air is invisible, and she needs to feel it push before she'll believe in it.**
> Four egg whites weigh nothing much and end up filling half a bowl, with
> nothing added but her arm. Children treat air as absence until something
> makes it act like a substance, and this morning it lifted a bowl's worth of
> foam over her own head. Preschoolers who get a physical demonstration of air
> taking up room start using it to explain other things: bubbles, balloons, the
> bread rising, wind against a coat. The demonstration has to be one she
> performed herself, which this was. She will bring it up again this week in an
> odd place, and that is the idea traveling.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Raw egg. She washes her hands after cracking and nobody licks
> the bowl, Kreston included. Hot fat spits the moment batter hits it, so she
> ladles from the side with your hand over hers and the pan handle turned in.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 333: One Cup Means One Cup 🌟
**📅 Monday, November 29, 2027**
**Theme:** Kitchen Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the butter out to soften, put the scale and the muffin pan on the table, and decide which low cupboard is coming out this afternoon.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Filling the Cup Four Ways
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Two Trays, One Guessed (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Heavy Pocket, Light Pocket (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Everything Out of One Cupboard (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Carrying the Plates to the Table
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Muffin Liners
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath, Then the Muffin She Saved
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Filling the Cup Four Ways

**🧰 You need:** 1 measuring cup or a mug · rice, water, sugar and cotton balls · 1 tray.

1. Fill the same cup four times over the tray: rice, water, sugar, cotton balls, all to the same line. She does the pouring and the stuffing.
2. Ask which cupful is heaviest. Let her lift each one and change her mind twice.
3. Tell her the cup holds the same amount every time whatever goes in it, and leave that sitting there. She tests it at 9:15 with flour.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Two Trays, One Guessed

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 cups self-rising flour (250 g), or all-purpose flour plus 2 tsp baking powder
- 1/2 cup sugar (100 g)
- 7 tbsp oil (100 ml), or 7 tbsp soft butter (100 g)
- 2 eggs
- 2/3 cup milk (150 ml)
- Kitchen scale or a measuring cup
- 1 tablespoon
- 2 mixing bowls
- 12 paper muffin liners
- 1 muffin pan
- Oven mitts
- 2 sticky labels and a pen

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Two bowls. She writes **1** on one sticky label and **2** on the other with the pen and sticks them on.
2. Bowl one, measured together: half the flour, half the sugar, half the oil or butter, one egg, half the milk. She reads the scale or fills the measuring cup to the line, and levels every tablespoon flat.
3. Bowl two is hers on her own. Same five things, same packets, no scale and no cup. She pours until it looks right to her. Say nothing.
4. Six paper liners per bowl in the muffin pan, a heaped tablespoon into each, and the labels moved onto the pan so you know which half is which.
5. Twenty minutes at 375°F (190°C). The pan goes in and comes out with your hands and she stays at the table while the door is open.
6. Cool them, then taste one from each side with whoever is in the house and take a vote.

> 💡 **Tip:** Hers may win, and if it does, say so. Measuring is how you make the same thing twice.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Heavy Pocket, Light Pocket

One coat pocket for heavy, one for light, one thing at a time. Stones, a wet
fir cone and a lump of frozen mud go one side. Dry leaves, a feather, a seed
case go the other. Walk the loop and let her feel her coat pull. Weigh both
piles in her hands on the doorstep before anything comes in.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and carries things the whole
> length of a walk now. Pick him one stone wider than his fist to hold for the
> whole loop and see whether he still has it at the gate. He will hand it to
> Azlyn for her pocket, and handing over on purpose is newer than picking up.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Everything Out of One Cupboard

One low cupboard comes out onto the floor, gets counted, and goes back in an
order she decides.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- One low cupboard
- 1 large tray or a clear patch of floor
- 1 damp cloth
- Paper and a pen
- Sticky notes
- 1 marker
- 1 bag for anything out of date
- 1 bag for the food bank

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She empties the cupboard onto the tray or the clear patch of floor, one thing at a time, passing each one to you.
2. The shelf comes up with the damp cloth. She does the flat middle and you do the corners.
3. Sorting is hers: cans, packets, jars, and a pile for whatever refuses to be any of those. Count each group and write the numbers on the paper.
4. Read the dates together. Anything gone over goes into the out-of-date bag and she carries it to the trash.
5. Three things nobody in this house is ever going to eat go into the food bank bag, and she picks them.
6. She decides where each group goes back, and the heavy cans go low because she has to lift them.
7. One sticky note per group, drawn with the marker and stuck inside the door, so tomorrow she puts things away without asking.

> 💡 **Tip:** Ninety minutes sounds long for one cupboard. She counts the cans twice, stacks them four ways, and runs the clock out on her own.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One shelf instead of the whole cupboard.
- Sort the cans by size, then by picture, then by weight.
- Pack the food bank bag and stop there.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The hill walk**, up the steep side with the muffins in a bag
- The riverside path, flat, for legs that have been up and down all afternoon
- The green space with a ball
- The corner store, and she carries the milk

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Keep Kreston clear while the cupboard is open,
> then give him three empty packets and a shelf of his own. At 17 months he
> puts things in and takes them out for ten or fifteen minutes, then comes back
> to it three times. On the hill he wants
> carrying at the steep part and walking at the top, which is the wrong way
> round for your back.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Pumping a tire is the first time she'll feel her own strength do something useful.**
> A bike pump is the usual version of this. Today it is a cupboard, emptied and
> put back by her arms, with the cans going on the low shelf because that is
> what she can lift. Children work out what they are capable of from jobs where
> the effort is theirs and the result stays visible afterwards, and a real
> household task does that in a way a toy cannot. Effort she can feel is the
> part that registers. She will open that cupboard tomorrow and see her own
> decisions in it. Give her the heavy end of things more often than feels
> necessary.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The oven and the hot pan are yours alone, and she stays at the
> table while the door is open. Cans come out of the cupboard one at a time and
> never stack where they can come down on her feet. Cotton balls, fir cones,
> seed cases and small stones are all the size Kreston chokes on at 17 months,
> so none of them go to him, the collecting pockets stay on Azlyn's coat, the
> only stone he carries is the wide one you picked, and both walk piles get
> weighed on the doorstep and left outside. Count the cotton balls out of the
> bag and back into it, and sweep the floor before he is down. Keep Kreston
> behind a gate while the cupboard is on the floor, and the out-of-date bag goes
> straight out to the trash rather than standing by the door.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 334: Taste It and Fix It 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, November 30, 2027**
**Theme:** Kitchen Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put five small bowls out with salt, sugar, dried herbs, pepper and a splash of vinegar in them, cover them with a plate, and find the can opener.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: One Pinch at a Time
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Fixing the Boring Bowl (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Following the Cooking Smells (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Pitchers, Funnels and a Tray of Oats (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Filling the Salt Shaker
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Little Bowls Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and Warm Milk
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: One Pinch at a Time

**🧰 You need:** the five covered bowls · 1 saucer · 1 glass of water.

1. Uncover the bowls and let her smell each one with her eyes shut. Name them as she goes.
2. A pinch of each onto the saucer, licked off a wet fingertip with a swig of water in between. She pulls a face at the vinegar and goes back to it twice.
3. Ask her which one she would put in food. Take the answer as it comes and tell her the bowl she is fixing arrives at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Fixing the Boring Bowl

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 can chopped tomatoes, or 2 boiled potatoes mashed with water
- 1 bowl
- Small bowls of salt, sugar, dried herbs, lemon juice or vinegar, black pepper
- 6 clean teaspoons
- 1 pitcher of water
- Bread for dipping
- Paper and a pen

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tomatoes into the bowl, or the two mashed potatoes loosened with water. She tastes it plain. Write her first word for it at the top of the paper.
2. The five small bowls go in a row with a teaspoon standing in each. The sixth spoon is hers for tasting and it gets rinsed between goes.
3. One thing, one pinch, stir, taste, then a mouthful of water from the pitcher. She chooses the bowl every time and you write down the order.
4. Keep going while she is interested. Leave the sugar alone even when she puts three lots in, because that is a result too.
5. Overdone is repairable. A splash from the pitcher pulls it back, and she does the fixing.
6. Read the list back in order, then dip bread in it and let everyone at the table taste what she built.

> 💡 **Tip:** Keep your face still. She reads you between spoonfuls, and one wince ends the experiment faster than the vinegar does.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Following the Cooking Smells

Cold air carries cooking a long way. Walk toward whatever you can smell and
name the door it came out of: the bakery, the takeout place, coffee, woodsmoke
off a chimney. She points before you do. On the way home ask which smell she
would eat and which one she would only stand near.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and pulls a face at sour
> things, so give him the smelling and none of the tasting. Hold each bowl
> under his nose for a second. Vinegar gets a whole-body reaction and he asks
> for it again, a joke he is old enough to be in on.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Pitchers, Funnels and a Tray of Oats

Ninety minutes that ask nothing of you. Set it up, sit down beside it, and let
her pour.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 deep tray or a dishpan
- 5 cups rolled oats (500 g)
- A handful of large dried pasta shapes
- 2 pitchers
- 1 funnel, or the top half of a cut plastic bottle
- 1 sieve
- 1 ladle
- 3 empty yogurt cups
- 1 dustpan and brush

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Deep tray or dishpan on the table, never the floor. All the oats in, and the pasta shapes stirred through by hand.
2. Hand her the two pitchers and nothing else for the first ten minutes. Pouring between two containers is the whole game and she runs it herself.
3. Add the funnel, or the cut bottle top. Show her once that a pitcher fills a yogurt cup faster through it, then leave her alone.
4. The sieve next. Oats fall through and the pasta stays behind, and she will do that eight times before she says anything about it.
5. Three yogurt cups and the ladle. Count the ladlefuls out loud and see how many fill one cup.
6. Sweep between rounds with the dustpan and brush. She does the sweeping and it counts as part of the play.
7. Bag the oats at the end. They keep, and the tray comes out again in the bad weeks.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say nothing for the first ten minutes. Every suggestion shortens the run, and a tray like this holds her twenty minutes at a stretch, twice over, if nobody organizes it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Warm water in the dishpan instead of oats.
- Dried pasta only, and she sorts it by shape.
- Pour in the bath tonight and skip the sweeping.
- Two pitchers, one sink, one dish towel.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the weekly one
- Indoor playground if the pool is closed for cleaning
- The library, for a book about food
- Home, with the tray again, on a week that has been long

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and swims by holding on and
> kicking hard, so take him under the arms and let his legs work. He kicks a
> ball on land now and the same movement turns up here. Twenty minutes, then
> out and warm before he goes quiet on you.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Finishing a week by using everything she made beats one more new thing.**
> This afternoon is a game she has played since she could sit up, with one new
> piece in it, the funnel. Familiar hands leave her attention free for the part
> that is new, which is why the second and third go at something teach more
> than the first. The same rule runs the rest of the week. On Thursday she
> cooks a dinner out of things she has already made, and none of it will be
> unfamiliar enough to frighten her. Repeating with a small change is how a
> three-year-old consolidates, and it looks like nothing much from the outside.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Oats and dried pasta end up on the floor, and Kreston at 17
> months puts everything in his mouth. Sweep between rounds and keep the tray
> on the table, not the floor. Salt as well: she is tasting pinch after pinch
> today, so keep the bowls small, and Kreston gets none of it. The pepper bowl
> gets the smallest pinch of the five, and it goes onto food rather than onto
> her tongue if it catches her throat.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 335: Her Own Kit 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, December 1, 2027**
**Theme:** Kitchen Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Move the puff pastry from the freezer to the fridge, and settle tonight which low drawer becomes hers in the morning.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Emptying the Bottom Drawer
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: What Goes in Her Drawer (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: What the Frost Got (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Cheese Straws, Two Tins (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Setting Out Tomorrow's Bowls
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Sorting Her Drawer Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Cheese Straw She Kept
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Emptying the Bottom Drawer

**🧰 You need:** the low drawer · 1 tray or a clear counter · 1 trash bag.

1. Tell her the drawer is hers from today and then let her empty it. Everything comes out onto the tray or the counter, one handful at a time.
2. Go through the pile with her: what belongs to the kitchen, what belongs upstairs, what belongs in the trash bag. She rules on each one.
3. Leave the drawer standing open and empty. She will look at it four times before 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: What Goes in Her Drawer

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 low drawer or cupboard shelf she can reach
- 1 damp cloth
- 1 small plastic pitcher
- 1 plastic bowl
- 1 butter knife
- 1 wooden spoon
- 1 small whisk
- 1 sieve
- 1 dish towel
- 1 hook or peg for her apron, with screws and a screwdriver, or adhesive pads
- 1 apron that fits her
- Card and a marker for the label

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She wipes the empty drawer out with the damp cloth, corners and all, and dries it with her hand.
2. Lay seven things on the table: the pitcher, the bowl, the butter knife, the wooden spoon, the small whisk, the sieve and the dish towel. She handles each one and decides where it lives in the drawer.
3. The eighth is hers to choose off this morning's pile. Take whatever she picks, a lid or a muffin liner included.
4. Stick or screw the hook on the end of the unit at her height and hang her apron on it.
5. Card and marker: she draws the label for the front. Ask what it says and write her words underneath in your handwriting.
6. Shut it, open it, and let her unpack and repack the lot twice while you stand there doing nothing.

> 💡 **Tip:** Nothing goes in that drawer without her say-so from today, and nothing comes out of it without asking her. The rule lasts longer than the drawer does.

### 🌳 Get Outside: What the Frost Got

First of December, and the frost has been through the yard. Walk her round
the things it flattened: the blackened dahlia, the collapsed nasturtium, the
soft edge on a fallen leaf. Then find what shrugged it off: the ivy, the
holly, the grass and her rosemary bush. Break the ice out of a bucket or a
bird bath in one sheet and let her carry it in gloves until the cold comes
through them.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and copies whatever job is
> going, so give him the second cloth and a low cupboard door to wipe while
> Azlyn does her drawer. He wipes one spot for a long time. Outside, put the
> ice sheet flat on the grass and let him stamp on it in boots.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Cheese Straws, Two Tins

Two trays go in and only one stays in this house. She decides who gets the
other one before she starts twisting.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 sheet ready-rolled puff pastry, or 1 2/3 cups flour (200 g) rubbed into 7 tbsp butter (100 g) with 4 tbsp water
- 1 cup grated cheese (100 g)
- 1 egg
- 1 small bowl and 1 fork for beating it
- 1 pastry brush or a teaspoon
- 1 rolling pin
- Her butter knife
- 2 baking trays
- Parchment paper
- Oven mitts
- 1 tin and 1 paper bag

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Ask who the second tin is for and let her name somebody. A neighbor, the woman at playgroup, whoever she says.
2. Unroll the pastry onto parchment paper, or roll the rubbed-in dough out with the rolling pin until it is as thick as her finger.
3. She beats the egg and paints it over the top with the pastry brush or the back of a teaspoon, edges included.
4. All the grated cheese scattered on by her, then pressed down with one pass of the rolling pin so it stays put.
5. She cuts long strips with her butter knife out of her drawer, holds each end, and twists. They come out wonky and bake fine.
6. Twelve minutes at 400°F (200°C) on the two lined baking trays. You open the oven and move the trays, she stays at the table.
7. Cooled, they split between the tin and the paper bag. She carries the bag herself and hands it over.

> 💡 **Tip:** Twisting is a two-handed job going opposite ways, which is hard at three. Hold one end for her until she asks you to stop.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Straight straws, no twist, and double the cheese.
- Cut the pastry into shapes with a cup rim instead.
- Bake one tray and freeze the other for a rough day.
- Draw a card for the person getting the bag.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **Indoor playground**, the quiet weekday session, before school lets out
- The library, and she can take her label idea for a book about cooking
- The park, boots on, for whatever is left of the ice
- Round to whoever the paper bag is for

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and kicks a ball with a
> proper swing now, so the quiet indoor playground session is the right one: room to
> run and nobody knocking him over. Give him a corner of cheese straw at snack
> time, broken small. He wants his own bag to carry and any bag will do.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **The moon changing shape is the first thing she'll notice that she can't touch.**
> Azlyn learns objects by acting on them, and today she got a drawer, a hook
> and a tin she can carry. The moon offers her none of that. She will point at
> it from the bathroom window this week, tell you it followed the car, and
> notice two weeks later that the shape is wrong. Watching a thing change
> that she cannot lift or fix is a different kind of thinking, and it is where
> patience over weeks starts. Nothing about the moon rewards her for hurrying,
> and that is new to her. Answer her questions about it straight, and say
> when you have no idea.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The hot oven and the trays are adult hands only, and Azlyn
> stays at the table while the door is open. She washes her hands after the
> raw egg, and none of it goes near Kreston. Gloves go on before she lifts
> the ice, and it comes off her hands the moment they sting. Keep Kreston off
> the ice sheet unless it is lying on grass. The screwdriver goes back in
> your pocket between turns on the hook.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="day-336"></a>

## 🌟 Day 336: The Dinner Is Hers 🌟
**📅 Thursday, December 2, 2027**
**Theme:** Kitchen Helpers

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Cut six cards out of a cereal box with your scissors and leave them on the table with the marker, and move her noodles from the freezer to the fridge.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Menu on the Fridge
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Six Jobs on Six Cards (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Trees, Bare Again (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: From the Pan to the Plates (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Serving the Bread
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Menu Cards
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Cookbook She Started
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Menu on the Fridge

**🧰 You need:** 1 sheet of paper · crayons · 1 magnet.

1. Tell her tonight's dinner is hers to cook and watch what her face does with that.
2. She draws the menu: what is in it, who is eating, and a dessert. Write her words beside each drawing without tidying them.
3. Stick it on the fridge with the magnet at her eye level. Everyone who comes in the kitchen today gets told about it.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Six Jobs on Six Cards

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6 index cards, or 6 pieces cut from a cereal box
- 1 marker
- 1 cutting board
- Her butter knife
- 1 vegetable peeler (**adult**)
- 1 bowl of water for washing
- Salad and vegetables
- 1 piece of hard cheese for grating
- 1 grater
- 3 tbsp vegetable oil
- 1 tbsp vinegar
- Measuring cups
- 1 whisk
- 1 jam jar with a lid
- 6 small trays or plates

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Six cards, one picture each in marker: a tap, a leaf, a peeler, a knife, a grater, a cup. She draws what she can. Lay them face up in a row with the six small trays behind them.
2. Card one: everything washed in the bowl of water onto the first tray. The card moves to the done pile.
3. Card two: salad torn onto the second tray, by hand, into pieces she thinks are the right size.
4. Card three: she holds the carrot flat on the cutting board while you take the skin off in ribbons with the vegetable peeler. Third tray.
5. Cards four and five: soft vegetables cut with her butter knife onto the fourth tray, then cheese grated onto the fifth, you holding the grater down and her pushing.
6. Card six: oil and vinegar in the measuring cups, tipped into the biggest one and whisked, then poured into the jam jar with the lid on. It stands by the plates until dinner.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her run the card order herself, even backwards. She turns six loose jobs into a sequence she can see.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Trees, Bare Again

Walk the route you walked on New Year's Day. The trees are back where they
started, bare and structural. Stand under the biggest one and take a picture
to sit beside January's. Ask what it looked like in the summer and see how
much of that she has kept.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and wants a job when he sees
> one going, so give him the sixth tray and one washed carrot to carry to the
> table. He drops it once. He walked none of this route in January and manages
> most of it now.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: From the Pan to the Plates

Six trays of prepped food and a menu on the fridge. She cooks, and the house
sits down hungry.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Everything she prepped this morning
- 1 large pan
- 1 colander
- 1 step stool
- 1 wooden spoon
- 1 tasting spoon
- Oven mitts
- 4 plates
- 1 ladle
- 1 dish towel
- A salt shaker
- The menu from this morning, on the fridge
- Her noodles, a muffin and the last of her cheese straws from earlier in the week, or whatever is in the fridge

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She lines the trays along the counter in the order things go in, checking the menu on the fridge for anything missing.
2. Fill the large pan, set it on the back burner with the handle in, and put her step at the side of the stovetop rather than in front.
3. Her noodles go in at the boil. She stirs with the wooden spoon and your hand stays over hers the whole time.
4. Cut vegetables in for the last two minutes. She counts them down out loud from twenty.
5. Lift some out with the tasting spoon and cool it. The salt shaker is hers: one pinch, taste again, and she says when it is right.
6. Oven mitts on you. The pan comes off the heat and drains into the colander, then the noodles go back in the pan on the folded dish towel while she ladles onto the 4 plates.
7. She carries the salad tray, the muffin and the cheese straws over, you carry the four hot plates, and everybody eats what she made.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her the ladle and let the plates come out uneven. Whatever nobody finishes goes into a covered bowl with her name on it, and she serves it again tomorrow.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- She plates up a cold dinner and skips the stovetop.
- One job at the stovetop, and you do the rest.
- Set the table and count out everything for six.
- Photograph each tray and start the cookbook with that.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The pharmacy**, then the park bench with a snack before the light goes
- The market for one thing she chooses for tomorrow
- Round the block with a flashlight each
- The library, for a book about something she cooked this week

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and eats what she cooked,
> cut small and cooled on his tray. Behind the gate while the pan moves, out
> again the second it is down. On the bench he wants to be off it kicking a
> stone along the path, so build in the extra fifteen minutes.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Distance is the part of space that nobody tells her about.**
> Somebody teaches her colors, numbers and shapes, and nobody sits her down
> about how far away things are. Her judgment of it is still rough. Children
> this age will try to climb into a toy car or reach a thing well past their arm,
> because size and distance are still being calibrated against a body that
> keeps changing. That is why today's stovetop rule is about where her feet go
> rather than about being careful. Walking the January route again gives her
> the other half of it, distance measured in her own steps, which is the
> version she can feel.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** She is at the stovetop as the cook for the first time. Handles turn
> in, the pan base stays hotter than it looks long after it comes off, and she
> carries the cold plates while you carry the hot ones. Kreston is strapped in
> or behind the gate the whole time pans are moving.

<a id="backup-nov"></a>

# 🌧️ November — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

These pages are for the November days the plan does not survive. Gray at
breakfast, cold rain that sets in before eight and never lifts, a temperature
on a small forehead, an afternoon gone dark by five. The two bad weather days
are full plans built to run with the door shut, on what the house already
holds, because the weather is the reason nobody is going to the store.
The two sick days ask almost nothing of her and not much more of you, and the
last page is eleven ideas at a time for the mornings when you have ten minutes
and no plan.

---

<a id="nov-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — Three Colors and the Gray Outside

Cold rain since before you woke up, and the forecast has it staying. November
hands her one long gray view out of every window in the house, so today you
paint it, and lunch happens on the floor under the lamps at one thirty because
the dark is back by five.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the paints, two jars for water and a stack of newspaper on the table, and put an empty egg carton and the widest brush you own beside them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Nine Grays in an Egg Carton
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Street in Three Colors (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Getting Warm Without a Coat (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Picnic That Never Went Outside (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🏠 Indoors Instead: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Curtains Across Every Window
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Grays That Are Left
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Warm Bath While It Keeps Raining
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Nine Grays in an Egg Carton

**🧰 You need:** 1 empty egg carton · white and black paint (blue and brown will do) · 1 spoon · 1 brush.

1. A spoon of white into each cup along the row. She does the spooning and it will not be even, which changes nothing.
2. One touch of black into the second cup, two into the third, and on down the row. She stirs each one with the handle of the brush and watches the row darken under her hands.
3. Carry the carton to the window and hold it up. Find the cup that matches the sky, then the roof, then the wet road. Leave the carton wet on the table.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Street in Three Colors

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The egg carton of grays
- 1 large sheet of thick paper, or the flat side of a cut-open box
- White paint, and one more color she picks
- 1 wide brush and 1 thin brush
- 1 jar of water and 1 old dish towel
- Newspaper under the whole lot
- 1 permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Two minutes at the window first. Ask her what is out there and take the list as it comes, gate and puddle and the neighbor's van included.
2. Say the rule out loud and put the rest of the paints back in the box in front of her: the grays, white, and one color of her choosing. She picks the color before a brush gets wet.
3. Big shapes first with the wide brush. Sky across the top, road along the bottom, and she covers the paper before anything gets detail. The brush goes through the jar of water and dries on the old dish towel between colors.
4. Then her list, in gray. Roofs, the van, the bare tree, the fence, whatever she named. Thin brush, and she works from the top down so her sleeve stays out of it.
5. The one color goes last and it has to be spent. She decides what deserves it: a front door, an umbrella, one lit window.
6. Prop it against the window to dry and go and look at it from the far side of the room. Write the date along the bottom in marker while she watches.

> 💡 **Tip:** The single color is the whole activity. Open the full set and you get a brown puddle by nine-forty, and she never once has to decide.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Getting Warm Without a Coat

The house is cold and she has not moved her whole body since breakfast. Clear
the hallway and build one round out of six things: ten jumping jacks, ten
stomps, ten arm circles, a lap of the living room on tiptoe, the laundry basket
carried the length of the hall, and a slow crawl back under the low table. Do
the round with her and count out loud. At the end of each one she puts the back
of her hand against her own cheek and says whether she is warm yet. The answer
changes by the third round. Give her the marker and the back of yesterday's
envelope and let her mark each round off as she finishes it. Five rounds takes
forty minutes with the arguing about tiptoe included, and she comes to lunch
pink and loud and ready to sit down.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and there is no version of
> this morning where he holds a loaded brush. Give him his own brush, a cup of
> plain water and a flattened box on the floor at 9:15, and let him paint the
> cardboard dark. It dries and he does it again. He walks the hallway rounds
> at 10:30 too, a lap behind her, stomping because she is stomping. Two-word
> combinations are starting, so expect *more water* the second the cup runs
> out.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Picnic That Never Went Outside

Morning was wet paint and standing up. This afternoon everybody sits on the
floor, the curtains come across, and lunch happens under a lamp at one thirty
because the dark is coming back at five anyway.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 blanket or an old sheet
- Cushions, one per person
- Real plates and cups, not the picnic set
- 1 tray
- Cold food the house already has: crackers, cheese, fruit, carrot sticks, dry cereal, a can of peaches, whatever is open in the fridge
- 1 small pitcher, half filled
- 2 dish towels
- 1 lamp

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She clears the middle of the living room floor. Move the low table out together and let her decide which way around the blanket goes.
2. She lays a place for everybody in the house, plus two toys she chooses, and everyone gets a real plate.
3. Food onto the tray, cold, no stove involved. She loads it and carries it in two hands, one trip, and you walk behind her.
4. Curtains across, big light off, lamp on. The room changes and she will notice before you say anything.
5. Everybody down on the floor with a cushion each, adults included, and nobody gets up for forty minutes. Phones go on the shelf.
6. She pours. Small pitcher, half full, one cup at a time, and a spill gets a dish towel rather than a comment.
7. Clearing is part of it. Everything back on the tray, blanket shaken out over the bath, cushions returned.

> 💡 **Tip:** Stay down. The picnic works because you are at her eye level for an hour, and it stops working the moment you start doing the dishes behind her.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Blanket over the kitchen table instead, and eat underneath it.
- Skip the food and take the books down there.
- One plate each, laid out on the floor in color order.
- Move the whole thing to the upstairs hallway, where the light is different.

### 🏠 Indoors Instead: **Pick one**
- **Hang the morning's paintings** along the hallway at her height, tape at all four corners
- Empty the coat closet and sit in it with a lamp
- Everybody's shoes in one line, biggest to smallest, front door to kitchen
- A phone call to whoever is furthest away, with three questions she prepares
- The linen closet laundry, sorted into piles by who it belongs to

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and a blanket on the floor
> is the best table he has met. Sit him at the edge with his own plate and cup,
> and expect him to walk through the middle of it twice carrying something.
> Give him the second dish towel to wipe with. He copies wiping now and does a
> worse job than the spill.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A constraint is what makes her choose instead of asking for everything.**
> Open the whole paint box and Azlyn uses every color inside five minutes, and
> the paper goes brown. Hand her three and something else happens. She holds
> the red back, looks at the roof, looks at the door, and decides which one is
> worth it, and that decision is the thinking you were hoping for. Three-year-
> olds get almost no practice at choosing, because most of the day arrives
> already chosen for them. A small fixed set gives her a real decision with a
> visible result at the end of it. The limit does the teaching, and it leaves
> you free to say yes to everything inside it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Paint water looks like drinking water to a 17-month-old, so
> the jars stay on the table and go down the sink the moment the brushes are
> washed. Use washable non-toxic paint only, because Kreston will get a
> brushful in his mouth at some point today. Wipe any drip off the floor as it
> happens; a wet floorboard with two children running on it is the real hazard
> in this room.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Pot That Cooks All Day

Gray sky, cold rain going sideways and no reason to open the door. Today she
does the chopping with a knife that works, dinner goes on the stove before
eleven and fills the house for six hours, and the afternoon takes something
apart on a towel while the light drains out of the windows.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand six things from the fridge and the cupboard on the counter, find the small serrated knife and the cutting board, and dig out one dead battery-powered thing nobody will miss.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Thumb Test
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Bridge and the Claw (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Knocking the Bottles Down (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: What's Inside the Broken Thing (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🏠 Indoors Instead: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: A Bowl at Every Place
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Screws in the Muffin Tin
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath While the House Smells of Dinner
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Thumb Test

**🧰 You need:** 6 things out of the fridge and the cupboard, 4 of them soft enough to take a thumbprint (mushroom, zucchini, banana, a ripe pear, canned peach halves, a slice of bread) and 2 that will not (onion, carrot, potato, a hard apple) · 1 tray.

1. Line them all along the counter and give her one instruction: press a thumb into each one, hard.
2. Two piles. The ones that give, and the ones that fight back. She sorts, you say nothing.
3. Tell her the giving pile is hers at 9:15 and the fighting pile is yours. Leave both on the tray.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Bridge and the Claw

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 small serrated table knife with a rounded tip (**adult supervision the whole time**)
- 1 cutting board and 1 damp dish towel to sit it on
- Her pile, the four that took a thumbprint
- Your pile, the two that did not (**yours**)
- 1 large bowl
- 1 heavy pot with a lid
- 1 can of tomatoes, or a jar of pasta sauce, or two spoons of tomato paste and an extra cup of water
- Oil, salt, 1 cup of water or stock
- 1 can of beans or a cup of dried lentils, if the six things looked thin in the bowl

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Damp towel under the board so it cannot slide. She stands at the counter with the board at elbow height, or sits at the table if the counter is too high.
2. Bridge grip first, on the softest thing in her pile. Her free hand arches over the top like a bridge, fingers down each side, and the blade goes through the gap under it. Show it once, say it once, then keep your hands off.
3. Claw grip next, on the longest thing she has, laid with a flat side down so it stays put. Knuckles forward, fingertips curled back, and the flat of the blade rests against her knuckles as it comes down.
4. One piece of food at a time and no hurrying her along. Every piece goes in the bowl, uneven, thick, fine, and it all cooks the same.
5. You take your two, standing beside her, because both of them roll. She watches and calls out which grip you are using.
6. Everything into the pot with the tomatoes, the oil, the salt and a cup of water. Tip the beans or the lentils in as well if the bowl came up short. Lid on, lowest heat, and it stays there until five o'clock.

> 💡 **Tip:** She never carries the knife anywhere. It lives on the board, it goes back on the board between every piece, and it comes off the board into your hand when the chopping stops.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Knocking the Bottles Down

Ten empty bottles and cans out of the recycling, stood in a triangle at the
far end of the hallway, and one soft ball. She rolls from a taped line, counts
what falls and stands them back up herself, which is half the game. Move the
line back a step every time she clears more than five. Give her the marker and
the envelope again if she wants to keep score.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 17 months and kicks a ball now, so he
> gets the same triangle and no line at all. He will walk up to the bottles and
> kick from a foot away, and that counts. Stand the bottles up for him as fast
> as he flattens them, and give him the word *down* every time, because two-
> word combinations are starting and *all down* is one he can reach.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: What's Inside the Broken Thing

Morning was sharp, careful and standing at the counter. This afternoon she
sits down with a screwdriver and finds out what has been inside the radio the
whole time.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 dead battery-powered object: a radio, a flashlight, a toy that stopped working, a wind-up clock
- 1 medium Phillips screwdriver and 1 small flathead
- 1 muffin tin or egg carton, for the screws
- 1 old towel and 1 tray
- 1 zip-top bag
- 1 piece of card, 1 marker, masking tape

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Batteries out first, in front of her, and up on a high shelf. You open nothing that plugs into the wall and nothing with a glass screen.
2. Towel on the table, tray on the towel. Everything that comes off the object lands on the tray and stays there.
3. Hunt the screws together. She points at each one, you break it loose with the Phillips, and she turns it out the rest of the way with both hands on the handle. The small flathead does the slotted screws and pries the case apart at the seam.
4. Every screw goes straight into one cup of the muffin tin. Count them in and count them out at the end.
5. Open it up. One part out at a time, laid along the tray biggest to smallest, and she does the lifting.
6. Ask what each part might do and write her answer on the card as she says it. The speaker cone is a drum and the spring is a snake, and both answers go down word for word.
7. Tape three parts to the card as a poster for her wall. The rest go in the zip-top bag with the screws, on the high shelf.

> 💡 **Tip:** Turning a screw out is heavy work for a three-year-old wrist and she will manage two out of six. Break each one loose for her and let the finishing be hers.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One screw only, then leave the rest and come back tomorrow.
- Take the batteries out of everything in the house and line them up by size.
- Draw round each part on paper instead of taping it down.
- Open an old ballpoint pen, which comes apart in four pieces and needs no tools.

### 🏠 Indoors Instead: **Pick one**
- **Taste the pot** with a teaspoon each, and let her say what it still needs
- The parts poster taped up in the hallway at her height
- Bottles back down the hall, this time bowling underhand from the kitchen door
- A blanket over two dining chairs and the parts tray carried inside
- Bread out of the cupboard, torn and stacked ready for the bowls at six

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Kreston is 17 months and every part on that tray
> is choke-size. He is out of this room while it is open, in the hallway with
> the bottles and a door between, or asleep. Bring him back once the bag is
> shut and the tray is cleared, and give him the empty muffin tin and a wooden
> spoon at floor level.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A sharp-enough knife is safer than a blunt one, and she can learn a grip.**
> A blunt knife slides. It skates off a tomato skin and lands in the hand
> holding the tomato, which is hers, because she leaned on it harder to make it
> work. A small serrated knife bites where she puts it, so she uses less force
> and keeps the line she aimed at. The grip carries more of the safety than the
> blade does. The bridge, her hand arched over the food with the blade passing
> underneath, keeps her fingers above the edge. The claw, knuckles forward and
> fingertips tucked back, gives the blade a wall to lean on. Show each one
> once, then sit beside her with your hands in your lap.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** You are within arm's reach of that knife for every second it
> is out of the drawer, and it goes back in your hand and into the drawer the
> moment the chopping ends. Never leave it on the board while you cross the
> room. Kreston stays out of the kitchen while she cuts and while the pot is
> on: the handle turns inward, the pot sits on a back burner, and the lowest
> heat still burns a hand that reaches. On the take-apart, batteries come out
> before the first screw, you open nothing that plugs into a wall socket, and
> you count the screws and small parts into the tin and bag them at the end.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="nov-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Worst Day of It

This is the day she cannot lift her head off the cushion, and there is nothing
in this book she needs. The plan is a warm room, one adult within reach and a
long sleep in the middle of the afternoon. You can stop any of it halfway
through and lose nothing, and none of it asks her to cut, build or leave the
spot you make for her.

### 🌙 Before You Come Downstairs
> Fill a small cup and stand it where her hand falls without her lifting her head. Put a bowl of cool water and two washcloths on the low table by the sofa, and her own pillow and the blanket she recognizes at the end of it.

### 🕗 The Shape of the Day

> *No clock times today. She sets the order and you follow her.*

- **Whenever she wakes.** Downstairs in her pajamas, blanket, and a drink already poured within her reach.
- **Before the first long sleep.** The cool cloth round, then one story with her eyes shut.
- **The long sleep.** The rest block, and it owns as much of the day as it wants.
- **When she asks for food.** Dry, plain and small, on a saucer rather than a plate.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** The sips, counted, and the same book as many times as she asks for it.
- **When the light goes.** Lamps low, bath skipped, bed early and yours if that is what she wants.

### 🛏️ The Rest Block

The middle of this day is a sleep, and it is the point of the day rather than
a gap in it. Make the sofa the bed: her own pillow off her bed, a blanket she
recognizes, the curtains across. Sit at the end of it with your hand on her
leg. She has dropped her nap for a year and she will fight the idea for four
minutes and go under for two hours. Take the two hours. Answer nothing that
can wait, and do not fill the room with the sound of the dishwasher being
emptied above her head.

### 🫗 Sips She Counts Herself

One small cup, filled a third of the way, and a straw if you have one. Set it
where her hand falls without her lifting her head. The job is little and
often, so every time you pass you say *one sip*, she takes one, and you both
count how many she has managed since the last sleep. Water, watered juice,
flat soda at room temperature, whatever she will take. Ice chips work on a day
when a cup is too much effort.

### 📖 The Story With Her Eyes Shut

Books are heavy today and her eyes ache. Tell her a story about herself
instead, with her eyes closed: the morning she found the frost on the gate,
the day the tower came down, the muddiest puddle on the lane. Slow, quiet, and
full of the things she recognizes. She will correct you when you get a detail
wrong, and that correction is the most she will do all day.

### 🧊 The Cool Cloth Round

The bowl and the two washcloths are on the low table from last night, so this
one starts where she is lying. Wring one out, lay it across her forehead,
count to twenty and swap it for the other. Wipe her hands and the back of her
neck. Three rounds, then the bowl goes down the sink and the cloths go over
the rail. It lowers nothing on a thermometer and it settles her, which is the
job.

> 👶 **Where Kreston Goes:** A sick sibling changes his day too. If a
> grandparent or a friend can take him from breakfast until dinner, this is the
> day to ask, and ask early. Failing that, run him in the next room with the
> door open and a gate across, his own cup that never crosses the doorway, and
> the toys that need no help. Wash your hands between the two of them every
> single time. He is 17 months and will climb on her if he gets the chance, so
> he does not sit on the sofa today.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Dark afternoons change the shape of the day, and the plan has to change with them.**
> Sunset comes before five for most of November, and the light sets the shape
> of a sick day here. Her body reads a fading afternoon as a signal. Melatonin
> arrives ahead of schedule, and the sleep pressure a fever already built
> climbs on top of it. You have the long sleep in the middle of the day and the
> lamps low by four, so the day ends where her body wants it to end. Bed before
> six counts as a bedtime this month. A child running a temperature spends most
> of her fuel on the fever, and an evening two hours short hands some of it
> back to her. Tomorrow starts early, and that suits her too.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** An open bowl of water on the floor is a drowning risk for a
> 17-month-old, so the cool bowl lives on the low table beside her and goes
> down the sink the moment the third round ends. Call your pediatrician the
> same day for any of these:
> a fever in a child this age that lasts beyond three days, breathing that is
> fast or noisy or pulls the skin in at her ribs, no wet diaper or trip to the
> bathroom in eight hours, a headache with a stiff neck, a rash that stays
> visible when you press a glass against it, or a child too drowsy to wake.
> Trust the pattern you know. Write down the time and the dose of anything you
> give her on a piece of paper on the counter, because a second adult on a long
> day is the way double doses happen.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="nov-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — The Day She Has Plans Again

The fever broke overnight, she is asking for things again, and she is nowhere
near ready to be back at it. This is the harder of the two days, because she
has energy for about eleven minutes at a stretch and none at all after that.
She does all of it lying down, on a lap or from under a blanket, one hand, no
setup.

### 🌙 Before You Come Downstairs
> Stand four teaspoons, a towel and a sheet of paper on the low table by the sofa, with the blanket and the book she knows by heart. Leave the drawer you plan to bring her by the door.

### 🕗 The Shape of the Day

> *No clock times today. She sets the order and you follow her.*

- **Whenever she wakes.** She will be brighter than yesterday and want the whole day at once. Slow it down before it starts.
- **After breakfast.** Four spoons, four words, and a small honest taste of food.
- **When she starts asking for jobs.** One drawer on the blanket, and it can stop after two minutes.
- **The rest block.** The sleep she says she does not need, and she still needs it.
- **Before the afternoon dip.** The list for when she is better, dictated by her.
- **When the light goes.** Warm water and a washcloth where she is lying, then a longer wind-down than usual.

### 🛏️ The Rest Block

She will argue about this one today, which is how you know she is on the mend.
Hold it anyway. Same sofa, same blanket, curtains across, and a rule that she
does not have to sleep and does have to stay lying down. Put the book she
knows by heart in her hands and go quiet. Most children are asleep by the
third page. A recovering three-year-old who skips this sleeps in bursts, then
crashes at four thirty, and tomorrow starts a day behind.

### 🥄 Four Spoons and Four Words

Four teaspoons, one taste on each, done from where she is lying with a towel
under her chin. A smear of honey on the first, a lick of salt on the second, a
drop of lemon juice or vinegar on the third, a scrape of unsweetened cocoa
powder on the fourth. Name each one as it goes in her mouth: sweet, salty,
sour, bitter. She will pull a face at the lemon and ask for it twice more.
Then the game: eyes shut, you load a spoon, and she names which of the four it
was. Nothing to clear up afterward but four spoons.

### 🗄️ One Drawer on the Blanket

Bring her a drawer. The kitchen drawer with the odds in it, the button tin,
the sock basket, the bag of bottle caps. Tip it on the blanket over her legs
and let her sort it into whatever groups she names, or leave it in a heap and
sort three things. This is a lap-sized job with a floor of two minutes and a
ceiling of forty, and either is a fine result today.

### 📝 The List for When She's Better

She has been indoors for days and she is full of plans. Take them down. Sit
with a sheet of paper and write the whole list as she says it, word for word,
including the trip to the moon. Read it back to her twice and pin it where she
can see it. Tomorrow, or the day after, she picks one off the list and you do
it, so keep at least one of them small enough to happen.

> 👶 **Where Kreston Goes:** He can come back into the room today, in short
> doses, with one rule: he stays on the floor and she stays on the sofa. He is
> 17 months and will want to climb up beside her within a minute. Give him a
> job at her feet instead, posting the sorted drawer back in one piece at a
> time while she directs him from above. Twenty minutes of that is plenty for
> both of them.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **She can name what she doesn't like once she has words for the tastes.**
> A recovering three-year-old turns food down and cannot tell you what is wrong
> with it. Sour, salty, sweet and bitter give her four handles. Put a smear of
> each on a spoon, name it while it is in her mouth, and inside a week *yuck*
> turns into *too sour*, which is something you can cook around. Her tongue is
> more sensitive than yours, bitter most of all, and that is why broccoli and
> medicine land harder for her than they do for you. Words for the tastes also
> give her a way to accept a thing she dislikes, because a thing with a name is
> a smaller thing.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Keep her home while a fever is still coming back in the
> afternoons, and for a full day after the last one, whatever the calendar
> says. Written doses stay on the counter, and the same rule holds today:
> nobody gives anything without reading the sheet first. Watch for the second
> illness that arrives on the back of the first, because a child who was mending
> and goes downhill again gets a fresh call to the pediatrician rather than
> another day on the sofa.

<a id="nov-extras"></a>

## 🎲 November — Extra Ideas

Ten minutes, no plan, cold rain on the glass and the lamps on at four. Pick a
line and start.

### 🎲 **Alternative Activities**

- **Fifty Steps Around the House**, counted out loud, then fifty back the other way.
- **The Mug She Carries Herself**, she picks it, stirs the warm milk and walks it to her own chair.
- **The Radiator Race**, wet mittens and hats laid out and checked to see which dries first.
- **Everything Blue in Four Minutes**, a timed hunt with a laundry basket and no rules about what counts.
- **The Chair Tunnel**, four dining chairs in a row under a blanket, with a job waiting at each end.
- **The Bell in the Next Room**, eyes shut, and she points at where the sound came from.
- **Two Minutes of Standing Still**, a contest nobody wins and everybody enters.
- **The Sofa Cushion Wall**, every cushion off the furniture and built into a wall across one doorway.
- **The Long Roll Down the Hallway**, a ball pushed back and forth sitting down, legs apart.
- **The Sock Skate Race**, socks on the smooth floor and the length of the kitchen crossed sliding.
- **The Newspaper Mountain**, a whole newspaper torn into strips and stuffed into a pillowcase.

### 🎨 **Alternative Arts & Crafts**

- **Rain Prints**, a sheet of paper held out under a drip for ten seconds and dried flat.
- **The Window Sign for the Street**, one big word drawn thick and taped facing out for whoever walks past.
- **Bubble Wrap Printing**, paint rolled over the bubbles and pressed onto paper.
- **The Foil Puddle**, foil pressed into a saucer and flooded with watered-down color.
- **Coffee Grounds Mud Paint**, used grounds stirred into glue for a brown that smells.
- **The Torn Paper Tree**, brown strips for a trunk and bare branches, because that is what is out there.
- **Candle Stub Lines**, wax scribbles that the paint refuses to cover.
- **The Odd Sock Draft Stopper**, stuffed with the rest of the odd socks and given a face.
- **Cotton Swab Dots**, one color per swab and no brushes allowed.
- **The Envelope Street**, old envelopes cut into lit windows and glued along a dark sheet.
- **Potato Stamps**, cut by you and printed by her onto a paper bag for wrapping.

### 👶 **Kreston's Turn**

- **The Ball Down the Hallway**, you sitting at one end, him kicking from the other.
- **Two Words at the Window**, *car gone* and *rain wet*, handed back to him each time he points.
- **Two Cups and the Clothespins**, dropped from one cup into the other and tipped out to start again.
- **The Pan Lid Drum**, one wooden spoon and one lid, at floor level, for as long as you can stand it.

## ⚠️ Quick Safety Reminders

- **Real flame**: the menorah on the 24th, the ice lantern on the 21st, the candle rules on the 27th, her cake on the 20th and your own cake on the 29th. Stay in the room while any of them burn, and the matches go back on a high shelf after every strike.
- **Button batteries**: the tea lights in the lit village on the 9th, and the one on the memory table on the 30th. Tape every cover shut and store them high, because a button battery swallowed at 18 months is a surgical emergency.
- **Small parts**: cork and clothespin villagers on the 4th, bottle caps on the 6th, birdseed and chopped nuts on the 10th, salt dough rounds on the 16th, foil coins on the 24th, hard candy on the 29th. Count them out, count them back into a box, and sweep the floor before Kreston goes down.
- **String and cord**: the bird feeders on the 10th, the name tags on the 11th and the paper cloud on the 18th all hang on it. Nothing stays looped within his reach, and the indoor ones come down at night.
- **Adult-only steps**: the craft knife on the 3rd, the 7th, the 9th, the 15th and the 26th, the kitchen scissors on the 26th and the 28th, melted fat on the 10th, the oven on the 16th and the 20th, the stove and the heated spoon on the 27th. Christmas cardboard hides staples in the seams, so run a hand down every panel first.
- **Winter specific**: the dark walks put them at the curb by half past three, so hold both their hands and stay off the road edge. Pond ice never holds a child, nothing red comes home off the collecting walks, and Kreston can drown in the inch of water in the river tray on the 23rd.

## Week 49: Storybook Village 📖
**📅 December 3 – December 9, 2027**

---

### 🎯 What This Week Is About

She builds a village this week and then moves into it. Friday nine boxes
become a street with doors that swing. Saturday the street gets a dozen
residents made out of clothespins, corks and wooden spoons. Sunday the land
goes down underneath all of it, a foil river and a gray road, and every
building moves across. From Monday the village is somewhere she talks from:
her own words in a book with a string binding, a story she winds past a
window, the rooms of your house wearing village names. Each day puts the same
question in front of her in a new shape: **who lives here, and what happens
to them?**

Nothing on the calendar lands this week. December does the work instead. The
first hard freeze puts a skin on the puddles Sunday morning, wreaths are
going up on half the doors on your block, and the front rooms are lit by half
past three, which Wednesday's walk uses. Kreston turns 18 months on Sunday
and pretend play starts with him, so watch what he does with a torn strip of
newspaper before he eats it. Pick where the village goes before Friday
morning. It holds that patch of floor for seven days, it grows hills on
Sunday and lit windows on Thursday, and a walking 18-month-old will flatten a
street built in a doorway.

---

### 🧒 What Azlyn Will Learn

- **A building has a front, a name and a number.** She marks the doors and windows, you cut on her marks, and every shop ends up with a sign she can find on her own feet.
- **Other people have insides.** She asks a dozen villagers one question, the same one every time, and you write down what each of them answers.
- **Her hands decide what a material is.** Foil, plastic wrap, blue paper and gray card for the river on Sunday; wax paper, candy wrappers and a freezer bag held to a flashlight on Thursday.
- **Talk can be kept.** She says a sentence at 9:20 on Monday and hears it back off the page at bedtime, in her order, with her wrong verbs still in it.
- **A story has an order and a voice.** Four pictures left to right through a window she winds herself, then one scene run three times over in a big voice, a squeaky voice and a whisper.

---

### 👩 What You'll Learn

- Asking what happens in it beats asking what it is
- The oldest teaching rituals put a child's question at the center
- Her hands know a sorting rule she cannot say yet
- Writing her words down shows her that talk can be kept
- One noticed detail does more for her than a round of applause
- Winter morning light is the strongest signal her body clock gets
- She asks for the wolf again because she already knows how it ends

---
