### 🌅 Opening Activity: Whose Name Is On It

**🧰 You need:** the presents · sticky notes · 1 pen.

1. She goes round the tree reading names she cannot read, matching first letters against the names you say out loud.
2. One pile per person. Hers gets counted four times and the count changes twice.
3. Write each name big on a sticky note, let her stick it on the right pile, and nothing gets opened until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: One Parcel at a Time

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The presents
- 1 trash bag for torn paper
- 1 shallow box for the paper worth keeping
- Scissors (adult only)
- 1 roll tape
- 1 notebook and a pen, to write down who gave what
- Sticky notes

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Everyone sits down. One parcel opens at a time and the rest stay in their piles, and the rule holds for the adults too.
2. She opens hers. Torn paper goes in the trash bag as it comes off, and she smooths any sheet worth keeping flat into the shallow box.
3. Ribbon, wire ties and taped seams are yours. Cut them with the scissors before she pulls, then put the scissors back up.
4. She plays with it. Five minutes on the floor at least, before anyone touches the next parcel.
5. Write in the notebook with the pen: who gave what, and what she said when she saw it, in her words.
6. A sticky note on each new thing with the giver's name. Tape the box it came in back together so the thing has somewhere to live tonight.

> 💡 **Tip:** Stop when she stalls, even at three parcels in. The rest keep, and a pile saved for the 27th makes that whole morning.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Who Else Is Out on Christmas Morning

Get out before noon, when the street belongs to the few with a reason to be on
it: somebody walking a dog in a coat, somebody riding a new bike with no
gloves, a car packed to the roof and idling. Say hello to every one.
Christmas morning is the one walk of the year where strangers answer.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months, and the wrapping outranks
> what came in it for another year. Give him one parcel wrapped in two
> layers with nothing breakable inside and let the tearing take as long as it
> takes. Pretend play is starting, so a bow on his own head gets a laugh he
> goes back for five more times.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Everything Alive in This House

She takes a clipboard round every room this afternoon and decides what counts
as alive.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Paper and crayons
- 1 piece of stiff cardboard as a clipboard
- 1 roll masking tape
- Your phone
- The new toy animals
- The houseplants and any pets

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tape a sheet of paper onto the cardboard. That is her clipboard and it stays in her hand for the hour.
2. Start in the kitchen and work through the house. One crayon mark per living thing. People count, and she will want a ruling on the fridge.
3. The new toy animals start an argument. Take her reasons and write them on her sheet in her words.
4. Back in one room, she splits them into groups she names. Two big squares of masking tape on the floor, and everything she can carry goes in the right one, houseplants included.
5. Anything too heavy to move gets a strip of tape beside it with her mark on it.
6. Now the photograph. Everything alive in one frame: plants carried in, a cat who declines, Kreston already leaving. Take six and keep the worst one.
7. Look at the picture and count who is missing. She will remember the plants upstairs.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say yes to her groups. *Things with faces* and *things that stay still* are working categories.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Water every houseplant in the house, one cup each.
- Line the new animals up biggest to smallest.
- Draw the family, pets included, on one long sheet.
- Count legs in the house, hers and everybody else's.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The lakeshore**, wrapped to the eyes, because the wind off the water is the point of going
- A drive to the highest spot nearby, and stay in the warm car
- The empty playground, cold slide and all
- Grandparents, or whoever is closest with a kettle on

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He will take the clipboard, so make him one from a
> spare piece of cardboard with a crayon taped to it. At 18 months he
> points and names, and the cat gets pointed at twenty times. Let him carry one
> houseplant to its square with both arms, and take the photograph on his
> terms.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sorting living things is harder than sorting objects, because they move.**
> Sorting blocks by color is a fixed problem. A cat that leaves, a brother who
> walks off, a plant that grows toward the window: those change while she is
> deciding about them. Children spend the years between three and six building
> the alive category, and they get there through motion first, then feeding,
> then growth. A toy dog with moving legs looks alive to her, and so does a
> stream. She sorts wrong for good reasons, and every ruling she makes out loud
> shows you how she is thinking. Ask her why the toy dog counts and you get
> the rule she is working from.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Christmas packaging is the hazard today and Kreston is loose
> in it. Button batteries out of new toys go up and out of the house, wire ties
> and plastic film go straight into the trash bag, ribbon does not stay on the
> floor. The scissors stay with you. Check every new toy for parts that came
> loose in the box.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Model on the Table

**🧰 You need:** one small toy from yesterday · paper · 1 marker.

1. She picks one thing she got yesterday. Small, hers, and already carried round the house once.
2. Stand it alone in the middle of the table and list its parts out loud between you. Write every part she names down the page.
3. Ask how many boxes it would take to build one as tall as the door. Write her number at the bottom. You test it at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Toy the Size of a Door

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4–6 flattened boxes from Christmas
- 1 roll packing tape
- 1 roll masking tape
- Heavy scissors or a craft knife (adult only)
- Markers
- Leftover wrapping paper
- String
- The small original as the model
- Her parts list from this morning

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Lay the flattened boxes across the floor and stand the original at the top, where she can see it from anywhere in the room.
2. Biggest part first. She points at it on the model, you cut the panel with the heavy scissors or the craft knife, and she stands back while you do.
3. Then part by part down her list. She looks at the original before each cut, and she is the one who says how big.
4. Packing tape holds the structure. Masking tape holds anything she may change her mind about, and she will change her mind twice.
5. Wrapping paper for the colored parts, torn and taped on in patches. Markers for the details she can see on the original and you cannot.
6. String for whatever hangs, ties or pulls. Stand it against the door and let her walk around it.

> 💡 **Tip:** Cut nothing she has not asked for. The wrong-looking proportions are her measurements.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Biggest Thing on the Street

Go out hunting for the largest version of ordinary things: the tallest tree on
the block, the biggest truck parked up, a flattened refrigerator box at the
curb, the dog that comes up to her shoulder. Use her body as the ruler at three
of them: waist, shoulder, over her head. December 26 puts more cardboard on the
sidewalk than any other day of the year.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and climbing, and a door-sized
> cardboard shape is the most interesting thing in the house. Give him a wide
> offcut flat on the floor as his own island and he will stand on it, get off,
> and get back on. Pretend play means he feeds the big one a block. Keep him
> off the finished build until the tape has set.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The One That Fits in a Matchbox

She makes it again, small enough to lose.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 matchbox or any small box
- Paper scraps
- 1 roll tape
- 1 pencil and crayons
- 1 bottle cap
- 1 pair of kitchen scissors (adult only)
- 1 scrap of foil
- Her parts list from this morning

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Empty the matchbox and push the tray out of the sleeve. Whatever she makes has to fit back inside with the lid closed.
2. Read her parts list back from this morning. Every part the enormous one has, the tiny one has.
3. Body first: a paper scrap folded or rolled to length, held with a strip of tape. You cut with the kitchen scissors, she folds.
4. The bottle cap does the work of one whole part. A head, a wheel, a base, whichever she names.
5. A thumbnail of foil for anything that shines.
6. Pencil for the marks too small for a crayon, crayons for the color.
7. Close the lid on it, then open it again, because she has to check it is still in there.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let her hold both at once, the door-sized one behind her and the matchbox in her fist. Same thing, same parts, two sizes apart.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Draw the toy life-size on a flattened box and leave it flat.
- Make a matchbox bed for it and nothing else.
- Line up five things in the house biggest to smallest.
- Trace round the big build on the floor with masking tape.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **A playground you have never been to**, twenty minutes' drive, empty on the 26th
- The woods, for the biggest tree the two of you can find
- The nearest hill, for the view of how small the houses go
- Indoor playground, or home with the biggest cardboard box the street produced

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** The matchbox and the bottle cap are choking
> hazards, so he works at the other end of the table with a shoebox, putting
> things in and taking them out. At 18 months that game outlasts anything you
> could buy him. At a new playground he wants the steps, holding one hand, up
> as many times as your back allows.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Making it enormous is how she checks she knows the parts.**
> Azlyn can recognize her new toy from across a room and still not know how it
> is put together. Building it door-sized forces the question part by part,
> because a wrong-sized wing shows up at that scale and hides at three inches.
> Educators call this working at a different grain. She has to look at the
> original with real attention, and she has to hold the whole shape in her head
> while she works on one piece of it. The matchbox version this afternoon runs
> the same check from the other end, and it is fiddlier, so she slows down.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The craft knife or the heavy scissors cutting big cardboard is
> adult-only work, and it happens with her standing back and knowing why.
> Christmas boxes carry staples in the seams, so run your hand along every
> panel before either child touches it. The scissors stay with you.

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Tray, the Cloth and the Cup of Water

**🧰 You need:** 1 metal tray · 1 cup of water · 1 wet washcloth · 1 hair tie.

1. Tie her hair back first, and say why while you do it.
2. She carries each thing to the table: tray in the middle, water and cloth on your side, inside your reach and not hers.
3. Ask what each is for. She gets the water first guess. Tell her the cloth smothers and leave that word with her until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: What a Flame Does

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 3 tea lights, or 1 dinner candle in a heavy holder
- 1 metal tray
- 1 glass jar taller than the candle
- 1 cup of water
- 1 wet washcloth
- 1 long-handled metal spoon
- Matches or a lighter (adult only)
- 1 hair tie

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tea lights on the tray, water and washcloth inside your reach, her hair in its tie. Both of you sit down, because nobody stands near a flame today.
2. Three rules: candles stay on the tray, only a grown-up strikes a match, tell a grown-up right away when something goes wrong. She says all three back.
3. Light one and put the matches back out of reach. She watches for a full minute with her hands under her legs.
4. Heat has a shape. Hold the metal spoon a hand's width above the flame for a count of ten, test the handle on your wrist, then let her feel it warm.
5. She blows it out. Watch the smoke rise in a line and fall apart. Relight it twice more.
6. Lower the glass jar over a lit one and watch it go out. Count the seconds. The wet washcloth does it faster.

> 💡 **Tip:** Say yes every time she asks to light it again. A flame she may look at loses its pull.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Her Shadow, Longer Than She Is

The sun stays low all day this week, so her shadow runs long at eleven in the
morning. Find pale sidewalk in full sun, stand her at one end, and pace out her
shadow in your feet, then hers. Turn her to face the sun and watch it swap
ends.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months, and a flame at his eye level
> is the one thing today he has no safe part in. Run the hour with him behind a
> closed door with another adult, or in the high chair an arm's length clear.
> Outside he chases his own shadow and cannot work out why it stays attached.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Handle Turns In

The stove gets the candle's treatment: a line on the floor, rules out loud, and
a real job at the end of them.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 2 cups milk
- 2 tbsp cocoa
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 1 small heavy pan
- 1 wooden spoon
- 1 step stool
- Masking tape for the floor line
- 2 mugs
- A cup of cooled milk for Kreston

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Masking tape across the floor an arm's length back from the stove. Past it belongs to whoever is cooking.
2. Milk, cocoa and sugar into the cold pan, off the heat. She measures, she pours, she gets cocoa on the counter.
3. Pan onto a front burner with the back burners empty and off, handle turned in and never out over the room. Have her check it.
4. Step stool to the stove, the one crossing of the tape line all day. Your hand on the pan handle, your arm behind her back, and she stirs with the wooden spoon.
5. Off the heat the moment it steams. Boiled cocoa skins over and she will not drink it.
6. Pour the two mugs. Stir a spoonful into Kreston's cup of cooled milk so he has what everyone else has.
7. Everyone drinks it on the far side of the tape line.

> 💡 **Tip:** Give her the whole stirring job and stay quiet. The cocoa is the excuse.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Cold cocoa shaken in a lidded jar.
- Melt a square of chocolate in a warm spoon.
- Draw the three candle rules for the fridge.
- Tape the floor line and practice standing behind it.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The green space with a ball**, because everyone here needs to run after three days indoors
- The riverside path, hats on, twenty minutes each way
- A walk to see whose tree is still up and whose is at the curb
- The yard or the garage, kicking a ball at a wall

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** Give him his cup of cooled milk in the high chair
> before the pan comes off the heat, so he is boxed in for the hot part. At 18
> months he kicks a ball with a real swing of the leg, so put one in front of
> him and stand back.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Fire and flame need rules, not avoidance.**
> Every four-year-old finds matches at some point, and the ones never allowed
> near a flame are the ones who experiment alone. Fire-safety researchers have
> said the same for decades: supervised handling, a short list of rules the
> child says out loud, and real jobs (blowing out, smothering, carrying the
> unlit candle) beat a blanket ban. She learned three rules this morning by
> saying them, and she has now seen what a jar does to a flame. Say yes to the
> birthday candles, the menorah and the stove, hands
> close and rules short. She is safer for having handled it with you standing
> there.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Open flame, matches and hot wax at 9:15, hot milk on a stove
> at 1:00, and an 18-month-old who pulls himself up on counters. The matches go
> back out of reach between every strike, on a high shelf and never the table.
> The heated spoon stays bowl end in your hand, because that end holds the heat
> long after the handle is warm. She touches the handle and nothing else, and
> the spoon goes on the tray to cool. Never leave the tea lights burning in an
> empty room. Kreston is behind a door or in the high chair for both.

## 🌟 Day 362: The Print It Leaves Behind 🌟
**📅 Tuesday, December 28, 2027**
**Theme:** Reflection & Winter Holidays

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the block of clay and a folded stack of newspaper on the table. Buy a small cake and a tub of frosting while you are out, for Wednesday.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: What Has a Pattern Underneath
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Clay Keeps the Shape (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Prints in the Frost (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Digging Up What She Made (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Drying the Spoons
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Ten Prints in a Row
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Bath and the Print of Her Own Hand
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: What Has a Pattern Underneath

**🧰 You need:** 1 fork · 1 shallow bowl · ten minutes of the house · her.

1. Turn a fork over and show her the back of it, then the sole of her shoe. Both carry a pattern.
2. Send her round the house for ten things with a pattern underneath: a comb, a coin, a bottle cap, a toy car, a key, a big leaf off the windowsill.
3. Line them up in the bowl in the order she found them. Every one leaves a copy of itself behind by lunchtime.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Clay Keeps the Shape

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 block modeling clay or air-dry clay
- A stack of newspaper, folded into a pad
- The ten pattern objects
- 1 wooden spoon, for the fine work
- 1 permanent marker
- 1 shallow bowl

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Fold the newspaper into a pad the size of a placemat. Everything happens on top of that, because clay picks up whatever it is lying on.
2. Warm the clay between your palms until it gives, then roll ten pucks the width of her hand and press each one flat, about a finger thick. She lays one puck out per object.
3. First object face down onto the first puck, and she presses it home with the flat of both thumbs, middle first and then out to the edges.
4. Back of the wooden spoon round the rim, rubbed slow. The comb teeth and the letters round the coin come up sharp.
5. Lift the object straight up while she holds the puck down with her other hand. A sideways pull drags the print out of shape.
6. Marker on the back of each: her initial, and a number matching its place in the line. All ten face up along the counter until 1:00.

> 💡 **Tip:** Press one object twice, once light and once hard, and lay the pair side by side. The hard one is the print she can still read after it has been buried.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Prints in the Frost

Morning frost sits on grass, car roofs and every shaded patch the low sun
misses. Walk her across a white lawn and turn round to look at her boot trail.
Find a set that is not hers: a dog, a bird, a bike tire. Press her hand on a
frosted hood and count how long the print lasts. Everything out here loses its
print by lunchtime, and the ten on the counter are not going anywhere.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and a pinch of clay goes
> straight in his mouth, so his part is one puck too big to swallow, held down
> under your hands and taken back into your pocket after. Press his whole hand
> into it, lift it out together, and write his name on the back while he
> watches. In the frost he stamps, looks, and stamps again in the same spot.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Digging Up What She Made

The ten prints are done, and now they go under the oats.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 deep tray or roasting pan
- 2.5 lb dry oats (or play sand)
- 1 spoon
- 1 clean paintbrush or old toothbrush
- The ten clay prints
- Index cards or card cut to size
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Oats into the deep tray three fingers deep, on the kitchen floor and off the carpet.
2. She turns her back. Bury the ten prints at different depths and rake the surface flat.
3. Show her once and hand it over: the spoon moves the oats, the brush clears the last of it. Dig wide, brush close.
4. Every print comes out face down. She turns it over, says what made it, then checks against the object.
5. Line the prints along the floor with their objects beside them.
6. One index card per print. She dictates and you write it with the marker, word for word: *the bottom of my shoe*.
7. Swap. She buries them for you and stands over the tray telling you where you are wrong.

> 💡 **Tip:** Sift the oats back into their bag. They get buried and dug out a dozen more times before they go gray.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Bury the prints in dry rice and use fingers.
- Rub a crayon over paper laid on each object instead, for a second set.
- Match the ten objects to the ten prints, face up.
- Stand two of the prints on the windowsill where the low sun rakes across them.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Swimming**
- **Swimming**, the last one of the year and the fifty-second
- Indoor playground, if the pool is shut for the holidays
- The library, for the books that have to go back before January
- A warm café and a window, if nobody has the energy for a swimsuit

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He swims too, at 18 months walking into the
> shallow end with both your hands and no idea water is different. Twenty
> minutes and out before he is cold. Hold him chest to chest for the first
> minute so the pool noise arrives with your face in front of him.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A copy of a thing teaches her what a fossil is.**
> Azlyn has looked at dinosaur bones all year without any idea how they got to
> be inside a rock. This morning she made ten of them: something soft took a
> shape, the object went away, and the shape stayed. That sequence is the whole
> idea, and she owns it because her hands did each step in order. The frost
> outside made the same prints and lost them by lunchtime, and that is the
> other half of it. Museums hand her the finished fossil. Pressing a shoe sole
> into clay hands her the process, and by Friday she will use the word on a
> rock in the yard.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Clay is not food and an 18-month-old will test that, so
> Kreston's piece is one puck too big to swallow, it stays under your hands, and
> it comes back to your pocket before he is put down. Pinch every loose crumb
> off the floor at the end. A tray of dry oats at floor height is a choking
> risk, so it goes on the counter the moment you step away. The coin and the
> bottle cap in her ten are choke-sized, so they get counted out onto the pad
> and counted back into the bowl, and he is in the high chair for the dig.
> Everybody washes hands before food.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

## 🌟 Day 363: Mom's Day Off 🌟
**📅 Wednesday, December 29, 2027**
**Theme:** Reflection & Winter Holidays

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Stand the cake, the frosting, the sprinkles and the candles on the counter, and put one wrappable thing from the house in a bag by the door.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Everything Sweet in the House
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: One of Every Kind in a Row (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Lights Left On in the Daytime (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Birthday Azlyn Runs (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Birthday Plates
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Wrappers She's Keeping
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Mom Reads, Nobody Moves
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Everything Sweet in the House

**🧰 You need:** 1 large tray or baking sheet · her · three trips.

1. Sit down on the sofa. That is your first job of the day and it holds until the walk.
2. Send her for every piece of candy in the house. Stockings, the cupboard, the bowl by the door, coat pockets. The top of the fridge is yours, pointed out from the sofa.
3. It all lands on the tray at your feet. She makes three trips and finds things you forgot you hid.

### 🎨 The Main Event: One of Every Kind in a Row

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Every piece of candy in the house
- 1 baking sheet or large tray
- 1 muffin tin or 6 small bowls
- Paper and a marker for labels
- 1 sandwich bag per person
- 1 roll tape

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip the tray out on the floor in front of her. You stay on the sofa the whole hour.
2. One kind per cup of the muffin tin. Her categories, so everything gold may end up together.
3. Count each cup out loud with her. She says the number, you write it on the paper with the marker.
4. She names each group. Write her name for it, tear the paper into labels, tape one to each cup.
5. Lay one of every kind in a row along the empty tray.
6. One sandwich bag per person, labeled and taped shut. She deals the shares out and decides what fair means. Kreston's goes on a high shelf, unopened.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not fix her groups. Gold-wrapped things belong together if she says so.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Lights Left On in the Daytime

Half the street has left its lights on in daylight this week and they look
washed out at eleven in the morning. Walk the block counting lit windows, then
count again at 5:00 to see how different the same houses look. It is your
birthday, so Azlyn pushes Kreston for a whole block.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and cannot have a single
> thing on that floor, so give him two of the small bowls and a wooden spoon in
> the high chair, up out of the candy and in your sightline. Filling and
> emptying is his game of the month. He will want a bag too, so tape one shut with a board
> book inside.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Birthday Azlyn Runs

Azlyn runs this from the frosting to the singing, and the one adult job is
lighting the candles.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 store-bought cake or plain loaf cake
- 1 tub of frosting
- Sprinkles
- Candles and matches (adult lights them)
- 1 knife for cutting the cake (adult only)
- 1 plate
- Paper and crayons
- Newspaper or wrapping paper
- Tape and ribbon
- One thing from the house to wrap

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Cake onto the plate. She spreads the frosting with her fingers and nobody smooths it after her.
2. Sprinkles next, the whole shaker, from whatever height she chooses. What lands on the plate stays on the plate.
3. Paper and crayons on the floor for the card. Nobody tells her what to draw.
4. The present: the thing from the house, wrapped in newspaper, taped by her, ribbon tied by you because a bow beats her fingers.
5. Candles in. She spaces them and counts them. You strike the matches, the only part she does not do.
6. She calls everyone to the table and says where each person sits, including you, on your own birthday.
7. Singing, blowing out, and the first slice is yours. She reads the card out loud and it will not match the drawing.

> 💡 **Tip:** Let it be worse than you would have made it. A lopsided cake and a present off your own shelf is the gift.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Store cake, candles in, straight to the singing.
- She makes the card and nothing else.
- A tea party with the good cups and no cake at all.
- Everyone draws Mom, and she picks the best one.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The indoor play center**, and you sit down with a coffee while somebody else's noise happens
- The library, warm and quiet, and she picks your book
- A café with cake, on the grounds that there is no such thing as too much
- Home on the sofa, if the birthday you want is a quiet one

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At 18 months he is in the birthday for real. He
> claps when the singing starts and blows before anybody else. Pretend play is
> coming in, so he feeds the cake to a toy. Keep the lit candles at the far
> side of the table from his chair.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sorting the candy is more interesting to her than eating it.**
> Hand a four-year-old a pile of mixed candy and watch what happens first. She
> lines it up. Children this age run a private census of the world, grouping
> and regrouping, and a heap of wrappers with colors, sizes and shapes in it is
> richer material than most toys sold for the purpose. The counting, the naming
> of groups and the one-of-each row are all real math, and she will do twenty
> minutes of it without you asking once, then come back to the tin after lunch.
> The eating comes after, and it comes slower, because she has an interest in
> the collection staying whole. The wrappers go into a bag she guards for a week
> after the candy is gone.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Hard candy, chocolate coins and foil wrappers across the floor
> are a choking hazard for an 18-month-old, so he spends the sorting hour in
> the high chair with his bowls, and the floor gets swept before he is down.
> Lit candles on a cake sit at his eye level and he will reach. Put his chair
> on the far side and blow them out early. The cake knife is yours, and it goes
> back in the drawer as soon as the slices are cut.

## 🌟 Day 364: The Table of Everybody 🌟
**📅 Thursday, December 30, 2027**
**Theme:** Reflection & Winter Holidays

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Find six to ten printed photos tonight, one of everybody including anyone who has died, and cut thick card into strips. No prints means she draws them tomorrow.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Naming Everybody Out Loud
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Photographs Standing Up (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: Cutting Green for the Table (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Letters to the People in the Photos (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Stamping the Envelopes
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Photo Box on Her Lap
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Last Books of the Year
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Naming Everybody Out Loud

**🧰 You need:** paper · 1 marker · a chair each.

1. Ask her to name everybody in the family. Write every name in the order she says it, and add nobody she has not named.
2. Read the list back. She remembers three more, one a friend from swimming and one somebody's dog.
3. Ask who is missing. The people who have died come up here, or at 9:15, and either is fine.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Photographs Standing Up

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 6–10 printed photos (or drawings of the people, if there are no prints)
- Thick card cut into folding stands
- 1 roll tape
- 1 small table or tray
- 1 cloth to cover it
- 1 battery tea light, or a flashlight under a jar
- 1 marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She picks the spot. A side table, a tray on a shelf, the end of the bookcase, out of the traffic and off the floor.
2. Cloth over it. She straightens it until she is satisfied.
3. One photo per name on her list. Anyone with no print, she draws on card.
4. Fold each card strip into an L, tape a photo to the upright, stand it up. She says each name out loud.
5. Marker under each stand: the name. She writes the letters she knows and you fill in the rest.
6. Battery tea light in the middle, or the flashlight face up under a jar. No flame on this table, and she switches it on herself. The greenery from the 10:30 walk goes round the base at 11:15, once you are both home with it.

> 💡 **Tip:** The people who have died get a stand the same size as everyone else's. She will ask a direct question. Answer it in one plain sentence, keep working, and expect it again four times this week.

### 🌳 Get Outside: Cutting Green for the Table

Take a bag and cut a handful of green for the table. Pine and spruce are the
easy ones at the end of December, and both smell of themselves when she
crushes a needle. Ivy off a fence holds its shape for a week. Cut low, cut
little, and ask before taking from a neighbor's yard.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and will have a photo stand
> off that table within the hour, so tape a spare photo of himself onto a card
> strip. He carries it around and turns it to face people, a new skill this
> month. On the walk he holds a sprig of pine and arrives with it in pieces.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Letters to the People in the Photos

The table is full of people who are somewhere else, and the mail still runs
tomorrow.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Folded card or plain paper
- Crayons
- Envelopes
- Stamps
- 1 pen for you to take dictation
- Stickers
- Your address list
- Your phone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Go round the table and pick out the living ones. Those are the letters. She will want to write to the others too, so say the truth: those stay on the table.
2. One folded card per person, drawn in crayon first. She decides who gets which drawing.
3. She dictates and you write it in pen, word for word, including the part that makes no sense.
4. She picks a sticker to seal each envelope, one per person.
5. Address them from your list. She puts the stamp on, top right corner, pressed with her thumb.
6. The stack goes in her hands to the post office at 2:30, and she mails them one at a time.
7. Anything she has not finished stays on the table for 4:00 and goes out tomorrow.

> 💡 **Tip:** Photograph each card before it goes in the envelope. Two of those people will keep hers on the fridge for a year.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- One card to one person, and stop there.
- Call two of them on video and let her hold the phone.
- Draw the whole family on one long sheet.
- Sort the photo box by who is in each picture.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Pick one**
- **The post office**, with the letters in her hands and the slot at her height
- The mailbox on the corner, if the counter line is out the door
- The grocery store for tomorrow, and she carries one thing
- A walk past the houses with the photos still in the windows

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** At 18 months a post office is a room full of lines
> and strangers, so twenty minutes is the budget. Give him one envelope to
> hold and he carries it like a job. He climbs the step there holding the rail,
> one foot at a time, new this month.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **A photo on a table gives a dead person a place, and that helps her more than an explanation.**
> At four, Azlyn still hears death as a temporary state and asks when the person
> is coming back. Abstract answers slide off her, and she will ask again in a
> week whatever you say. A photo on a covered table gives her something she can
> handle: a spot in the house where that person is, a name she says out loud,
> greenery she cut herself laid round the base. Grief researchers who work with
> young children lean on rituals for this reason. She gets to include somebody,
> the part she was asking for underneath the question. Set the table up once
> and leave it standing as long as she wants it.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Holly, yew and mistletoe berries are poisonous and Kreston
> mouths everything he picks up, so cut pine, spruce or ivy only and go through
> the bag before it comes indoors. No berries on that table at all. The battery
> tea light needs its screws done up tight, because a button battery swallowed
> at 18 months is a surgical emergency.

## 🌟 Day 365: The Box and the Bottle 🌟
**📅 Friday, December 31, 2027**
**Theme:** Grand Finale

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Dig out the eleven handprint sheets and stand them on the table with the paint, the brush and the scissors. Leave the box and the bottle on the shelf. She gets them down herself in the morning.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Getting Them Down Off the Shelf
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Opening the January Box (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Walk, Bare Trees Again (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: What the Bottle Was Holding (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🌳 Out Again: **Playgroup** (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Forks, the Last Set of the Year
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: Everything Out of the Box, Again
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: The Book She Picked in January
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Getting Them Down Off the Shelf

**🧰 You need:** the January box · the July bottle · 1 chair she can stand on · 1 pen · 1 envelope.

1. She drags the chair over. Stand behind her while she lifts the box down with both hands, then the bottle, both to the table.
2. Read the lid out loud with her: **OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2027**. Then read today off the calendar. She has waited a year for this, so give her the minute.
3. She shakes the box and guesses what is in it. Write every guess on the envelope and stand it against the lid until 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Opening the January Box

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The sealed January shoebox
- 1 pair of scissors (**adult only**)
- Fresh paper, 2 sheets
- 1 pen and crayons
- The envelope of guesses
- Your phone

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Scissors through the packing tape, yours, all the way round. She lifts the lid off and looks in before either of you reaches.
2. One thing out at a time, laid in a row, no digging. The photograph, the drawing, her answers, and the January walk treasure last.
3. Ask the four questions in the same order and write the answers word for word before she hears the old ones: favorite color, favorite food, favorite song, what she wants to do this year. Leave her grammar where it lands.
4. Unfold January's and read them out, then lay the sheets side by side. Read them in pairs, January's answer and then today's, and let the difference sit there.
5. Fresh paper and crayons, and she draws the family again with January's beside her. She will tell you who she left off.
6. Check the guesses against what came out, then photograph the table before anything moves.

> 💡 **Tip:** Her answers before January's. Read January's out first and she copies herself, and the copy tells you nothing.

### 🌳 Get Outside: The Same Walk, Bare Trees Again

Walk the January route the same way round and let her call every turn. The
trees are back to the shape she met on the first walk of the year, bare and all
structure, and she has names for two of them. Hand her a paper bag and the
same instruction: one thing worth keeping. She will tell you where it is going
before you do.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and 26 days, and on the first
> walk of the year he rode facing out with empty hands. He walks a good stretch
> of the route today and collects into his own paper bag. He has more than
> twenty words and *box* is worth handing him this morning. Give him the lid to
> carry and he takes the job as far as the door.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: What the Bottle Was Holding

The bottle went up beside the box in July and she has asked about it since
October. The door frame and the eleven sheets of hands follow it.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- The sealed July bottle
- 1 pair of scissors (**adult only**)
- The eleven handprint sheets, January through November
- 1 fresh sheet of thick paper
- Washable non-toxic poster paint and 1 wide soft brush
- 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
- 1 pencil and 1 hardback book
- A long strip of paper to cut the year from
- The empty shoebox, packing tape and a permanent marker

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Scissors through the tape round the cap, yours. She tips the strips out and unties every ribbon.
2. Read her July strips out loud in the order she hands them over. She will not remember saying any of it, and she will argue with two.
3. One strip is folded, and that one is yours. She hands it over and you read it out this time.
4. Door frame. Shoes off, heels back, book flat on her head, pencil mark, **DEC 31** beside it. Cut a strip of paper from January's line to today's and hand her both ends.
5. Draw round her flat hand beside January's outline, then let her put her palm inside the old one. The gap round the edge is the year.
6. December's handprint on the twelfth sheet: paint her palm, press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write **December** and **4**.
7. All twelve sheets on the floor in order, January at one end and today's still wet at the other. Then today goes in the shoebox, taped shut, **OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2028** on the lid.

> 💡 **Tip:** Stand the new box where the old one stood, high and in her sightline. She checked that shelf all year, and a year runs better with something on it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- The four questions on the sofa, recorded on the phone.
- Open the bottle and leave the box until tomorrow.
- Lay the twelve handprints out and let her find January.
- Photograph the table and put it all back unsorted.

### 🌳 Out Again: **Playgroup**
- **Playgroup**, if yours runs on New Year's Eve, and many do not
- A friend's house, the same one from the first week of January
- The store before it shuts early, and she carries one thing for tonight
- The January route once more in the last light, and ask what is different

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He went on that door frame lying down on Day 1 and
> stands for it today, heels against the wood and your hand flat on his head.
> His January print sits under Azlyn's, made while somebody held his fist open.
> He presses his own palm down now and lifts it off himself, and one sheet
> comes back with a footprint on it.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **She won't remember most of this year, and that isn't the point.**
> Ask her at twenty about the tower or the bottle and you will get nothing
> back. Memory researchers call the gap childhood amnesia, and it takes almost
> everything before three or four. Her autobiographical memory is starting to
> hold its own contents. The rest of it went somewhere harder to point at: the
> words she has, the pause before she gives up on a hard thing, the assumption
> that an adult comes when she calls, hands that can press and tape and stir.
> None of it arrives with a date on it, and she cannot call it up as an
> episode. The year went into her. The box on the table is for you.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** The scissors open two sealed things today, so they go back up
> out of reach between the two and never onto the table. The January contents
> are choking-sized: the walk treasure, the ribbon round each strip, the sand
> and the stones in the bottom of the bottle. Kreston is at the table for all
> of it, so tip the sand into the trash yourself and the ribbons into your
> pocket as they come off. She is on a chair at 8:00 to reach the shelf, so
> keep both hands on the chair while she is up there and bring the box and
> the bottle down one at a time. Washable non-toxic paint only.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>
<a id="backup-dec"></a>

# 🌧️ December — Backup Days & Extra Ideas

These are the December days the plan cannot survive. Ice on the sidewalk,
snow coming down sideways, dark by four thirty and a car you would rather
not move, or a kid on the sofa who wants nothing except you sitting near her.
Two full indoor days sit here, two sick days that ask almost nothing of
either of you, and a page of one-line ideas for the morning you open this
with ten minutes and no plan. Take one and put the week's page back in the
drawer until tomorrow.

---

<a id="dec-weather-1"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 1 — Hot Water on the Coldest Morning

Snow came down all night, the steps are under it, and the cold has the car
doors frozen shut. Nobody is going out. The warmest thing in the house today
is a sink of water at her height, and she gets to stand in it up to her
elbows for as long as she wants. Put a towel down first and the whole day
costs you one wash load.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Push the step stool to the sink, fold two old towels on the floor in front of it, and stand the dish soap and a scrub brush where she can see them.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: The Basket of Grubby Things
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: The Sink at Her Height (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Ten Trips Without Spilling (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: The Sock Mountain (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: Putting the Dry Cups Away
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Last Bowl of Suds
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Warm Bath, Warm Room
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: The Basket of Grubby Things

**🧰 You need:** 1 laundry basket · her · every room in the house.

1. Give her the basket and one rule: anything that goes in it has to survive a soak. Plastic plates, cups, toy animals, blocks, the tea set, a doll with hair you can dry.
2. Walk the house with her. She decides. Take the wooden spoon out if she picks it and tell her why, then let her put something else in its place.
3. Stand the full basket by the sink and tell her the water goes on at 9:15. She will ask four times before then, so give her a job in the meantime: line the dirtiest ones up along the counter, worst first.

### 🎨 The Main Event: The Sink at Her Height

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 1 step stool, steady, pushed tight against the cupboard
- The sink filled a third full, plus 1 dish pan or big bowl of clean rinse water
- 1 teaspoon dish soap, no more
- 1 scrub brush and 1 sponge
- 2 old towels for the floor, 1 dish towel for the clean plastic and her hands
- 1 tray or drying rack for the clean ones
- The basket of grubby things

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Run the water to warm on your own wrist before she gets on the stool. She tests it after you, and she never touches the faucet.
2. Show her the order once: wash in the sink, rinse in the bowl, stand it on the tray. Then step back and let the order fall apart.
3. Hand her the brush for the ridged things and the sponge for the flat ones. She will use the brush for everything, which is fine.
4. Once the foam is gone she washes with gray water and does not care. Tip it, refill it warm, and let her count how many things one bowl of soap gets through.
5. Ask her to find the dirtiest thing left in the basket and do that one next. Naming it turns the last twenty minutes into a hunt.
6. Dry the plastic together on the dish towel and carry the tray to the table. She put a stack of dirty things through and came out with a stack of clean ones, and the tray is the proof.

> 💡 **Tip:** One teaspoon of soap. A squeezed bottle gives you a sink of foam with no water under it, and the foam is what she plays with instead of the job.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Ten Trips Without Spilling

The walk is off, so the movement has to come from somewhere. Set a full cup
of warm water on the counter and an empty bowl at the far end of the hall,
and send her back and forth. Ten trips, counted out loud, walking flat and
slow. The bowl fills a finger at a time and she learns that fast hands empty
the cup before she gets there. Race her on trip eight. Lose.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and wants the sink he cannot
> reach. Set his own dish pan on a towel on the kitchen floor, an inch of
> warm water, one cup and one plastic animal. Pretend play has started, so
> he will wash the animal because he watched Azlyn wash hers, and he will tell
> you about it with the words he has. Stay in the room the whole time, and tip
> the bowl out the moment he walks away from it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: The Sock Mountain

Morning was wet to the elbows. This afternoon is dry, warm and sitting down,
and it ends with every sock in the house paired for the first time since
August.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Every clean sock in the house, out of every drawer
- 1 laundry basket, emptied onto the rug
- 1 small basket or bag for the odd ones
- 4 paper bags, or 4 plastic grocery bags, one per person
- 1 marker for the names
- Her, the rug and a warm room

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Tip the lot into a heap in the middle of the rug and let her get into it. The heap is half the appeal and it costs you nothing.
2. Start with the easy rule: hers or not hers. Two piles, and she can tell by size before she can tell by pattern.
3. Move to pairs. Hold one up, she hunts the match. Say the pattern out loud as you go, stripes and spots and the gray ones with the hole.
4. Anything without a partner goes in the odd basket. Tell her the partner might turn up, and mean it.
5. Roll each pair together. Her rolls will come apart in the drawer, and they go in as they are.
6. Write a name on each bag with the marker while she watches you write it, then sort the pairs in. She reads the names off the first letter, and Kreston's bag she knows by size.
7. Deliver the bags room by room. She empties each one into its drawer, and the job is finished in a way that morning jobs almost never are.

> 💡 **Tip:** Do not re-pair the ones she got wrong. A blue sock married to a green one is her decision, and correcting it in front of her ends the sorting for the afternoon.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Pair her socks only and leave the adult heap for another day.
- Line the odd socks up longest to shortest and stop there.
- Stuff four odd socks with the others to make a soft ball each.
- Read in the sock heap, which is warmer than it sounds.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He is 18 months and posting things is close to his
> favorite thing. Hold his named bag open and let him drop socks in, then
> carry a rolled pair to a room and hand it over. He has twenty-some words, so
> ask him whose it is before you tell him, and wait through the pause. Keep him
> out of the heap while Azlyn is working in it or the pairs come apart faster
> than she makes them.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Doing the dishes is water play with a result, and she'll do it for the water alone.**
> Hand her a bowl of warm water on a housebound morning and she stays at it
> for forty minutes, which no craft you set up this month has managed. Warm
> water on skin settles a small body, the same reason a bath rescues a bad
> evening, and the sink adds weight, resistance and a job with a visible end.
> She is running a real experiment on how much soap makes how much foam. The
> plates come out clean or they do not, and either way she has moved a stack
> of dirty things into a stack of clean ones at adult height, doing adult
> work. Put the towels down before she climbs up and stay within arm's reach.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Set the water warm on your own wrist first, and she never
> touches the faucet. No knives, glass, graters or anything with a blade goes
> into the wash, and check the sink with your hand before she puts hers in.
> Kreston's bowl holds one inch and gets tipped out the second he leaves it,
> because a toddler can drown in less water than that, and he is never in the
> kitchen with standing water and no adult. Wet tile is slippery, so the towels
> stay down all morning and shoes come off.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="dec-weather-2"></a>

## 🌧️ Bad Weather Day 2 — The Floor Is the Job

Freezing rain over the last of the snow, black ice on the steps, and a
three-year-old with a full tank and nowhere to empty it. Today she works with
her feet. She polishes the hallway, climbs the stairs a dozen times, and by
lunch she is worn out in the way a cold walk would have worn her out.

### 🌙 Prep Tonight
> Put four old towels and two pairs of thick socks by the hall door, and clear the hallway floor of everything with a corner on it.

### ⏰ At-a-Glance Schedule
- **8:00–9:00 AM** — 🌅 Opening Activity: Which Floors Slide
- **9:00–9:15 AM** — Morning Meeting (15 min)
- **9:15–10:15 AM** — 🎨 The Main Event: Polishing the Hall on Two Towels (60 min)
- **10:15–10:30 AM** — Snack (15 min)
- **10:30–11:15 AM** — 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Everything That Lives Upstairs (45 min)
- **11:15–11:45 AM** — Free Play (30 min)
- **11:45 AM–12:00 PM** — 🤸 Wiggle Time (15 min)
- **12:00–12:30 PM** — Lunch
- **12:30–1:00 PM** — 📚 Book Time
- **1:00–2:30 PM** — 🎨 Second Main Event: Everybody's Feet in a Row (90 min)
- **2:30–3:30 PM** — 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives (60 min)
- **3:30–4:00 PM** — Snack & Free Play
- **4:00–4:15 PM** — 🧹 Her Job: The Boots Lined Up by the Door
- **4:15–5:00 PM** — Quiet Play: The Paper Feet
- **5:00–5:45 PM** — 🛁 Wind-Down: Lights Low, Feet Up
- **6:00 PM** — **Dinner**

### 🌅 Opening Activity: Which Floors Slide

**🧰 You need:** 2 old towels · thick socks · every floor surface in the house.

1. Towel under each foot, hands free, and walk her onto the kitchen tile. She slides. Let her fall over twice before you say anything about it.
2. Take her to the carpet and try the same thing. Nothing moves. Then the hall, then the bathroom, then the rug by the door.
3. Ask her which floor is the fastest and let her rank all of them out loud. She picks which end of the hall gets the finish line, and you tape it there at 9:15.

### 🎨 The Main Event: Polishing the Hall on Two Towels

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- 4 old towels, two dry and two damp
- Thick socks, hers and yours
- 1 spray bottle of water, or a bowl to dip a corner in
- Masking tape for the start line, or a folded dish towel laid across it
- 1 empty laundry basket as the turning post
- A clear stretch of hard floor, nothing underfoot

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. Stand the basket at the end she picked and tape a start line at the other. That is the course, and the walls are out of bounds.
2. Wet two towels with the spray bottle, or dip a corner in the bowl and wring them out. Thick socks on both of you, one damp towel under each of her feet. She pushes from the start line to the basket, around it, and back, and the floor behind her comes up clean.
3. Send her over the same strip four or five times. Skating is the fun part and the cleaning happens whether she means it or not.
4. Swap to the dry towels for the buffing run. Tell her the job now is shine, and let her hunt for the streaks she left.
5. Load her up: hand her something to carry across on the return trip so her arms work as well as her legs.
6. Finish with one slow run where she balances with nothing to hold, then look down the hall together with the lights on low. The floor is different because of her, and she can see it.

> 💡 **Tip:** Damp, not wet. A soaked towel puts water on the boards and turns a fun morning into a slick you have to mop before anybody walks it.

### 🏠 Instead of Getting Outside: Everything That Lives Upstairs

Fill the basket with everything downstairs that belongs on another floor:
laundry, books, a hairbrush, three cups, a stray boot. She carries it up one
armful at a time and puts each thing where it lives. Count the trips out loud
and let her decide when she is done. Stairs are the best climbing frame in
the house on a day like this, and by trip six she is breathing hard.

> 👶 **Infant Integration:** Kreston is 18 months and climbs stairs holding on,
> one foot at a time, so he goes up with the others. Stay one step below him,
> hands off, and let it take as long as it takes. Downstairs, give him a dry
> washcloth of his own to push around on hands and knees while Azlyn skates,
> and keep him well off the polished stretch while she is moving on it.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

### 🎨 Second Main Event: Everybody's Feet in a Row

Morning ran through her legs. This afternoon her feet stay still and get
drawn around, and the year shows up in the size of them.

**🧰 Complete Materials List:**
- Flattened cardboard, cereal boxes or a roll of paper, enough for six outlines
- 1 pencil and thick markers
- Blunt scissors for her, heavy scissors for you (**adult only**)
- Masking tape
- Every pair of shoes and boots by the door, plus the summer ones from the closet

**📝 Step-by-Step Instructions:**
1. She stands on the cardboard with her sock off and you draw around her foot. Hold the pencil upright and expect her to giggle and move.
2. Do everybody: yours, hers, Kreston's, anyone else in the house. Write the name inside each outline while she watches you write it.
3. Cut them out, you on the thick card and her on the easy edges. Names face up.
4. Lay them on the floor smallest to biggest. She will want hers next to yours, so let her hold both up and compare them face to face.
5. Dig out her summer sandals and stand them on her outline. They do not fit any more, and this is the first time she has seen a whole year as a measurement.
6. Tape the row along the baseboard at her height, biggest at one end. Write the month beside each one.
7. Let her try on every shoe by the door, including yours, and walk the polished hall in them.

> 💡 **Tip:** Draw around the foot rather than the shoe. A shoe outline is a shoe, and a foot outline with her name in it is her, which is the reason she keeps looking at it.

### 🎯 Afternoon Alternatives
- Her foot and your foot, cut out, taped up, done in fifteen minutes.
- Trace hands instead, and put them beside January's handprint sheet.
- Measure the hall in her feet, heel to toe, and write the number on a card by the door.
- Draw around her whole body on flattened boxes and let her color it in.

> 👶 **Kreston's Afternoon:** He is 18 months, and pretend play is running now,
> so he will put your boots on and take four steps before he goes over. Sit
> beside him and let him do it. Name each shoe as he tries it and wait for his
> version of the word. His outline goes in the row too. Stand him on the
> cardboard, hold one hand so he keeps still, and draw fast.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Doing a job with her feet is how she gets her whole body into it.**
> Ask a three-year-old to sit and color on a housebound day and you get
> eleven minutes. Give her a job that runs through her feet and you get an
> hour. Pushing, bracing and sliding send steady pressure through her joints,
> and that load settles a body with nowhere to run, which is the whole trouble
> with a dark December morning. Her feet carry her weight, so a foot job pulls
> in her legs, hips and back at the same time, and the work is heavy enough to
> matter. She finishes worn out the way a cold walk would have worn her out.
> Hand her the towels, name the finish line and stay out of the route she
> picks.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Towel skating happens on a clear straight run with no stairs
> at either end and no glass, no radiator corner and no table leg in the path.
> Close the stair gate before she starts. Damp towels only, and mop any water
> she leaves before the next run. On the stair trips, stay one step below
> Kreston with your hands free, and send one child at a time. The heavy
> scissors are yours and go back on a shelf between cuts.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="dec-sick-1"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 1 — The Day She Runs It From the Sofa

This is the flat day. She has a fever, she wants you in the room, and she
will not stay with anything for longer than four minutes. Nothing here needs
cutting, baking or a cleanup she has to be part of, and you can drop any of
it halfway through without wasting a thing. Your whole job today is fluids,
rest and being close by.

### 🛋️ Set Up Once, Before Anything Else
> Sofa nest, a cup with a lid on the floor beside it, a bowl within reach, a towel over the cushion, and the thermometer and medicine on a high shelf. Build it once and you will not have to get up for the rest of the morning.

### ⏳ The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes** · straight to the sofa, not the table. Water first, food later or not at all.
- **After the first long sleep** · one quiet thing on her lap, ten minutes, then let it go.
- **When she asks for food** · dry toast, a clementine, a yogurt. Anything she names is the right answer.
- **The long middle** · the rest block. Nothing is scheduled against it.
- **Before the afternoon dip** · a drink, a wet cloth on her forehead, the curtains closed.
- **When it goes dark at four thirty** · lamps on low, television if that is what gets you both to six.
- **Whenever she has had enough** · bed early, and take the win.

### 😴 The Rest Block

The center of today is a long stretch where nothing is asked of her. Two
hours, maybe three, on the sofa or in your bed, curtains half closed and one
lamp on. She may sleep and she may lie there watching the ceiling, and both
count. Sit within reach with your phone or a book. A feverish three-year-old
who cannot find you spends her energy checking where you are, so stay in the
room and let her feel you there. Line Kreston's nap up with this block and
you get the quietest ninety minutes of the day.

### 🛋️ Building It Where She Points

**🧰 You need:** every cushion and blanket in the house · her voice · your arms.

1. Ask her where the nest goes and take the answer, whether it is the sofa, the floor or the corner behind the armchair.
2. She names each piece and where it lands. You carry, you fold, you tuck. Do it wrong once and let her correct you.
3. Once she runs out of instructions, ask where the next thing goes rather than filling it in yourself.
4. The nest stays up until she is well, so nothing here goes back tonight.

### ✏️ The Picture She Orders Up

**🧰 You need:** paper on a book · 1 pencil or crayon · her lying flat.

1. Tell her you will draw anything she says, and she does not have to lift her head.
2. She talks, you draw. A dog with six legs comes out as a dog with six legs.
3. Ask her one question per picture: what color, how big, what is it standing on.
4. Write her title along the top in her words and put it where she can see it from the sofa.

### 📖 The Story You Get Wrong

**🧰 You need:** a story she knows by heart · her eyes shut.

1. Tell it from memory with her lying down and the lamp off.
2. Get one thing wrong on purpose every few lines. The wolf knocks on the wrong door, the bear eats the porridge cold.
3. She will correct you flat on her back with her eyes closed, which is the most she can give today and it costs her nothing.

### 🎯 If She Will Not Settle
- Move the whole nest to your bed and start again there.
- One long audiobook or a familiar movie, with you on the sofa beside her.
- A cool washcloth on the back of her neck and the window cracked for one minute.
- Name every animal she can think of, out loud, taking turns until she stops.

> 👶 **Kreston Today:** He is 18 months, he wants to climb on her, and he cannot
> be in that room unsupervised for a second. Move his nap earlier so it lands
> inside her rest block. If somebody can take him out for two hours, today is
> the day to ask. Keep him going with things that need no setup from you:
> stairs with you one step below, his own basket to empty, a spoon and a bowl
> and a toy that gets fed. Separate cups, and wash your hands between the two
> of them.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Directing an adult is the strongest evidence of competence she can get.**
> Flat on the sofa she has lost every job she owns. She cannot carry, climb,
> pour or fetch, and a three-year-old measures herself with those. Directing
> you hands it back. She names the cushion, the corner, the color of the
> blanket, and an adult moves. That loop tells her she still has an effect on
> the world on a day her own body has stopped cooperating with her. Follow her
> instructions to the letter, including the ones that make no sense, and give
> it back to her when she stalls by asking where the next one goes. She is
> doing the thinking and you are supplying the arms, and she knows the
> difference.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Fluids matter more than food today. Small sips often, and
> count the wet diapers or trips to the bathroom. Call your doctor for a fever
> that will not come down, a rash that does not fade under pressure, breathing
> that looks like hard work, a stiff neck, refusing to drink for hours, or a
> child you cannot rouse. Medicine goes back on a high shelf between doses,
> never on the sofa arm or the floor, and write the time of each dose on a
> piece of paper. No hot drink within her reach or Kreston's.

<div style="page-break-after: always;"></div>

<a id="dec-sick-2"></a>

## 🤒 Sick Day 2 — Bored and Not Better Yet

Day three or four. The fever has gone, she is fed up, and she cannot manage
anything you would call a day. This is the harder one to get right, because
she will demand more than she can handle and then fall apart at two o'clock.
Give her a smaller version of normal and keep the rest block, even though she
says she does not need it.

### 🛋️ Set Up Once, Before Anything Else
> Leave the sofa nest up. Put a lap tray or a big book beside it, a cup with a lid, and a bowl of clementines and whatever else is sour in the fridge.

### ⏳ The Shape of the Day
- **Whenever she wakes** · she will be up before you want her to be. Sofa, water, and no expectations for an hour.
- **Once the first hour is behind you** · one thing on the lap tray, sitting up, twenty minutes at most.
- **When she asks for food** · say yes to whatever she names. Appetite coming back is the news of the day.
- **Before the afternoon dip** · the rest block, and hold the line on it.
- **After the rest block** · the one small job, which is the whole point of today.
- **When it goes dark at four thirty** · lamps low, and no visitors.
- **Bedtime** · earlier than she thinks she needs, because tomorrow is the day she overdoes it.

### 😴 The Rest Block

She will argue about this one. Do it anyway: an hour on the sofa after lunch
with the curtains half closed and something she has heard forty times playing
low. The rebound day is where families lose the recovery, because a child who
feels better at eleven is back on the sofa by three and back to square one on
Thursday. Say it out loud as a rule rather than a suggestion. Lie down with
her if that is what makes it happen.

### 🍋 One Sour Thing at a Time

**🧰 You need:** a clementine · a lemon wedge · plain yogurt · a pickle or a spoon of cranberry sauce · 1 saucer. With no citrus in the house, an apple wedge and a cracker with a drop of vinegar on it do the same job.

1. Put them on a saucer on her lap and let her go in whatever order she likes.
2. Try each one yourself, out loud, before you say anything about hers.
3. Ask her to put them in order, most sour to least, and take her order as final.
4. Come back to the lemon at the end. Most children go back a second time once the surprise has gone.

### 🍊 Peeling for the Whole House

**🧰 You need:** 4 or 5 clementines, or any fruit in the house with a skin she can get off · 1 bowl for the peel · her lap.

1. Start each one for her with a thumbnail and hand it over. Peeling is slow work with one hand and she has all day.
2. One segment for each person in the house, laid out on the tray in named piles.
3. Let her deliver them, or call people over if she is not up to standing.
4. Keep the peel in the bowl on the radiator. The room smells of it for the rest of the afternoon.

### 📝 The Card That Says What's Next

**🧰 You need:** 1 index card or a piece of thick paper · 1 marker · her ideas.

1. Ask what she wants to do on the first proper day back and write it down word for word.
2. Cap it at three things. A recovering child who plans six wakes up owing herself six.
3. She draws one small picture beside each line, or tells you what to draw.
4. Tape it where she can see it from the sofa and read it back whenever she asks.

### 🎯 If She Is Climbing the Walls
- Sofa to the window and twenty minutes of naming what goes past.
- Everything in one drawer emptied onto the tray and put back in a new order.
- A phone call to somebody who will let her do the talking.
- Ten minutes of her leading and you following, room to room, at her pace.

> 👶 **Kreston Today:** He comes back in short doses. He is 18 months and full
> of pretend play, so give him a spoon, a bowl and a toy that needs feeding,
> and set him up on the rug where she can watch without being climbed on.
> Twenty minutes together, then move him on before it goes wrong. He may well
> be the next one down with it, so keep the cups separate and expect a broken
> night. If he has been shut out of her room for two days, he will want you,
> and ten minutes of your full attention buys you the afternoon.

---

> 🧠 **A Little Parenting Insight**
> **Sour is the taste she'll learn to like on purpose, and that's a new experience.**
> Sour reads as a warning to a small child, and a three-year-old spits out
> lemon on reflex. Then she watches you eat a wedge, tries it again, and
> something switches over. Learning to like a taste on purpose is a new kind
> of experience for her, and she is the one running it. A mouth coming off
> three flat days is dulled, and sour cuts through where sweet slides past, so
> this is the week it lands. Give her a clementine, a lick of lemon and a spoon
> of plain yogurt and let her rank them. If her throat is still raw, leave the
> lemon out and come back to it in a few days.

> ⚠️ **Safety:** Keep the fluids going, because a child on the mend drinks
> less once she stops being watched. Citrus stings a raw throat and a cracked
> lip, so let her stop the moment she says so. Kreston gets clementine segments
> broken in half with the seeds out and the pith pulled off, and he sits up to
> eat them with you next to him. Whole segments, grapes and lemon rind are all
> choking hazards at 18 months. If she gets worse again after a day of
> improving, call your doctor rather than waiting it out.

## 🎲 December — Extra Ideas

### 🎲 **Alternative Activities**

- **Both Sides of the Front Door** · one hand flat on the inside of the door, one on the storm door glass, and she calls the difference.
- **Paper Snowball Fight** · a stack of newspaper crumpled into ammunition, the sofa as the wall.
- **The Practice Wrap** · a shoebox, a sheet of leftover paper and as much tape as she wants to use.
- **Four O'Clock Lights Off** · every lamp off at the moment it goes dark outside, then one back on at a time.
- **Guess Which Hand** · a small thing hidden in one fist, three guesses, then she hides and you guess.
- **The Cupboard Orchestra** · a pan, a wooden spoon and a jar of rice, played loudest to quietest.
- **The Bed Picnic** · lunch upstairs on a towel, and nobody goes back down until it is finished.
- **Heavier or Lighter** · two cans, one in each hand, and she calls it before the scale does.
- **Freeze When It Stops** · three rounds of music and stopping, then she works the button and you freeze.
- **Everything That Came Out of a Box** · a hunt for what arrived this month, packing paper and all.
- **The Laundry Basket Boat** · a basket, a cushion and a wooden spoon for an oar.

### 🎨 **Alternative Arts & Crafts**

- **Cotton Balls on Blue Paper** · glue and stick, no cutting, snow that stays up till spring.
- **The Star You Cannot Plan** · paper folded in four, one cut across the corner, and the shape shows up when it opens.
- **Wrapping Paper Collage** · leftover paper torn small and glued into one big sheet.
- **The Card for Somebody Far Away** · folded card, her drawing, your envelope and her stamp.
- **Two Crayons, One Cold** · one crayon out of the freezer and one off the radiator, drawn side by side on the same page.
- **The Salt Snow Picture** · glue squeezed in lines, salt poured over, the loose stuff tipped off.
- **Pipe Cleaner People** · bent into a family and stood up on a jar lid.
- **Buttons Pressed Into Playdough** · the tin emptied out and pushed in row by row.
- **Circles Without a Brush** · the bottom of a cup dipped in paint and printed across a page.
- **The Hallway Drawing** · a long strip of paper taped to the wall at her height, added to all week.
- **A Bag of Snips** · scissors, scrap paper and nothing to make, which is the point.

### 👶 **Kreston's Turn**

- **The Bottom Three Stairs** · up and down holding the rail, with you one step below, as many times as he wants.
- **Feeding the Bear** · a spoon, an empty bowl and a toy that gets a whole meal.
- **Lids Through the Slot** · a shoebox with a slot cut in the lid and a pile of jar lids to post.
- **Naming What He Hands You** · he brings things one at a time, you say the word and wait for his version.

# 🎁 Keepsake Tracker

Eight threads in this book run past December 31. This page is the record of
them, so the box, the door frame, the twelve sheets of hands and the four walk
photographs stay findable after the booklets go in a drawer. Fill it in on the
page, in pen, and keep the page with the box.

---

## 1. 📦 The Time Capsule

You sealed it on Day 1 with packing tape and **OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2027** across
the lid, then cut it open on Day 365 with scissors. Inside it went her drawing
of the family, the four answers in her own words, the treasure she picked up
on the first walk of the year, and a photograph. You photographed the contents
before the lid went on, and those pictures are still on your phone. On the
afternoon of Day 365 you taped the same shoebox shut again with **OPEN
DECEMBER 31, 2028** on the lid and stood it back on the shelf she watched all
year.

## 7. 🎂 Birthday Interviews

Kreston turned one on Day 156 and Azlyn turned four on Day 354. Ask the same
questions on every birthday from here on, write the answers word for word,

## 💛 The Last Page


Brooklyn, you got to the end of it. I wrote these mornings a long way from
your kitchen, with a calendar and a set of guesses about what 8:00 costs on
a Tuesday in March with both of them awake and one of them teething. You
paid it 365 times. The book planned the days and you ran them.

Keep this copy, the one with the pencil in it. The crossed-out days tell you
more than the printed ones, and Kreston gets his turn in a few years, so the
margins are for you first and then for him. The backup pages hold up in any
year: two bad weather days a month, two sick days, an extras page you may
never have opened. Nothing in there goes stale.

She started the year with a tower that fell at four blocks and finished it
telling you which tree on the walk belongs to her. Kreston sat propped on
the rug in January and came up the stairs behind her in December. You were
in the room for all of that.

Plenty of days this year nothing got made and nothing got crossed off. She
had you for the whole of those days, and that was the curriculum from the
start.
